If any of these works have a grip on you, confess them to God, who is faithful and just to forgive, and seek the help of mature believers in your local church as you walk in the light.

question: How can an unmarried person relieve sexual tension in a non-sinful way?
answer:
God designed sexual desire as a good gift to be expressed in the one-flesh covenant of marriage between a man and a woman (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). An unmarried person is called to holiness and self-control, not to sexual release outside that covenant (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5).

There is no God-honoring sexual climax or “relief” outside the marriage bed. Sexual union belongs to husband and wife. Lust in the heart is already adultery, according to Jesus (Matthew 5:28). Practices that typically involve lustful thoughts or images, including pornography and masturbation, do not honor God; they usually deepen the struggle rather than resolve it in holiness.

Scripture’s path is to flee sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:18) and to learn to control your own body in holiness and honor, not in passionate lust (1 Thessalonians 4:4-5). Pray for the Holy Spirit to produce the fruit of self-control (Galatians 5:22-23). Guard your eyes and fill your mind with what is true, honorable, and pure (Job 31:1; Philippians 4:8). Steward your body through work, exercise, rest, and service instead of idleness. Live in the fellowship of a local church, where isolation is harder to maintain.

If you find yourself burning with passion and unable to exercise self-control, it is better to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9). Seek counsel from your church’s elders about whether marriage in the Lord is the wise next step for you.

This tension is a real and common struggle. If you have sinned in thought or action, Jesus Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose again; He offers forgiveness and power to walk in newness of life to all who repent and trust Him. A concrete next step is to speak this week with a pastor or a mature same-gender believer in your church so they can pray with you and walk with you in accountability. Read 1 Thessalonians 4 slowly in prayer each day, asking God to make His will for your sanctification real in your life.

question: What does it mean to be devout?
answer:
To be devout is to live with sincere, wholehearted devotion to God, marked by reverent awe, consistent worship, prayer, and a life of obedience that flows from genuine faith rather than empty ritual.

Scripture portrays devout people as those who fear God and seek Him earnestly, such as Cornelius, who “was a devout man and one who feared God with all his household, who gave generously to the people and prayed to God continually” (Acts 10:2). True devotion is not a way to earn standing with God; it is the fruit of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, as the Holy Spirit produces progressive sanctification and godliness in the believer (1 Timothy 4:7-8). The fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom, lies at the heart of this piety (Proverbs 9:10). It also shows itself in practical love and holiness: “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world” (James 1:27).

A concrete next step is to set a simple daily rhythm of reading a short portion of Scripture (such as a Psalm) and praying in response, then living that out in your family, work, and local church.

question: Are we supposed to use musical instruments in church?
answer:
The use of musical instruments in gathered church worship is a non-essential tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree. The New Testament neither commands nor forbids instruments in the assembly, so differences arise from how we apply the regulative principle of worship (doing only what God has prescribed) and how we see continuity with Old Testament temple practices.

One historic view, held by groups such as the Churches of Christ and some exclusive-psalmody Presbyterians, is that instruments should not be used. They argue that instruments belonged to the ceremonial worship of the Old Covenant temple, now fulfilled in Christ, and that the New Testament only commands vocal singing of psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). Adding what is not prescribed, they believe, goes beyond Scripture.

Another view, common among Baptists, most evangelicals, and many Reformed churches, is that instruments may accompany congregational singing. They note that the Psalms repeatedly call for instruments in praise (Psalm 150:3-5) and that the New Testament does not prohibit them, so this falls under Christian liberty in disputable matters (Romans 14:5-6), provided the instruments serve the congregation rather than become a performance.

In either practice the priority remains the same: worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24), with the whole church singing from the heart as the Word of Christ dwells richly in us. Instruments (or their absence) must never distract from Christ, the Word, or the congregation’s own voice.

A wise next step is to talk with the elders of your local church, open Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 together, and pray that whatever your congregation does would honor God and build up His people in unity.

question: What does the Bible say about miscarriage?
answer:
The Bible affirms that God personally forms and knows every child in the womb, treating unborn life as real and precious, even though it does not give a long, separate teaching on miscarriage itself. Psalm 139:13-16 says, “For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well. My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be.” Jeremiah 1:5 adds, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart.” Luke 1:41 and Luke 1:44 show John the Baptist leaping for joy in the womb at the presence of Christ, confirming that the unborn child is already a living person known by God.

Scripture also records the sorrow of losing a child before or at birth. Job 3:16 speaks of being “hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight.” Ecclesiastes 6:3 compares a long but empty life unfavorably to a stillborn child. These passages treat the loss as real grief, not as something insignificant. In 2 Samuel 12:23, after his infant son dies, David says, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me,” expressing hope of reunion with the child in God’s presence.

The Bible does not give a detailed map of the eternal destiny of every miscarried child. It does reveal God as perfectly just, merciful, and the One who delights in little ones (Matthew 19:14). Many Christians therefore rest in His character and in the hope that such children are kept by His grace. Others emphasize God’s sovereign election even here. In either case the child’s worth does not depend on our understanding, but on the God who formed them.

If you are carrying the grief of a miscarriage, the Lord is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18). Bring that sorrow to Him in prayer, perhaps lingering in Psalm 139 or Psalm 13. Share it with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk with you. God’s providence over every life, including the shortest, is a comfort we can cling to even when we do not have every answer.

question: Is religion the cause of most wars?
answer:
No, religion is not the cause of most wars. The great majority of conflicts in history have been driven by political power, territory, resources, ethnicity, or secular ideology rather than religious conviction.

It is understandable to think otherwise when looking at the Crusades, the Thirty Years’ War, or modern religious terrorism. Those events involved real violence done in the name of faith, and they remain a scandal that Christians must lament rather than excuse.

Yet even many of those wars mixed religion with deeper political and economic aims. Meanwhile, the deadliest conflicts of the last century, including both World Wars and the mass killings under communist regimes, were fueled primarily by nationalism, racism, and atheistic ideologies. Historians who have surveyed recorded wars consistently find that purely or primarily religious motives account for only a small fraction.

The Bible locates the true source of war not in religion itself but in the sinful human heart: “What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?” (James 4:1). Every person, religious or not, is a sinner whose desires for power, wealth, and revenge erupt into violence (Romans 3:23). Jesus Himself commanded His followers to love their enemies and to be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:44), and He died and rose to reconcile sinners to God, which is the only lasting foundation for peace among people.

Christians are therefore called to pursue justice and peace in a fallen world while pointing others to the One who alone can change the heart.

question: What does it mean to “in all your ways acknowledge Him” in Proverbs 3:6?
answer:
To “acknowledge Him” in all your ways means to know, recognize, and submit to the Lord in every decision, relationship, and ordinary activity of life rather than relying on your own insight.

Proverbs 3:5-6 says, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight.” The Hebrew word behind “acknowledge” is yada, which speaks of knowing God relationally in a way that produces obedient recognition of His authority. In the wisdom setting of Proverbs, “ways” and “paths” describe the whole course of a person’s life and choices, so this is not limited to religious moments. It is the practical outworking of the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). God does not promise an easy road, but He does promise to direct those who know and yield to Him.

A concrete way to live this is to pause before both large and small choices, bring them to God in prayer, and measure them by Scripture rather than your own understanding. You might begin this week by taking one ordinary part of your day, such as your work or a conversation, and deliberately acknowledging the Lord there by seeking His will and aiming to honor Him in it.

question: Does God still give visions to people today? Should believers expect visions to be a part of their Christian experience?
answer:
No, believers should not expect visions as a normal or necessary part of Christian experience today, because God has given His people a complete and sufficient Word rather than ongoing revelatory visions.

Continuationists argue that we remain in the last days begun at Pentecost, so the Spirit still grants visions as Joel 2:28 promised and Acts 2:17 records, for the church's ongoing edification and guidance.

I hold the cessationist view as one faithful option within historic Christianity: extraordinary revelatory gifts such as visions that convey new divine revelation ceased with the apostles, whose ministry formed the church's once-for-all foundation (Ephesians 2:20). God formerly spoke in various ways through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken fully and finally by His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2), and the completed Scriptures now equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). New visions would add to that closed canon, which Scripture itself forbids. God remains sovereign and may work as He pleases, yet we walk by faith in the written Word rather than seeking extra-biblical experiences that can easily mislead.

A wise next step is to devote yourself to the ordinary means of grace: read Scripture daily (perhaps beginning in the Gospels or Psalms), asking the Holy Spirit to illumine it, and talk with your local church elders about any questions this raises.

question: Is physical abuse an acceptable reason for divorce?
answer:
Physical abuse is not listed in Scripture as a ground for divorce. Some Christians argue that unrepentant, ongoing violence so abandons the duties of the one-flesh covenant that it should be treated as desertion under 1 Corinthians 7, thereby permitting divorce. I believe we must not add grounds beyond the two Jesus and Paul actually name (sexual immorality and desertion by an unbeliever), because marriage is a lifelong covenant God has joined and we are not to go beyond what is written.

God designed marriage as a permanent one-flesh union: “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6). Jesus allowed an exception only for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9). Paul added that if an unbelieving spouse leaves, the believer “is not bound in such cases” (1 Corinthians 7:15). Physical abuse is a grievous sin that God hates; it directly contradicts the husband’s call to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25) and the command that no one do harm. It is never acceptable, and the civil magistrate exists as God’s servant to punish such evil (Romans 13:4).

An abused spouse is not required to remain in physical danger. Immediate separation for safety, involvement of the church for discipline of the offender, and protection of any children are right and necessary. Genuine repentance, proven over time and with accountability, is the only path toward possible reconciliation; safety must never be sacrificed for it. The local church elders should surround the victim with care, apply church discipline to a professing believer who abuses, and help the innocent party walk in wisdom.

If you or someone you love is in immediate danger, contact emergency services at once and get to a safe place. Then speak with a trusted pastor or a certified biblical counselor. Pray directly to the Lord for protection, wisdom, and healing, using passages such as Psalm 46 and Psalm 23 as you do so.

question: Why is “You shall not steal” in the Ten Commandments?
answer:
“You shall not steal” is in the Ten Commandments because God, the Creator and owner of all things, forbids taking what He has entrusted to another person. This eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15) requires us to honor our neighbor’s property as an act of justice and love, since people are made in God’s image and what they possess is a stewardship from Him.

God gave this law at Sinai after redeeming Israel from Egypt, calling them to live as His holy people rather than repeating the oppression they had suffered. “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein” (Psalm 24:1), so theft is an assault on God’s order. The New Testament restates the same moral demand: the commandments, including “You shall not steal,” are summed up in “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13:9), and the former thief must now work with his own hands so that he may share with those in need (Ephesians 4:28).

This command therefore exposes our sin (none of us has perfectly respected others’ goods or remained fully content) while also showing the character of God, who gives rather than takes. Honor it today by being honest in small matters, paying what you owe, working diligently, and giving generously as a grateful response to Christ’s grace.

question: What does it mean that “His mercy endures forever” (Jeremiah 33:11 and Psalm 136)?
answer:
The phrase “His mercy endures forever” means that God’s covenant love never fails, expires, or depends on our fluctuating worthiness. In the Berean Standard Bible this is often rendered “His loving devotion endures forever,” both phrases translating the Hebrew word hesed, which speaks of God’s loyal kindness, compassion, and unbreakable faithfulness to His people.

Psalm 136 uses the refrain after every line as Israel thanks God for creation, the exodus, victory over enemies, and daily provision. Each mighty act is presented as flowing from this same unending hesed (Psalm 136:1). Jeremiah 33:11 places the identical words on the lips of a restored people after exile: they will again hear joy in Jerusalem and bring thank offerings, singing, “Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever,” because God keeps His promise to rebuild what judgment had broken.

This reveals God’s immutability. He does not change, so the mercy He has pledged cannot be exhausted (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). For those in Christ it is the ground of perseverance: the same God who saved you by grace will keep you by that grace. When guilt or fear presses in, you can still give thanks, because His hesed is not a mood but His settled character.

A simple next step is to read Psalm 136 slowly this week, pausing after each refrain to name one specific mercy you have received, then thank God for it in your own words and share that thanksgiving with a mature believer in your local church.

question: Is the Church of God in Christ (COGIC) a good biblical church?
answer:
The Church of God in Christ (COGIC) is a Pentecostal denomination that affirms the core doctrines of the Christian faith, including the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Jesus Christ (the hypostatic union), His virgin birth, His penal substitutionary atonement, His bodily resurrection, and justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. In that sense, COGIC congregations are Christian churches, and many genuine believers belong to them.

That said, several of its distinctive teachings and practices do not align as closely with Scripture as they should. COGIC teaches a baptism in the Holy Spirit subsequent to conversion, with speaking in tongues as the initial evidence. The Bible teaches that every true believer is baptized in the Spirit at conversion: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). Tongues is a gift not given to all (1 Corinthians 12:30), and the New Testament instances involved known languages that served the spread of the gospel.

Historic Christianity includes both cessationist and continuationist views on miraculous gifts. Continuationists hold that such gifts continue for the church today. Cessationists (my position) hold that the sign gifts authenticated the apostles and the new revelation they brought, and that they ceased with the close of the canon (Hebrews 2:3-4). The specific Pentecostal requirement of a subsequent experience with tongues as evidence goes beyond Scripture and can create an unhelpful two-tier view of Christians.

COGIC also comes from the Holiness tradition and teaches entire sanctification as a second definite work of grace. Scripture instead describes progressive sanctification, in which the Holy Spirit continually conforms believers to Christ through the ordinary means of grace (the Word, prayer, and fellowship) throughout the Christian life (Philippians 1:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

On church government, COGIC is episcopal, with bishops exercising oversight. Other historic churches have practiced this model, seeing it as providing needed unity and accountability. The New Testament pattern, however, is a plurality of elders leading an autonomous local congregation (Acts 14:23; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9), which is the view I hold as more faithful to the text.

Like any large denomination, individual COGIC churches vary. Some may add extra-biblical revelations, legalistic holiness codes, or prosperity emphases that distort the gospel. A good biblical church is marked by the faithful preaching of the whole counsel of God, the right administration of believer’s baptism and the Lord’s Supper, church discipline, and the sufficiency of Scripture as the final authority.

If you are considering a COGIC congregation, listen carefully to whether the gospel of Christ’s finished work is proclaimed without additions, and test everything by Scripture (Acts 17:11). Pray for wisdom, and seek the counsel of mature believers in a local church that exposits the Word and holds to historic Christian doctrine.

question: What is the voice of one calling in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3; John 1:23)?
answer:
The voice of one calling in the wilderness is John the Baptist, who in John 1:23 identified himself as the fulfillment of Isaiah 40:3, serving as the forerunner who prepared the way for the Lord Jesus Christ.

Isaiah 40:3 announces a herald preparing a highway for the LORD in the wilderness. John applied this directly to his own ministry of calling Israel to repentance and baptism, making hearts ready for the Messiah. By using a prophecy about preparing the way for Yahweh and applying it to Jesus, John testified to the deity of Christ, the One who is truly God and truly man.

This prophetic fulfillment displays the unity of Scripture and God’s faithfulness to send His Son. John’s work pointed people to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). As those who follow Christ, we prepare the way in our own lives by turning from sin and pointing others to Him.

question: What is neonomianism?
answer:
Neonomianism is the teaching that the gospel functions as a new law, making faith, repentance, and sincere evangelical obedience the conditions of a sinner’s justification before God rather than the empty-handed reception of Christ’s finished work.

This view is historically associated with the Puritan Richard Baxter, who sought to guard against antinomianism yet recast the gospel as a milder covenant of works. Scripture instead teaches that God justifies the ungodly by grace through faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). Justification is God’s forensic declaration that imputes the righteousness of Christ to the believer, not a reward for performing new-covenant duties (Romans 4:4-5; Philippians 3:9; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

Neonomianism therefore confuses the instrument of faith with a meritorious condition and undermines both the sufficiency of Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement and the freeness of justification. The biblical gospel calls us to rest in Jesus alone, whose death and resurrection fully satisfy divine justice, rather than looking to our own obedience as the ground of acceptance.

If you are studying this for assurance of salvation, read Romans 3–5 slowly and talk with a pastor in a local church that holds the historic Protestant doctrine of justification by faith alone.

question: What does it mean that neither height nor depth separates us from the love of God (Romans 8:39)?
answer:
Neither height nor depth in Romans 8:39 means that no extreme of space or existence, from the highest heavens to the lowest depths, can separate believers from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Paul stacks these words with death and life, angels and powers, present and future, to show that God's love, secured by Christ's atoning death and bodily resurrection, stands unbreakable over every created thing (Romans 8:38-39).

In the immediate context of Romans 8, this climax follows the Spirit's help in weakness, God's purpose in suffering, and the unbreakable chain from foreknowledge to glorification. Height and depth simply complete the picture of all creation, much as Psalm 139:8 already confessed that neither the heavens nor Sheol can hide us from God. The language also echoes the vast dimensions of Christ's love in Ephesians 3:18, yet here the point is not merely how great that love is, but that nothing can sever those who are in union with Christ from it.

This assurance rests on justification by grace through faith, not on our changing feelings or circumstances. When life lifts you high in success or drops you into deep sorrow, the promise still holds because it is anchored in Christ's finished work, not in your grip on Him. Read Romans 8:31-39 slowly this week, then pray directly to the Lord, asking Him to settle this truth in your heart and to help you rest in His love rather than in your own strength. Share the passage with a mature believer in your church so you can encourage one another in it.

question: What is the doctrine of preterition?
answer:
The doctrine of preterition teaches that in His eternal counsel God sovereignly passes by some sinners, withholding the special grace of election and leaving them to the just condemnation their sins deserve.

Many Arminian believers reject preterition, holding instead that God elects those He foresees will freely respond to His universally offered grace, thereby preserving both His desire for all to be saved and human free will.

As a Reformed Baptist I hold that preterition is a biblical doctrine because it flows from texts such as Romans 9:18, where God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills, showing that His choice is free and not based on anything in the creature. This understanding does not make God the author of sin, for those passed over perish because of their own willful unbelief, as John 3:19 states that people loved darkness rather than light. The concrete implication is that Christians should give all glory to God for their salvation and labor in evangelism with the confidence that He will save every one of His elect through the preaching of the gospel.

question: Are there supposed to be any rituals in Christianity?
answer:
Christianity is not a religion of rituals performed to earn God's favor. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by ceremonies or works (Ephesians 2:8-9). The Old Testament's many ceremonial laws, sacrifices, and feasts were shadows pointing forward to Christ; they are fulfilled in Him and no longer bind the church (Hebrews 10:1; Colossians 2:16-17).

Jesus did command two ordinances for His people: baptism and the Lord's Supper. These are not empty rituals or meritorious acts. Baptism is the outward sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, administered to believers (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3-4). The Lord's Supper proclaims His body given and blood shed for sinners until He returns (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). They function as means of grace that strengthen faith as we look to the finished work of the cross, not as additions to it.

The early church gathered simply around the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42). True worship is in spirit and truth, not elaborate ceremony (John 4:23-24). Faithful Christians differ on how structured or informal gathered worship should be; that belongs to the realm of Christian liberty rather than a test of orthodoxy (Romans 14:5-6). What unites us is the Gospel itself, not extra traditions.

If you are seeking to understand these practices, start by reading the accounts of baptism and the Lord's Supper in the Gospels and Acts, then visit a local church that preaches the Bible clearly so you can see them observed in light of Christ's finished work. Pray that the Lord would give you a heart that treasures Him rather than mere forms.

question: What is the Presbyterian Church in America (PCA), and what do they believe?
answer:
The Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) is a conservative Reformed Presbyterian denomination founded in 1973 by churches that withdrew from the Presbyterian Church in the United States over concerns about theological liberalism and the authority of Scripture. It is a confessional body that adopts the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms as subordinate standards under the Bible.

The PCA believes the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments are the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, the only rule of faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16-17). They confess one God eternally existing in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and will return personally to judge the living and the dead.

Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from works (Ephesians 2:8-9). The PCA holds the doctrines of grace, including God's sovereign election, particular redemption, effectual calling, and the perseverance of the saints. They affirm covenant theology, viewing baptism as a covenant sign administered to believers and to the infant children of believers (typically by sprinkling or pouring, though other modes are permitted). The Lord's Supper is a means of grace in which Christ is spiritually present to His people. Church government is Presbyterian, with teaching and ruling elders forming a local session, regional presbyteries, and a national General Assembly. Only qualified men serve as pastors and elders.

These convictions place the PCA firmly within historic Reformed Christianity, sharing the same gospel of justification by faith with other confessional Reformed churches while differing from Baptist churches on the subjects of baptism and aspects of church order. Faithful believers in the PCA can be received as brothers and sisters in Christ. If you are considering a PCA congregation, visit a local church, sit under the preaching of the Word, and speak with the elders about membership.

question: Where is God now? Where is God when it hurts?
answer:
The ache in asking where God is when it hurts is real, and Scripture never pretends that pain is small or that God’s nearness always feels obvious.

God is not absent. He is present everywhere by His omnipresence, and He draws especially near to the brokenhearted. Psalm 139:7-10 says, “Where can I go from Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence? If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there. If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea, even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast.” Psalm 34:18 adds, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the crushed in spirit.”

You may wonder how a loving, powerful God can allow such hurt, or why He can feel silent when the pain is loud. Those questions are honest. The Bible shows a world broken by human sin, yet a God who did not stay distant. In the incarnation, the eternal Son took on true humanity, lived among us, and entered our suffering. Jesus is the High Priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). On the cross He bore sin in our place, cried out in anguish, and was raised bodily on the third day, so that those who trust Him are never finally abandoned.

If you belong to Christ, He is with you now by His Spirit, and He intercedes for you at the Father’s right hand. Even in the hurt, He remains holy, sovereign, and good, working all things for the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28), though that does not make the pain itself good or easy to understand.

If this suffering has left you unsure where you stand with God, the way to know His nearness forever is not by trying harder but by turning from sin and trusting in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for the forgiveness of sins and new life.

A concrete next step is to open Psalm 13 or Psalm 22 today, speak the hurt to God in your own words (He already knows it), and share what you are carrying with a pastor or mature believer in a local church so you do not walk through it alone.

What particular pain are you facing right now?

question: What is the just war theory?
answer:
Just war theory is a historic Christian ethical framework that sets out when a war may be morally justified and how it must be conducted if it is to remain within bounds of justice. It was shaped especially by Augustine of Hippo and later by Thomas Aquinas as they sought to honor both God’s call to peace and the reality of a fallen world in which governing authorities must restrain evil.

The theory typically distinguishes two sets of criteria. Jus ad bellum (justice in going to war) requires a just cause such as defense against aggression, legitimate public authority, right intention, last resort after other means have failed, a reasonable prospect of success, and overall proportionality. Jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war) requires discrimination between combatants and non-combatants and proportionality in the force used. These principles attempt to apply God’s justice while limiting the destruction that always accompanies armed conflict.

Scripture presents God as both a God of peace and a God who has given the civil magistrate the sword to punish wrongdoers: “For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). At the same time Jesus declares, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9), and He teaches His followers not to resist an evildoer in personal vengeance (Matthew 5:38-48).

Faithful Christians have therefore differed on how these truths apply to war. The just war tradition, held by Augustine, Aquinas, and most of the historic church including Reformed thinkers, holds that limited, defensive war can be a necessary last resort to protect the innocent and restrain evil. Christian pacifism, held by Anabaptists and others, concludes that Jesus’ commands to love enemies and refuse personal retaliation preclude believers from participating in war, since the church’s calling is to bear witness as a people of peace. These differences arise because the Bible clearly teaches God’s justice, human sin, and the pursuit of peace, yet it does not furnish a detailed modern checklist for nation-states. The matter therefore belongs among those disputable issues in which Christians may exercise liberty without breaking fellowship (Romans 14:1-12).

A believer facing questions of military service, national policy, or personal conscience can profitably study Romans 13 and the Sermon on the Mount in their literary and historical contexts, pray for wisdom, and seek counsel from pastors and mature members of a local church.

question: What does it mean that women should have a gentle and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:4)?
answer:
In 1 Peter 3:4, a gentle and quiet spirit means an inner heart of meekness and peaceful trust in God, rather than a restless, harsh, or self-promoting manner, and this unfading beauty is of great worth in His sight.

Peter writes to Christian wives (many likely married to unbelieving husbands) that their adorning should not be merely external, such as elaborate hair, gold jewelry, or fine clothes, but “the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:3-4). The surrounding verses show that this conduct, lived without a word of argument, can even win a husband (1 Peter 3:1-2). “Gentle” describes a humble, not harsh or easily provoked character, the same quality Jesus claimed for Himself: “Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). “Quiet” describes a tranquil, peaceable spirit that is not agitating, fearful, or driven to control, because it hopes in God rather than in circumstances (1 Peter 3:5-6).

This is not a command that women must be voiceless, personality-less, or without influence. The same letter calls every believer to be ready to give a reason for the hope within (1 Peter 3:15), and the New Testament records women serving, teaching in appropriate settings, and speaking with courage. The point is the hidden person of the heart: a spirit that does not stir strife or live in anxiety, which is precious because it reflects faith rather than self-reliance. These traits belong to the fruit of the Spirit for every Christian (Galatians 5:22-23), yet Peter highlights them here for wives in a setting of potential household tension.

Grow in this by looking to Christ rather than trying to manufacture meekness in your own strength. A concrete next step is to read 1 Peter 3:1-6 slowly this week, noticing Sarah’s hope in God, and then talk with a mature sister in your local church about how a gentle and quiet spirit can look in ordinary conversations at home. Ask the Lord in prayer to produce this fruit by His Spirit as you abide in His Word.

question: What does it mean to be free from sin?
answer:
To be free from sin means that, through union with Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection, a person is no longer under sin’s penalty or its ruling power, and is instead set apart to belong to God, though the complete removal of sin’s presence waits until glory.

In the first-century world Paul knew, slavery was a vivid everyday reality, so he used that language to describe our former bondage and our new liberty. Romans 6:18 says, “You have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness.” Romans 6:22 adds, “But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness, and the outcome is eternal life.” This is not mere self-improvement. It is the result of Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement: He bore the wrath our sins deserved so that those who trust Him are justified (declared righteous) and no longer condemned (Romans 8:1; Romans 8:2).

Freedom from sin’s penalty happens at conversion. Freedom from sin’s power grows through sanctification as the Holy Spirit enables us to put sin to death and walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4; Romans 6:11–14). Freedom from sin’s presence will be complete only when Christ returns and we are glorified. Until then, 1 John 1:8 is honest: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” We are no longer slaves, yet we still fight.

This liberty is not permission to sin. Galatians 5:13 warns us not to use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but to serve one another in love. John 8:36 promises, “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died as our substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by our works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to read Romans 6 slowly this week, asking God to help you reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to Him, and to speak with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about walking in that freedom. What part of this freedom feels most needed or most confusing to you right now?

question: Is God man-made? Did man create the idea of God?
answer:
No, God is not man-made. The Bible teaches that the eternal God created mankind in His image, rather than humans inventing the true God as an idea.

You may wonder if belief in God is merely a human invention, perhaps arising from our need for comfort, meaning, or explanations before science developed. The many religions across cultures can also make it seem as though people have simply projected their own thoughts or desires onto a divine being.

Scripture presents the opposite. God exists from eternity, independent of us. Genesis 1:1 says, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." Psalm 90:2 declares, "Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God." This is the Creator-creature distinction, grounded in God's aseity (His self-existence). We depend on Him; He does not depend on us. Acts 17:24-25 records Paul saying, "The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands. And He is not served by human hands, as if He needed anything, because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else."

People do invent false gods. Romans 1:20-23 teaches that God's eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen from creation, so that we are without excuse, yet humanity exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and animals.

God has not left us to invent Him. He has revealed Himself in Scripture and fully in Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. All of us have sinned and fall short of the glory of the holy God (Romans 3:23), leaving us separated from Him. Jesus lived a perfect life, died on the cross as the substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works or our ideas of God.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

What has prompted this question for you?

question: What is the significance of the statement “God is within her; she will not fall” in Psalm 46:5?
answer:
In Psalm 46:5 the Berean Standard Bible reads, “God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns.” This means Zion, the city of God, remains secure and unshaken because the Lord Himself dwells in her midst.

Psalm 46 sets this promise against a world in upheaval. God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble, so His people need not fear even if the earth is transformed and the mountains topple into the seas (Psalm 46:1-3). Verse 4 then describes a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells. God’s presence there (His covenant immanence among His people) is the reason she will not be moved. In Israel’s history this encouraged God’s people when enemies threatened Jerusalem, reminding them that the living God was not a distant idol but truly in their midst.

This finds its fuller meaning in Christ. The church is now the temple of the living God, a dwelling place for God in His Spirit (2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:21-22). Jesus promised that He would build His church and the gates of Hades would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). Because God is within her by the Holy Spirit, the church will not fall, and those truly united to Christ are kept by His power.

When the ground feels like it is giving way around you, remember that if you belong to Christ, God is within you. Read Psalm 46 slowly today and thank Him for His nearness, then ask a mature believer in your church to pray with you for a fresh sense of His presence.

question: What does the Bible say about worship?
answer:
The Bible teaches that worship is the exclusive honor, praise, and obedient service due to the one true God, offered from the heart in spirit and in truth. God alone is worthy of this, for He is the holy Creator and Redeemer who will not share His glory with idols or any rival.

From the beginning, Scripture forbids worship of anyone or anything else: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3). Jesus Himself reaffirmed this when He said, “Worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10). True worship is not empty ritual or mere emotion; Jesus told the Samaritan woman, “A time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23-24). This means worship involves the whole person, our affections, minds, and wills, directed toward God as He has revealed Himself.

The New Testament also shows that worship is not confined to a building or a song. Paul writes, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1). Everyday obedience, gratitude, and holiness become worship when they flow from faith in Christ. At the same time, God calls His people to gather: we sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, hear the Word, pray, and remember the Lord’s death until He comes (Colossians 3:16; Hebrews 10:24-25; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). Heaven itself is filled with this worship, as the redeemed cry, “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power” (Revelation 4:11).

Because Jesus is truly God, the Bible records people worshiping Him without rebuke (Matthew 28:9, 17; John 9:38). Trinitarian worship, then, is offered to the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit. This is not a later invention but the outworking of who God is.

A simple next step is to open Psalm 95 or Psalm 100 this week, read it slowly, and speak its words back to God in your own prayer. Then gather with a local church on the Lord’s Day, not as a spectator but as one who comes to ascribe to the Lord the glory due His name. Faithful Christians may differ on music styles or liturgy, yet we are united in this: God is seeking worshipers who love Him with all they are.

question: What is more important, the death of Christ or His resurrection?
answer:
Neither the death of Christ nor His resurrection is more important than the other. Both are equally essential and inseparably joined in the one saving work of the Gospel.

Scripture presents them together as of first importance. Paul writes that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification (Romans 4:25).

The cross is the place of penal substitutionary atonement, where the sinless Son bore the wrath our sins deserved. The resurrection is God's public declaration that the sacrifice was accepted, that death is defeated, and that those united to Christ are justified and given new life. Remove either, and the Gospel collapses. A death without resurrection would leave us unvindicated and still under condemnation. A resurrection without the atoning death would leave sin unpaid.

Hold both together in your faith and worship. Read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly this week, asking the Lord to deepen your rest in the finished work of Christ who died and rose for you.

question: What is the emerging / emergent church movement?
answer:
The emerging church movement (sometimes distinguished as the emergent church) was a loosely connected late-1990s to 2010s effort to reimagine Christian faith and practice for postmodern culture. It emphasized conversation over creeds, community over institutional structures, narrative and experience over propositional doctrine, and cultural deconstruction of traditional church forms.

Some participants remained closer to historic evangelical methods while updating style and mission. Others, especially those associated with Emergent Village and writers such as Brian McLaren, moved toward questioning or redefining core Christian teachings. The Bible treats Scripture as the inspired, inerrant, and sufficient Word of God that does not change with culture (2 Timothy 3:16-17; Isaiah 40:8). Where the movement treated biblical claims as merely one perspective among many, or recast penal substitutionary atonement as optional or even abusive, it departed from the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3).

Christians are commanded to hold fast to sound doctrine and to test every spirit and teaching against the written Word (Titus 1:9; 1 John 4:1; Acts 17:11). Cultural relevance in methods can be wise, yet the gospel itself (Christ’s real incarnation, substitutionary death for sinners, burial, and bodily resurrection) is not renegotiable (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). If you encounter teaching that treats the Bible’s authority, Christ’s exclusive mediation, or justification by faith alone as outdated, measure it by Scripture rather than by conversation or cultural mood, and seek counsel from a local church that confesses these truths without apology.

question: What does the Bible say about underage drinking?
answer:
The Bible does not name a legal drinking age, because that is a modern civil category rather than a biblical one. Scripture does, however, forbid drunkenness, require self-control, and command submission to governing authorities.

Ephesians 5:18 says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” Proverbs 20:1 adds, “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise.” Drunkenness belongs to the works of the flesh, and those who practice it will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19–21). Alcohol itself is not treated as inherently sinful for adults who can receive it with thanksgiving and without being mastered by it (1 Corinthians 6:12; 1 Timothy 4:4–5), yet it easily becomes a snare, especially for the young who lack mature self-control.

Where civil law sets a drinking age, that law is to be obeyed as an ordinance of God unless it directly contradicts His Word. Romans 13:1–2 teaches, “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God. Consequently, whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves.” Underage drinking therefore violates both wisdom and the duty to honor parents and magistrates (Exodus 20:12; 1 Peter 2:13–14).

Faithful Christians have long differed on whether adult believers should drink in moderation or abstain entirely; that is a matter of Christian liberty (Romans 14). Underage drinking, however, is not an exercise of that liberty. The path of wisdom for those under the legal age is abstinence, growing in the fruit of self-control by the Spirit rather than experimenting with what Scripture calls a mocker.

If this question is personal, speak openly with a parent or a mature believer in your church, and ask the Lord for a heart that loves His ways more than the world’s. Pray through Galatians 5:16–25, asking the Spirit to produce self-control and to keep you from being mastered by anything.

question: Will there be a great apostasy / falling away during the end times?
answer:
Yes, the Bible teaches that a falling away from the faith will occur in connection with the last days. In 2 Thessalonians 2:3 Paul writes that the day of the Lord will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed. Jesus likewise warns in Matthew 24:10-12 that many will turn away from the faith, and 1 Timothy 4:1 states that in later times some will abandon the faith.

This belongs to eschatology, a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree. Scripture clearly warns of apostasy yet does not give a complete, undisputed timeline, so differences arise from how prophetic texts are read. In such non-essentials we can extend Christian liberty (Romans 14) while remaining united on Christ’s certain return and final judgment.

Some Christians, particularly those holding a dispensational premillennial view, anticipate a distinct, large-scale apostasy immediately before or during a future tribulation, coinciding with a single future Antichrist. Other Christians, including many amillennial and historic Reformed believers, see apostasy as characteristic of the entire church age between Christ’s first and second coming, with possible intensification near the end, and they often understand the man of lawlessness as a recurring principle of opposition rather than solely one future individual.

I hold that Scripture points to real and increasing departure from sound doctrine in the visible church as we move toward Christ’s return, yet those truly justified by grace through faith will persevere because they are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5). Those who finally fall away were never truly of us (1 John 2:19). This is one faithful reading among others within historic Christianity.

The call for every believer is therefore the same: hold fast to the gospel, test every teaching by Scripture, and remain watchful. A concrete next step is to read 2 Thessalonians 2 slowly this week, asking God directly for wisdom and a steadfast heart, and to stay closely connected to a local church that faithfully preaches the Word.

question: Should all pronouns referring to God be capitalized?
answer:
No, Scripture does not require that pronouns referring to God be capitalized. This is a non-essential matter of English style and personal reverence where faithful Christians may disagree, because the original Hebrew and Greek texts had no capital letters to mark divine pronouns, and the Bible gives no rule about later English typography.

One common Christian practice capitalizes pronouns such as He, Him, His, You, and Your when they refer to God. Many see this as a small, visible way to honor His holiness and to help readers quickly recognize a divine referent, a convention found in some older translations and in much traditional hymnody and writing.

Another widespread practice, followed by many modern translations, does not capitalize those pronouns. This approach treats them according to ordinary English grammar, avoids adding a visual distinction that is not present in the original manuscripts, and keeps the focus on the content of the words rather than on later orthographic custom.

In such disputable matters of practice, each person should be fully convinced in his own mind and do what he does unto the Lord (Romans 14:5–6). The real issue is the holiness of God, not the typeface. Jesus taught us to pray, “hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9). Whether you capitalize or not, let even this small choice remind you to treat His name with the reverence His character deserves, and do not bind another believer’s conscience over a convention Scripture never commands.

question: What is Kabbalah?
answer:
Kabbalah is a mystical tradition that developed within medieval Judaism, claiming to uncover hidden, esoteric meanings in the Hebrew Scriptures through symbols, numerology, contemplative practices, and ideas such as the ten sefirot (divine emanations) arranged on a Tree of Life.

It is extra-biblical. The Scriptures themselves present God's revelation as public, sufficient, and centered on Jesus Christ rather than secret codes or inner techniques. God has spoken in many times and in various ways through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). The Bible is the inspired, inerrant Word of God, profitable for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Scripture therefore warns against being taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition rather than according to Christ (Colossians 2:8). True knowledge of God comes through the incarnate Word, Jesus Christ, who is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature (Hebrews 1:3; John 1:18). Christians rest in the finished work of Christ and the ordinary means of grace (the Word, prayer, and the gathered church) rather than mystical systems.

If you are seeking a deeper knowledge of God, open the Gospel of John and read of Jesus, who fully reveals the Father.

question: Should a Christian be a prepper or in any way involved with doomsday prepping?
answer:
Faithful Christians may disagree about how far to go with prepping, because Scripture gives principles of wisdom, provision, and trust rather than a required stockpile list, making the details a matter of Christian liberty (Romans 14:1-6).

Some believers treat storing food, water, skills, and basic supplies as ordinary stewardship. They point to Joseph storing grain in years of plenty so people could survive famine (Genesis 41:33-36) and to the ant that prepares its food in summer (Proverbs 6:6-8). They also cite the duty to provide for one's household (1 Timothy 5:8), which can include planning for storms, job loss, or disruption.

Other believers warn that intense doomsday focus (collapse scenarios, bunkers, isolation, endless stockpiling) often grows from fear rather than faith. Jesus told His disciples not to worry about tomorrow (Matthew 6:25-34), and He warned against the rich fool who stored up goods yet was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16-21). They emphasize seeking first the kingdom and living generously in community rather than self-sufficient survivalism.

A balanced Christian approach uses ordinary means without anxious unbelief. Reasonable preparedness (a few weeks of food and water, basic skills, savings) can honor God as a steward and help you love family and neighbor in hard times. Obsessive doomsday prepping that feeds panic, conspiracy thinking, or withdrawal from the local church usually does not. God is sovereign; history is in His hands, not ours. We do not know the day of Christ's return, so we live faithfully now, occupy until He comes, and refuse to let fear of the future rule the present.

Examine your motives. If the drive is panic about the end of the world, bring that anxiety to the Lord and ask Him for contentment in His providence. If it is simply practical care for those God has given you, hold the plans loosely and stay ready to share. Talk with your pastor or a mature elder in your church this week, and read Matthew 6 slowly, asking God to show you where worry has taken root so you can rest in Him rather than in supplies.

question: What is the church?
answer:
The church is the assembly of God’s redeemed people, united to Jesus Christ as His body and bride, both as the universal company of all true believers and as local congregations of those who have been justified by grace through faith.

The New Testament word “church” comes from the Greek ekklesia, meaning a called-out assembly. It refers first to the universal church of every person who belongs to Christ by faith, of which He is the head (Ephesians 1:22-23; Colossians 1:18), and second to particular local churches of baptized believers who gather for the preaching of the Word, prayer, fellowship, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:41-42; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Jesus promised, “I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). He purchased the church with His own blood (Acts 20:28) and loves her as His bride, giving Himself up to make her holy (Ephesians 5:25-27). The church is the household of God and the pillar and foundation of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15), called to display God’s wisdom and to make disciples of all nations (Ephesians 3:10; Matthew 28:19-20).

Every Christian is therefore called to belong to a local church rather than walk in isolation, using the gifts God has given to build up the body (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Hebrews 10:24-25). If you are not yet part of one, seek a congregation that faithfully proclaims Christ’s death and resurrection, and commit yourself to its life and mission.

question: Does a cashless society have anything to do with the end times?
answer:
A cashless society is not mentioned anywhere in Scripture, so the Bible does not explicitly tie it to the end times. Questions like this belong to eschatology, a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree without compromising the essentials of the faith, because passages such as Revelation use apocalyptic imagery rather than a detailed forecast of twenty-first-century technology.

Some Christians, especially those who read Revelation in a primarily futurist way, see a cashless system as a possible means by which the second beast could enforce the economic control described in Revelation 13:16-17, where no one can buy or sell without the mark. They view current moves toward digital currency as a potential setup for that future reality.

Others, including many amillennial and historicist interpreters, understand the mark as a symbol of allegiance to anti-Christian power and idolatry rather than a prediction of any particular payment method. They note that Revelation was written to first-century churches under Roman pressure, using vivid pictures to assure them that God remains sovereign over every empire until Christ returns.

What Scripture states plainly is that Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11; 2 Timothy 4:1). We are commanded to watch and live holy lives, not to map every headline onto prophecy (Matthew 24:36; Matthew 24:42). God has not given us a spirit of fear (2 Timothy 1:7), and our hope rests in Christ’s finished work and coming kingdom, not in any form of currency.

In practical terms, handle whatever money God gives you as a steward, seeking first His kingdom (Matthew 6:33; 1 Timothy 6:17-19). A wise next step is to read Revelation 1–3 slowly, noting how Jesus speaks to His churches, then talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about how your congregation understands these texts. Pray for the Spirit’s help to handle the Word accurately (2 Timothy 2:15) rather than anxiously.

question: I am a former Catholic. Should I continue to go to Catholic Church so I can reach people for Christ?
answer:
No, you should not continue attending the Catholic Church as your regular place of worship, even with the good desire to reach people for Christ.

Your longing to see others know Jesus is a gift from God, and it honors Him. At the same time, the local church exists first for the gathered worship of God’s people in spirit and truth, the preaching of the Word, the right use of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and mutual encouragement under faithful elders (Hebrews 10:24-25). The Roman Catholic Church officially teaches a way of justification that mixes faith with works, sacraments, and ongoing cooperation as necessary to be made right with God. That is not the Gospel. Scripture is clear that we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8-9; Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28). Paul warns that even an apostle or an angel preaching another gospel is to be accursed (Galatians 1:8-9). The Mass itself is presented as a re-presentation of Christ’s sacrifice, yet Hebrews teaches that by a single offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:10-14). Regular participation would place you in worship that contradicts the finished work of Christ and the doctrine of justification.

You can still love and reach Catholic family and friends without making that church your spiritual home. Spend time with them, share meals, listen well, tell them how Christ saved you by His death and resurrection, and invite them to hear the Word preached where the Gospel of grace is clear. Do not hide your convictions, yet speak with patience and respect. Many Catholics sincerely love Jesus and hold to the Trinity and His deity; begin there, then gently show that Scripture locates our right standing with God in Christ’s finished work received by faith, not in our performance or the sacramental system.

Find a local church that holds to the authority of Scripture and justification by faith alone, become a member there, and ask the pastor or elders for counsel on how to share Christ with those still in Catholicism. Pray directly to God for wisdom, open doors, and softened hearts among the people you love. He is faithful to use a life rooted in a true church far more than a life divided between two gospels.

question: What does the Bible say about world missions?
answer:
The Bible presents world missions as God’s plan to bless all peoples through the gospel and as the church’s commission to proclaim Christ to the ends of the earth. From the beginning God promised Abraham, “all peoples on earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3), and the prophets called Israel to “Declare His glory among the nations” (Psalm 96:3) while looking to a light for the Gentiles that would reach “the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

Jesus fulfilled and commanded this worldwide purpose after His resurrection: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:18-20). He also told His disciples, “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The apostle Paul later asked, “How then can they call on the One they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach?” (Romans 10:14). Scripture’s vision ends with a countless multitude “from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” standing before the Lamb (Revelation 7:9).

This missionary mandate flows from the gospel itself: Christ’s death and resurrection are sufficient for sinners of every people, and the church is sent as His ambassadors until He returns. A concrete next step is to ask your local church how you can pray, give, or serve in its missions efforts this month.

question: How should we live our lives in light of our identity in Christ?
answer:
Our identity in Christ means we have been justified by grace through faith, adopted as God's children, and united to Jesus in His death and resurrection, so we now live as new creations who walk in holiness and love by the Spirit's power rather than our own effort. The old self has been crucified with Christ, and we are called to put it off while putting on the new self created after God's likeness in true righteousness and holiness. As Paul writes, "Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!" (2 Corinthians 5:17). This union with Christ is the foundation for progressive sanctification, in which the Holy Spirit conforms us to Jesus over time.

Because we have been raised with Christ, we set our minds on things above rather than earthly things, considering ourselves dead to sin but alive to God (Colossians 3:1-3; Romans 6:11). We clothe ourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, and especially love, forgiving others as the Lord has forgiven us (Colossians 3:12-14). We walk in a manner worthy of our calling as God's chosen people, a royal priesthood set apart to proclaim His excellencies (Ephesians 4:1; 1 Peter 2:9). This is not a way to earn God's favor, since we already have it in Christ, but the natural fruit of belonging to Him. He who began this good work in us will complete it (Philippians 1:6).

In daily life this looks like speaking words that build others up, fleeing temptation by remembering you belong to Jesus, and serving your family, church, and neighbors as one in whom Christ lives (Galatians 2:20). A concrete next step is to read Colossians 3:1-17 this week, asking the Lord to show you one specific area (such as speech, anger, or relationships) where you can put on Christlike character, then share that application with a mature believer in your local church for encouragement and prayer. Pray directly to God, thanking Him for your identity in Christ and asking the Spirit to help you live it out each day.

question: How do I know the Bible is not just mythology?
answer:
The Bible is not mythology because its authors present it as historical testimony of real events, people, and places, not as invented tales. The apostle Peter wrote, "For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty" (2 Peter 1:16).

You may wonder, as many do, whether the Bible resembles the imaginative stories of Zeus, Gilgamesh, or other ancient religions, especially given its miracles and distant setting. Some also assume modern scholarship has shown it to be late legend. Yet the Bible differs sharply in genre and claim. The Gospels function as ancient biographies grounded in eyewitnesses, and Luke opens by explaining he investigated everything carefully "so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught" (Luke 1:1-4). Paul likewise recites the early creed of Christ's death, burial, and resurrection, listing named witnesses still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

Archaeology has repeatedly confirmed details once doubted, such as the existence of King David, Pontius Pilate, and the Hittites. The Bible also shows a unique unity across centuries and authors, a linear view of history rather than cyclical myth, and hundreds of specific prophecies fulfilled in Jesus. Scripture itself claims to be God-breathed and useful for teaching (2 Timothy 3:16-17), the inspired, inerrant Word that reveals the living God rather than human invention.

This historical reliability matters because the Bible's central message is the Gospel: we are sinners separated from a holy God, yet Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as our substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

A helpful next step is to read the Gospel of Luke slowly, noting its concrete historical details, and ask God for wisdom as you do (James 1:5). What particular part of the Bible most makes you wonder if it is only mythology?

question: What does it mean that the Bible is infallible? What is biblical infallibility?
answer:
Biblical infallibility means that the Bible, as the inspired Word of God, is completely trustworthy and incapable of error or failure in all that it affirms. It cannot lead us astray and will always accomplish the purposes for which God gave it.

This truth rests on the character of God Himself, who cannot lie and whose Word is therefore truth. All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Jesus treated Scripture as unbreakable (John 10:35) and declared that not the smallest letter would pass away until all is fulfilled (Matthew 5:18). The law of the LORD is perfect and His testimony is trustworthy (Psalm 19:7); every word of God is flawless (Proverbs 30:5); and His Word will not return empty but will accomplish what He desires (Isaiah 55:11). Your word is truth (John 17:17).

Infallibility is closely joined to the Bible’s inerrancy (its freedom from error in the original writings) and its verbal plenary inspiration (every word of every part given by God). Together these truths mean Scripture is the sufficient, certain, and final authority for faith and life. We therefore read it with humble confidence rather than sitting in judgment over it.

A practical next step is to open Psalm 119 this week, asking God to grow your trust in His Word as you read, and then to bring any lingering questions to a faithful pastor or mature believer in a local church that holds the Scriptures as God’s infallible Word.

question: What does the Bible mean when it says something is unclean?
answer:
When the Bible says something is unclean, it refers primarily to a state of ritual impurity under the Mosaic law that made a person or object temporarily unfit to approach God’s holy presence in worship, and it also names the moral defilement that sin produces.

The Hebrew term ṭāmēʾ (unclean) stands opposite ṭāhôr (clean) and governs large sections of Leviticus concerning foods, childbirth, skin diseases, and bodily discharges (Leviticus 11–15). These laws were not mainly hygiene rules or arbitrary taboos. They taught Israel that the Lord is holy and that death, decay, and disorder cannot mix with His presence; contact with the dead or certain animals required washing, waiting, or sacrifice before a person could reenter worship (Leviticus 11:44-45; Numbers 19:11-13). Other ancient cultures had purity customs, yet Israel’s laws uniquely tied ritual purity to covenant loyalty and the character of Yahweh.

Jesus later declared all foods clean (Mark 7:18-19) and showed by touching lepers and the dead that He, the Holy One, overcomes uncleanness rather than being defiled by it. The ceremonial system served as a type pointing to the deeper need for purification that only Christ’s atoning work supplies. In the new covenant the focus shifts to the heart: what truly defiles a person is not food or ritual contact but the evil that comes from within (Mark 7:20-23). Believers are made clean by the blood of Christ and are still called to pursue holiness of life (Hebrews 9:13-14; 1 Peter 1:15-16).

These passages therefore remind Christians that God remains holy. We no longer keep the food laws or ritual washings, yet we still confess sin and seek purity of heart through faith in the One who makes the unclean clean.

question: What is the meaning of life?
answer: The meaning of life is to know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent, glorifying Him and finding lasting joy in fellowship with Him. You may wonder whether any single answer can fit such a large question, or whether suffering and the seeming randomness of the world leave life without real purpose. Those concerns are understandable. The Bible teaches that God created us in His image for relationship with Himself (Genesis 1:26-27), yet our sin has separated us from Him (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). In His love God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. He lived a sinless life, died on the cross as our substitute in penal substitution, bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Through faith in Him we are justified by grace alone, reconciled to God, and given eternal life, which is knowing Him (John 17:3; Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. What has your search for meaning looked like so far?

question: How can there be subordination in the Trinity?
answer:
The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, equal in essence, power, and glory, with no inferiority of being among them. What Scripture reveals is an order of personal relations and, in the work of redemption, the Son’s willing obedience to the Father.

It is understandable to wonder how any kind of order or submission could exist without making one person less divine than another. The Bible holds both truths together. The three persons share the one undivided divine nature (homoousios, of the same essence), as when Jesus says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) and Paul writes that “in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (Colossians 2:9). At the same time the persons are distinct: the Father is unbegotten, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (John 1:14, 18; John 3:16), and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (John 15:26). These relations of origin (sometimes called taxis, or order) do not divide the essence or rank the persons by worth.

In the economy of salvation the eternal Son took on true humanity and submitted Himself to the Father’s will, even to death on a cross (Philippians 2:5–8). When Jesus said, “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), He spoke as the incarnate, sent Son, not as one who lacked full deity. After all things are put under His feet, “the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put everything under Him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). This is the ordered working of the one God, not a lesser god serving a greater one.

This mystery of unity and distinction calls us to worship rather than to master every detail. A concrete next step is to read John 14–17 slowly, noticing how Jesus speaks of both His oneness with the Father and His going to the Father, and then to pray that God would increase your awe of His triune glory through His Word.

question: Why are there so many religions? Do all religions lead to God?
answer:
The variety of religions in the world is real, and many people hope that sincere paths of any kind all lead to God, since claiming one way can feel narrow or unkind.

The Bible teaches that God has made Himself known through creation and conscience, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). Yet because of sin, humanity suppresses that truth, exchanges the glory of the true God for idols of our own making, and invents ways to reach Him or explain life (Romans 1:21-25). That is why so many religions exist: they are fallen human attempts, often sincere, yet they contradict one another on who God is, what is wrong with us, and how we can be made right with Him. They cannot all be true.

Christians believe there is one holy God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We have all sinned and fall short of His glory, and our sin separates us from Him (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, was born of the Virgin Mary, lived a sinless life, and died on the cross as our substitute, bearing the penalty our sins deserved (penal substitutionary atonement). He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, proving His victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by religious works or sincerity.

Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). The apostles declared, “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What has shaped your view of Jesus and His claim to be the only way?

question: Do Mormons believe in the Trinity?
answer:
No, Latter-day Saints (commonly called Mormons) do not believe in the Trinity as historic Christianity confesses it from Scripture.

They teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are three separate and distinct beings (three gods) who are one only in purpose and will, not one God sharing the same divine essence. Historic Christianity, by contrast, holds that there is one God who eternally exists as three co-equal, co-eternal persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is a core doctrine, not a secondary or optional view. Denial of it places a group outside orthodox Christianity.

Scripture reveals both the oneness of God and the full deity and distinct personhood of Father, Son, and Spirit. "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus commanded baptism "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), using a singular "name" for the three. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Holy Spirit is likewise God (Acts 5:3-4). These truths together are what the church has always meant by the Trinity: one God in three persons.
