This matters because the God we worship, and the Christ who saves, must be the God of Scripture. Jesus is truly God and truly man, whose sacrificial death and bodily resurrection reconcile sinners to the Father. If you are speaking with Latter-day Saint friends, listen with respect, open the Bible with them, and hold fast to what God has actually revealed about Himself.

question: Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?
answer:
The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments. God delivered them by His own voice at Mount Sinai and wrote them on two tables of stone after first redeeming Israel from Egypt, so that obedience would flow from grace rather than merit (Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21).

The first four commandments summarize our duty toward God, and the remaining six our duty toward our neighbor. Jesus further reduced this summary to the two great commandments of loving God with all our heart, soul, and mind, and loving our neighbor as ourselves, on which all the Law and the Prophets hang (Matthew 22:37-40; Romans 13:8-10). This same moral standard was originally written on the human heart at creation and remains the perpetual rule of righteousness (Romans 2:14-15).

For those justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, the Ten Commandments function as the third use of the law: a guide for grateful obedience in progressive sanctification, not a means of earning standing with God. Regularly examine your life by them in prayer, asking the Spirit to show remaining sin and to conform you more fully to Christ.

question: What does it mean to be contrite? What is contrition?
answer:
To be contrite is to have a heart crushed by the weight of sin against a holy God, marked by humble, sincere sorrow rather than mere regret over consequences. Contrition is that inner brokenness of spirit which God receives as the true sacrifice He desires.

In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the idea is often expressed by a word meaning to crush or pulverize, picturing a heart broken into pieces under conviction. Psalm 51:17 records David after his sin: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise." The Lord Himself promises to dwell with such people in order to revive them (Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 66:2).

This is godly sorrow, distinct from worldly sorrow that produces only death; it leads to repentance and life without regret (2 Corinthians 7:10). It is the Spirit’s gracious work of conviction, not something we produce by our own effort, and it prepares the heart to rest in Christ’s finished work rather than in our feelings.

If you sense this brokenness, do not hide it or try to manage it alone. Confess the specific sin to God, using Psalm 51 as a guide for your own prayer, and stay connected to a faithful local church where the Word, prayer, and fellowship can strengthen you.

question: What does it mean that “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11)?
answer:
In Psalm 16:11, “at Your right hand are pleasures forevermore” means that God Himself is the fountain of unending joy, and that those who belong to Him will enjoy His presence in the place of highest honor, blessing, and delight that never ends.

David wrote this as a confession of trust: the Lord is his portion, his cup, and his security, so that even in the face of death he is not shaken. The “right hand” in Scripture is the place of power, favor, and royal honor (Exodus 15:6; Psalm 110:1). To be there is to live in God’s immediate presence, where there is “fullness of joy.” The Hebrew words speak of pleasant delights that last in perpetuity, not fleeting earthly comforts.

This hope is fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Peter quoted Psalm 16:8-11 on Pentecost to show that God did not abandon His Holy One to the grave, but raised Jesus and exalted Him to His right hand (Acts 2:25-33). Christ’s bodily resurrection and session at the Father’s right hand guarantee that death is not the end for those united to Him. Believers therefore look forward to glorification: we will be with the Lord forever, see Him as He is, and share in the pleasures of His presence (1 John 3:2; Revelation 21:3-4).

Even now you can taste a foretaste of that joy by setting the Lord always before you, as David did (Psalm 16:8). A simple next step is to read Psalm 16 slowly this week, asking God to make the path of life known to you and to fill you with His presence. Talk to Him directly about this hope, and if you belong to a local church, share it with a mature believer who can pray with you.

question: What is divine providence?
answer:
Divine providence is God’s sovereign, wise, and continual work of preserving, governing, and directing all things in creation according to His holy purposes and for His glory.

The Bible teaches that the Lord “works out everything to its end” and that He “upholds all things by His powerful word” (Ephesians 1:11; Hebrews 1:3). Not even a sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father, and the very hairs of your head are all numbered (Matthew 10:29–30). This is neither cold fate nor distant deism; it is the personal, fatherly rule of the triune God who remains intimately involved with His world.

This doctrine flows from God’s character as sovereign, faithful, and good. He uses both ordinary means and secondary causes (what theologians call concurrence) so that human choices, weather, nations, and even suffering serve His wise ends without making Him the author of sin.

In practice, this means you can face an unexpected job loss, a hard diagnosis, or a change of plans without despair, because nothing is random and God is working all things for the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28). A simple next step is to read Psalm 103:19 and Matthew 6:25–34 this week, then thank God specifically for one ordinary detail He has already governed in your life.

question: In what ways is the Christian life like the Olympics?
answer:
The Christian life resembles the Olympics because Scripture itself uses the imagery of athletic contests to describe our calling to follow Christ with disciplined endurance.

Athletes train with strict self-control for a perishable wreath, and Paul applies this to believers who exercise themselves for godliness in progressive sanctification. "Everyone who competes in the games exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one. Therefore I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air. No, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:25-27). "Train yourself for godliness. For physical training is of some value, but godliness has value for all things, holding promise for both the present life and the life to come" (1 Timothy 4:7-8).

We run a race that requires endurance, throwing off every weight and the sin that clings so closely, while looking to Jesus as the pioneer and perfecter of our faith. "Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God" (Hebrews 12:1-2). An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules, so we live by the Word of God rather than our own preferences (2 Timothy 2:5).

The prize is not salvation earned by our performance, for we are already justified by grace through faith in Christ's finished work. The race is the lifelong pursuit of knowing Christ more fully and receiving the imperishable reward He gives those who finish well by His keeping power. "I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:14). "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing" (2 Timothy 4:7-8).

This week, identify one specific encumbrance or lingering sin that slows your run, confess it to the Lord, and ask a mature believer in your local church to help you lay it aside as you fix your eyes on Jesus in daily Scripture reading.

question: What should be the Christian perspective on nudity in art?
answer:
The question of nudity in art is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture gives no direct command about artistic depictions of the unclothed body. It therefore falls under Christian liberty and the careful application of broader principles rather than a test of orthodox faith.

Some Christians hold that such art can honor the Creator when it portrays the dignity of the human form without erotic purpose. God made mankind in the imago Dei, male and female, and declared His creation very good. The body is fearfully and wonderfully made, and before the Fall Adam and Eve were naked and unashamed (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:25; Psalm 139:14). In this view, skillful, non-lustful representation can point back to that original goodness.

Other Christians argue that, after the Fall, nakedness is bound up with shame and covering, and that in a world marked by lust such images too easily become a snare. They therefore choose to avoid creating or viewing artistic nudes in order to keep their thoughts pure and to refuse any participation in objectifying those made in God’s image (Genesis 3:7; Genesis 3:21).

In either case the heart remains decisive. Jesus teaches that looking with lustful intent is already adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). We are called to dwell on whatever is pure and lovely, to flee sexual immorality, and to glorify God in our bodies, which are temples of the Holy Spirit (Philippians 4:8; 1 Corinthians 6:18-20). We must also refuse to put a stumbling block in a brother’s way (Romans 14:13).

Christian liberty therefore requires that we neither despise nor judge one another on this point, but that each be fully convinced in his own mind and walk in love (Romans 14:3-5). A wise next step is to examine how any particular work actually affects your own thoughts, then talk it through with a pastor or mature believer in your local church while asking God for a guarded heart and genuine holiness.

question: Should we allow false teachers into our home?
answer:
No, we should not receive false teachers into our homes in a way that welcomes, supports, or platforms their ministry.

The apostle John writes, "If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or even greet him. Whoever greets him shares in his wicked work." (2 John 1:10-11) This teaching is the doctrine of Christ, that Jesus has come in the flesh, truly God and truly man in the incarnation. In the first-century setting, traveling teachers stayed in homes and were given a platform, so receiving them meant aiding their work and treating them as brothers. Doing so would share in their deception.

Scripture also commands us to test the spirits, because "many false prophets have gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1), and Jesus warned, "Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves." (Matthew 7:15) Even an angel preaching another gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8). The principle remains: do not give false teachers lodging, influence, or implied fellowship that advances error, especially around your family.

This is not a command to be unkind or to refuse all conversation. We can still speak the Gospel with gentleness at the door, pray for their repentance, and treat them as people who need Christ. Hospitality to ordinary neighbors and strangers remains a Christian duty (Hebrews 13:2). The line is crossed when we treat a false teacher as a fellow believer or let them teach in our household.

If you are facing this, talk with the elders of your local church for counsel, and ask God for discernment as you hold fast to the true Gospel of Christ’s death and resurrection.

question: How is God’s Word a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105)?
answer:
God’s Word is a lamp to your feet because it gives enough clear light for the next obedient step in a dark world, showing you God’s will so you do not stumble into sin or confusion. Psalm 119:105 says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.”

In the psalmist’s world, a traveler at night carried a small oil lamp that lit only the ground immediately ahead, enough to keep from falling, even if the whole road remained unseen. Scripture works the same way: it is sufficient for today’s faithfulness (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The Spirit uses the Word to expose sin, correct our thinking, and train us in righteousness so that we are equipped for every good work. It is also “a light to my path,” giving the larger direction of a life that honors Christ rather than the world’s darkness (Psalm 19:8; Proverbs 6:23).

This is why Christians receive the Bible as the inspired, inerrant, and sufficient authority for faith and practice. Feelings, culture, and even our own wisdom can mislead us, but God’s Word does not. When you face a decision about speech, work, relationships, or purity, search the Scriptures first and let them set the next step.

Open Psalm 119 this week and read a stanza each day, asking the Lord to show you one concrete act of obedience for that day. Pray to Him directly, using the psalm’s own words as your guide, and share what you see with a mature believer in your local church so you walk in the light together.

question: Why were the people guilty for a priest’s sin?
answer:
The people were guilty for a priest’s sin because the anointed priest stood as their covenant representative before God, so his transgression in that office brought corporate guilt on the congregation he represented (Leviticus 4:3).

In Israel’s worship, the high priest did not act merely as a private individual. He bore the names of the twelve tribes on his breastpiece as a memorial before the Lord (Exodus 28:29), approaching God on behalf of the whole people. When he sinned, the holiness of the sanctuary and the standing of the nation were compromised together. That is why the law required him to offer a young bull, the same costly offering prescribed when the entire congregation sinned (Leviticus 4:13–14). Scripture treats this as real covenantal solidarity, not a mere symbol: the head’s unfaithfulness implicated the body.

This same principle of representation appears throughout the Bible. Adam’s sin brought death to those united to him (Romans 5:12); a king’s or father’s actions could bring blessing or judgment on those under his care. The priest’s guilt therefore was not arbitrary unfairness but the outworking of God-appointed mediation. It also showed how seriously God regards the holiness of those who draw near on behalf of others.

All of this prepares us for the greater High Priest. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, never sinned and therefore never brought guilt on His people. Instead He offered Himself once for all, so that those who trust Him receive His righteousness rather than condemnation (Hebrews 4:14–15; Hebrews 7:26–27). Human pastors and elders still matter, and their sins can wound a congregation, which is why we ought to pray for them and hold them to the Word. Yet our standing before God rests finally on Christ’s perfect representation, not on any earthly priest.

A wise next step is to read Hebrews 7–9 slowly, asking the Lord to show you both the seriousness of sin in those who lead and the sufficiency of the sinless Savior who intercedes for you.

question: What is spiritual mapping?
answer:
Spiritual mapping is a modern practice, mainly among some charismatic and Pentecostal Christians, of researching a city or region's history, culture, sins, and religious patterns in order to identify alleged demonic strongholds or territorial spirits and then pray against them.

It is often connected with what is called strategic-level spiritual warfare. Proponents sometimes appeal to Daniel 10:13 and Daniel 10:20 (the "prince of the kingdom of Persia" and the "prince of Greece") or to Ephesians 6:12: "For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world's darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms." Scripture, however, never commands or models mapping geographic areas this way, nor does it instruct believers to research local history in order to bind territorial spirits.

This is a non-essential practice where faithful Christians disagree, largely because the Bible gives less explicit detail on method than on the reality of spiritual conflict itself. Some continuationist Christians view it as a strategic application of intercession for cities. Many other Christians, especially in Reformed and cessationist traditions, see it as extra-biblical speculation that can shift attention from Christ's finished work and the ordinary means of grace.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, spiritual warfare is real, yet the New Testament directs us to resist the devil by standing firm in the faith, putting on the armor of God, and taking thoughts captive to Christ rather than by geographic mapping (Ephesians 6:10-18; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8-9; 2 Corinthians 10:3-5). A wise next step is to pray regularly for your neighborhood from Scripture, share the gospel with those around you, and walk in holiness within a local church, resting in Christ's victory rather than in techniques the apostles never taught.

question: What is God’s design for marriage?
answer:
God designed marriage as a lifelong covenant between one man and one woman. He instituted it at creation when He formed Eve as a helper corresponding to Adam, so that the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:18–24).

Jesus Himself reaffirmed this original pattern, teaching that God made them male and female from the beginning and that a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, the two becoming one flesh; what God has joined together, man must not separate (Matthew 19:4–6). This one-flesh union is also a profound mystery that points to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Husbands are called to love their wives sacrificially as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, while wives are to submit to their own husbands as the church submits to Christ (Ephesians 5:22–25). Marriage was ordained for mutual help, the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue, and as a safeguard against sexual immorality.

This covenantal design therefore calls husbands to lead in self-giving love and wives to respond in respectful partnership, both resting in the gospel and walking in the Spirit. If you are married, a concrete next step is to read Ephesians 5:22–33 together this week and ask the Lord to shape your home according to that pattern.

question: What is the value of group Bible study?
answer:
Group Bible study is valuable because it lets believers examine Scripture together, sharpen one another’s understanding, and put God’s truth into practice in real community rather than in isolation. The church is called to this kind of shared life around the Word. Hebrews 10:24-25 says, “And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” The early church devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship (Acts 2:42). Colossians 3:16 likewise urges, “Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom.”

This kind of gathering is one of the ordinary means of grace God uses in progressive sanctification. The Holy Spirit applies the Word more fully when brothers and sisters teach, correct, and encourage one another, much as iron sharpens iron (Proverbs 27:17). Individual reading remains essential, yet the body of Christ is designed so that no member grows in isolation.

A concrete next step is to speak with the elders or pastors of your local church this week about joining an existing small-group Bible study, or about gathering a few members to begin one. If you are not yet part of a congregation, seek a Bible-preaching church that takes the Word and fellowship seriously. Ask the Lord to give you a hunger for His Word in the company of His people.

question: How can I overcome a feeling of spiritual emptiness?
answer:
Feeling spiritual emptiness can be a wearying experience that leaves the soul dry and searching. The Bible gives voice to this very longing: "As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs for You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God" (Psalm 42:1-2).

God designed us for Himself, and nothing else can ultimately fill that space. Jesus Christ, fully God and fully man, invites the thirsty to Himself: "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst" (John 6:35). If this emptiness reflects a life still separated from God by sin, the Gospel is the answer. We have all sinned and fallen short of His holiness. Yet Christ lived perfectly, died on the cross as our penal substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By grace through faith in Him alone, not by our works, we are justified and brought into union with Christ. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

Even those who belong to Christ can pass through seasons of spiritual dryness, whether from unconfessed sin, neglect of God's Word, isolation, or simply the trials He uses to refine us. If there is known sin, confess it, for "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). Remember that your justification rests on Christ's finished work, not fluctuating feelings, and He who began a good work in you will complete it (Philippians 1:6). Return to the ordinary means of grace: Scripture, prayer, and the gathered church.

A practical next step is to open Psalm 63 today, read it slowly, and then speak to God in your own words about this emptiness, asking Him to draw you near and satisfy you with the knowledge of Christ's love (Ephesians 3:19). If you are not already part of a local church, visit one this Lord's Day where the Bible is faithfully preached, and share this struggle with a pastor or mature believer so they can pray with you (Hebrews 10:24-25).

How has this feeling of emptiness been affecting your walk with the Lord lately?

question: How can I, a Muslim, become assured of paradise?
answer:
The desire for real assurance of paradise is a deep and honest one. You may feel that even sincere faith, the five pillars, and a lifetime of good deeds still leave the outcome uncertain, because final judgment rests with God's will and no one can fully know it in advance.

Christians believe the Bible teaches that lasting assurance does not come from weighing our own efforts, but from what God has already done in Jesus Christ. God is perfectly holy and just. Every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory (Romans 3:23), and that sin separates us from Him. Our best works cannot remove the guilt or pay the debt, because they themselves are stained.

Out of love the Father sent His eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, lived a sinless life, and then died on the cross as our substitute, bearing the penalty our sins deserved (this is called penal substitutionary atonement). He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, showing His victory over sin and death. Salvation is therefore by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Those who repent and trust Him are justified (declared righteous) and given eternal life as a gift.

Jesus Himself said, "Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life" (John 5:24). The apostle John later wrote so that believers "may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). Assurance rests on Christ's finished work, not on our fluctuating performance.

You may have been taught that Jesus was only a prophet who was not crucified, or that God becoming man is unthinkable. The New Testament writers, who knew Him, testify that He did die, that He rose, and that He is the one Mediator between God and humanity (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Turn from relying on your own striving and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and the gift of assured eternal life with God.

A simple next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking God to show you whether these things are true. What thoughts or questions does this raise for you?

question: What is the spiritual gift of miracles?
answer:
The spiritual gift of miracles (also called the working of miracles) is a special enablement of the Holy Spirit by which certain believers performed supernatural acts of power that went beyond ordinary means, as listed among the charismata in 1 Corinthians 12:10 and 1 Corinthians 12:28.

These works served as authenticating signs of the apostolic gospel in the founding of the church. Continuationists argue that this gift remains available today because the Holy Spirit still indwells the church, God still acts supernaturally, and Scripture never states that such gifts have ended. As a Reformed Baptist I hold that the miraculous sign gifts, including this one, ceased with the apostles, because they confirmed the new revelation now complete in Scripture and belonged to the unique foundational era of the church (Hebrews 2:3-4; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Ephesians 2:20).

God remains free to work miracles according to His sovereign will, yet believers today are called to the ordinary, abiding gifts and means of grace (the Word, prayer, and fellowship) rather than expecting a standing gift of miracles as in the apostolic age. A wise next step is to read 1 Corinthians 12–14 slowly, asking the Lord to help you treasure His sufficient Word and serve His people with whatever gifts He has given you.

question: What does it mean that God is merciful?
answer:
God is merciful means that He looks on sinners with holy compassion and withholds the judgment we deserve, instead showing kindness and providing forgiveness we could never earn. This is not God ignoring sin or weakening His justice. His wrath against sin is real, and His mercy is displayed most clearly where justice is fully satisfied, in Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement on the cross.

Scripture presents this as central to who God is. He proclaimed Himself to Moses as “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The psalmist repeats the same truth: “The LORD is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Psalm 103:8). In the New Testament this mercy is bound to salvation itself: “But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved!” (Ephesians 2:4-5). At the cross God remains both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26).

Because God has shown us such mercy, we are called to live it out: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). Practically, this means coming to Him in honest confession of sin, knowing He is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), and extending the same undeserved kindness to those who have wronged us.

question: Who is the head of the church, biblically speaking?
answer:
Jesus Christ is the head of the church. The New Testament consistently presents Him as the supreme authority over His people, who form His body.

Paul writes that God “put everything under His feet and appointed Him as head over everything for the church, which is His body” (Ephesians 1:22-23). He adds that “Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior” (Ephesians 5:23) and that “He is the head of the body, the church” so that He might have preeminence in all things (Colossians 1:18). This headship of Christ means the church belongs to Him, lives by His life, and answers to His Word rather than to any human figure as ultimate authority.

Elders and pastors serve as under-shepherds who point the flock to the Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4). In the life of a local congregation this means measuring teaching, worship, and decisions by Scripture so that Christ, not tradition or personality, remains Lord.

question: Who is the ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9?
answer:
The ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9 is Satan, also called the devil and the great dragon, the one who deceives the whole world. Revelation 12:9 identifies him directly: “And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, who leads the whole world astray. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him.”

This is the same serpent who appeared in the Garden of Eden in Genesis 3:1, tempting Eve and bringing sin and death into the world. The New Testament writers treat that event as real history, not mere symbol, and they see Satan as a personal, fallen adversary who accuses, tempts, and opposes God’s people (see also 2 Corinthians 11:3; John 8:44). Revelation 12 places this ancient enemy in the larger story of Christ’s victory: the male child (Jesus) is caught up to God, the dragon is thrown down, and the promised crushing of the serpent’s head in Genesis 3:15 is shown as already accomplished at the cross and resurrection, even while the church still waits for the final, public end of his power.

Because Satan is a real but defeated foe, believers need not live in terror of him. Resist him by standing firm in the gospel, drawing near to God in prayer and the Word, and remembering that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (James 4:7; Romans 16:20).

question: Book of 1 John - Bible Survey
answer:
The Apostle John wrote 1 John as a pastoral letter to believers, most likely in Asia Minor near the end of the first century, to assure them of eternal life and to expose false teachers who denied that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh.

John writes as an eyewitness of the incarnate Son: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). He states his purpose plainly: “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). The letter also aims at complete joy through genuine fellowship with the Father and the Son (1 John 1:3–4).

The historical setting involved early heresies (often linked to proto-Gnostic or Docetic teaching) that treated the material body as unworthy of God, so some denied the true incarnation and atoning death of Jesus. John answers this by insisting that every spirit confessing “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2) and by calling such deniers antichrists (1 John 2:18–22; 1 John 4:3).

Major themes include walking in the light rather than darkness (1 John 1:5–7), the reality of sin and the need for confession (1 John 1:8–10), God’s love displayed in the sending of His Son as propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2; 1 John 4:10), the new-birth marks of faith, love, and obedience, and confidence before God on the day of judgment. Genuine children of God do not make a practice of sin (1 John 3:4–10) and love the brothers (1 John 3:14–18; 1 John 4:7–21). Those who left the church showed they were never truly of it (1 John 2:19), which undergirds the perseverance of the saints.

A simple outline follows the letter’s flow:
- The Word of Life and the basis of fellowship (1 John 1:1–4)
- Walking in the light, confessing sin, and keeping God’s commands (1 John 1:5–2:17)
- Warnings about antichrists and remaining in the truth (1 John 2:18–27)
- The children of God, righteousness, and brotherly love (1 John 2:28–3:24)
- Testing the spirits and the love of God (1 John 4:1–21)
- Faith that overcomes the world and the certainty of eternal life (1 John 5:1–21)

1 John therefore defends core truths of the incarnation (Jesus is truly God and truly man) and of penal substitutionary atonement while giving believers three practical tests of authentic faith: right doctrine about Christ, a life of growing holiness, and love for fellow Christians. Read the letter slowly this week, asking the Lord to show you these marks in your own walk, and discuss what you see with a mature believer in your local church.

question: What happens at the final judgment?
answer:
At the final judgment, Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to raise all the dead and to judge every person, the living and the dead. Those justified by grace through faith in Him will enter eternal life, while the unrepentant will face eternal punishment, after which God will renew all things in a new heaven and new earth.

Jesus taught this plainly: He will come in His glory, sit on His glorious throne, and separate people as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats (Matthew 25:31-46). Those who belong to Him inherit the kingdom prepared for them, while others go away into eternal fire. He also said a time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29). Revelation 20:11-15 describes the great white throne, where the dead are judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books, and anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire.

This judgment displays God’s holiness, justice, and faithfulness. Believers in Christ face no condemnation, because Jesus bore the penalty of their sin in His sacrificial death on the cross and rose bodily on the third day (Romans 8:1; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Their works will be assessed for reward, yet salvation itself is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by those works. All people have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), so every one of us needs this Savior.

Because that day is certain, the fitting response now is to repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. How does knowing this coming judgment shape the way you live and hope today?

question: In what ways is becoming a Christian becoming an entirely new man / woman?
answer:
Becoming a Christian means God makes you a new creation in Christ through regeneration by the Holy Spirit, so the old self of sin dies and a new heart, identity, and life begin. This is not self-improvement or a new set of habits, but a supernatural work of God that unites you to Jesus in His death and resurrection.

Jesus taught that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again (John 3:3). God promised, I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). He saved us... through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17).

This newness includes several realities. You receive a new standing before God through justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone: you are declared righteous, forgiven, and reconciled because Jesus died as your substitute and rose again. You receive a new identity and family: you are adopted as a child of God, no longer defined by former sins or the world’s values (Romans 8:15; Galatians 2:20). You receive a new nature and direction: the Holy Spirit begins progressive sanctification, enabling you to put off the old self with its practices and put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator (Colossians 3:9-10; Ephesians 4:22-24). You also receive a new destiny: from spiritual death and condemnation to walking in newness of life and the sure hope of glorification (Romans 6:4).

The change is real and decisive, yet not complete until Christ returns. Remaining sin still wars against the new heart, which is why we must daily walk by faith, using the means of grace (the Word, prayer, and the local church). When old temptations rise, remember you are already a new creation in Christ and live from that identity rather than toward it.

A concrete next step is to read 2 Corinthians 5:14-21 and Ephesians 4:17-32 this week, then pray, asking God to help you see yourself as He now sees you in Christ and to walk accordingly. If you have not yet trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

question: What are the Pauline epistles?
answer:
The Pauline epistles are the thirteen New Testament letters written by the Apostle Paul to churches and individuals in the first century.

They are Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, and Philemon.

These letters teach core truths of the Gospel, including justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, the nature of the church as Christ’s body, and the call to holiness by the Holy Spirit. Paul wrote them in the Greco-Roman world to address real congregations and people, yet they remain the inspired Word of God for the whole church. The Apostle Peter treated them as Scripture when he wrote, “And consider that the patience of our Lord means salvation, just as our dear brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes the same way in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters. His letters contain some things that are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:15-16). All Scripture, including these epistles, is God-breathed and useful for training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Reading even one of them slowly this week, asking the Lord to apply its truth to your own life and church, is a simple way to grow in that same grace.

question: How can I be sure I am praying according to the will of God?
answer:
You can be sure you are praying according to the will of God when your requests are shaped by Scripture, offered in humble submission through Christ, and helped by the Holy Spirit. Scripture is the revealed, preceptive will of God, showing His character, commands, and promises so that we do not guess in the dark.

The Bible gives this confidence: "And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us" (1 John 5:14). His secret decree remains His own (Deuteronomy 29:29), but He has not left us without light. Jesus taught us to pray, "Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10), and He Himself submitted in Gethsemane, "Yet not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39). The Holy Spirit intercedes for us according to that same will when we do not know how to pray as we ought (Romans 8:26-27). As we abide in Christ and His words abide in us, our asking is brought into line with His heart (John 15:7).

Prayers that chase selfish pleasure miss the mark (James 4:3). Prayers that seek wisdom, holiness, daily bread, the advance of the Gospel, and thanksgiving align with what God has already said He desires (James 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). Even when a specific outcome is unclear, we can still pray, "If the Lord wills," and rest that He works all things for the good of those who love Him.

A concrete next step is to take one Psalm or a short Gospel passage each day this week, read it slowly, and turn its truths into your own requests, asking God to make His will your delight (Psalm 37:4). Share this desire with a pastor or mature believer in your local church so they can pray with you and help you grow. In your own prayer, simply ask the Lord to search your heart and teach you to pray (Psalm 139:23-24). He is a gracious Father who hears His children because of Christ.

question: What does the Bible say about busyness / being too busy?
answer:
The Bible cautions against a life of anxious, distracted busyness that crowds out God, rest, and what matters most, as when Jesus told Martha she was worried and upset about many things while Mary had chosen the good portion of sitting at His feet (Luke 10:41-42). God Himself rested after creating the world (Genesis 2:2-3) and commanded His people to remember the Sabbath day (Exodus 20:8-11). Jesus invited His weary disciples to come away to a quiet place and rest (Mark 6:31), and He still calls, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Scripture also says, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain, and He grants sleep to those He loves (Psalm 127:1-2). It is better to have one handful with rest than two handfuls with toil (Ecclesiastes 4:6), and we are warned not to wear ourselves out chasing riches (Proverbs 23:4).

This rest is more than a day off. It flows from justification by grace through faith in Christ alone, whose atoning death and bodily resurrection free us from striving to earn God’s approval by our productivity. In progressive sanctification the Holy Spirit teaches us to cease from our own works and enter the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9-11).

If your days feel frantic, prayerfully review your schedule this week and ask the Lord where busyness has become an idol. Talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about healthier rhythms of work and rest, and speak directly to God about your burdens, perhaps lingering over Psalm 46.

question: What are the seven baptisms mentioned in the Bible, and what do they mean?
answer:
The Bible mentions baptism in several distinct ways, and some have identified seven such baptisms. They are the baptism into Moses, John's baptism of repentance, Jesus' baptism, baptism with the Holy Spirit, baptism with fire, Jesus' baptism of suffering, and the baptism of Christian believers.

The baptism into Moses describes how the Israelites were identified with Moses as their deliverer when they passed through the cloud and the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1-2). John's baptism was an immersion of repentance, preparing Israel for the Messiah's arrival (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3). Jesus Himself was baptized by John to fulfill all righteousness, at which the Spirit descended and the Father declared His pleasure, displaying the Trinity (Matthew 3:13-17). Baptism with the Holy Spirit is Christ's work of pouring out the Spirit, placing every believer into the one body of Christ (Matthew 3:11; Acts 1:5; 1 Corinthians 12:13). Baptism with fire, spoken of by John alongside the Spirit, points to God's purifying and judging work, as He gathers the wheat and burns the chaff (Matthew 3:11-12). Jesus called His coming death a baptism He must undergo, the sufferings of the cross that accomplished our redemption (Luke 12:50; Mark 10:38-39). Christian baptism is the immersion of those who have believed, done in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as a public sign of union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3-4; Acts 8:36-38).

These various baptisms all involve identification with a person or work of God, and they ultimately direct us to the Gospel: Christ died, was buried, and rose again so that sinners might be justified by grace through faith in Him alone. Ephesians 4:5 speaks of "one baptism," which in the life of the church is this ordinance given by Christ.

Many Christians who baptize infants see water baptism as the new-covenant sign that replaces circumcision and may therefore be applied to the children of believers as members of the covenant community. I hold that baptism is for believers only, by immersion, because the New Testament pattern is baptism after repentance and faith, vividly picturing the individual's personal union with Christ rather than conveying grace to an infant. This is one faithful understanding among orthodox Christians who all seek to obey the Lord's command.

If you have trusted Christ and have not yet been baptized as a believer, speak with the elders of a local church about taking that step of joyful obedience.

question: What do you think about the Bible codes? Is there any validity to them?
answer:
Bible codes, meaning hidden messages supposedly found by skipping letters at equal distances in the Hebrew text, have no validity as extra revelation or as a way to interpret the Bible. God has spoken clearly in the words He inspired, and we are to receive what is written rather than hunt for secret patterns.

Deuteronomy 29:29 says the secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may follow all the words of this law. Scripture’s perspicuity and sufficiency mean the Holy Spirit’s intended meaning is found in the grammar, context, and literary form of the text itself, not in letter skips. Jesus and the apostles quoted and applied the Old Testament according to that plain sense, seeing Christ in the actual promises, types, and fulfillments God had given (Luke 24:27; 2 Peter 1:20-21). Biblical prophecy is given openly so it can be tested, not decoded after events occur (Deuteronomy 18:21-22). Adding hidden layers also runs against the warning not to add to God’s words (Proverbs 30:5-6).

The desire for such codes often comes from a sincere wish to see the Bible’s supernatural character confirmed. That longing is understandable, yet the decisive confirmation God has given is the public, historical resurrection of Jesus Christ, together with the Scriptures that already testify of Him. Patterns of letters can appear in any lengthy text and do not constitute new prophecy or a second Bible.

The real treasure is the Gospel itself: we are sinners before a holy God, Christ took on flesh, lived without sin, died as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, and we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Read the Bible for that message. A simple next step is to take a Gospel such as John, read it in context with a local church that preaches the Word plainly, and ask the Lord to help you hear and obey what He has already revealed.

question: How can I see the hand of God moving in my life?
answer:
God's hand is always at work in the lives of His people through His sovereign providence, even when it is not obvious in the moment. Jesus said, "My Father is always at His work to this very day, and I too am working" (John 5:17). We perceive this most clearly by faith as we trust His Word rather than demanding constant visible signs, for "we walk by faith, not by sight" (2 Corinthians 5:7).

The greatest display of God's hand is the sending of His Son, who lived a perfect life, died as a substitute for sinners, and rose bodily on the third day. If you belong to Christ by grace through faith, that saving work is the surest evidence that He has already moved toward you in love. In daily life His providence appears in ordinary mercies (breath, provision, relationships, and even hard seasons that refine us), for "every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights" (James 1:17). He also works through the local church, the preaching of Scripture, prayer, and the Lord's Supper. Scripture promises that "in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose" (Romans 8:28).

This week, take ten minutes each evening to write down two or three specific mercies you received that day, thank God for them in your own words, and ask Him to open your eyes as the psalmist did: "Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law" (Psalm 119:18). Share what you notice with a mature believer in your church so you can grow together in recognizing His faithful care.

question: Are we to love the sinner but hate the sin?
answer:
Yes, we are to love the sinner but hate the sin. This reflects God’s own character: He loves the people He created while remaining holy and opposed to the evil that destroys them.

The Bible never treats people as disposable, because every human being is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27). At the same time, it never treats sin as harmless. “Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good” (Romans 12:9). Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners and ate with them, yet He came “to call sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32). In John 8:11 He neither crushed the woman caught in adultery nor left her in her sin; He showed mercy and said, “Go and sin no more.”

True love seeks a person’s eternal good. Approving or remaining silent about what God forbids is not compassion; it is indifference. Sin is rebellion that enslaves and leads to death (Romans 6:23). We therefore hate it in ourselves first, then in others, while still treating the person with dignity because Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:8). This is the call to repentance: a turning from sin toward the Savior who bore our guilt in penal substitution on the cross and rose bodily so that we might be justified by grace through faith.

If this question arises from a specific relationship, begin with your own heart. Ask the Lord to search you (Psalm 139:23-24), confess any pride or harshness, then pray by name for the person involved, asking God for wisdom to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). Talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church so you do not walk this alone. We all stand as sinners in need of the same grace.

question: Is the Buddhist concept of Zen compatible with the Christian faith?
answer:
The Buddhist concept of Zen is not compatible with the Christian faith. Zen, as a school of Mahayana Buddhism, typically aims at satori (sudden enlightenment) through practices like zazen, seeking to realize emptiness, non-self, and an impersonal or non-dual reality, without a personal Creator, without sin as rebellion against God, and without a Savior.

The Bible presents a different reality. God is the personal, triune Lord who created all things and who speaks (Genesis 1:1; Matthew 28:19). Human beings are made in His image yet fallen in sin, separated from Him and unable to save themselves (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died as a penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by meditation, self-realization, or any technique (Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus Himself said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6); there is one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5; Acts 4:12).

Some people notice surface similarities, such as an emphasis on stillness or presence in a noisy world, and they may treat Zen methods as neutral tools. Biblical meditation, however, is not emptying the mind or dissolving the self; it is filling the mind with God’s Word and responding to the living God who has revealed Himself (Psalm 1:2; Joshua 1:8). Mixing the two worldviews does not produce a deeper Christianity; it replaces the Gospel with another path.

If you are drawn to Zen because you long for rest, clarity, or meaning, that longing itself points beyond technique. Christ invites the weary: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Turn from self-effort and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A simple next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking God to show you who Jesus is, and to speak with a pastor in a local church that holds to the Bible as God’s Word. What in particular about Zen has been drawing your attention?

question: What is the Wailing Wall / Western Wall?
answer:
The Western Wall, also called the Wailing Wall, is a surviving section of the massive Herodian retaining wall that supported the Temple Mount platform in Jerusalem. It is the closest accessible remnant of the Second Temple complex, and Jews gather there to pray and mourn the Temples’ destruction.

Jesus Christ plainly foretold that destruction: “Do you see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down” (Matthew 24:2). The Romans fulfilled that word in AD 70, razing the Temple itself while leaving outer retaining walls standing. That event closed the old-covenant sacrificial system, because Christ’s once-for-all atoning death on the cross has already provided the perfect sacrifice (Hebrews 10:10–14). Jesus Himself is the true temple (John 2:19–21), and those who trust Him become living stones in God’s spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). Believers therefore approach God with confidence through Christ alone, not through any remaining wall (Hebrews 4:16).

question: What is Taizé worship, and is it biblical?
answer:
Taizé worship is a meditative style of prayer and song that arose from the ecumenical Taizé Community in France, founded by Brother Roger in 1940. It typically includes short, repetitive chants (often drawn from Scripture and sung in several languages), extended silence, brief Bible readings, intercessory prayer, and a quiet atmosphere with candles, all aimed at fostering personal encounter with God and visible Christian unity, especially among young people.

Questions of worship style such as this are tertiary matters on which faithful Christians may disagree. Scripture clearly requires worship in spirit and in truth and supplies the ordinary elements God has given His people (the Word, prayer, singing, the ordinances), yet it does not prescribe every musical form or gathering atmosphere. John 4:24

Some Christians, including many Catholics, mainline Protestants, and some evangelicals, receive Taizé as a biblical help toward stillness, simple Scripture-soaked song, and reconciliation. They point to the call to let the word of Christ dwell richly through psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and to the invitation to be still before God. Colossians 3:16; Psalm 46:10

Others, especially those who hold the regulative principle of worship, judge that Taizé adds elements Scripture does not command for gathered worship: mantra-like repetition that can become the “vain repetitions” Jesus warned against, prolonged silence treated as a central means rather than a supporting posture, and an ecumenical framing that often minimizes rather than clarifies doctrinal differences on the gospel itself. Matthew 6:7

From a Reformed Baptist conviction I share the second concern more than the first. Singing God’s Word and praying together are commanded and precious, yet worship must remain regulated by Scripture rather than by atmosphere, repetition, or a lowest-common-denominator unity. The ordinary means of grace in a local church (the preached Word, prayer, and the ordinances) remain the primary way Christ has appointed for our growth, and any practice that blurs the distinction between justification by faith alone and other gospels deserves caution.

If Taizé songs or gatherings attract you, the next concrete step is to read Colossians 3:16 and John 4:24 slowly, then talk with your pastor or elders about how your church already seeks to worship according to the Word. Let that conversation, rather than any single style, shape your participation.

question: Does the Old Testament truly predict a second advent of the Messiah?
answer:
Yes, the Old Testament truly predicts a second advent of the Messiah. Prophets describe both a humble, suffering King who would come to save and a glorious King who will return to judge, reign, and renew all things.

It is understandable that some readers, including many traditional Jewish interpreters, see the prophets as expecting only one messianic coming that would immediately restore Israel and bring worldwide peace. The two-advent pattern can therefore look like a later Christian attempt to explain why Jesus died rather than immediately established the kingdom.

Yet the Scriptures themselves show the Messiah’s work unfolding in two stages. The prophets, moved by the Spirit of Christ, “predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:10-11). They often saw the mountain peaks of His first and second comings without clearly distinguishing the valley of time between them. The New Testament writers, under the same Spirit, make the distinction plain.

Isaiah 61:1-2 announces the Anointed One who would “proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance.” When Jesus read this in the synagogue He stopped after “the year of the Lord’s favor” and declared it fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18-21), leaving the day of vengeance for His return. Daniel 7:13-14 portrays “One like a Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” to receive an everlasting dominion; Jesus applied this scene to His future coming (Matthew 26:64). Zechariah 9:9 depicts the King arriving humble and riding on a donkey, while Zechariah 14:4 looks ahead to the day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives. Psalm 110:1 places the Messiah at the Lord’s right hand “until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,” implying an interval after His exaltation before the final subjugation.

These texts, read in their own literary context and as the apostles interpret them, reveal the Messiah’s first advent in humiliation to atone for sin and His second advent in power. Because of human sin and our separation from a holy God, the first coming was necessary: Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as a substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Those who repent and trust in Him alone are justified by grace through faith and will be ready to meet Him with joy rather than fear.

This hope of His personal, bodily return should shape daily life. Read Isaiah 61, Daniel 7, and Zechariah 9 and 14 this week alongside the Gospels, asking the Lord to deepen your confidence in both advents. Pray through those passages, thanking God for the Savior who came and the King who is coming. If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, do so today for forgiveness and new life. How has this question arisen for you, and which passages have you been considering?

question: Contemporary Christian music - is it honoring to God? Should it be used in church services?
answer:
The honoring of God through music depends on whether the words are faithful to Scripture, the heart is sincere, and the aim is His glory rather than human performance or entertainment. Whether contemporary Christian music belongs in a church service is a non-essential matter of worship style on which faithful Christians may disagree, because the Bible commands singing that teaches truth and stirs gratitude but does not prescribe particular instruments, rhythms, or cultural forms.

Some believers prefer psalms and historic hymns, holding that they better guard doctrinal depth, keep the focus congregational rather than on a stage, and avoid associations with worldly entertainment. Others receive well-written contemporary songs as a fitting way to sing a new song to the Lord, so long as the lyrics remain biblically sound and the gathering stays centered on God rather than a concert atmosphere.

Romans 14:19 urges us to pursue what makes for peace and mutual upbuilding in such disputable matters. Scripture itself directs the church: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God (Colossians 3:16). We are also told to speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making music in our hearts to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19), and to worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:24), with everything done decently, in order, and for the edification of the body (1 Corinthians 14:26; 1 Corinthians 14:40).

The real test is therefore content and fruit, not the date a song was written. Does it exalt God's holiness, our need of a Savior, Christ's atoning work, and the call to faith? Does it help the whole congregation, young and old, actually sing together rather than watch? Songs that are man-centered, theologically thin, or turn worship into a show hinder the church no matter the style; songs that let the word of Christ dwell richly can serve well in either traditional or contemporary dress.

A practical next step is to take one song you hear this week, old or new, and measure its lyrics against Colossians 3:16. If the question is creating tension in your local church, speak with your elders in humility, seeking the unity of the gospel rather than uniformity of preference.

question: What does it mean to test the spirits?
answer:
To test the spirits means to examine every teaching, claim of revelation, or spiritual influence against the Scriptures, so you can discern whether it comes from God or from a deceptive source.

The apostle John gives the command plainly: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). In its original setting, John was confronting teachers who denied that Jesus Christ had truly come in the flesh. The decisive test he gives is Christological: “By this you know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3). That confession upholds the incarnation, that the eternal Son took on true humanity (the hypostatic union) without ceasing to be God.

Scripture supplies further marks of a genuine work of the Spirit. It will agree with the apostolic Gospel of Christ’s death, burial, and bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), produce the fruit of righteousness rather than lawlessness, and submit to the written Word as the final authority (Isaiah 8:20; Acts 17:11). The Bereans modeled this when they examined Paul’s preaching daily against the Scriptures. Likewise, “test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

A concrete way to practice this is to take any new teaching, impression, or movement and ask: Does it confess the biblical Jesus (truly God, truly man, crucified and risen)? Does it contradict or add to the finished work of the cross and justification by faith alone? Measure it by the whole counsel of God rather than by feelings, popularity, or apparent power. If you are unsure, bring the matter to your local church elders, who are charged to guard the flock with sound doctrine.

Ask the Lord for the wisdom He promises to those who seek it (James 1:5), and let Scripture, not every voice that claims spiritual origin, have the last word.

question: Why should I get married?
answer:
Marriage is a good gift from God, created for companionship, fruitfulness, and as a living picture of Christ’s love for His church. The Lord Himself said it is not good for the man to be alone, so He made a suitable helper and joined husband and wife in a one-flesh covenantal union (Genesis 2:18; Genesis 2:24).

This union gives a holy setting for sexual intimacy, the raising of children, and mutual help in growing in holiness, while pointing beyond itself to the Gospel: “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:31-32; 1 Corinthians 7:2; Hebrews 13:4). At the same time, remaining unmarried can also be a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord, so marriage is honorable yet not required of every Christian (1 Corinthians 7:7; 1 Corinthians 7:32-35).

If you are considering marriage, look for a spouse who shares your faith in Christ and prepare to love sacrificially as Christ loves the church. A wise next step is to pray for the Lord’s wisdom, read Genesis 2, Ephesians 5, and 1 Corinthians 7, and talk with your pastor or a mature married couple in your local church.

question: Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath?
answer:
Faithful Christians disagree on whether Sunday is the Christian Sabbath, and this is a non-essential matter. The New Testament never uses that exact phrase, the transfer of the day is inferred rather than explicitly commanded, and Romans 14:5-6 treats the observance of days as an area of personal conviction under Christian liberty.

One historic view, held by many Reformed and Puritan Christians (including the tradition that shaped historic Baptists), is that the Sabbath is a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:2-3) and part of the moral law in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8-11). After Christ’s resurrection the day of rest and worship shifted to the first day of the week, now called the Lord’s Day, which functions as the Christian Sabbath. The apostles gathered then (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), and the whole day is to be kept holy in rest from ordinary labor and in public and private worship.

Another common view among Lutherans, many evangelicals, and those who emphasize New Covenant discontinuity is that the Sabbath pointed forward to Christ, who is our true rest (Hebrews 4:9-10) and Lord of the Sabbath (Matthew 12:8). The ceremonial and civil aspects of the Mosaic Sabbath were fulfilled (Colossians 2:16-17), so Sunday is simply the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10) on which the church gathers for worship. Strict Sabbath restrictions do not bind believers, and each person should be fully convinced in his own mind without judging others.

Neither position is required for orthodox Christian faith. What unites us is that Christ rose on the first day, the church has gathered then from the beginning, and we rest in Him rather than in our own works. A wise next step is to read the passages above in their context with your local church and consider how you can set apart the Lord’s Day for gathered worship, Scripture, prayer, and works of mercy, whatever your precise view of the Sabbath.

question: What does it mean that those who humble themselves will be exalted (Matthew 23:12)?
answer:
Jesus teaches that God Himself will bring down those who proudly lift themselves up, while He will honor and raise those who willingly take a lowly place of submission and service. In Matthew 23:12 He says, “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

This word comes as Jesus rebukes the scribes and Pharisees for craving titles, the best seats, and public praise while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:1–7). The same principle appears throughout Scripture: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Those who humble themselves under God’s mighty hand will be exalted in due time (1 Peter 5:6; James 4:10).

Jesus Himself is the supreme pattern. Though equal with God, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:6–9). This movement from humiliation to exaltation is the shape of true discipleship and progressive sanctification. Genuine humility begins when we see our sin and receive justification by grace through faith in Christ alone, which leaves no room for boasting (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Look this week for one quiet way to serve someone in your family or church without seeking notice, trusting the Father who sees in secret. Ask Him to search your heart for pride and to form in you the mind of Christ.

question: How should poetry in the Bible be interpreted?
answer:
Poetry in the Bible should be interpreted according to its literary genre, attending to parallelism, metaphor, and other figures of speech, while still receiving it as the true and inspired Word of God. Large portions of Scripture are poetry, including Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, and much of the prophetic books.

Hebrew poetry rarely uses rhyme or a fixed meter. It relies instead on parallelism, in which one line restates, contrasts, or develops the thought of another. Synonymous parallelism appears in Psalm 19:1: "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands." Antithetic parallelism often appears in Proverbs, setting wisdom against folly. These devices concentrate meaning and invite meditation rather than supplying a simple prose report.

Poetic language also employs vivid figures of speech. Metaphors and similes describe God and reality without being woodenly literal. "The Lord is my shepherd" (Psalm 23:1) truly teaches God's personal care and guidance, even though He is not a herdsman. Hyperbole can intensify emotion, as in Psalm 6:6: "I am weary with my groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears." Such language expresses real distress and real faith; it is not fiction. The truths poetry teaches about God's character, human sin, and the hope of redemption remain historically and theologically reliable because all Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16).

Read each poem in its immediate literary and historical setting, note the type of psalm or oracle it is (lament, praise, wisdom, prophecy), and let Scripture interpret Scripture. The New Testament writers treat Old Testament poetry as authoritative revelation, not as mere ornament. This approach honors the Holy Spirit's chosen form while guarding against both over-literalizing imagery and dissolving the text into vague symbolism.

When you next open a psalm or proverb, pause to name the main image or the kind of parallelism at work, then ask what it shows you of God's holiness, mercy, or call to trust. Let that insight shape a brief, honest prayer of your own.

question: What is the significance of the statement in Romans 1:22 that “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”?
answer:
In Romans 1:22, Paul describes the tragic irony of fallen humanity: although they claimed to be wise, they became fools. This statement shows how people suppress the truth about God that is clearly seen in creation, then boast in their own intellect, only to sink into spiritual and moral folly.

The verse sits in a larger argument (Romans 1:18-23) that God's wrath is revealed against those who suppress the truth. Although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks, so their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming wisdom, they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man, birds, animals, and reptiles. In the first-century Roman world, this struck at the heart of Greek and Roman pride in philosophy while the culture remained steeped in idolatry. The Greek term behind "became fools" (emōranthēsan) points not merely to intellectual error but to moral dullness, the same biblical "fool" who says in his heart there is no God (Psalm 14:1).

This illustrates the noetic effects of sin: rebellion against God darkens the mind itself, so that autonomous human reason, detached from the fear of the Lord, produces idolatry rather than true knowledge. Paul later contrasts this with Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Worldly claims of wisdom that deny the Creator or His moral order still follow the same downward path today.

In practice, this calls us to submit our thinking to Scripture rather than conforming to the age's prevailing "wisdom." A concrete next step is to read Romans 1:18-32 slowly this week, asking the Lord to reveal any place where you may be exchanging His truth for cultural or intellectual idols, then to pray for the wisdom that begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10; James 1:5).

question: What does it mean that sin is lawlessness?
answer:
Sin is lawlessness means that sin is the transgression of God’s holy law, a real act of rebellion against His righteous authority rather than a mere mistake or weakness. The apostle John states this directly in 1 John 3:4: “Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.”

John wrote to believers facing false teachers who claimed close fellowship with God while continuing in unrepentant sin, as if God’s commands did not apply to them. The Greek word anomia, rendered “lawlessness,” describes a state of living without or against God’s law, whether the moral instruction given through Moses or the full revelation of His will in Scripture. In that setting, John was showing that genuine new birth produces a life that no longer treats God’s law as optional.

This definition rests on God’s own character. He is holy and just, and His law expresses who He is. Therefore every person is a lawbreaker: “for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and “whoever keeps the whole law yet stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it” (James 2:10). Jesus Christ, however, perfectly obeyed that law in our place and then became the penal substitutionary atonement for our lawlessness, dying on the cross and rising bodily so that sinners who trust Him are justified by faith alone.

Those who have been born of God still battle remaining sin, yet they do not continue in a lifestyle of lawlessness because God’s seed remains in them and they are being progressively sanctified by the Holy Spirit (1 John 3:9; 1 John 1:8-9). A concrete application is to stop treating any known disobedience as small. Confess it to God according to 1 John 1:9, then take the next step of speaking with a pastor or mature believer in your local church so you can receive prayer and accountability as you pursue obedience.

question: Has anyone ever seen God?
answer:
No one has ever seen God in His full, unveiled glory. God is spirit and dwells in unapproachable light, so no one can see His face and live. John 1:18; Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16.

Yet God has repeatedly made Himself known through theophanies, real visible appearances in history. Moses saw the Lord’s back after God covered him in the cleft of the rock. Exodus 33:23. Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted. Isaiah 6:1. The apostle John later explains that Isaiah saw Jesus’ glory. John 12:41. These were genuine encounters, not mere symbols, yet they remained mediated so that the observers would not be consumed.

The clearest revelation came in the incarnation. The eternal Son took on true human nature, so that those who saw Jesus saw the Father. John 14:9. He is the image of the invisible God and the exact representation of His nature. Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3. Because of the hypostatic union, Jesus is truly God and truly man; therefore seeing Him is seeing God.

We behold that same glory now by looking to Christ in Scripture. God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of His glory in the face of Jesus Christ. 2 Corinthians 4:6. One day every believer will see Him as He is. 1 John 3:2.

question: Are books such as 90 minutes in Heaven and 23 minutes in Hell biblically based?
answer:
No, books such as 90 Minutes in Heaven and 23 Minutes in Hell are not biblically based. They are extra-biblical personal accounts of alleged near-death experiences, not the inspired and inerrant Word of God.

Scripture alone is our sufficient and final authority for knowing what God has revealed about heaven and hell. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). We are not to add to His words (Proverbs 30:5-6). Jesus Himself taught that the testimony of Scripture is enough: if people will not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). The apostle Paul was caught up to paradise yet was not permitted to tell what he heard (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Even Peter, who witnessed the transfiguration, pointed us to the prophetic word made more certain (2 Peter 1:19).

These popular accounts often add unverifiable details, conversations, and imagery that go beyond (and at times sit uneasily with) the Bible’s own descriptions. Heaven is the unhindered presence of God, where He will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more (Revelation 21:3-4). Hell is the place of eternal punishment prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41; Matthew 25:46). We test every claim by the closed canon of Scripture rather than treating private experiences as new revelation.

If these stories have stirred your curiosity about eternity, open the Bible itself and read what God has already made clear. A simple next step is to read John 14, 2 Corinthians 5, and Revelation 21–22 this week, asking the Lord for wisdom to discern truth from error (James 1:5), and talk it over with a pastor or mature believer in your local church.

question: Why does God not seem to care about the millions of starving children in the world?
answer:
The suffering of starving children is heartbreaking, and it is understandable that it can make God seem distant or uncaring. Many people who raise this question wonder how a God who is both all-powerful and loving could permit such pain among those who have done nothing to deserve it, or they conclude He must not notice or must not exist.

The Bible teaches that God does care. He "executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry" (Psalm 146:7). He is "a father to the fatherless, a defender of widows" (Psalm 68:5). This world is not the way God first made it. Humanity's rebellion against Him brought a curse on creation, so that scarcity, toil, and death entered (Genesis 3:17-19). The whole creation now groans under that bondage (Romans 8:20-22). Much of today's hunger flows from human sin (war, greed, corruption, and injustice), though a fallen order also includes drought and disaster. God is not the author of evil. He is sovereign, just, and patient, delaying final judgment so that people might repent rather than perish (2 Peter 3:9).

The clearest demonstration of His care is that the Son of God took on human flesh, knew hunger Himself, fed the crowds, identified with the poor, and died on the cross as a substitute for sinners. He rose bodily and will return to make all things new. Then "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain" (Revelation 21:4). Until that day God works through His people to relieve suffering, calling us to feed the hungry as unto Christ (Matthew 25:35-40).
