If this burden is shaking your trust, bring it honestly to God in prayer the way the psalmists did in their laments, and read the book of Job. A helpful next step is to share the question with a pastor at a Bible-preaching local church and to consider practical ways you can serve the hungry. God proved His love in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for forgiveness and new life.

What about this suffering feels heaviest to you right now?

question: What is postmodern therapy, and is it biblical?
answer:
Postmodern therapy refers to counseling approaches such as narrative therapy and solution-focused brief therapy that arise from postmodern philosophy. These methods treat identity, problems, and even reality itself as socially constructed stories shaped by language, so the therapist collaborates with the client to deconstruct old narratives and co-create new ones rather than diagnosing according to any objective standard.

This approach is not biblical. Scripture presents itself as the inspired, inerrant Word of God that reveals objective truth about God, humanity, sin, and salvation (John 17:17; 2 Timothy 3:16-17). Postmodern therapy’s rejection of metanarratives and absolute truth stands against the Bible’s claim that Jesus Christ is the truth and that every human philosophy must be measured by Him (John 14:6; Colossians 2:8). The human heart is deceitful above all things, and our deepest problems flow from sin rather than from unhelpful social stories or oppressive language (Jeremiah 17:9; Mark 7:21-23). Lasting change comes through repentance and faith in Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement, followed by the Holy Spirit’s work of sanctification as He renews the mind by Scripture, not through inventing a preferred identity (Romans 12:2; Ephesians 4:22-24).

Christians therefore look to the sufficiency of Scripture and to biblical counseling within the local church rather than to methods built on a contrary worldview. If you are facing personal struggles, speak with a pastor who can apply God’s Word to your situation and begin reading Psalm 139 and Ephesians 1, which ground identity in the Lord’s sovereign design rather than in constructed stories.

question: I am a Christian who is addicted to smoking. How can I quit?
answer:
Addiction is a heavy bondage, and the fact that you want to quit as a Christian is already a mercy from God. Scripture never names tobacco, yet it does command us not to be mastered by anything and to glorify God with our bodies, which are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:12; 1 Corinthians 6:19-20). When a habit controls you, it has become a rival master, and that is not the freedom Christ purchased.

Jesus died and rose so that we would no longer be slaves to sin. In union with Him we have died to sin’s dominion, and we now walk in newness of life by the Spirit (Romans 6:6; Romans 6:14; Romans 8:13). This is progressive sanctification: the Spirit enables us to put to death the deeds of the body, including habits that have enslaved us. The struggle is real, both spiritually and physically, yet God is faithful and will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear; He always provides a way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

I cannot give medical advice, so please consult a doctor about the physical dependence. Spiritually, fight with the ordinary means of grace: daily prayer in which you confess the hold this has on you and ask the Spirit for strength, regular reading of Scripture (especially Romans 6–8), and honest fellowship in your local church.

This week, tell your pastor or a mature believer in your congregation what you are facing and ask them to pray with you and check in regularly. We are not meant to fight alone. The Lord who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6). He is patient with His people.

question: What is mortification of sin / the flesh?
answer:
Mortification of sin (or of the flesh) is the believer’s Spirit-empowered work of putting remaining indwelling sin to death as an essential part of progressive sanctification.

The apostle Paul commands this directly in Romans 8:13: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Colossians 3:5 likewise says, “Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature.” In Paul’s letters, “flesh” often refers to the remaining sinful principle still at work in Christians, not merely the physical body. This ongoing battle flows from union with Christ, in whom the old self has already been crucified (Romans 6:6; Galatians 5:24), yet it continues because sin still dwells in us until we are glorified.

Unlike justification, which is God’s once-for-all declaration of righteousness received by faith alone, mortification is the lifelong weakening of sin’s power so that we grow in holiness. Practically, this means naming a specific remaining sin, starving it of opportunity, and turning immediately to prayer and Scripture rather than relying on willpower alone. Ask the Holy Spirit today to expose one particular sin in your life, then take one concrete step of obedience against it in dependence on Christ.

question: Is God’s love reckless?
answer:
No, God’s love is not reckless. Reckless means acting rashly, without wisdom or regard for consequences, yet God is perfectly wise, sovereign, and purposeful in all He does (Isaiah 46:10).

Some use the word, as in a well-known worship song, to describe God’s extravagant pursuit of sinners, drawing from the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one (Luke 15:4). The intent is often to highlight how God seeks the lost despite our unworthiness. Even so, that parable shows determined, joyful, and wise love, not carelessness. The ninety-nine are already His, and the search is not a gamble.

Scripture presents God’s love as eternal, planned, and holy. He chose His people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). He sent His Son at the appointed time as the atoning sacrifice, demonstrating His love while we were still sinners (John 3:16; Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10). This is penal substitution, the holy God dealing justly with sin at the cross, not an impulsive or thoughtless act. God’s love is covenantal and steadfast; it never fails because it flows from His unchanging character (Malachi 3:6; Lamentations 3:22).

You can rest in this. God’s love for those who are in Christ is not a reckless gamble but a sure, wise, and costly commitment. When we speak of Him, we do well to let Scripture, not catchy phrases, set the terms. A simple next step is to read 1 John 4:7-21 slowly this week and ask the Lord to deepen your grasp of His love as it is actually revealed in Christ.

question: Does the Bible teach that there is a gift of celibacy?
answer:
Yes, the Bible teaches that God gives some people a gift of remaining unmarried, often called the gift of celibacy or singleness.

In 1 Corinthians 7:7 the apostle Paul, himself unmarried, writes, “I wish that all of you were as I am. But each of you has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.” In context he presents both marriage and celibacy as charisma, gracious gifts from God. Those who lack the gift of celibacy and “burn with passion” are told it is better to marry (1 Corinthians 7:9). Jesus likewise spoke of those who remain unmarried “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,” adding that “not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:11-12).

This enablement is not a command for all, nor does it make marriage second-class. Marriage remains honorable and a good gift (Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 7:28). The point is simply that God equips some to live contentedly single so they may serve Him with undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). Faithful Christians may therefore be called differently in this area; we honor both paths as we exercise Christian liberty (Romans 14).

If you are weighing this for your own life, pray through 1 Corinthians 7, examine your actual desires and circumstances before the Lord, and talk it over with mature believers in your local church.

question: What did it mean that Satan wanted to be like the Most High in Isaiah 14:14?
answer:
Isaiah 14:14 records the boast, “I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” In its immediate setting this is the arrogant claim of the king of Babylon, who sought to elevate himself to divine status. Many Christians have also seen in these words a picture of Satan’s original rebellion, when he, a created angel, desired to take the unique place that belongs to God alone.

This desire meant that Satan wanted to seize God’s unique sovereignty, to receive the worship due only to the Creator, and to determine his own will independently of the Lord. God is the Most High, incomparable in holiness, power, and glory (Isaiah 40:25; Isaiah 46:9). No creature can become like Him in essence. The series of “I will” statements in Isaiah 14:13-14 reveal a heart of pride that refused to remain in the high position God had given him. The Bible teaches that pride was the devil’s condemnation (1 Timothy 3:6). This same lie, “you will be like God,” was used to tempt Eve in Genesis 3:5.

Every time we insist on our own way over God’s Word, we echo that same rebellious desire. The Lord opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). A practical next step is to read Isaiah 14:4-23 in its full context, then contrast it with Christ’s humility in Philippians 2:5-8, and ask the Lord to expose any pride in your own heart so that you may walk in the lowliness that honors Him.

question: What does the Bible say about the hornet?
answer:
The Bible mentions the hornet in three Old Testament passages, where the Lord sends it as His instrument to drive the Canaanite nations out of the land promised to Israel. Exodus 23:28 records God's promise: "I will send the hornet before you to drive the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites out of your way." Deuteronomy 7:20 continues, "Moreover, the LORD your God will send the hornet against them until even the survivors hiding from you have perished." Joshua 24:12 looks back on the fulfillment: "I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your sword or bow."

The Hebrew word behind "hornet" is tsir'ah, a stinging insect, and the text presents God employing it in real history as part of His covenant faithfulness. These verses display the sovereignty of God, who uses even a small creature to keep His word to Abraham's descendants and to bring judgment on the idolatrous peoples of Canaan. Israel's conquest was not achieved by human strength, as Joshua 24:12 makes plain.

This same Lord still rules over every detail of creation and fights for His people. Trust His providence in your own battles rather than leaning on your own resources, and ask Him to help you rest in His power as you walk with Him today.

question: What were the key events in the life of Jesus Christ?
answer:
The key events in the life of Jesus Christ include His virgin birth in Bethlehem, His baptism by John the Baptist, His public ministry of teaching and miracles, His crucifixion, burial, bodily resurrection on the third day, and His ascension into heaven. These events, recorded as historical reality in the Gospels, reveal Jesus as truly God and truly man in the hypostatic union and accomplish the atonement for sinners.

Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem, fulfilling prophecy (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 2:1-7; Micah 5:2). This is the incarnation, in which the eternal Son took on human nature (John 1:14).

Around the age of thirty He was baptized in the Jordan River. The Holy Spirit descended on Him like a dove and the Father declared Him the beloved Son, displaying the Trinity (Matthew 3:13-17; Luke 3:21-22). He then endured forty days of temptation in the wilderness yet remained without sin (Matthew 4:1-11).

Jesus called disciples, preached the kingdom of God, and performed miracles such as healing the sick, feeding the five thousand, walking on water, and raising Lazarus from the dead (Matthew 4:18-22; John 11:1-44). He taught with authority, including the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:1-7:29). Near the close of His ministry He was transfigured, revealing His glory (Matthew 17:1-8).

In His final week He entered Jerusalem to praise (Matthew 21:1-11), instituted the Lord’s Supper (Matthew 26:26-29), prayed in Gethsemane, was arrested and tried, and was crucified at Golgotha under Pontius Pilate (Matthew 26:36-27:56; John 19:16-37). His death was the penal substitutionary atonement, in which He bore God’s wrath against sin in the place of His people (Isaiah 53:5-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

He was buried, yet on the third day God raised Him bodily from the dead, as witnessed by many (Matthew 28:1-10; Luke 24:1-12; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8). After forty days of appearances He ascended into heaven (Acts 1:3, 9-11; Luke 24:50-53).

These events fulfill God’s plan of redemption. A helpful next step is to read one of the Gospels, such as Mark, to encounter these events in Scripture itself.

question: Do Christians need a day of rest?
answer:
Christians need rest because God made us that way in creation and because our deepest rest is found in Jesus Christ Himself. Whether a particular calendar day must be kept as a required Sabbath of rest is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, largely because the New Testament emphasizes fulfillment in Christ and Christian liberty rather than repeating the old covenant Sabbath command in the same form.

Many Reformed believers see the Sabbath as a creation ordinance and a continuing moral principle, now observed on the Lord’s Day (Sunday) for worship and rest from ordinary work. Many other Protestants, including Lutherans and a wide range of evangelicals, hold that the Sabbath pointed forward to Christ, who is our rest, so that no specific day is mandated even though the church’s gathering on the first day of the week is the New Testament pattern and rest remains wise.

Scripture leaves room for this difference: “One person considers one day more sacred than another; another considers every day alike. Each of them should be fully convinced in their own mind” (Romans 14:5). Paul also wrote, “Therefore do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day. These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17). At the same time Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27), and Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath-rest that remains for the people of God as we rest from our own works in Him.

A concrete way to live this out is to gather with the church on the Lord’s Day, as the early believers did (Acts 20:7), and to treat rest as a gift rather than either a legal burden or an excuse to neglect worship. Speak with your pastor or a mature believer in your local church about how they approach the Lord’s Day, and this week take one practical step such as setting ordinary work aside so you can worship, reflect, and receive rest. Come to Jesus with your weariness, for He says, “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

question: How can I be a good Christian?
answer:
Wanting to live as a faithful Christian is a good desire, yet it does not begin with our own moral effort. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). God is holy and just, and our sin separates us from Him and deserves His wrath. In love He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life and died on the cross in penal substitutionary atonement, bearing the penalty our sins deserved. He was buried and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works. As Scripture says, "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

If you have already trusted Him, then a faithful Christian life is progressive sanctification: the Holy Spirit continually conforms you to Christ as you abide in Him. Jesus said, "I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). This happens through God's ordinary means of grace: reading and hearing Scripture, prayer, and gathering with a local church so that we spur one another on to love and good deeds (Hebrews 10:24-25). Good works then follow as fruit of union with Christ, not as the basis of our standing with God (Ephesians 2:10).

A concrete next step is to read one chapter of the Gospel of John each day this week and to pray, asking God to help you know and follow Jesus more closely. If you are not already connected to a Bible-preaching church, visit one and speak with a pastor about walking with Christ.

What has stirred this desire in you, or which part of following Jesus feels most unclear right now?

question: What does the Bible say about lawsuits / suing?
answer:
The Bible, particularly in 1 Corinthians 6:1-8, instructs believers not to take disputes with fellow Christians before secular courts, but to resolve them within the church, since having lawsuits among yourselves is already a defeat and it is better to be wronged than to bring shame on the gospel. Paul reminds the Corinthians that the saints will one day judge the world and even angels, so they ought to be able to settle ordinary matters among themselves rather than airing grievances before unbelievers.

Jesus likewise taught His disciples to settle quickly with an adversary and even to give more than is demanded rather than insist on their rights (Matthew 5:25; Matthew 5:40). Scripture also warns against hasty litigation that can lead to shame (Proverbs 25:8) and calls believers not to repay evil for evil but to leave room for God’s wrath (Romans 12:17-19). At the same time, God Himself established earthly authorities and courts as His servants to punish wrongdoing and uphold justice (Romans 13:1-4), and the apostle Paul lawfully appealed to Caesar when his life and ministry were at stake (Acts 25:11). The distinction, then, is not a blanket ban on every use of the legal system, but a call to pursue peace, protect the church’s witness, and refuse revenge or greed.

If a conflict involves a fellow believer, first go privately as Jesus taught, then with one or two others, and if needed involve the church (Matthew 18:15-17). Talk with your pastor or elders for counsel before considering any legal step, and pray for wisdom to honor Christ even if it costs you personally.

question: What is kingdom now teaching?
answer:
Kingdom Now teaching is a view, found mainly in some charismatic and Pentecostal circles, that the church is to take dominion over earthly institutions such as government, education, media, and culture in the present age in order to establish the Kingdom of God now, rather than waiting for its full manifestation at Christ's personal return.

This teaching often includes restored apostolic and prophetic offices, the Seven Mountains Mandate for cultural takeover, and an emphasis on believers exercising present authority to bind demonic powers and bring heaven's rule to earth.

Eschatology (including how and when the kingdom comes in fullness) is a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture gives less detailed sequencing of future events than it does on the person of Christ or the way of salvation. Historic views include premillennialism (Christ returns before a future earthly millennial reign) and amillennialism or postmillennialism (greater present or future gospel triumph in this age before His return). Kingdom Now theology is a distinctive charismatic emphasis on realizing the kingdom through the church's present dominion. Some see it as consistent with postmillennial hopes; others regard it as an over-realized eschatology that underplays the "not yet."

Jesus announced that the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:15) and is in the midst of His people (Luke 17:20-21), yet He also taught us to pray "Your kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10) and declared, "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). The wheat and tares grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30, 36-43). All orthodox Christians affirm that Jesus will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). The church's clear commission is to make disciples of all nations through the gospel (Matthew 28:18-20), living as salt and light in the world (Matthew 5:13-16) while our citizenship remains in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

A concrete next step is to read the kingdom parables in Matthew 13 with a mature believer in your local church and ask how they shape faithful witness now, without confusing the church's mission with seizing earthly power.

question: What is The Infinite Way?
answer:
The Infinite Way is a spiritual teaching developed by Joel S. Goldsmith (1892–1964), a former Christian Science practitioner, and first presented in his 1947 book of the same title. It describes itself as a non-organizational way of life rather than a church or religion, centered on silent meditation, inner stillness, and the realization that God is an infinite presence or consciousness already within every person, producing peace and spiritual healing.

This teaching draws from New Thought, Christian Science, and various mystical sources. It is not historic Christianity. The Bible presents God as the personal, holy Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), not an impersonal infinite consciousness. We are separated from Him by sin, and reconciliation comes only through the incarnation of Jesus Christ (truly God and truly man), His penal substitutionary atonement on the cross, His burial, and His bodily resurrection. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by realizing an already-existing oneness.

Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). The apostle Paul summarized the Gospel this way: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

If you have encountered The Infinite Way, a wise next step is to read the Gospel of John for yourself and weigh its claims about the historical Jesus against any other spiritual path. Pray directly to God for light from His Word, and consider discussing these questions with a pastor in a local church that holds to the Scriptures.

question: Does God have favorites?
answer:
No, God does not have favorites the way people do, preferring some because of status, ethnicity, appearance, or performance. Scripture teaches that God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11; Acts 10:34; Deuteronomy 10:17).

He judges justly and the gospel of Christ is for all kinds of people. At the same time, God freely chose a people for Himself, first Israel and then all who are in Christ, not because they were better or more deserving, but according to His own purpose and love (Deuteronomy 7:7-8; Ephesians 1:4-5). This is often called unconditional election: His choice rests in His mercy, not in anything He saw in us, since all have sinned (Romans 3:23; Romans 9:15-16).

Some historic Christians hold that God elects those He foreknew would believe, stressing human response. I believe the Reformed reading better fits the whole of Scripture, because it keeps salvation entirely of grace so that no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8-9). Either way, this is not the petty favoritism of men. It is the holy, wise, and merciful will of God.

This should produce humility, not comparison. If you belong to Christ by faith, you are His beloved child because of who He is, not because you outperformed others. Read Romans 9 through Romans 11 slowly this week, ask the Lord to show you His character, and talk it through with a mature believer in your church.

question: How can I live a holy life?
answer:
Living a holy life begins with being made new in Christ, then growing in progressive sanctification by the Holy Spirit. We all fall short of God's holiness because of sin, yet Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as our substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By grace alone through faith alone in Him, we are justified and given new hearts from which true holiness flows. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

God calls those who belong to Him to be holy because He is holy: "But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy.”" (1 Peter 1:15-16). This is not a way to earn God's favor. Having been justified, we work out our salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in us to will and to act (Philippians 2:12-13). Walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:16). Put off the old self, be renewed in your mind, and put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness (Ephesians 4:22-24).

Immerse yourself in Scripture, which God uses to sanctify us (John 17:17). Pray continually, confessing sin and depending on His strength. Gather with a faithful local church for the Word, fellowship, the Lord's Supper, and accountability. Flee sin and pursue what pleases the Lord.

This week, read Romans 6 slowly, noting that you have died to sin with Christ, then choose one specific area of remaining sin to put to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). Share that commitment with a mature believer in your church who can pray with you and walk alongside you. Pray directly to God, asking Him to give you a love for holiness and the power to obey, resting in His promise that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

What has stirred this desire in you, or what particular area of life are you hoping to bring more fully under Christ's lordship?

question: What is the sinner's prayer?
answer:
The sinner's prayer is a short prayer of repentance and faith often used in evangelical settings, in which a person confesses their sin, trusts that Jesus Christ died and rose for them, and asks Him to forgive them and be their Savior and Lord.

The Bible does not prescribe any set formula of words. It does, however, call sinners to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15) and promises that “if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. For with your heart you believe and are justified, and with your mouth you confess and are saved” (Romans 10:9-10). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by reciting a prayer (Ephesians 2:8-9). The Holy Spirit must give new birth (regeneration) so that genuine repentance and justifying faith follow (Titus 3:5). The words themselves do not save; only union with the crucified and risen Christ does.

Some Christians find such a prayer a useful way to put faith into words. Others caution that it can produce false assurance if it is treated as a ritual rather than the fruit of the Spirit’s work and the beginning of a life of discipleship.

question: How can a Christian avoid being a doormat for other people?
answer:
A Christian avoids being a doormat by practicing sacrificial love under God’s authority rather than under other people’s demands. Scripture never treats meekness as unlimited availability or people-pleasing. The fear of man is a snare, but the one who trusts in the Lord is kept safe (Proverbs 29:25). Paul asks, “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). True service flows from the fear of God, not from anxiety about disappointing others.

Jesus Himself loved perfectly yet refused to let crowds, family, or even well-meaning disciples set His course. After healing many, He withdrew to pray and then told His disciples He must go on to other towns to preach, because that was why He had come (Mark 1:35–38). He spoke truth in love, confronted hypocrisy, and sometimes simply walked away. Christians are called to the same pattern: look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others (Philippians 2:4). That “also” matters. You remain a steward of the time, energy, body, family, and calling God has given you. Enabling laziness, sin, or manipulation is not love; it can even become a failure to provide for those God has first entrusted to you (1 Timothy 5:8; 2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

Speak a clear yes or no (Matthew 5:37). When a request conflicts with your God-given responsibilities, a gracious refusal is not unkind. It is often the loving thing, because it refuses to pretend you can be God for someone else. Grow in this through the ordinary means of grace: stay in Scripture, pray for wisdom (James 1:5), and walk with a local church where mature believers can help you see the difference between Christlike service and being used.

This week, identify one recurring demand that consistently drains you without aligning with your actual calling. Pray over it using Galatians 1:10 and James 1:5, then practice one clear, kind “no” (or a delayed “let me pray about that”) rather than an automatic yes. If the pattern involves genuine harm or abuse, involve wise church leaders and, where needed, proper authorities. God formed you in His image; He does not ask you to erase that dignity in the name of niceness.

question: What does it mean that the workers are few (Matthew 9:37)?
answer:
In Matthew 9:37, Jesus means that a great number of people stand ready to hear and respond to the Gospel of the kingdom (the plentiful harvest), yet comparatively few of His followers are actively laboring to proclaim it and gather them in.

This word comes immediately after Jesus saw the crowds and was moved with compassion, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). The harvest picture, drawn from ordinary farming life, points to the present opportunity to bring people into God’s kingdom through the preaching of the good news. Jesus therefore commands His disciples, “Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest” (Matthew 9:38). God Himself owns the field and sends the laborers in answer to prayer.

The same urgency appears later when Jesus gives the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19–20). Every believer is called to this work, not only vocational ministers. A concrete next step is to pray daily that the Lord would raise up and send more workers, while looking for one specific opportunity this week to speak of Christ in your own family, workplace, or neighborhood, and to do so in fellowship with a local church.

question: What was the purpose of the Levitical Law?
answer:
The purpose of the Levitical Law was to reveal God’s holiness, set Israel apart as His covenant people, provide a temporary system of priestly mediation and sacrificial worship, and expose sin while pointing forward to Jesus Christ.

After God redeemed Israel from Egypt, He gave these laws so that He might dwell among them as a holy nation. He commanded, “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). The detailed instructions concerning the Levitical priesthood, the tabernacle, ritual purity, and the various offerings taught a sinful people how to approach a holy God without being consumed by His just wrath.

These ceremonial provisions were never the final answer. They functioned as types and shadows. Hebrews 10:1 states that the law is only a shadow of the good things to come and could never make worshipers perfect through repeated sacrifices. The blood of bulls and goats illustrated substitutionary atonement, in which an innocent life was given in place of the guilty, looking ahead to the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.

The law also served a pedagogical purpose. Paul explains that it was added because of transgressions until the promised Seed came, and that “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:19; Galatians 3:24). By revealing the depth of human sin and the impossibility of perfect obedience, it prepared hearts for the Savior who would fulfill the law and become our great High Priest.

In this way the Levitical Law finds its goal in the new covenant, where Christ has offered Himself once for all and now intercedes for all who trust in Him. We cannot draw near to God by ritual or our own merit, but only through faith in the finished work of Jesus.

question: What does the Bible say about confession of sin to a priest?
answer:
The Bible teaches that Christians confess their sins directly to God, who alone forgives, and also to one another for healing and accountability. It does not require or describe confession to a priest as the means of receiving pardon.

First John 1:9 says, "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." This confession is made to God Himself. James 5:16 adds, "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed." The New Testament presents Jesus as our one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5) and great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), so that we may "approach the throne of grace with confidence" (Hebrews 4:16). All believers share in the royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9); there is no continuing special class of priests who stand between the Christian and God.

Some Christians understand John 20:23 ("If you forgive anyone’s sins, their sins are forgiven; if you do not forgive them, they are not forgiven") as establishing a priestly power to grant absolution in private confession. The surrounding context, however, shows Jesus sending the apostles to proclaim the gospel: those who repent and believe are declared forgiven, while those who refuse remain in their sins. The book of Acts records no practice of private auricular confession to apostles or elders for sacramental pardon; instead the apostles preached repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus.

Christ’s penal substitutionary death is sufficient. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not through a human intermediary. If you are carrying guilt, go first to God in prayer, naming the sin and resting on His promise in First John 1:9. Then, as James 5:16 encourages, share with a trusted fellow believer or an elder in your local church for prayer and accountability. That ordinary means of grace, not a priestly rite, is the pattern Scripture gives us.

question: Should Christians go to nightclubs? Is clubbing a sin?
answer:
Nightclubs are not named in Scripture, so attending them is a matter of Christian liberty and applying holiness, where faithful believers may differ in conscience because culture and personal weakness vary.

Many Christians conclude that typical nightclubs should be avoided. These venues commonly feature drunkenness, immodest or sensual dancing, music that does not honor God, and an atmosphere that stirs lust and worldliness. Scripture calls us to flee sexual immorality, make no provision for the flesh, and not love the world or its desires (1 Corinthians 6:18; Romans 13:14; 1 John 2:15-17; Ephesians 5:18).

Other Christians hold that a believer might attend in some settings if they remain sober, modest, and uncompromised, viewing it as permissible under liberty so long as it does not violate conscience or cause a weaker brother to stumble (Romans 14:1-23; 1 Corinthians 10:23-31). They emphasize that all things are lawful, yet not all are beneficial or build up.

I counsel most believers to stay away from ordinary nightclubs. Progressive sanctification means we pursue holiness rather than putting ourselves in places designed for worldly pleasure. We are not to be conformed to this world, and we are to do all to the glory of God (Romans 12:2; 1 Corinthians 10:31; 1 Peter 1:15-16). Ask whether the environment helps you love Christ more or makes provision for temptation.

Talk with your pastor or a mature believer in your local church about your specific situation and motives. Pray that God would search your heart and give wisdom (Psalm 139:23-24; James 1:5), then choose fellowship and rest that actually strengthen your walk with Him.

question: Does the statue outside the United Nations have any connection to the beast of the end times?
answer:
No, the statue outside the United Nations has no connection in Scripture to the beast of the end times. The Bible never mentions the United Nations or any modern sculpture, and it does not identify any particular artwork as the fulfillment of prophecy.

Revelation 13:1-2 describes a beast rising from the sea that resembles a leopard, with feet like a bear and a mouth like a lion, receiving power from the dragon. This draws on the animal imagery of Daniel 7 and portrays a blasphemous kingdom or ruler that opposes God and persecutes the saints. Later in the chapter, an image of the beast is mentioned that people are compelled to worship (Revelation 13:14-15). These are prophetic symbols in apocalyptic literature, written first to churches facing Roman pressure, and they point ultimately to Christ’s victory over every anti-God power.

Christians have understood these passages in different ways across history. Some read them as describing first-century Rome, others as a still-future figure, and others as a recurring pattern of opposition to God. Specific identifications of current events, buildings, or statues as “the beast” or its image go beyond what the text itself requires. Eschatological details like this are a non-essential matter where faithful believers may disagree, because the Bible gives less explicit information on the timing and exact form of these symbols than it does on core truths such as Christ’s bodily return, the resurrection, and final judgment.

The Lord Jesus Himself warned against being alarmed by every rumor of fulfillment (Matthew 24:6) and against setting dates no one can know (Matthew 24:36). Our calling is to watch, remain faithful, and keep our eyes on Him rather than on speculative connections. If this question has left you uneasy, a good next step is to read Revelation 12–14 slowly in context, perhaps with a pastor or mature believer from your local church, and to pray for the Spirit’s wisdom and peace as you do. God is sovereign over every nation and every age, and those who belong to Christ are kept by His power.

question: What is the sign of Jonah?
answer:
The sign of Jonah is Jesus Christ’s burial for three days and nights followed by His bodily resurrection, which He compared to Jonah’s time in the great fish.

When the scribes and Pharisees demanded a miraculous sign to prove His authority, Jesus answered that none would be given except the sign of the prophet Jonah. He said, “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40; see also Matthew 12:39; Matthew 16:4; Luke 11:29–30). Jonah 1:17 records that “the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish.” This is biblical typology: Jonah’s descent and deliverance prefigure Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection as the greater reality.

Jesus is greater than Jonah (Luke 11:32). The resurrection is God’s public vindication of His Son, confirming that His sacrificial death on the cross truly atoned for sin and that He has conquered death. Like the Ninevites who repented at Jonah’s preaching, this generation is called to repent at the preaching of the One who died and rose again.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. How does this sign shape the way you see Jesus?

question: What does it mean to walk worthy?
answer:
To walk worthy means to live each day in a manner that matches the calling God has given you in the gospel of Jesus Christ, conducting yourself with holiness, humility, and love as those already united to Him.

The apostle Paul uses this language repeatedly. In Ephesians 4:1 he writes, "As a prisoner for the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received." He adds in Colossians 1:10 that we are to "walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God," and in 1 Thessalonians 2:12 he urges believers "to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory."

This is not a way to become acceptable to God. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, whose penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection have already made us righteous. Walking worthy belongs instead to progressive sanctification: the Holy Spirit's ongoing work of conforming us to Christ as we put off the old self and put on the new.

Paul immediately shows what this looks like in Ephesians 4:2, calling us to "all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love." In daily life that means choosing truth-telling over gossip, forgiveness over bitterness, and diligence over laziness, whether at home, work, or church.

This week, read Ephesians 4:1–16 slowly each day. Ask the Lord to show you one specific attitude or habit that does not yet match your calling, then talk with Him about it in prayer and share it with a mature believer in your local church for encouragement and accountability.

question: What is a divine appointment?
answer:
A divine appointment is an encounter or circumstance that God sovereignly arranges according to His providence, not by chance, often to advance the gospel, provide help, or encourage His people.

The Bible never uses that exact phrase, yet it plainly teaches that the Lord directs our steps and orders events for His purposes. Proverbs 16:9 says, “A man’s heart plans his way, but the LORD determines his steps.” A clear picture appears when the Spirit sent Philip to the desert road, where he met the Ethiopian official who was already reading Isaiah and needed the gospel explained (Acts 8:26-35).

This is the doctrine of divine providence: God is not a distant spectator but the wise and good King who works all things according to the counsel of His will. Because of that, ordinary meetings are never merely random.

When an unexpected conversation or interruption arises, pause and ask how God might be at work, then look for a simple way to listen well or point to Christ. Ask Him each morning to make you alert to the people He places in your path.

question: What is the Qur’an?
answer:
The Qur’an is the central holy book of Islam, consisting of 114 chapters (surahs) that Muslims believe to be the literal, uncreated word of God revealed to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel in the seventh century and later compiled into its present form.

Christians believe the Bible is the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, the unique and final written revelation that centers on Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man, whose sacrificial death and bodily resurrection secure salvation by grace through faith alone (2 Timothy 3:16; John 1:1; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Qur’an and the Bible differ on these core truths, including the Trinity, the incarnation, the crucifixion, and the way of salvation.

If you are comparing the two, a wise next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly and ask God to show you who Jesus truly is.

question: What would have happened “if the Lord had not been on our side” (Psalm 124:2)?
answer:
If the LORD had not been on our side when men rose up against us, they would have swallowed us alive when their anger flared against us; then the flood would have engulfed us, the torrent would have overwhelmed us, and the raging waters would have swept us away (Psalm 124:2–5). We would have been given as prey to their teeth and caught like a bird in the snare of the fowlers (Psalm 124:6–7).

This song of ascents recounts God’s sovereign deliverance of His people from overwhelming enemies, using images of being swallowed, drowned, and trapped that were common for describing certain destruction. The psalm then blesses the LORD who did not abandon them, declaring, “Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 124:8). It displays God’s providence and covenant faithfulness, preserving His people when they had no strength of their own.

When opposition or trial feels like a flood that could sweep you away, read Psalm 124 aloud and thank God that He is for those who belong to Him in Christ. You might also pray through the psalm, asking Him to keep your heart remembering that your help is in His name.

question: What did Jesus mean when He said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven?
answer:
Jesus meant that it is humanly impossible for those who trust in their riches to enter the kingdom of God, just as a camel cannot pass through the tiny eye of a sewing needle. He used this vivid hyperbole right after a wealthy young man walked away sorrowful rather than give up his possessions to follow Christ (Matthew 19:21-22). Jesus then told the disciples, "Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God" (Matthew 19:24).

The disciples were astonished, because many in their first-century Jewish setting viewed wealth as a sign of God's blessing. They asked who then could be saved. Jesus answered that what is impossible with man is possible with God (Matthew 19:25-26). A later legend claimed He meant a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye, where camels had to unload and kneel, but no such gate existed in His day, and that idea would weaken His point of complete impossibility apart from divine power.

This teaching does not mean no rich person can be saved (Abraham and Joseph of Arimathea were wealthy yet belonged to God). It shows that riches easily become an idol that keeps people from depending on the Lord, and that no one, rich or poor, can earn entrance into the kingdom. All have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Romans 3:23). We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works, wealth, or self-reliance (Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as the atoning sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day.

Turn from sin (including any trust in money or self) and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. One practical step is to ask the Lord to show you where your security really lies, then use whatever resources He has given you with open hands for His kingdom rather than clutching them as your hope. How does this word of Jesus land on your own view of money and what it takes to be right with God?

question: How do we decide which books belong in the Bible since the Bible does not say which books belong in the Bible?
answer:
The books belong in the Bible because God inspired them as His Word, and the people of God recognized them by their apostolic origin, doctrinal consistency, widespread use in the churches, and the Holy Spirit’s witness. Scripture itself does not contain one verse that lists every book, yet that does not leave the canon to human invention.

Some people object that this sounds circular, or that we must therefore depend on an infallible church to tell us which books count. The historic Christian answer is that God determined the canon by inspiration; the church discovered and received what He had already given. Jesus treated the Hebrew Scriptures as a settled collection when He spoke of “the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). The apostles quoted those same books as the Word of God. Within the New Testament itself, Peter already refers to Paul’s letters as Scripture (2 Peter 3:15-16), and Paul cites a saying from Luke’s Gospel as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18). The early churches received writings that came from apostles or their close companions, that agreed with the gospel already preached, and that were read in worship across many congregations. Later councils simply confirmed the books that had already been recognized.

The extra books found in some Bibles (often called the Apocrypha or deuterocanonical books) were not part of the Hebrew canon Jesus used, are not quoted as God’s Word in the New Testament, and contain teachings that sit uneasily with the rest of Scripture. Protestants therefore regard them as historically useful but not inspired. The sixty-six books display a remarkable unity that centers on Christ, and the same Spirit who inspired them continues to confirm their authority in the hearts of believers (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

God has preserved His Word for His people (Isaiah 40:8; Matthew 24:35). If this question has left you uncertain, a wise next step is to read one of the Gospels or a New Testament letter slowly, asking the Lord to show you Christ in it, and then talk with a pastor in a local church about the history of how these books were received. Pray that God would give you growing confidence in the Scriptures He has given.

question: What does it mean to walk by the Spirit (Galatians 5:16)?
answer:
Walking by the Spirit means conducting your daily life in dependence on the Holy Spirit’s power and guidance, so that you will not gratify the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:16). This is not a vague feeling or a way to earn God’s favor. It is the Spirit-enabled path of progressive sanctification that follows justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ.

Paul writes this in the context of Christian freedom. Believers are no longer under the law as a means of being right with God, yet that liberty is not an opportunity for the flesh. Instead we serve one another through love (Galatians 5:13). The flesh and the Spirit remain in conflict within every Christian, so that we often do not do what we want (Galatians 5:17). Those who belong to Christ have already crucified the flesh with its passions and desires (Galatians 5:24). As we walk by the Spirit, He produces His fruit in us: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23).

This walking happens as we set our minds on the things of the Spirit rather than the things of the flesh (Romans 8:5). It is not self-powered willpower. It is the Spirit applying the finished work of Christ to our daily conduct, putting sin to death and making us more like Jesus.

A concrete picture is this: when irritation rises in a conversation, you pause, remember you belong to Christ, and ask the Spirit to produce gentleness instead of a sharp reply. That is walking by the Spirit in that moment.

Open Galatians 5:16-26 today, pray through the fruit of the Spirit, and ask the Lord to produce one of those qualities in a specific relationship or temptation you will face this week. Stay closely connected to a local church where the Word is preached and you can walk this out with other believers.

question: What does the Bible mean when it says "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'"?
answer:
The Bible means that a person who inwardly denies God is a moral fool whose life produces corruption, not merely someone making an intellectual mistake, as Psalm 14:1 and Psalm 53:1 both declare: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’ They are corrupt; their acts are vile. There is no one who does good.”

The Hebrew word nabal (“fool”) describes spiritual and ethical insensitivity rather than low intelligence, the same character seen in the man Nabal of 1 Samuel 25:25 whose name itself meant “fool.” Saying this “in his heart” points to a settled inner stance that God will not see, intervene, or judge, which immediately bears fruit in vile deeds. Scripture later explains this as the noetic effects of sin, in which people suppress the truth God has made plain in creation and become futile in their thinking (Romans 1:18-21).

This is practical atheism: living as though the holy, just God of Scripture does not exist. Even those who profess belief can slip into it whenever daily choices ignore His presence. A concrete next step is to read Psalm 14 in full, then ask the Lord to search your own heart as Psalm 139:23-24 invites, so that the fear of the Lord (the beginning of knowledge, Proverbs 1:7) would mark every area of life.

question: What is onanism? Is onanism a sin?
answer:
Onanism takes its name from Onan in Genesis 38. After his brother Er died, Judah told Onan to fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law by going in to Tamar and raising up offspring for his brother. Onan knew the child would not be counted as his, so whenever he slept with Tamar he spilled his semen on the ground. What he did was wicked in the Lord’s sight, so the Lord put him to death (Genesis 38:8-10).

Onan’s sin was willful, selfish disobedience to the levirate duty God had given to preserve family lines in Israel, not merely a particular physical act.

Later the word “onanism” came to be used for masturbation. Scripture never names masturbation. It does, however, teach that lust is adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27-28), that sexual intimacy belongs inside the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4), and that we must flee sexual immorality because our bodies belong to God as temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:18-20). Masturbation ordinarily involves lustful thoughts and seeks sexual pleasure apart from that covenant, so it is sinful.

All of us have sinned and fall short of God’s glory. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Turn from this sin and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

If this is a personal struggle, confess it to the Lord using Psalm 51 as a guide, and seek accountability from a pastor or mature brother in your local church.

question: Is Israel and the church the same thing? Does God still have a plan for Israel?
answer:
No, national Israel and the church are not the same thing, though the church is the true people of God who inherit the promises in Christ.

Dispensational Christians argue that God keeps two distinct peoples with separate programs, so that national Israel retains unfulfilled land and kingdom promises the church does not assume.

I hold covenant theology as a Reformed Baptist, in which there is one people of God across the covenants: the church is the Israel of God, yet God has not rejected ethnic Israel and still plans to bring many of them to faith in Christ.

Paul writes, “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1) and later, “a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25-26). Gentiles have been grafted into the olive tree of God’s covenant people, and natural branches can be grafted in again (Romans 11:17-24). In Christ the dividing wall is broken down so that Jew and Gentile become one new man (Ephesians 2:14-16); Galatians 6:16 therefore speaks of “the Israel of God.”

This is one faithful historic Christian reading, not the only one. It should produce humility rather than pride toward Jewish people. Pray for their salvation, share the gospel with them, and remember they need the same Savior we do. A concrete next step is to read Romans 9–11 this week, noting God’s faithfulness, then pray specifically for Jewish people to trust Jesus as Messiah.

question: Are Catholic beliefs and practices biblical?
answer:
Catholicism shares several core Christian beliefs that Scripture clearly teaches, including the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Jesus Christ (the hypostatic union), His virgin birth, atoning death, and bodily resurrection. Many individual Catholics sincerely love Jesus and want to follow Him.

Yet a number of distinctive Roman Catholic doctrines and required practices are not taught in the Bible and in some cases contradict its plain meaning. The Bible presents itself as the sufficient, final authority for faith and practice. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work. The New Testament church tested teaching by the written Word. Acts 17:11 Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true. Catholic teaching adds equally binding Sacred Tradition and the Magisterium, including later dogmas such as papal infallibility.

On the Gospel itself, Scripture teaches that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from works. Romans 3:28 For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Ephesians 2:8-9 For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast. Official Catholic teaching includes the necessity of cooperating with grace through works and sacraments in order to be justified, which adds human merit to the finished work of Christ.

Other practices lack New Testament support. There is one mediator between God and men. 1 Timothy 2:5 For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Prayer is directed to God, not to Mary or the saints. Christ’s sacrifice was once for all and is not re-offered. Hebrews 10:10 And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Purgatory is absent from Scripture; after death comes judgment. Hebrews 9:27 And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment. Mary herself spoke of God as her Savior. Luke 1:47 and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior. The New Testament pattern is believer’s baptism as a sign of already-received grace, not infant baptism that confers it.

These differences are not minor, because they touch the Gospel. Galatians 1:8-9 But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be under a curse.

All people have sinned and fall short of God’s holiness, and no amount of religious observance can remove that guilt. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is received by turning from sin and trusting in Him alone, not in the church, sacraments, or our own efforts.

Read Romans and Galatians for yourself this week, asking God to make His Word clear. Seek a local church that treats Scripture as the final authority and preaches Christ crucified and risen as sufficient.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Simeon?
answer:
The tribe of Simeon teaches that the Lord hears the afflicted, yet He judges fierce anger and violence by scattering those who live by it, even while He mercifully preserves a remnant among His covenant people.

Leah named her second son Simeon because “the LORD has heard that I am unloved” (Genesis 29:33). His name itself proclaims that God listens. Yet Simeon, together with Levi, later answered the defilement of their sister Dinah with deceit and slaughter at Shechem (Genesis 34). Jacob’s dying words named the sin plainly: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence. \ldots Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:5-7). That word came true. Simeon’s inheritance was carved out inside Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1, 9), Moses’ tribal blessing in Deuteronomy 33 omits them entirely, and their numbers collapsed after the plague that followed the Simeonite leader Zimri’s public immorality (Numbers 25:14; Numbers 26:14).

God’s holiness and justice are on display: uncontrolled wrath does not produce righteousness, and sin shrinks a people’s influence. At the same time His covenant faithfulness appears, for Simeon is still listed among the sealed of Israel (Revelation 7:7). The scattering that judged Levi became a blessing when the Levites were dispersed as priests and teachers; Simeon’s scattering was quieter absorption. Both outcomes remind us that the Lord remains free to chasten and to keep.

In your own walk, ask the Spirit to search any leftover anger or thirst for personal vengeance. Confess it, using Psalm 139:23-24 as a guide in prayer, and invite a mature believer in your local church to help you pursue the gentleness that marks those who belong to Christ.

question: What is the hypostatic union?
answer:
The hypostatic union is the biblical doctrine that Jesus Christ is one Person who possesses two complete natures, fully divine and fully human, united forever. These natures remain distinct, without mixture, change, division, or separation.

Scripture presents this clearly: the eternal Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1; John 1:14). He who existed in the form of God took the form of a servant and was made in human likeness (Philippians 2:6-7). In Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form (Colossians 2:9). The Greek term hypostasis, meaning person or essential nature, appears in Hebrews 1:3, where the Son is the exact representation of God’s nature. The church later used “hypostatic union” to summarize this revealed truth and to guard against errors that would deny either Christ’s full deity or His full humanity.

This union is essential to the Gospel. Only one who is truly man could represent us, live a sinless life in our place, and die as our substitute. Only one who is truly God could offer a sacrifice of infinite worth and rise bodily from the dead, conquering sin and death. Because of the hypostatic union, Jesus is the one Mediator between God and man.

When you pray or face temptation, you come to a Savior who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, and who now holds all power as God (Hebrews 4:15-16). Read John 1 this week and ask the Lord to show you the glory of Christ as both God and man. Turn from sin and trust in this Jesus, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. How does this truth about who Jesus is shape the way you approach Him today?

question: Doubting God — how can I overcome doubt in my relationship with God?
answer:
Doubt in your relationship with God can feel heavy, confusing, and isolating. You are not alone in this; Scripture records faithful people who wrestled with similar questions and still found God near.

God is not threatened by honest doubt. A desperate father once cried out to Jesus, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus met him with compassion rather than condemnation. Even when we are faithless, He remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:13). Your relationship with God does not rest on the strength of your feelings or the absence of questions. It rests on Christ’s finished work: He died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Faith is strengthened as we use the means of grace God has provided: His Word, prayer, and fellowship with other believers. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). We have a sympathetic High Priest, so we may approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:14-16). Isolation often deepens doubt, while the church is called to show mercy to those who doubt (Jude 22).

This week, read Psalm 13 slowly each morning. Then speak directly to God about the specific doubts you are carrying, asking Him to meet you there through His Word. Afterward, share this struggle with a pastor or mature believer in your local church who can pray with you and remind you of truth. God is at work even now and will complete the good work He has begun (Philippians 1:6).

What particular doubts have been weighing on you most right now?

question: Did God create other people in addition to Adam and Eve?
answer:
No, the Bible does not teach that God created other original people besides Adam and Eve. Scripture presents them as the first man and woman, the sole progenitors of the entire human race.

Genesis 1:27 records that God created mankind in His image, male and female. Genesis 2 then gives the detailed account of that sixth-day work: the Lord God formed Adam from the dust of the ground and later made Eve from his rib (Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:21-22). Eve is called “the mother of all the living” (Genesis 3:20). The apostle Paul later confirmed this when he told the Athenians that God “from one man made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth” (Acts 17:26).

This historical reality undergirds the doctrine of original sin and Adam’s federal headship. Through one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, just as through the obedience of the one Man, Jesus Christ, the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). All of us therefore share both the image of God and the same fallen condition that only the last Adam can remedy.

A frequent question is where Cain found a wife. Genesis 5:4 simply states that Adam “had other sons and daughters,” so early marriages were among close relatives, which was neither forbidden nor genetically hazardous at that stage of human history.

Every person you meet is therefore a fellow descendant of that first pair, equally made in God’s image and equally in need of the Savior.

question: What does the Bible say about self-discipline?
answer:
The Bible presents self-discipline (also called self-control or temperance) as a vital fruit of the Holy Spirit and a necessary mark of a life being made holy. It is not mere human willpower, but grace-enabled restraint that helps believers resist sin, order their desires, and pursue godliness.

Paul lists self-control among the fruit the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ (Galatians 5:22-23). He uses the image of an athlete: everyone who competes exercises self-control in all things for a perishable wreath, so how much more should we discipline our bodies and keep them under control for an imperishable prize (1 Corinthians 9:24-27). God has given us a spirit of power, love, and self-discipline, not fear (2 Timothy 1:7). His grace itself trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age (Titus 2:11-12). A person without self-control is like a city with broken-down walls, exposed and vulnerable (Proverbs 25:28). Peter likewise urges believers to supplement faith with self-control as they grow in Christ (2 Peter 1:5-6).

This belongs to progressive sanctification: the Holy Spirit steadily conforms us to the image of Christ, using the ordinary means of grace (Scripture, prayer, and the gathered church) rather than leaving us to strive in our own strength. Self-discipline therefore shows itself in concrete places such as our speech, appetites, time, and thought life. When we fail, we do not despair; we return to the finished work of Christ, who perfectly obeyed where we do not, and we keep walking by the Spirit.

A simple next step is to pick one area this week (perhaps a daily time in the Word or a specific habit of speech), ask the Lord for the Spirit’s help as you read 1 Corinthians 9, and invite a mature believer in your local church to walk with you in it. Pray directly to God, asking Him to produce this fruit in you as you abide in Christ.

question: What is original sin?
answer:
Original sin is the inherited guilt and corruption of nature that every human being receives from Adam’s first disobedience, so that all are born sinners, spiritually dead, and under God’s just wrath apart from grace.

Scripture presents Adam as the federal head of the human race: “Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). David confesses the same reality: “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5). This imputation of Adam’s sin, together with the resulting total depravity of our nature, means we cannot make ourselves right with God by our own efforts.

Because of original sin we stand in desperate need of a Savior. Jesus Christ, the last Adam, lived a perfect life, died as a penal substitution for sinners on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing justification by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

This truth calls us to humble ourselves daily, confessing our need rather than relying on our own righteousness, and to rest in Christ’s finished work. How has this doctrine shaped the way you see yourself before God?

question: Are intrusive thoughts sin? Are spontaneous violent, sexual, or blasphemous thoughts sin?
answer:
Intrusive thoughts of this kind can leave you feeling guilty, frightened, and unsure whether you have sinned against a holy God.

The Bible teaches that sin includes the thoughts and desires of the heart, not only outward actions. Jesus said, "But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). Likewise, "For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness. All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man" (Mark 7:21-23).

At the same time, Scripture distinguishes temptation from sin. Jesus "has been tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). James explains the process: "But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is fully grown, gives birth to death" (James 1:14-15). A spontaneous, unwanted thought (violent, sexual, or blasphemous) that you did not invite, that you immediately reject, and that you hate is typically temptation or a remnant of remaining sin in our fallen nature, not a willful transgression. Sin occurs when the will consents, when we dwell on the thought, or when we take pleasure in it. Unwanted blasphemous thoughts that horrify you are not the unpardonable sin, which is a settled, knowing rejection that attributes the Holy Spirit’s work to Satan (Matthew 12:31-32).

These struggles reveal the ongoing presence of sin in the heart and our need for a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as the atoning sacrifice (penal substitution) for our sins including every sinful thought, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. All who repent and trust in Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Turn from any known sin (including any time you have entertained such thoughts) and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

Take every thought captive to make it obedient to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5). Set your mind on whatever is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely, and admirable (Philippians 4:8). When an intrusive thought comes, refuse it at once, turn to the Lord in prayer (ask Him to search your heart, as in Psalm 139:23-24), and fill your mind with His Word.

Speak with the elders or a mature believer in your local church so they can pray with you and offer counsel. I do not provide medical or psychiatric advice; if these thoughts are intense or persistent, please also consult a qualified professional. A practical next step is to write out Philippians 4:8, keep it where you can see it, and recite it whenever an unwanted thought arises. How have these thoughts been affecting your walk with the Lord?

question: Book of 1 Corinthians - Bible Survey
answer:
The book of 1 Corinthians is a letter written by the apostle Paul around AD 55 from Ephesus to the church he had planted in Corinth. Paul writes as an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, addressing a congregation he founded on his second missionary journey, a church already showing both the fruit of the gospel and deep disorders (1 Corinthians 1:1-2; 1 Corinthians 16:8; Acts 18:1-11).

Corinth was a prosperous Roman colony and major port, known for trade, philosophy, and open immorality. The church there faced factions, sexual sin, lawsuits between believers, confusion about marriage and idol food, disorder in worship, misuse of spiritual gifts, and some who denied the bodily resurrection. Paul confronts these issues not with mere rules but with the wisdom of God displayed in Christ crucified, which is foolishness to the world yet the power of God for those who believe (1 Corinthians 1:18-25).

The letter moves from greeting and thanksgiving, to a call for unity around the gospel rather than human leaders, then to holiness in the body (the church as a temple of the Holy Spirit), answers to their questions, the supremacy of love, proper use of gifts, the Lord’s Supper as a proclamation of Christ’s death, and a majestic defense of the resurrection. At the heart of it all stands the gospel Paul received and delivered as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

This epistle shows that justification by grace through faith in the risen Christ must produce a holy, unified, and loving church. Believers are not their own; they were bought with a price and are called to glorify God in body and spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The same letter that rebukes pride and disorder also holds out the sure hope that our labor in the Lord is not in vain because Christ has been raised (1 Corinthians 15:58).

As you read 1 Corinthians, ask the Lord to show you how the message of the cross should shape your own relationships, purity, and hope within your local church.

question: How do I identify my spiritual gift?
answer:
Spiritual gifts (often called charismata) are abilities the Holy Spirit gives every believer to serve others and build up the church for the common good. You identify yours chiefly by studying the relevant Scriptures, praying for wisdom, serving actively in a local church, and receiving confirmation from mature believers rather than relying on a personality quiz.

The New Testament lists gifts such as teaching, serving, encouragement, giving, leadership, and mercy (Romans 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:4-11; 1 Peter 4:10-11). The body-of-Christ image in 1 Corinthians 12 shows that these gifts differ yet all contribute to the health of the whole, so effectiveness and fruit in actual ministry often reveal them more clearly than self-assessment alone.

Faithful Christians disagree on whether the miraculous sign gifts (tongues, prophecy, healings as described in the apostolic era) continue today. Continuationists argue that 1 Corinthians 12–14 still applies in full, so a believer might prayerfully seek and test those gifts in community as well.

I hold the cessationist view common in Reformed Baptist churches: those sign gifts authenticated the apostles and the new revelation now complete in Scripture (Hebrews 2:3-4; Ephesians 2:20), so they have ceased. Identification therefore focuses on the ongoing gifts of service that edify the church through ordinary means.

A concrete next step is to read 1 Corinthians 12 this week, ask God to show you where He has already been using you, then speak with your pastor or an elder about a specific serving opportunity (hospitality, teaching children, practical helps, or administration). Try it, watch for fruit and joy in others, and invite feedback. Using the gift God has given you brings both usefulness to the body and personal delight in His grace.

question: What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24)?
answer:
Nothing of redemptive or atoning value is lacking in Christ’s afflictions; His sacrificial death is complete and fully sufficient. In Colossians 1:24 Paul means the remaining sufferings appointed for Christ’s body, the church, as it continues the gospel mission in this age.

He writes, “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of His body, which is the church” (Colossians 1:24). This cannot mean the cross itself was unfinished, for Jesus declared, “It is finished” (John 19:30), and “by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The penal substitutionary atonement of Christ fully satisfies divine justice and needs no addition.

What remains is the overflow of those afflictions into the members of His body through our union with Him. “The sufferings of Christ overflow to us” (2 Corinthians 1:5), and we are called to share in them (Philippians 3:10; Romans 8:17). Paul, imprisoned for the gospel, takes his appointed share of those tribulations so that the church may be strengthened and the mystery of Christ made known.

Our hardships for the sake of others therefore display the power of the finished work rather than completing it. Read Colossians 1 slowly this week and ask the Lord to help you see any present trials as service to His body, while you rest in the completeness of the cross. Pray directly to God, thanking Him for that finished atonement and asking for joy in any suffering that serves His people.

question: How can I get my prayers answered by God?
answer:
God answers prayer as a sovereign, wise, and loving Father, not because we discover a technique that obligates Him. He hears those who come to Him through His Son, Jesus Christ. If you have not yet trusted Christ, that is the first prayer God always welcomes: turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.
