Scripture is clear that sin separates us from God, yet Christ, truly God and truly man, lived perfectly, died as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Those who repent and believe are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone and adopted as God’s children, so they may call Him Father (John 14:6; Romans 5:1; Romans 8:15; 1 John 5:14).

Once you belong to Christ, the Bible gives these marks of prayer that God delights to answer according to His will:

Pray according to God’s revealed will in Scripture rather than merely your own desires. “This is the confidence we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). Abide in Christ and let His words shape your requests (John 15:7). Pray in Jesus’ name, which means asking in line with His character and authority, not as a magic phrase (John 14:13–14).

Come with a repentant heart. Unconfessed sin hinders prayer: “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18). Confess quickly, receive His cleansing, and keep short accounts with God (1 John 1:9). Check your motives; God does not grant requests aimed at selfish pleasure (James 4:3).

Pray with faith in God’s character, persistence, and thanksgiving. Ask, seek, and knock (Matthew 7:7–8). Bring everything to Him with gratitude (Philippians 4:6). Remember that “no” or “wait” is still an answer from a Father who knows what is best; Paul’s thorn was not removed, yet God’s grace proved sufficient (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

A concrete next step: open Matthew 6:9–13 today, pray through the Lord’s Prayer slowly as a model (adoration, surrender to God’s will, daily dependence, confession, protection), then take one specific request to Him while asking Him to align your heart with His Word. Share that request with a mature believer in a local church so you can pray together. God uses the means of grace (His Word, prayer, and fellowship) to conform us to Christ. Keep coming to Him; He is faithful.

question: What is the more excellent way (1 Corinthians 12:31)?
answer:
The more excellent way in 1 Corinthians 12:31 is love. After urging the Corinthians to desire the greater gifts, Paul immediately turns to this surpassing path in 1 Corinthians 13, showing that agape (self-giving, God-like love) is greater than any spiritual gift.

The Corinthian church was divided and proud over tongues, prophecy, and other gifts, so Paul redirects them: even if someone speaks with angelic tongues, prophesies all mysteries, has mountain-moving faith, or gives everything away, it amounts to nothing without love (1 Corinthians 13:1-3). Love is patient and kind, it does not envy or boast, it is not arrogant or rude, it does not insist on its own way, and it never fails, even though gifts will pass away (1 Corinthians 13:4-8). Faith, hope, and love remain, but the greatest of these is love (1 Corinthians 13:13).

This is not mere sentiment. It is the fruit of the Spirit and the very character of God displayed in Christ’s penal substitutionary death for sinners. In practice, pursue this love in your local church by using whatever gifts God has given you to serve others rather than to be seen, putting their good ahead of your own preference or recognition.

question: What is the open heaven concept?
answer:
The open heaven concept in Scripture refers to God revealing His presence, sending the Holy Spirit, or granting visions of His glory, as when the heavens opened at Jesus’ baptism and the Spirit descended on Him (Matthew 3:16). Ezekiel likewise wrote that “the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God” (Ezekiel 1:1), and Stephen, as he died, saw “heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56).

Some Christians, especially in Pentecostal and charismatic settings, use “open heavens” for seasons of revival, miracles, or abundant blessing, sometimes drawing on Malachi 3:10 and the Old Testament language of God opening or closing the heavens for rain as a sign of favor or judgment (Deuteronomy 28:12).

The New Testament shows that the greatest opening of heaven is Jesus Christ Himself, truly God and truly man, the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). Through His incarnation, atoning death on the cross, and bodily resurrection, believers have access to the Father by one Spirit (Ephesians 2:18) and may approach the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). Jesus is the true connection between heaven and earth (John 1:51). You can therefore pray and read Scripture today, trusting His finished work rather than waiting for a special atmosphere.

question: What is the origin of baptism?
answer:
Christian baptism originates with John the Baptist, who immersed people in the Jordan River as a public sign of repentance in preparation for the Messiah, and it was instituted by Jesus Christ Himself as a standing command for His disciples.

The Greek word *baptizo* means to immerse or dip, which matches the practice of plunging into water. John preached a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 3:1-6; Mark 1:4-5). Jesus, though sinless, submitted to John's baptism to fulfill all righteousness and identify with the people He came to save; at that moment the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father's voice declared His pleasure in the Son, revealing the Trinity (Matthew 3:13-17). After His resurrection Jesus commanded, "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The early church immediately obeyed, as when about three thousand were baptized on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:41).

Ritual washings for ceremonial purity existed in the Old Testament and in later Jewish practice (such as the mikveh), yet John's baptism and Christian baptism are distinct: they are a one-time act of repentance and identification with Christ rather than repeated ceremonial cleansing. Baptism is an ordinance, an outward sign of the inward grace of union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4).

If you have trusted Christ and have not yet been baptized, speak with the elders of a faithful local church about taking that step as a public testimony of faith.

question: What is historical criticism?
answer:
Historical criticism is a scholarly method of studying the Bible that investigates a text’s origins by asking who wrote it, when, from what sources, and in what historical and cultural setting, often tracing how the writing may have developed over time.

Understanding a passage’s original setting can serve faithful interpretation, yet much historical-critical work has treated Scripture as a merely human product and has assumed that miracles and predictive prophecy did not occur. The Bible itself claims far more: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16), and “no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation, because no prophecy was ever brought about by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:20-21). Christians therefore receive the grammatical-historical sense of the text while submitting to its divine authority and treating its narrative claims as real events rather than as evolving religious traditions.

When you study a passage, note its historical background and literary form, then let the text’s own claims about God, sin, and salvation govern your reading rather than naturalistic theories about how the document “must” have arisen. Seek out teachers and commentaries that honor the inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture so that historical insight serves, rather than undermines, confidence in God’s Word.

question: What does the Bible say about paying taxes?
answer:
The Bible teaches that Christians should pay taxes to civil authorities as part of honoring God’s ordained government. Jesus, when trapped by a question about the imperial tax, said, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matthew 22:21). Paul likewise commands, “This is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, who give their full time to governing. Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due” (Romans 13:6-7).

These passages rest on the truth that God Himself institutes civil government for order and justice (Romans 13:1-4; 1 Peter 2:13-14). Paying taxes is therefore not merely a civic duty but an act of submission to the Lord, who remains sovereign over every ruler. Jesus Himself paid the temple tax, though as the Son He was exempt, so as not to give unnecessary offense (Matthew 17:24-27).

In practice this means filing honestly, paying what is lawfully owed, and doing so as unto Christ rather than merely to avoid penalties. When a government’s demands would require personal sin, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), yet ordinary taxation, even under imperfect or pagan rulers, remains a Christian obligation.

question: Should Christian women wear pants?
answer:
The Bible does not require Christian women to avoid pants in favor of only skirts or dresses. This is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty where faithful believers may disagree, because Scripture emphasizes principles of modesty, clear distinction between men and women, and a godly heart rather than a fixed list of garments for every culture.

Some conservative Christians interpret Deuteronomy 22:5 as forbidding pants for women, since trousers were historically men's clothing, and they therefore encourage dresses or skirts to preserve visible gender distinctions and promote modesty. Many other Christians, including most Reformed and evangelical believers, note that clothing styles are largely cultural; women's pants today are not the same as a man putting on a woman's cloak, so the command is honored when dress remains modest, feminine in character, and not an attempt to erase the sexes God created (Genesis 1:27).

Romans 14:5 reminds us that in disputable matters each person should be fully convinced in his own mind, and Romans 14:13 warns us not to put a stumbling block in a brother's way. The New Testament focus is inner godliness expressed in respectable apparel: 1 Timothy 2:9-10 calls women to adorn themselves with modesty and self-control rather than costly display, and 1 Peter 3:3-4 points to the hidden person of the heart with a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God's sight.

Pants themselves are not sinful, yet clothing that is tight, revealing, or deliberately androgynous can violate modesty and the created order. Our standing before God is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by the cut of our clothes; justification does not come from skirts or trousers. A helpful next step is to read 1 Timothy 2:9-10 and 1 Peter 3:3-4, then prayerfully ask the Lord to search your motives in dressing and to give wisdom for your own setting. If you belong to a local church, talk with a mature sister or an elder about how these principles look in your congregation, so that you walk in unity and love.

question: Why wasn't Jesus named Immanuel?
answer:
Jesus was given the personal name Jesus by the angel’s command because it means “the Lord saves,” highlighting His mission to rescue sinners, while Immanuel is a title meaning “God with us” that describes His identity rather than serving as His legal name (Matthew 1:21). The Bible presents this as fulfillment, not a contradiction: Isaiah promised a child who would be called Immanuel as a sign of God’s nearness (Isaiah 7:14), and Matthew shows that people would recognize Jesus this way because in Him God truly dwells with humanity (Matthew 1:22-23).

Some notice the different names and wonder whether the prophecy failed. The text itself distinguishes the two: Joseph is told, “you are to give Him the name Jesus,” while the prophet says “they will call Him Immanuel.” In Scripture a person can have a given name and also be known by titles that reveal who he is (Son of David, Christ, Lord). Jesus (from the Hebrew Yeshua) points to His saving work; Immanuel (Hebrew immanu-El) points to the incarnation, God the Son taking on true human nature so that He is both fully God and fully man.

Because Jesus is Immanuel, God is not distant. He has come near in the flesh, lived among us, and remains with His people by His Spirit (John 1:14; Matthew 28:20). When loneliness or fear presses in, you can remember that the One who saves is also the God who is with you. Read Matthew 1 slowly this week and thank the Father that He has drawn near in His Son.

question: How is choosing a good name better than choosing riches (Proverbs 22:1)?
answer:
A good name is better than riches because it is a reputation of integrity and godliness that endures, brings lasting favor, and honors the Lord, while wealth is fleeting and cannot purchase character or true peace.

Proverbs 22:1 states, "A good name is more desirable than great riches; favor is better than silver and gold." In the world of ancient Israel, a person's name (the Hebrew shem) stood for their character and standing in the community, affecting trust, family honor, and daily dealings far more than silver ever could. Riches can sprout wings and fly away (Proverbs 23:4-5), but "the memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot" (Proverbs 10:7). This good name grows from the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7), and it produces favor with God and people that no amount of gold can buy.

This wisdom finds its deepest fulfillment in Christ, who though He was rich became poor so that we might become rich in Him (2 Corinthians 8:9). His perfect name covers us, and we are called to live in a way that reflects His righteousness rather than chasing earthly gain. Practically, this means choosing honesty in a business deal, faithfulness in a hard conversation, or contentment in your work even when a shortcut to more money tempts you.

This week, ask one mature believer in your local church how they have seen your character, then pray through Psalm 139:23-24, asking God to show you any place where you might trade a good name for passing riches.

question: What is the lust of the eyes?
answer:
The lust of the eyes is the sinful craving for what we see, whether possessions we covet or people we desire in ways God has forbidden, as 1 John 2:16 describes it among the things that belong to the world rather than to the Father.

This is not mere noticing of beauty or provision, but a grasping desire that seeks to possess, consume, or enjoy what God has not given. The Greek term in 1 John 2:16 is epithumia, a strong craving that, in this context, is disordered and opposed to love for God. Scripture shows it in Eve, who saw that the tree was pleasing to the eyes and took of it (Genesis 3:6), and in the tenth commandment’s prohibition of coveting (Exodus 20:17). Jesus likewise taught that looking at a woman to lust after her is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28). It therefore includes both material greed and sexual immorality stirred by sight.

These desires wage war against the soul (1 Peter 2:11) because they treat created things as ultimate rather than receiving them with thanksgiving under God’s lordship. They are an expression of remaining concupiscence, the corruption of the heart that believers must put to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). The world and its lusts are passing away, but the one who does the will of God lives forever (1 John 2:17).

Set your mind on things above, not on earthly things (Colossians 3:1-2). A concrete next step is to pray through Psalm 119:37, asking God to turn your eyes from worthless things and to revive you by His Word, while making a covenant with your eyes as Job did (Job 31:1) and filling your vision with Scripture in the fellowship of a local church.

question: What does the Bible say about Voodoo? How should a Christian view Voodoo?
answer:
The Bible never names Voodoo, which developed long after the New Testament as a blend of West African spirit worship, ancestor veneration, and ritual magic (often mixed with Catholic images). Scripture does, however, speak with unmistakable clarity against the practices at its center: consulting spirits, witchcraft, sorcery, necromancy, and the worship of any being besides the one true God.

Deuteronomy 18:10-12 forbids anyone who “practices divination or conjury, who interprets omens, who practices sorcery, who casts spells, who is a medium or spiritist, or who consults the dead,” calling these things “detestable to the LORD.” Leviticus 19:31 likewise commands, “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them.” In the New Testament, Galatians 5:19-21 lists sorcery among the works of the flesh that exclude people from the kingdom of God, and 1 Corinthians 10:20-21 warns that pagan sacrifices are “offered to demons, not to God,” so that believers “cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.”

A Christian must therefore view Voodoo as occult idolatry, not as harmless culture, folklore, or an alternative spirituality. The loa and other spirits invoked in Voodoo are not God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; they are either empty inventions or actual demonic powers that oppose Christ. Participation, even out of family custom, curiosity, or a desire for protection or healing, is spiritual adultery against the God who says, “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3). Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5), and He alone has authority over every spirit.

If you have ever taken part in such practices, the same Scriptures that warn also offer hope: Christ died as a penal substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily, so that all who repent and trust in Him alone receive forgiveness and new life. Turn from every rival power and rest in Him. Stay far from Voodoo objects, rituals, and consultations; instead, bring every fear and need to the Lord in prayer and His Word, and walk in the fellowship of a local church that holds fast to Scripture.

question: What is the meaning of Lent?
answer:
Lent is a traditional 40-day season of fasting, prayer, and repentance observed by many Christians before Easter, recalling Jesus' 40 days of fasting and temptation in the wilderness as He prepared for His public ministry (Matthew 4:1-11).

This practice is a non-essential matter of church custom where faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture nowhere commands a specific pre-Easter fast even though it does commend fasting, repentance, and self-examination as ongoing spiritual disciplines.

Many in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and some Lutheran traditions keep Lent as a helpful time of penitence and preparation, often beginning on Ash Wednesday, with fasting or self-denial, extra prayer, and charity, viewing it as a way to follow Christ's example and ready the heart to celebrate His resurrection.

Many Reformed, Baptist, and other evangelical Christians do not observe a formal Lenten season, holding that repentance and the ordinary means of grace (the Word, prayer, and the Lord's Supper) belong to the whole Christian life rather than a special calendar period, and that adding extra-biblical seasons risks legalism (Romans 14:5-6; Colossians 2:16-17).

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, Lent is a matter of Christian liberty rather than a requirement. It is not necessary for faithful Christianity, and it must never be treated as meritorious, since we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. If someone uses a focused season of fasting and prayer to grow in sanctification and gratitude for Christ's penal substitutionary atonement, that can be a legitimate personal discipline so long as it does not bind others' consciences.

Whether you keep Lent or not, a wise next step is to read the Gospel accounts of Jesus' temptation, His journey to the cross, and His resurrection, asking the Lord to deepen your daily repentance and joy in His finished work.

question: What doth every sin deserve?
answer:
Every sin deserves God’s wrath and curse, both in this life and that which is to come. God is holy and just, so every transgression of His law brings real guilt and the penalty of death, making sinners subject to spiritual, temporal, and eternal misery apart from Christ. Scripture says, “For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23). It also warns that “because of these things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 5:6) and “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law” (Galatians 3:10).

This is why we need a Savior. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and we cannot pay the debt ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we failed to live, then offered Himself in penal substitutionary atonement, bearing the wrath and curse we deserved on the cross. He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, proving His victory over sin and death. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. How does seeing sin’s true desert change the way you rest in Christ’s finished work today?

question: What does the Bible say about diligence?
answer:
The Bible presents diligence as faithful, persistent effort that God blesses in daily work and in growing in godliness, while laziness brings want and missed fruit.

In the wisdom of Proverbs, this is a repeated theme of fearing the Lord in practical life: "Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth" (Proverbs 10:4). "The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor" (Proverbs 12:24). "The slacker craves yet gets nothing, but the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied" (Proverbs 13:4). Solomon even points to the ant, which works steadily without a ruler over it (Proverbs 6:6-8).

The New Testament carries this into both vocation and spiritual growth. Believers are told, "Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men" (Colossians 3:23), and "Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord" (Romans 12:11). Peter calls us to "make every effort" to add virtue, knowledge, and self-control to our faith so that we will not be ineffective or unfruitful (2 Peter 1:5-8). Hebrews urges the same diligence to the end, so that hope remains sure (Hebrews 6:11-12).

This is part of progressive sanctification: the Holy Spirit enables us to put off sloth and live as faithful stewards of the time, gifts, and callings God has given. A concrete application is to treat ordinary duties (work, home, study of Scripture) as service to Christ rather than mere tasks to finish.

Ask the Lord this week to show you one area of sluggishness and to give you a diligent heart there, perhaps beginning each day with a few verses from Proverbs as you pray for His help.

question: What is agnosticism?
answer:
Agnosticism is the view that the existence of God is unknown or unknowable. The term comes from Greek roots meaning "not knowing," and it typically describes either personal uncertainty ("I do not know") or the stronger claim that such knowledge is impossible in principle. It differs from atheism, which denies God's existence outright.

Christians believe, on the authority of Scripture as the inspired Word of God, that God has not left Himself unknown. Romans 1:19-20 teaches that what may be known about God is plain because God has made it plain, and His eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen from the creation of the world, understood from His workmanship, so that people are without excuse. This is general revelation in nature. God has also given special revelation through the Scriptures and, supremely, in His Son. Hebrews 1:1-2 states that God spoke in the past through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.

Some people hold agnostic views because they feel the evidence is insufficient, or because they wrestle with God's apparent hiddenness and the reality of suffering. Scripture answers that the testimony of creation is already clear, yet people suppress the truth (Romans 1:18), and that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, has made the Father known through His life, atoning death, and bodily resurrection.

A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John, which presents Jesus as the one who reveals God.

question: What does it mean to “be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4)?
answer:
To “be angry and do not sin” means anger is not automatically sinful, yet it must not produce ungodly words, revenge, or lingering bitterness. Psalm 4:4 says, “Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. Selah.”

David wrote this as an evening prayer amid distress and opposition. The Hebrew verb can mean tremble or be agitated; the call is to let holy agitation drive you to quiet self-examination before God rather than to sinful outburst. The New Testament takes up the same wording in Ephesians 4:26–27: “Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold.” Paul places it inside the call to put off the old self of bitterness and wrath (Ephesians 4:31) as part of progressive sanctification.

Jesus Himself displayed righteous anger at hardness of heart (Mark 3:5) without ever sinning, showing that indignation against evil can be holy. Our anger, however, is often mixed with pride or self-interest, so Scripture warns us to keep it short and submitted.

When anger rises, follow the psalm: pause, search your own heart before God in prayer, and refuse to speak or act until you have done so. If this is a repeated battle, speak with a pastor or mature believer in your local church and walk through Ephesians 4 together.

question: How will the covenant with death be annulled (Isaiah 28:18)?
answer:
The covenant with death in Isaiah 28:18 will be annulled by the Lord GOD Himself. He will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the plumb line, so that hail sweeps away the refuge of lies and water floods the hiding place; then that false agreement with Sheol will not stand, and the overflowing scourge will trample those who trusted it (Isaiah 28:17-18).

This takes place as God lays a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion as a sure foundation: “the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament identifies this stone as Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:6; Romans 9:33). The rulers of Jerusalem had boasted of a pact that would keep the coming judgment from touching them, hiding in lies rather than in the Lord (Isaiah 28:14-15). God exposes that refuge as worthless and brings the very judgment they thought they had escaped.

Historically this was realized in the invasions that overtook Judah despite their schemes. The same principle stands for every generation: any hope of safety apart from the Lord (whether political alliances, self-made religion, or moral effort) is a covenant with death and will fail. True security is found only by believing in Christ the cornerstone.

If this passage has raised questions about where you yourself are resting, open Isaiah 28 and 1 Peter 2, ask the Lord to show you any false refuge, and speak with a pastor in a local church who can walk with you in the Word.

question: What is the Hindu caste system?
answer:
The Hindu caste system is a traditional, hereditary social hierarchy in Hindu society that classifies people mainly by birth, family occupation, and ideas of ritual purity. It is organized around four main varnas: Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers, merchants, and artisans), and Shudras (laborers and servants), with many people historically treated as outside the system altogether (often called Dalits or, in older language, untouchables). In daily life this has usually operated through thousands of local jatis, or subcastes, that shape marriage, work, and social contact.

The pattern is associated with ancient Hindu texts such as the Rigveda and later law codes like the Manusmriti. India’s constitution formally abolished caste-based untouchability and discrimination, yet social effects of the system still appear in many communities.

The Bible teaches that every human being is created in the image of God and therefore possesses equal dignity, regardless of birth or social rank (Genesis 1:27). In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, for all who belong to Him are one (Galatians 3:28). That truth stands against any ranking of people by ancestry.

question: What does the Bible say about rest and relaxation?
answer:
The Bible presents rest as a gracious gift from God, patterned after His own rest in creation, commanded for our good, and fulfilled in the soul-rest Jesus Christ gives to those who come to Him.

After finishing His work of creation, God rested on the seventh day, blessed it, and made it holy (Genesis 2:2-3). He later commanded His people, “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:8), tying weekly rest both to creation and to His redeeming work. This was never meant as empty ritual. Jesus, Lord of the Sabbath, taught that “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). He Himself withdrew to lonely places to pray (Luke 5:16) and invited His weary disciples, “Come with Me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest” (Mark 6:31).

The deepest rest the Bible offers is not merely a day off. Jesus says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28-29). Hebrews explains that a Sabbath-rest still remains for the people of God; we enter it by faith in Christ’s finished work rather than by our own striving (Hebrews 4:9-10). At the same time, Scripture rebukes both anxious overwork that forgets God “gives sleep to those He loves” (Psalm 127:2) and lazy idleness that refuses honest labor (Proverbs 6:9-11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10). Enjoying the fruit of our work and simple gifts of food, family, and creation is itself a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 5:18).

True rest, then, is an act of trust: we cease from treating ourselves as sovereign and remember that God is. Faithful Christians have differed on the exact form of weekly Sabbath observance, yet all agree that rest is part of wise stewardship of the body and soul God has given us.

This week, set aside ordinary labor for a stretch of time, gather with God’s people if you can, and pray through Matthew 11:28-30, asking the Lord to teach you to rest in His finished work rather than in your own productivity.

question: What is deism? What do deists believe?
answer:
Deism is the belief that a Creator God exists and made the universe, yet does not intervene in it afterward, leaving the world to operate solely by natural laws like a clockmaker who winds a clock and walks away.

Deists typically hold that this God is known through human reason and observation of nature rather than through Scripture, miracles, or personal revelation. They generally reject the Trinity, the incarnation of Jesus Christ, His atoning death, and His bodily resurrection as supernatural claims, along with any ongoing divine involvement such as answered prayer or providence. Religion, in this view, often reduces to ethics drawn from natural order.

The Bible teaches a different God, one who is both transcendent Creator and personally present. In Him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28). He upholds all things by His powerful word (Hebrews 1:3), and in Him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17). The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). This is divine providence, God’s active, personal rule over creation, not absenteeism.

Unlike the distant deity of deism, the God of Scripture draws near, calls sinners to Himself, and has acted in history through Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection. This means prayer is conversation with a Father who hears, not an unused mechanism. If this contrast raises questions about knowing God personally, a next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly and ask Him to show you who He is.

question: Is the distinction between clergy and laity biblical?
answer:
The New Testament does not establish a clergy-laity distinction that divides Christians into a priestly class and ordinary people, though it does appoint qualified men as elders and deacons to serve among the people of God.

Many in Catholic, Orthodox, and some Anglican traditions argue that Christ and the apostles instituted a distinct clerical order of bishops, priests, and deacons, continued through succession, as essential for valid sacraments and the church's visible order.

As a Reformed Baptist, I hold this as one faithful option within historic Christianity: every believer shares in the priesthood of all believers through union with Christ, while elders function as undershepherds and teachers within the flock rather than a separate caste.

Scripture calls the whole church "a royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9) and a kingdom of priests (Revelation 1:6), because there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). New Testament leaders are called elders or overseers who shepherd the flock they belong to (Acts 20:28; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9), and deacons who serve practical needs (1 Timothy 3:8-13); the term for priest is reserved for Christ and all saints, not for church officers. Pastors and teachers exist "to equip the saints for works of ministry, to build up the body of Christ" (Ephesians 4:12), so the congregation itself does the work of ministry. Jesus told His disciples they are all brothers and must not exalt themselves with titles (Matthew 23:8).

This means you have direct access to God in prayer without any human priest, you honor those who labor in the Word (1 Timothy 5:17; Hebrews 13:17), and you use your own gifts to serve the body. A helpful next step is to read 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 this week, noting the qualifications of officers, then talk with a trusted elder in your church about how these roles function among the whole congregation.

question: What does it mean to have a wilderness experience?
answer:
A wilderness experience is a season of testing, isolation, scarcity, or spiritual dryness that God uses to humble His people, expose what is in the heart, and teach them to live by His Word rather than by their own strength or visible provision.

In Scripture the LORD led Israel through the wilderness for forty years “to humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments” (Deuteronomy 8:2). He fed them with manna so they would learn that “man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus Himself was “led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1), where He answered every temptation with Scripture and succeeded as the faithful Son where Israel had failed (Matthew 4:4). These accounts treat the wilderness as a real place of both danger and divine purpose, not mere metaphor.

Such seasons belong to God’s work of sanctification. They are not proof that He has abandoned you; they are often the very means by which He weans us from self-reliance and deepens our trust in Christ, who already walked the wilderness for us. Trials produce perseverance and maturity (James 1:2-4), and a loving Father disciplines those He receives as sons (Hebrews 12:5-11).

If you are in such a season, stay with the ordinary means of grace: daily Scripture, honest prayer, and the gathered church. A concrete next step is to read Deuteronomy 8 slowly this week, noting every way God provided, then talk to Him about those same provisions in your own life and share what you see with a mature believer in your local church. He remains faithful even when the path feels barren.

question: What does Malachi 2:16 mean when God says, ‘I hate divorce’?
answer:
When God says “I hate divorce” in Malachi 2:16, He is condemning the faithless, violent breaking of the marriage covenant, not merely expressing a general dislike of hardship. In the Berean Standard Bible the verse reads, “For I hate divorce,” says the LORD, the God of Israel, “and him who covers his garment with violence,” says the LORD of Hosts. So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith.

The immediate setting is Malachi 2:10-16, where the men of Judah were dealing treacherously with “the wife of your youth” (Malachi 2:14), often putting her away in order to marry foreign women. The LORD Himself had been “a witness between you and the wife of your youth\ldots though she is your companion and your wife by covenant.” Divorce in that context was covenant treachery (the Hebrew idea of faithlessness), an act that left the discarded wife vulnerable and “covered” the husband’s own life with violence and injustice. God therefore commands His people to guard their spirits and refuse such unfaithfulness.

This hatred of divorce flows from God’s original design: “a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Jesus later confirmed that what God has joined, man must not separate, and that Moses’ permission of divorce was a concession to hardness of heart, “but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:6, 8). Marriage is meant to display God’s own covenant faithfulness; tearing it apart distorts that picture and inflicts real harm.

Christians therefore treat marriage vows as a sacred, lifelong covenant rather than a disposable contract. If you are married, the concrete next step is to ask the Lord to help you love your spouse with the same steadfastness He shows His people, and to seek the counsel and prayers of your local church elders if the relationship is strained. Guard your spirit; do not break faith.

question: How transparent should church finances be?
answer:
Church finances should be handled with integrity and enough openness to the members that the congregation can see the church is faithfully stewarding what belongs to the Lord, without even the appearance of greed or secrecy. Paul took pains to do this when administering a large gift: “We hope that no one will find fault with us concerning this generous gift that we are administering. For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of men” (2 Corinthians 8:20-21). Elders and deacons must not be lovers of money (1 Timothy 3:3; 1 Timothy 3:8), and every steward must be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2).

The precise form of that openness (full line-item reports, summarized budgets, or whether individual salaries are listed) is a matter of wisdom and local church practice rather than a command every congregation must follow in the same way. Faithful churches have used different methods while still honoring these principles. Some share detailed reports with members so the body can approve the budget together; others keep certain personal figures more limited to guard against envy or unnecessary comparison, while still providing clear accountability through elders and a finance team.

In an elder-led congregational church, members ordinarily review and approve the budget, which requires a real (not token) level of transparency to those who belong to the church. If this question has arisen in your own congregation, a good next step is to speak privately with an elder, asking how finances are currently reported and offering to pray for those who carry that responsibility (Hebrews 13:17). Do so as a supportive member, not an accuser, and continue giving cheerfully yourself as an act of worship.

question: Is intinction the correct way to do communion?
answer:
Intinction (dipping the bread into the cup so both elements are received together) is a non-essential matter of church practice where faithful Christians may disagree, because the New Testament clearly institutes the Lord's Supper with bread and the cup yet does not command one exclusive physical method of distribution.

Many historic churches, especially Eastern Orthodox, some Anglican, Lutheran, and Catholic congregations, have long used intinction as a unified way to receive both elements at once, often citing early church custom, practicality, or the desire that every communicant partake of both bread and wine.

Reformed, Baptist, and many evangelical churches typically give the bread first to be eaten and then the cup to be drunk separately, following the two distinct actions Jesus took at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26-28; 1 Corinthians 11:23-25), where He said “Take and eat” and afterward “Drink from it, all of you.”

Romans 14:1-6 calls us to extend charity and liberty in such disputable practices that do not touch the gospel. What is essential is that we receive both elements in remembrance of Christ’s body given and blood shed, examining ourselves and spiritually feeding on Him by faith as a means of grace (1 Corinthians 11:26-29). The spiritual presence of Christ is enjoyed by those who come in faith, not by the precise mechanics of how the elements reach the mouth.

If your church uses intinction, receive it with thanksgiving focused on the cross; if it uses sequential distribution, do the same. A wise next step is to open Matthew 26 and 1 Corinthians 11 with your pastor or elders and ask how your congregation’s practice seeks to honor the biblical institution while keeping unity in the gospel.

question: What is the church suffering?
answer:
The church suffers because it is united to Christ in a world that rejected Him. Jesus told His disciples, “If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (John 15:18), and “In this world you will have tribulation. But take heart! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). All who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12), and it has been granted to believers not only to believe in Him but also to suffer for His sake (Philippians 1:29).

This includes open persecution (imprisonment, violence, and martyrdom in many nations), cultural hostility and legal pressure in others, the ordinary trials of a fallen creation that still groans (Romans 8:22–23), and even wounds from false teaching, division, and unrepentant sin inside congregations. Yet this is not meaningless. Believers share in Christ’s sufferings so that they may also share in His glory (Romans 8:17); God uses it to produce perseverance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3–5). Paul even spoke of filling up in his flesh what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, the church (Colossians 1:24), meaning the church continues to bear witness through costly faithfulness until Christ returns.

Remain in a faithful local church that preaches the Word, prays, and practices the ordinances. Pray for brothers and sisters who suffer more intensely, remembering those in prison as if you were there with them (Hebrews 13:3), and look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him (Hebrews 12:2).

question: What does it mean that a person will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-11)?
answer:
To not inherit the kingdom of God means to be excluded from eternal life and the future blessings of God's reign, remaining under judgment rather than receiving the inheritance promised to His people. Paul writes, "Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God" (1 Corinthians 6:9-10). Those whose lives are characterized by unrepentant practice of these sins will not enter the kingdom.

This is not a denial that anyone who has ever fallen into such sins can be saved. Paul immediately adds, "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11). The same warning appears elsewhere: those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:21; Ephesians 5:5). The point is a settled pattern of unrepentant wickedness, not a single stumble followed by godly sorrow. True justification (God declaring a sinner righteous through faith in Christ) is never without sanctification (the Spirit making a person holy). A life that continues in these sins without turning from them shows that a person has not been born again.

The kingdom here is the eschatological inheritance of those united to Christ, who become heirs with Him. God is holy and just, and His wrath against sin is real, yet He is also gracious and merciful. We all have sinned and fall short of His glory. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as the substitute bearing the penalty for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works.

If these sins describe your present life, turn (repent) from them and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. If you belong to Christ, remember that you are no longer defined by what you once were; pursue holiness by the Spirit, putting sin to death. A wise next step is to open 1 Corinthians 6 and 1 John in prayer, asking God to search your heart, and to speak with a pastor in a local church that holds to the Bible's teaching. How does this land with you?

question: Is it wise for Christian teens to be dating?
answer:
Whether Christian teens should date is a tertiary matter of wisdom and Christian liberty rather than a core command of Scripture, so faithful believers may differ without breaking fellowship (Romans 14:5). Scripture gives clear principles of purity, parental honor, and marriage as a covenant, yet it does not prescribe or forbid modern dating by name.

Some Christians hold that recreational dating is unwise for teens and prefer family-involved courtship only when marriage is a realistic near possibility. They see casual pairing-off as stirring affections too soon and exposing young people to unnecessary temptation.

Others believe dating can be a legitimate way for older, mature teens to grow in discernment if it stays group-oriented, parent-supervised, and strictly bounded against impurity, treating it as character assessment rather than romance.

I believe typical dating is generally not wise for Christian teens. Most are not yet in a position to enter the lifelong covenant of marriage, and pairing off often awakens love and passions Scripture tells us not to stir until the proper time (Song of Solomon 2:7). God's will is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace (2 Timothy 2:22). Guard your heart, for it is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23). Honor your father and mother (Ephesians 6:2). These commands call for holiness now, not practice at romance.

A concrete way to live this out is to invest this season in group friendships, serving in your local church, and growing in the knowledge of God rather than seeking a boyfriend or girlfriend. Talk openly with your parents (or a trusted church elder if you are a parent considering this for your teen) about what godly companionship looks like at this age, and ask the Lord together for a heart that treasures Christ above any relationship, using Psalm 119:9 as a starting point for prayer: "How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word."

question: Why does God allow us to go through trials and tribulations?
answer:
The weight of trials and tribulations can leave us weary and wondering why a good God permits such pain. It is natural to question how a loving and all-powerful God could allow suffering.

The Bible teaches that God is sovereign, holy, and good. Sin entered the world through Adam, bringing the curse of toil and sorrow (Genesis 3:17-19), yet God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, conforming them to the image of His Son (Romans 8:28-29). Christ Himself entered our suffering, offering Himself as a penal substitutionary atonement on the cross, and rose bodily so that we have forgiveness and the sure hope of a glory where tribulation will end.

God uses trials to refine our faith like gold in the fire (1 Peter 1:6-7), to produce perseverance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3-5; James 1:2-4), and as a Father's loving discipline so we may share His holiness (Hebrews 12:7-11). His grace proves sufficient in our weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). This belongs to our progressive sanctification, and He keeps those who are truly His through every storm.

Bring your specific trial to the Lord in prayer, asking for the wisdom He promises (James 1:5), then share the burden with a trusted elder or mature believer in your local church (Galatians 6:2; James 5:16). You can pray through the honest lament and trust of Psalm 13.

question: What does Deuteronomy 10:12 tell us God requires of us?
answer:
Deuteronomy 10:12 tells us that the LORD our God asks of us to fear Him by walking in all His ways, to love Him, and to serve Him with all our heart and with all our soul.

This is Moses’ plain summary of covenant loyalty after reminding Israel of God’s gracious choice of them. The fear of the LORD is reverent awe that produces obedient love rather than mere ritual, and Moses immediately adds that keeping God’s commandments is “for your own good” (Deuteronomy 10:13). Jesus later identified this same wholehearted love as the greatest commandment: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37).

Because of sin we fall short of this perfect devotion, yet Christ fulfilled the law in our place through His sinless life, atoning death, and bodily resurrection. Those who trust in Him are justified by grace through faith and are given the Holy Spirit to walk in new obedience (Romans 8:3-4). Read Deuteronomy 10:12-13 slowly today and ask God Himself to grow this fear and love in your heart as you attend to His Word.

question: Is it okay to get tattoos if they are of a Christian nature?
answer:
Getting a tattoo, even one of Christian nature such as a cross, a Bible verse, or a symbol of faith, is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty where faithful believers may disagree. The New Testament does not give a direct command on tattoos, and Christians interpret the relevant Old Testament text differently regarding whether it still binds us.

Some Christians hold that tattoos remain forbidden. They point to Leviticus 19:28, which says, "You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead or put tattoo marks on yourselves. I am the LORD." They connect this to the New Testament teaching that the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, bought at a price, so we must glorify God with it (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). In this view, even a Christian tattoo can still treat the body as a canvas for self-expression rather than stewardship, and it may carry associations with worldly or rebellious culture that hinder a clear witness.

Other Christians hold that the command in Leviticus 19:28 was tied to pagan mourning rituals in the ancient Near Eastern world and, like other ceremonial laws (dietary rules or clothing mixtures), does not bind New Covenant believers. They see a Christian tattoo as potentially a way to remember God's truth, start Gospel conversations, or publicly identify with Christ, provided the motive is to honor Him. Scripture calls us to do whatever we do, in word or deed, in the name of the Lord Jesus and to the glory of God (Colossians 3:17; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

In disputable matters like this, Romans 14:5 and Romans 14:13 teach that each person should be fully convinced in his own mind and that we must not put a stumbling block in a brother's way. We are not to judge one another over such things, nor use our freedom to cause others to stumble.

Whatever you decide, the heart motive matters most. Ask whether this would truly glorify Christ, write His Word more deeply on your heart, and serve as a faithful witness, or whether it might reflect vanity, trend-following, or a desire to fit in. Tattoos are permanent, so consider how they could affect ministry opportunities, cultural contexts where tattoos carry negative associations, or fellowship with believers who see them differently.

A wise next step is to talk this through with the elders or a mature believer in your local church, who can help you apply biblical wisdom to your specific situation. Spend time in prayer, asking God to search your heart and reveal any mixed motives (Psalm 139:23-24), and let His Word, not personal preference, shape the decision.

question: What day is the Sabbath, Saturday or Sunday?
answer:
The biblical Sabbath is the seventh day of the week, Saturday, set apart by God at creation and commanded in the Ten Commandments as a day of rest (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11). The New Testament church, however, gathered on the first day of the week, Sunday, which it called the Lord's Day, because that is the day Jesus rose from the dead (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Which day Christians should set apart for rest and gathered worship is a tertiary, non-essential matter on which faithful believers may disagree. The New Testament does not restate the Sabbath command in the same form as the Old Covenant, and it treats the choice of days as an area of Christian liberty rather than a test of orthodoxy (Romans 14:5-6; Colossians 2:16-17).

One historic view, held by Seventh-day Adventists and some other Sabbatarian Christians, is that Saturday remains the Sabbath because the fourth commandment belongs to God's unchanging moral law and Scripture never explicitly transfers the day. Another major view, held by most historic Protestant churches (Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican, and many Baptist congregations), is that the Sabbath principle of one day in seven now belongs to Sunday, the Lord's Day, following the resurrection and the apostolic pattern of gathering on the first day.

The heart of the matter is not the calendar date but resting in Christ's finished work, for He Himself is our Sabbath rest (Hebrews 4:9-10). Whatever day your church observes, the call is to cease from ordinary labor, hear the Word, pray, and worship with God's people. A wise next step is to read those passages in context, pray for wisdom, and talk with the elders of a Bible-believing local church about how they understand and practice the Lord's Day.

question: Why did God punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie (Genesis 12:17)?
answer:
God afflicted Pharaoh’s household with severe plagues because Pharaoh had taken Sarai into his house as a wife, and the LORD was protecting her and the covenant promise He had just given Abram, not because Pharaoh invented the deception.

Abram, fearing for his life in Egypt, asked Sarai to say she was his sister (Genesis 12:11-13). Pharaoh then took her, and “the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai” (Genesis 12:17). The affliction was tied directly to her presence as another man’s wife. God had promised Abram offspring and land (Genesis 12:2-3; Genesis 12:7), and Sarai was essential to that line. The plagues exposed the truth so Pharaoh would return her unharmed, preserving both the marriage and the promised seed that would culminate in Christ.

Pharaoh was not entirely without responsibility. Even in ignorance he had taken a married woman into his household, an act God does not overlook. The later parallel with Abimelech makes the same point more explicitly: God withheld the king from sinning against Him by touching Sarah and then required her return (Genesis 20:3-7). Here the plagues served a similar revealing and restraining purpose. Abram’s fear-driven half-truth was a real failure of faith, yet God remained faithful to His own word. He did not abandon the covenant because His servant stumbled.

This account therefore displays both God’s holiness (He will not allow the defilement of the marriage through which the Messiah would come) and His covenant faithfulness (He keeps His promises even when His people do not). When fear tempts us to manage outcomes ourselves rather than trust what God has said, the same LORD still guards His purposes. A concrete next step is to read Genesis 12 alongside Genesis 20 and ask the Lord to show you where you, like Abram, are tempted to protect yourself instead of resting in His word.

question: Christmas Story — Day 4 — Do Christians worship Mary?
answer:
No, Christians do not worship Mary. Worship belongs to God alone, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus Himself said, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10).

Mary holds an honored place in the Christmas story as the humble young woman God chose to bear His Son. The angel called her “highly favored,” and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, declared, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” (Luke 1:28; Luke 1:42). All generations call her blessed because she believed God’s word and submitted to His plan: “I am the Lord’s servant. May it happen to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). Yet Mary herself magnified the Lord and rejoiced in God her Savior (Luke 1:46-47). She was a sinner who needed grace, just as we do. She is not divine, not a co-redeemer, and not a mediator. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

Some Christian traditions, especially Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox, give Mary a very high honor they call veneration (not worship), seeing her as the God-bearer (Theotokos) and often asking her to intercede. They insist this is distinct from the worship due to God. Historic Protestant Christianity, however, finds no biblical command or example for praying to Mary or ascribing her roles that belong to Christ alone, and it warns that such practices can easily confuse the honor due a faithful creature with the worship due the Creator.

In the nativity, Mary points us away from herself to the child in the manger. That child is Immanuel, God with us, truly God and truly man, born to save His people from their sins (Matthew 1:21-23). This Christmas, read Luke 1–2 slowly and notice how every detail, including Mary’s faith, serves to exalt Jesus. Thank God for her obedience, then worship the Son she bore.

question: What is Kemetic spirituality / Kemetism?
answer:
Kemetic spirituality, or Kemetism, is a modern reconstructionist pagan movement that revives the polytheistic religion of ancient Egypt (called Kemet, meaning "black land"). Practitioners typically worship the netjeru (gods such as Ra, Osiris, Isis, and others), seek to live by ma'at (order, truth, and justice), offer rituals drawn from temple and funerary texts, and often include ancestor veneration or heka (ritual power).

This stands in direct conflict with the Bible's revelation of the one true God. Scripture commands, "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Exodus 20:3), and declares that "all the gods of the nations are idols, but the LORD made the heavens" (Psalm 96:5). The LORD judged Egypt's gods in the Exodus to display His unique sovereignty (Exodus 12:12).

Some are drawn to Kemetism to reclaim African heritage (seeing ancient Egypt as a high Black civilization) or as an alternative to Christianity they associate with colonialism. Those concerns are understandable given real historical sins by professing Christians, yet the God of Scripture is the Creator of every people, not a Western invention; He acted in Egypt itself and sent the Gospel to Africa from the first century onward.

God is holy and just. All people have sinned and stand separated from Him, unable to restore themselves by rituals, ma'at, or any other path. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died as the penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation comes by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works or other deities.

Turn from sin (including idolatry) and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What has drawn you to look into Kemetism?

question: Should Christians be concerned about the idea of Sharia Law?
answer:
Yes, Christians should be concerned about Sharia Law as a comprehensive civil and religious system, because its classical sources and historical applications frequently clash with biblical justice, the equal dignity of every person made in God’s image, and liberty of conscience.

Sharia draws from the Quran, the Hadith, and later legal schools to regulate worship, family, crime, and public life. In practice this has often meant restrictions on Christians and other non-Muslims (dhimmi status, jizya tax, limits on church building and public witness), death penalties for apostasy or blasphemy in some jurisdictions, and unequal legal standing for women and non-Muslims. These outcomes contradict the God-given role of civil government to punish actual evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4) and the New Testament’s insistence that faith cannot be coerced. Jesus Himself said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36), and the apostles never called the church to wield the sword of the state to enforce worship.

At the same time, not every Muslim desires a fully implemented Sharia state, and many live peaceably under secular law. The deeper issue remains theological: Islam denies the Trinity, the deity of Christ, His substitutionary death, and His bodily resurrection. Those denials place it outside orthodox Christianity. The Bible therefore calls us to speak the truth in love rather than to treat all religions as equally saving paths (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Fear is not our posture; Christ has already overcome the world (John 16:33). Yet love of neighbor requires us to protect the vulnerable, to pray for those living under harsh applications of Sharia, and to seek the conversion of Muslims through the Gospel of grace rather than through political power.

A concrete next step is to pray regularly, using 1 Timothy 2:1–4, for governing authorities, for the persecuted church, and for Muslim neighbors to hear of Christ’s finished work. Then look for one ordinary way to show hospitality and to share the hope of the resurrection with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

question: What is the meaning of the foxes in Song of Solomon 2:15?
answer:
The little foxes in Song of Solomon 2:15 are destructive pests that spoil vineyards just as they begin to bloom. The verse says, “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in bloom” (Song of Solomon 2:15).

This is poetic imagery in a book that celebrates the love between a bride and groom. Faithful Christians have understood the foxes in more than one way, since Song of Solomon uses rich symbols rather than plain historical narrative, and such details are not essential to the faith. Some see the little foxes as small problems, unkind words, or neglected duties that can erode a marriage if left unaddressed. Others, drawing on the church’s long tradition of reading the Song as a picture of Christ and His bride, take the foxes as little sins, false teachings, or worldly distractions that threaten the fruit of God’s people.

In ancient Israel, foxes and jackals were known to damage young vines, so the picture would have been vivid. In either reading the call is the same: be watchful and catch what would ruin what God has made to flourish. This illustrates the Christian duty of watchfulness and the mortification of sin, even the small ones that hinder fruitfulness (Romans 8:13). A practical next step is to ask the Lord to show you any “little foxes” in your own life or relationships, then bring them to Him in repentance and seek help from mature believers in your local church.

question: What is the false cause fallacy?
answer:
The false cause fallacy is a logical error in which someone claims that one event or thing caused another without sufficient evidence of a real causal connection.

This informal fallacy often appears as assuming that because one event followed another, the first must have caused the second (post hoc ergo propter hoc), or as treating mere correlation as proof of causation.

A simple example is concluding that a lucky shirt caused a team’s victory simply because the wearer put it on before the game.

Scripture calls us to careful, truthful thinking rather than hasty assumptions. Proverbs 18:13 warns that answering a matter before hearing it is folly and shame. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 likewise urges believers to test all things and hold fast to what is good. Sound reasoning honors the God of truth.

question: Is it a sin to share copyrighted material on the internet?
answer:
Yes, sharing copyrighted material on the internet without the owner’s permission is a sin. It violates the command, “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15), and it fails to submit to the governing authorities God has appointed (Romans 13:1).

Copyright exists to protect the fruit of another person’s labor. Distributing their songs, films, books, software, or other work without authorization takes what belongs to them and withholds the payment or control they are due. That is a form of theft, even when no physical object changes hands. Christians are also called to honor civil law unless it requires disobedience to God; in ordinary cases, copyright law does not.

The fact that “everyone does it,” that it feels victimless, or that it happens in private does not make it righteous. God sees the heart and calls His people to integrity in hidden things as well as public ones (Ephesians 4:28).

If you have done this, the path of repentance is clear: stop, delete what you should not possess, and, where you can, obtain the work lawfully or simply do without it. Bring the matter to the Lord in prayer, asking Him for a clearer love of honesty and of your neighbor’s good. If the conviction lingers, speak with a pastor in your local church for further counsel.

question: What does the Bible say about Christian fathers?
answer:
The Bible presents Christian fathers as spiritual leaders who must raise their children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord without provoking them to anger, provide for their families, and lead their households in following God (Ephesians 6:4; 1 Timothy 5:8; Genesis 18:19).

In the Greco-Roman world of the New Testament, fathers held extensive household authority, yet Scripture uniquely restrains that power by forbidding provocation and centering fatherhood on the Lord's teaching rather than mere control (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21). Godly fathers diligently teach God's commands to their children throughout daily life so the next generation sets its hope in God (Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Psalm 78:4-7). They train children in the way they should go (Proverbs 22:6) and display the compassion the Lord Himself shows as Father (Psalm 103:13).

This calling is an expression of a father's loving headship in the home, exercised as he points his family to Christ. One concrete step a Christian father can take is to set a regular time, even a few minutes each evening, to read a short passage of Scripture with his children and pray specifically for their hearts to know the Lord.

question: What was the process of deciding on the Old Testament canon?
answer:
The Old Testament canon was recognized over centuries as God’s people received the writings He inspired through Moses and the prophets, rather than being fixed by one later council. By the first century, the Jewish Scriptures stood as the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings, which Jesus treated as God’s authoritative Word (Luke 24:44).

This recognition displays the inspiration of Scripture: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). The Jewish people were entrusted with these oracles of God (Romans 3:2). The Torah was received as immediately binding; prophetic books were added as they were given and tested against prior revelation; the Writings completed the collection. New Testament writers quote or allude to this body of books, and first-century Jewish testimony (such as Josephus) describes a closed set corresponding to the 39 books Protestants receive.

The early church inherited this Hebrew canon. The Greek Septuagint contained additional writings later called the Apocrypha or deuterocanonicals. Some church fathers cited them, and later Western councils included them in lists. These extra books, however, were not part of the Hebrew collection Jesus used and were not received as prophetic in the same way. Protestant churches therefore receive the 39 books that match the Hebrew Scriptures; Catholic and Orthodox traditions include the additional books on the basis of later ecclesiastical lists. Faithful Christians have differed on these boundaries, yet the essential confession remains that God has spoken inerrantly in the Scriptures that reveal His holiness, our sin, and the promised Messiah.

Read the Old Testament as the living Word that prepares the way for Christ. A simple next step is to open Luke 24, note how Jesus interprets “Moses and all the Prophets,” then ask God to help you see the same fulfillment as you read a portion of the Law or the Prophets this week.

question: Is cyber-sex / phone sex a sin?
answer:
Yes, cyber-sex and phone sex are sin. They fall under sexual immorality and lust, which God forbids.

Jesus taught that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5:27-28). The apostle Paul commands, “Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18). God designed sexual intimacy for the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman, and He will judge the sexually immoral (Hebrews 13:4; Genesis 2:24). These activities typically involve lustful descriptions, fantasies, or acts with someone who is not your spouse, violating that holy design.

I know this can be a real struggle in a digital age, with loneliness, easy access, and strong temptation. Many people battle these desires. Yet God’s standard remains clear, and true love does not approve of what He calls sin.

All of us have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as our substitutionary atonement, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By grace alone through faith alone in Him, we are justified and receive forgiveness and new life, not by our own efforts.

Turn from this sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

If this is a present struggle, a wise next step is to confess it honestly to God, then seek a pastor or mature believer in a local church for accountability and help walking in holiness. You can also pray directly to God, asking Him for strength to flee temptation and to love His design for purity (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5). How is this affecting you right now?

question: Do unbelievers immediately go to hell when they die?
answer:
Yes, Scripture teaches that the souls of unbelievers go immediately upon death into a place of conscious torment (often called Hades), while their bodies await the resurrection and Christ’s return for final judgment.

This involves the intermediate state, a point of some discussion among Christians because the Bible emphasizes the certainty of judgment more than every chronological detail, and phrases like “fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:13) can be read in more than one way. Faithful Christians agree, however, that those who die without faith in Christ face God’s just and eternal punishment.

One major historic view (held across most Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox teaching) is that there is an immediate particular judgment: the souls of the wicked enter torment in Hades, reserved until the great day, after which death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire (Luke 16:22–23; 2 Peter 2:9; Revelation 20:13–15). Another view, held by some groups, is that the dead remain unconscious until the resurrection, at which time unbelievers are judged and punished.

The account Jesus gave of the rich man and Lazarus, together with the immediate presence of believers with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23), points to conscious existence right after death for both the righteous and the lost. There is no second chance after death: “Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).

This is a sobering reality because God is holy and His wrath against sin is real. Every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works.

If you have not trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. You may wonder whether this is fair, especially for those who never heard, yet God has made Himself known in creation so that all are without excuse (Romans 1:20), and He now commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30).

Read Luke 16 and John 3, pray directly to God asking Him to give you understanding of His Word, and speak with a pastor in a Bible-believing local church.

question: How should Christians react to persecution against the LGBTQ community?
answer:
Christians must never join in violence, hatred, or unjust harm against anyone, including people who identify as LGBTQ. Every human being is made in the image of God and therefore possesses real dignity that we are bound to honor (Genesis 1:27). Jesus commands us to love our neighbor as ourselves and even to love those who oppose us (Mark 12:31; Matthew 5:44). We do not repay evil with evil, and we must not participate in bullying, assault, or cruelty (Romans 12:17-21).

At the same time, love does not mean affirming what God forbids. Scripture presents sexual activity as reserved for the covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6). Homosexual practice, like all other sexual immorality, is sin (Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10). Gender is given by God as male and female; rejecting that created order is not a path of life. True love warns of danger rather than celebrating it. We speak this plainly because the same God who made us also calls us to repentance and offers mercy.

The hope of the Gospel remains open to every sinner. All of us have fallen short (Romans 3:23). Christ died for the ungodly, was buried, and rose bodily (Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). In the Corinthian church some who had practiced homosexual acts were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11). That same grace is offered today: turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to pray for specific people you know who identify this way, asking God to give you both compassion and courage, then to seek one ordinary opportunity this week to treat them with kindness while remaining faithful to Scripture. Stay connected to a local church that holds both truth and love together, and let your elders help you walk this out.

question: How did Satan and other angels sin if heaven is sinless?
answer:
The Bible teaches that Satan and the other fallen angels were created good by God yet chose to rebel against Him in pride, after which they were expelled so that heaven, as the dwelling of the holy God, remains without sin. Heaven’s holiness does not mean created beings there lacked the capacity to choose; it means God does not permit iniquity to remain in His presence. Jude 6 speaks of “the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling.” 2 Peter 2:4 states that God “did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment.” Revelation 12:7-9 describes the resulting war in heaven, after which the dragon (Satan) and his angels were thrown down.

Scripture points to pride as the root: 1 Timothy 3:6 warns against conceit that leads to “the condemnation of the devil.” Passages such as Ezekiel 28:15 (“You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created until iniquity was found in you”) and Isaiah 14:12-15, though spoken against earthly kings, use language that many faithful readers have long seen as also describing this angelic fall. God is not the author of sin; the first iniquity arose in the creature’s own will. The details of that first choice remain partly mysterious, yet the outcome is clear: the holy angels continue in God’s presence while the rebels do not.

This warns us that even great privilege and a perfect environment cannot keep a heart from pride. Guard against it by daily humility before Christ, who defeated the devil through His death and resurrection, and by staying close to the means of grace in a local church.

question: What is the greatest sin?
answer:
The Bible identifies blasphemy against the Holy Spirit as the unforgivable sin (Matthew 12:31-32). Jesus taught that every other sin and blasphemy can be forgiven, yet this persistent, knowing rejection of the Spirit’s clear witness to Christ cannot, because it hardens the heart against the only source of pardon.

Jesus also named loving the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind as the greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38). The fundamental sin, therefore, is failing to love God, which appears as unbelief, idolatry, and pride. Every sin is an offense against God’s holiness and justly deserves His wrath.

All of us have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. If this question stirs anything in your own heart before God, open the Gospel of John this week and speak with a pastor in a Bible-preaching local church.

question: What does the Bible say about sedition?
answer:
