The Bible condemns sedition as sinful rebellion against the civil authorities God has appointed, while also requiring that believers obey God rather than men whenever a ruler commands what God forbids.

Romans 13:1-2 states, "Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God. Consequently, whoever resists the authority is opposing what God has instituted, and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves." The same chapter explains that the magistrate is "God’s servant for your good" who "does not bear the sword in vain" (Romans 13:4). First Peter 2:13-14 likewise commands, "Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good." Proverbs 24:21 warns, "My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not associate with those who rebel."

In Galatians 5:19-21 the works of the flesh include "hatred, discord, jealousy, rage, rivalries, divisions, factions," and those who practice such things "will not inherit the kingdom of God." Older English translations such as the King James Version render the Greek term *dichostasiai* as "seditions," capturing the idea of factious revolt. Scripture also records God’s judgment on actual rebellions, such as Korah’s uprising against Moses (Numbers 16:1-35) and Absalom’s conspiracy against David (2 Samuel 15:1-12; 2 Samuel 18:9-15).

At the same time, when human commands directly contradict God’s law, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29; see also Acts 4:19-20). Daniel’s friends refused idolatry (Daniel 3:16-18) and Daniel continued praying (Daniel 6:10) even under threat of death; they did not raise an armed revolt. Jesus Himself distinguished rendering to Caesar what is Caesar’s from rendering to God what is God’s (Matthew 22:21) and did not lead an insurrection against Rome.

God’s sovereignty therefore both establishes government as a common-grace restraint on evil and sets its limits. A concrete next step is to pray regularly for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2) and to honor them in speech and conduct (1 Peter 2:17), while remaining ready to suffer rather than sin if a law requires disobedience to Christ. Seek counsel from the elders of a local church if you face a specific conflict of conscience.

question: What is the International Christian Church (ICC), and what do they believe?
answer:
The International Christian Church (ICC), also called the SoldOut Movement, is a restorationist Christian group founded in 2006 by Kip McKean after his departure from the International Churches of Christ. It seeks to restore what it sees as first-century Christianity through aggressive evangelism, highly structured one-on-one discipleship, and a call for members to be fully “sold out” in commitment.

They affirm several historic Christian truths: one God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary, who died as a sacrifice for sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day; and the Bible as the inspired Word of God. They practice believer’s baptism by immersion and emphasize making disciples of all nations.

A central distinctive is their teaching that water baptism is necessary for the forgiveness of sins and entrance into salvation, drawing especially from Acts 2:38. They also require ongoing, directive “discipling” relationships in which a more mature member often exercises significant authority over another’s decisions, time, relationships, and finances. These practices flow from a view that true faith must be proven by total obedience and fruitfulness.

Scripture teaches that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:28; Romans 4:5). Baptism is a commanded sign of the inward grace already received by faith, not the instrument that obtains that grace. Adding any human act as a condition for justification mixes law with gospel and cannot save. The ICC’s intense control over members’ lives also risks replacing the freedom of the Spirit with human authority (Galatians 5:1; Colossians 2:20-23).

If you or someone you love is involved with the ICC, compare their teaching directly with the whole counsel of God, especially the letters of Paul on justification. Seek out a local church that clearly preaches Christ crucified and risen, and talk with its pastors. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

question: Do some Christmas traditions have pagan origins?
answer:
Yes, some Christmas traditions have historical ties to pagan or pre-Christian practices, such as the selection of December 25 near Roman winter festivals or the use of evergreens in ancient seasonal customs, though historians debate how much was direct borrowing, coincidence, or a later Christian alternative.

This is a tertiary matter of tradition and Christian liberty, not a core doctrine, because Scripture neither commands nor forbids a feast for Christ's birth, so faithful Christians may disagree in good conscience without it affecting the gospel or fellowship (Romans 14:5-6).

One historic Christian view holds that we should reject Christmas customs because of possible pagan roots, in order to keep worship free from any mixing with the practices of the nations (Deuteronomy 12:29-32).

Another historic view, equally within orthodox Christianity, is that we may celebrate the incarnation with joy and even adapt cultural elements, provided they now honor Christ rather than idols, since the present meaning and our freedom in non-essentials outweigh distant origins (Colossians 2:16-17; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

As one faithful option, I see liberty to remember Jesus' birth with gratitude and simple family observances that highlight the biblical incarnation, while staying cautious of superstition or commercial excess, because God the Son truly took on human nature and that event is worth treasuring.

Do not judge one another over days or customs, but pursue peace (Romans 14:13; Romans 14:19). A practical next step is to read Luke 2:1-20 and Matthew 1:18-25, then talk with your local church about how your household can honor Christ this season according to a clear conscience.

question: Where does the Old Testament predict the coming of Christ?
answer:
The Old Testament predicts the coming of Christ, the Messiah, in many passages that describe His lineage, birth, life, suffering, death, resurrection, and eternal reign. These messianic prophecies, from Genesis through Malachi, are fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth and display the unity of Scripture in God's plan of redemption.

Genesis 3:15 promises a descendant of the woman who would crush the serpent's head, pointing to Christ's victory over sin and Satan. Genesis 49:10 and 2 Samuel 7:12-16 identify Him as the ruler from Judah and the son of David whose throne would be established forever. Isaiah 7:14 and Micah 5:2 foretell His virgin birth in Bethlehem as Immanuel, God with us. Isaiah 9:6-7 presents the child born as Mighty God and Prince of Peace. Isaiah 53:4-6, 53:10-12 describes the suffering Servant who would bear our iniquities as a guilt offering, the heart of penal substitutionary atonement. Psalm 22:16-18 details the piercing of His hands and feet and the dividing of His garments. Zechariah 9:9 and Zechariah 12:10 portray the humble King who would be pierced.

These texts reveal that we are sinners in need of a Savior. Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as our substitute on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A helpful next step is to read Isaiah 53 slowly, then compare it with the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion. What stands out to you as you consider these promises?

question: What is spiritual adultery?
answer:
Spiritual adultery is unfaithfulness to God by giving worship, trust, or deepest love to idols, false gods, or the world rather than remaining exclusively devoted to Him. Scripture uses marriage imagery, with God as the faithful Husband and His people as His bride, so turning from Him is treated as adultery.

In the Old Testament the prophets charged Israel with this sin when they worshiped Baal and other gods (Hosea 2:2; Jeremiah 3:6-9; Ezekiel 16:15-32). James applies the same language to believers who love the world: "You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God" (James 4:4). Paul likewise describes the church as betrothed to Christ as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2). This is covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry, a breach of God's exclusive claim on His people (Exodus 34:14).

In daily life it can appear as trusting money, success, relationships, comfort, or even religious activity more than Christ Himself. Ask the Lord to search your heart using Psalm 139:23-24, and talk with a mature believer in your local church about any competing loves He exposes.

question: How can we rely on the power of God?
answer:
We rely on the power of God by turning from self-reliance to humble dependence on Him through faith in Christ, prayer, His Word, and the work of the Holy Spirit. Scripture shows that this power is not something we generate, but something we receive as we abide in Jesus, whose resurrection life is at work in those who belong to Him (Ephesians 1:19-20; John 15:5).

God often displays His strength most clearly in our weakness. The apostle Paul learned this when the Lord told him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). We therefore stop pretending we are sufficient and instead confess our need, asking the Father to strengthen us with power through His Spirit in our inner being (Ephesians 3:16). That is why we are told, “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts” (Zechariah 4:6). Faith looks away from our resources to His, trusting that those who wait on the Lord will renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31).

Practically, this happens through the ordinary means of grace. We pray, bringing every anxious thought to Him rather than striving in our own wisdom (Philippians 4:6-7; Proverbs 3:5-6). We read and meditate on Scripture so that faith is fed and our minds are renewed. We walk in fellowship with other believers, because God often supplies His power through the body of Christ. Progressive sanctification is not self-improvement; it is the Spirit applying the finished work of Christ to our daily battles with sin, fear, and weariness.

A simple next step is this: tomorrow morning, before you face the day’s demands, read Ephesians 3:14-21 slowly and pray in your own words, asking God to grant you strength according to His glorious might for the specific tasks and temptations ahead. Then tell a mature believer in your local church what you are learning so they can pray with you. God delights to meet those who come to Him in dependence, and He will not fail you.

question: What does it mean that Jesus fulfilled the law, but did not abolish it?
answer:
Jesus fulfilled the Law and the Prophets without abolishing them by bringing every command, type, and prophecy to its complete and intended goal in His person and work. In Matthew 5:17 He says, "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them."

"Fulfill" means to complete, accomplish, and fill out their full meaning, not to cancel their validity. Jesus did this through His perfect, lifelong obedience to every precept (His active obedience), His death as the true sacrifice that the temple rituals and priesthood foreshadowed, and His teaching that exposed the heart-level demands of God's commands rather than mere external compliance. He immediately adds that until heaven and earth pass away, not the smallest letter or stroke of a pen will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished (Matthew 5:18). This shows real continuity: God's moral standards, rooted in His unchanging holy character, remain.

The ceremonial aspects of the Law, such as animal sacrifices and food laws, find their fulfillment and thus their end in Christ, as Hebrews 10:1 explains that the law is only a shadow of the good things to come. The civil laws given to Israel as a nation are not binding on the church. Yet the moral law continues as the rule of life for believers, now written on our hearts in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10). This is why Paul can say that Christ is the culmination of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes (Romans 10:4), and yet that we do not nullify the law by this faith but uphold it (Romans 3:31).

Believers are not under the law as a covenant of works for justification. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, whose perfect righteousness is imputed to us. The law now serves as a guide for our sanctification as we walk by the Spirit. Some historic Christian views, particularly certain dispensational approaches, emphasize a sharper break, seeing the Mosaic Law as entirely fulfilled and set aside so that Christians live only under New Testament commands. The Reformed view, which I hold as one faithful option within historic Christianity, sees greater continuity in the moral law as an expression of God's eternal character, while recognizing the new covenant's distinctiveness in how that law is administered through Christ and the Spirit.

This frees us from both legalism (trying to earn God's favor by rule-keeping) and lawlessness (ignoring God's standards). A practical next step is to read Matthew 5:17-48 this week, asking the Lord to show you both how Jesus has fulfilled these commands for you and how the Spirit now enables you to live them from the heart.

question: What are the Major Prophets and Minor Prophets?
answer:
The Major Prophets are Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Daniel. The Minor Prophets (also called the Twelve) are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

These names simply distinguish the longer books from the shorter ones. They do not rank importance, since all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). These prophets spoke God’s Word to Israel and Judah across centuries of covenant unfaithfulness, exile, and return. They announced His holiness and just wrath against sin, called the people to repentance, and held out sure hope of restoration through the coming Messiah. All of that finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the true and final Prophet, through whom God has now spoken fully (Hebrews 1:1-2; Luke 24:27). As you read them, look for how they prepare the way for Christ’s atoning death and resurrection and for the new covenant He established.

question: Why believe in Jesus?
answer:
You may find it challenging to believe in Jesus when many voices treat all spiritual paths as equally valid, or when He is viewed only as a wise teacher rather than God Himself. Those reactions are understandable in a world full of competing claims.

The Bible teaches that God is holy, just, and loving, yet His wrath against sin is real. Every person has sinned and falls short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), leaving us separated from Him; the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and no amount of good works can bridge that gap. In His mercy God sent His Son: Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union), who took on human nature in the incarnation, lived a sinless life, and died on the cross as a penal substitutionary atonement for our sins. He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, proving His victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 3:16). He is now the exalted Lord.

Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus declared, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

A helpful next step is to read the Gospel of John, asking God to show you the truth about Jesus as you do, and to connect with a local church that faithfully teaches the Bible. What has shaped your view of Jesus so far?

question: What is a Bible Baptist Church, and what do Bible Baptists believe?
answer:
A Bible Baptist Church is typically an independent Baptist congregation that names itself this way to stress the Bible as the inspired, inerrant, and sufficient Word of God (sola Scriptura) together with historic Baptist convictions, especially the baptism of professing believers by immersion.

Many such churches grew out of the twentieth-century fundamentalist movement that defended the core truths of Scripture against theological liberalism. They commonly belong to or resemble fellowships such as the Bible Baptist Fellowship International, remaining autonomous while cooperating in missions and church planting.

Bible Baptists affirm the essential doctrines of the faith. They believe in one God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union), conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, who lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and will return personally (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Those who truly trust Him are kept by God’s power and will not finally fall away.

They practice two ordinances given by Christ: believer’s baptism (credo-baptism) by immersion as a public testimony of faith and union with Christ (Acts 8:36-38; Matthew 28:19), and the Lord’s Supper as a memorial of His death (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). The local church is autonomous and congregational, led by pastors and served by deacons, with a strong emphasis on evangelism, discipleship, and the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18-20; Acts 2:41-42).

On secondary and tertiary matters they often hold a dispensational reading of Scripture, a premillennial view of Christ’s return (frequently with a pretribulational rapture), and a practice of personal and ecclesiastical separation. Faithful Christians may differ on these points of eschatology and church practice without compromising the gospel; they belong to the realm of Christian liberty where conscience and charity should prevail (Romans 14:1-6). Some Bible Baptist churches also prefer or require the King James Version, though this is not universal.

If you are considering such a church, the most helpful next step is to visit, hear the preaching of the Word, and speak with the pastor about how they handle Scripture, the gospel, baptism, and membership.

question: What is sexual ethics?
answer:
Sexual ethics is the set of moral principles that govern right and wrong in sexual thoughts, desires, and actions.

Scripture teaches that God created sexuality as a good gift, to be expressed exclusively within the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 1:27-28; Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6). In that union it pictures Christ’s love for the church and serves fruitfulness and one-flesh unity (Ephesians 5:31-32). Sexual activity outside this design, including fornication, adultery, and homosexual practice, is sin against God’s holy standard (Hebrews 13:4; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Romans 1:26-27).

The Gospel still offers real hope: those who repent and trust in Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection are washed, sanctified, and justified, then called to honor God with their bodies by fleeing sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:11; 1 Corinthians 6:18-20).

question: What is spiritual sickness? What does it mean to be spiritually sick?
answer:
Spiritual sickness is the Bible’s way of describing the soul under the power of sin: a condition that corrupts our thoughts, desires, and will, cuts us off from the holy God, and leaves us unable to make ourselves spiritually well.

To be spiritually sick means to be a sinner who needs Jesus Christ as Physician rather than a person who can heal or justify himself.

Jesus put it plainly: “It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:31-32). The Old Testament already pictured this: “The whole head is injured, the whole heart is sick. From the sole of the foot to the head, there is no soundness—only wounds and welts and festering sores” (Isaiah 1:5-6). Jeremiah adds that “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure” (Jeremiah 17:9). This is the fruit of the Fall: every part of us is affected, so that we are spiritually dead in trespasses even while we still breathe (Ephesians 2:1).

The only cure is the Gospel. Christ was pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities; “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness (1 Peter 2:24). His bodily resurrection proves the healing is real and complete for all who are united to Him by faith. This is not self-improvement but regeneration by the Holy Spirit, justification by grace through faith, and then progressive sanctification as we walk with Him.

If you sense this sickness in yourself, the next step is to bring it honestly to God in prayer, asking Him to search your heart (Psalm 139:23-24) as you read a passage such as Psalm 51 or Romans 3, and to speak with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk with you.

question: What is fellowship with God?
answer:
Fellowship with God is the believer’s living communion with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a shared life of love, truth, and purpose made possible through union with Christ.

The apostle John writes, “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3). This sharing (the New Testament word often translated fellowship) is not a distant acquaintance or a mere claim of spirituality. John immediately clarifies that those who walk in darkness while claiming fellowship with God are lying, yet “if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:6-7). Paul likewise points to its Trinitarian shape: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).

This communion rests on Christ’s finished work and is enjoyed as we abide in Him, like branches remaining in the vine (John 15:4-5). Practically, it is cultivated by turning to God in honest prayer, receiving His Word, confessing sin, and walking in obedience with other believers in a local church. Open 1 John this week and pray through it, asking the Lord to make this fellowship more real in your daily life.

question: What role does Iran play in the end times?
answer:
The Bible mentions Persia, corresponding to modern Iran, as one of the nations allied with Gog in a prophesied conflict against Israel in Ezekiel 38:5. This belongs to eschatology, a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, because prophetic texts often use vivid, symbolic language and do not always give exhaustive detail tying every ancient name to a specific modern nation-state.

One major view, common among dispensational premillennial Christians, is that Iran will join a northern coalition to invade Israel in the last days, after which God Himself will intervene and destroy the attackers to display His glory (Ezekiel 38:16; Ezekiel 38:18-23; Ezekiel 39:21-22). Another historic view, held by many amillennial and some historic premillennial Christians, treats Ezekiel 38–39 as portraying the climactic hostility of worldly powers against God and His people, which may unfold spiritually across the church age or at the final rebellion, without requiring a one-to-one match with today’s Iran. Revelation 20:8 uses similar Gog and Magog language for a last uprising, supporting a more typological reading.

In these non-essentials we have Christian liberty (Romans 14:5). What Scripture makes plain, and what unites believers, is that Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead. A helpful next step is to read Ezekiel 38–39 in its full context, noting the Lord’s complete sovereignty over the nations, and to pray for the Iranian people, that many would trust in Christ for forgiveness and new life.

question: What does Jesus mean when He says, “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” in the gospels?
answer:
When Jesus says “Truly, truly” or “Verily, verily,” He is solemnly declaring that the words that follow are absolutely certain, reliable, and spoken with His own divine authority.

The phrase translates the Greek “amēn amēn legō hymin,” drawn from the Hebrew “amen,” meaning “truly,” “it is firm,” or “so be it.” In first-century Jewish practice, people normally used “amen” at the end of a statement to confirm someone else’s words. Jesus uniquely places it at the beginning of His own teaching, claiming that He Himself is the source of truth rather than merely affirming another.

This doubled form appears most often in the Gospel of John (about 25 times) to introduce weighty revelations about new birth, eternal life, His relationship with the Father, and His identity as the Son (John 3:3; John 3:5; John 5:24; John 6:47). It functions as a verbal seal of self-attestation, underscoring that Jesus is the Truth incarnate whose words we may trust completely (John 14:6).

When you meet these words in Scripture, slow down and receive them as the Lord’s own voice. Read one of the “truly, truly” sayings in John this week, and ask God to help you believe and obey what Jesus has made sure.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Asher?
answer:
The tribe of Asher teaches us that God gives His people rich covenant blessings and calls us to receive them with gratitude, use them to serve others, and pursue complete obedience rather than partial faithfulness.

Asher’s name means “happy” or “blessed,” given when Leah rejoiced at his birth (Genesis 30:13). Jacob later prophesied, “Asher’s food will be rich; he will provide royal delicacies” (Genesis 49:20). Moses added that Asher would be “most blessed of sons,” favored among his brothers, bathing his feet in oil, with gates bolted in iron and bronze and strength matching his days (Deuteronomy 33:24-25). Their allotted land along the northern coast was fertile and oil-rich, a real fulfillment of the Abrahamic land promise in its Ancient Near Eastern tribal setting.

Yet they did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants of their towns (Judges 1:31-32) and, in Deborah’s day, “remained at the seacoast and stayed in his harbors” (Judges 5:17). That incomplete conquest pictures remaining sin that must be put to death; it reminds us of the need for progressive sanctification by the Holy Spirit through the ordinary means of grace. God still preserved a remnant: some from Asher humbled themselves and came to Hezekiah’s Passover (2 Chronicles 30:11), and the prophetess Anna of the tribe of Asher waited faithfully in the temple and recognized the infant Christ (Luke 2:36-38). Even Asher appears among the sealed people of God in Revelation 7:6.

In Christ we have far richer spiritual food than olive oil and royal delicacies. Receive those gifts without apology, then spend them for others rather than coexisting with lingering compromise. This week read Deuteronomy 33:24-25 and Luke 2:36-38, thank God directly for one concrete blessing He has given you, and ask Him to make your strength equal your days in serving your local church.

question: Why does the Bible speak against braided hair?
answer:
The Bible does not forbid braided hair as something sinful in itself. In 1 Timothy 2:9 and 1 Peter 3:3 the apostles warn Christian women against using elaborate braided hairstyles (along with gold, pearls, and costly clothing) as a way to display wealth, status, or vanity, and they call them instead to modest apparel and the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit.

In the Greco-Roman world of the first century, ornate braided styles interwoven with jewels were often a mark of luxury and sometimes associated with immorality or social climbing. Paul and Peter contrast that kind of outward show with the unfading beauty of a heart transformed by Christ (1 Peter 3:3-4; 1 Timothy 2:9-10). The concern is the heart’s orientation in sanctification: our appearance should not compete with or contradict a life of good works and humility before God.

This is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty and the application of modesty, where Scripture gives a principle more than a detailed dress code, so faithful Christians have differed. Some groups have taken the verses as a standing rule against braiding hair or wearing jewelry, seeing simplicity itself as a required mark of holiness. Others have understood the passages as culturally specific examples of a lasting call to avoid ostentation and self-promotion, so that modest braids today are a matter of conscience rather than a command.

Romans 14 teaches us not to pass judgment on one another in disputable matters of this kind. A helpful next step is to ask whether your own choices in appearance seek to honor Christ and serve others without drawing undue attention, then talk it over with a mature sister or the elders in your local church as you pursue the inner adornment that is precious in God’s sight.

question: What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?
answer:
A contract is a mutual legal agreement that depends on both parties meeting specified conditions and can be canceled if those terms fail. A covenant, especially as God makes them in Scripture, is a solemn, binding relationship that God Himself initiates and guarantees by oath and often by blood, establishing a gracious bond that He upholds even when His people do not.

This distinction matters because the Bible presents God's dealings with humanity through covenants rather than contracts. He swore a covenant to Abraham while Abraham slept, walking alone between the pieces as the greater party who bound Himself (Genesis 15:17-18; Hebrews 6:13-18). The new covenant is likewise secured by Christ's blood, not by our performance (Luke 22:20; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:6-13). The theological term that captures this is the covenant of grace, in which God unilaterally promises redemption through the Mediator, Jesus Christ.

Because our standing with God is covenantal rather than contractual, failure does not void the relationship. You can therefore rest in Christ's finished work instead of treating obedience as a bargaining chip, and you can pray the promises of the new covenant back to God as a child rather than a negotiator.

question: If Jesus was God, why did He say "No one is good but God alone"?
answer:
Jesus was not denying His deity when He said, “Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18). He was pressing a man who had just called Him “Good Teacher” to face what that word truly means.

Some hear this as Jesus distancing Himself from God, as if He were admitting He was only a good man or correcting a title He did not deserve. The context and the rest of Scripture show otherwise. The rich young ruler ran up, knelt, and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus first directed him to God’s unique goodness, then to the commandments. When the man claimed he had kept them all, Jesus looked at him with love and told him to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow Him (Mark 10:17–22). By claiming the authority to demand total allegiance and to grant treasure in heaven, Jesus was acting as God, not as a mere teacher.

Jesus elsewhere calls Himself “the good shepherd” who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). The New Testament repeatedly affirms that He is without sin (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). The statement therefore fits the hypostatic union: Jesus is truly God and truly man. As man He points people to the Father; as God He shares the Father’s unique goodness.

This encounter also exposes our own condition. The young man thought he was already good enough. Jesus showed that no one is. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). We cannot inherit eternal life by our works. Jesus, who is God, took on human nature, lived a perfectly good life, died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What do you make of Jesus’ identity after looking at this passage in its setting?

question: What does it mean that God will reveal the hidden things (Daniel 2:22 and 28)?
answer:
God revealing the hidden things in Daniel 2:22 and Daniel 2:28 means that He alone knows and discloses mysteries, secrets of the heart, and future events that no human wisdom or pagan practice can uncover. In the immediate setting, God made known to Daniel both the forgotten content of King Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and its interpretation about successive kingdoms, which the Babylonian wise men could not discover.

This displays God’s omniscience, for “He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him” (Daniel 2:22). The secret things belong to the Lord, yet He reveals what His people need (Deuteronomy 29:29). Unlike the court magicians, the God of heaven “reveals mysteries” and showed the king “what will happen in days to come” (Daniel 2:28), pointing finally to the everlasting kingdom God Himself would set up (Daniel 2:44). All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are now found in Christ (Colossians 2:3).

When you face what is hidden or uncertain, follow Daniel’s example by gathering with other believers to seek God in prayer (Daniel 2:17-18). Ask Him for wisdom, which He gives generously (James 1:5), and rest in what He has already made plain in Scripture rather than in speculation.

question: What items should be included in a church constitution?
answer:
A church constitution should include the church's name and purpose, a statement of faith, membership processes, officer qualifications and duties, meeting procedures, the ordinances, church discipline, and an amendment process. These elements help a local church live under Christ's headship with clarity and order, as Scripture requires that all things be done in a fitting and orderly way (1 Corinthians 14:40).

A statement of faith should confess the core doctrines of the faith, including the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, the authority of Scripture, justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and the Gospel of Christ's atoning death and bodily resurrection. Membership articles typically describe how a person joins (a credible profession of faith, together with believer's baptism by immersion in a Baptist context), the duties of members, and the process of restoration or exclusion, following the pattern of Matthew 18:15–17. Officers should be defined by the qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:1–13 and Titus 1:5–9, with elders leading the congregation while the members participate in major decisions.

Other historic churches organize authority differently. Presbyterian constitutions, for example, often give greater standing to a session and broader connectional courts because they see that structure as a wise application of shared elder rule across congregations.

From a Reformed Baptist perspective, an elder-led congregational constitution best reflects the New Testament pattern of qualified local elders shepherding a gathered body of believers who together affirm key matters of doctrine, membership, and mission (Acts 14:23; 1 Peter 5:1–4). This preserves both biblical leadership and the priesthood of all believers without requiring a particular tertiary detail such as exact meeting frequency or property language.

If you are drafting or revising such a document, gather with your elders or a few mature members, pray together for wisdom (James 1:5), and read the relevant passages as a group before comparing a sample constitution from a like-minded church. Speak directly to the Lord about unity and faithfulness as you work.

question: What is topical preaching? Should a pastor preach topically?
answer:
Topical preaching is a method in which a pastor selects a subject (such as prayer, holiness, marriage, or the attributes of God) and then gathers and explains various passages of Scripture that address that theme, rather than unfolding one continuous passage in its original literary context.

Whether a pastor should preach topically is a matter of pastoral wisdom and Christian liberty, not a test of orthodoxy. Scripture commands pastors to preach the word and to declare the whole counsel of God (2 Timothy 4:2; Acts 20:27), yet it does not prescribe only one homiletical form. Faithful Christians have therefore differed.

One historic approach, common among many Reformed and Puritan ministers, treats consecutive exposition of entire books as the ordinary diet of the church. This keeps the preacher bound to the text’s own agenda, supplies balanced teaching over time, and helps the congregation hear Scripture in context.

Another historic approach, used by many evangelists and pastors including Charles Spurgeon, treats topical preaching as a legitimate and often powerful way to apply the Bible to particular needs, to proclaim the gospel on a given theme, or to address urgent pastoral questions.

A pastor may preach topically, especially for evangelistic services, special occasions, or specific congregational needs. At the same time, the regular Lord’s Day ministry is wisest when it is primarily consecutive exposition, so that God’s people receive the whole counsel of God rather than a preacher’s preferred topics. In either method the texts themselves must still be handled according to their original meaning.

If you are considering this for your own preaching, begin by praying through 2 Timothy 4:1-5, talk it over with your fellow elders, and let the congregation’s actual spiritual diet (not merely your preferences) guide the mix of consecutive and topical sermons.

question: What are tribulation saints?
answer:
Tribulation saints typically refers to people who come to saving faith in Jesus Christ during a future period of intense global suffering called the Great Tribulation. The phrase itself does not appear in Scripture but is drawn from passages such as Revelation 7:13-14, where an elder identifies a great multitude: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

This language is most common in dispensational premillennial eschatology, which sees the church raptured before a distinct seven-year tribulation, after which many Jews and Gentiles believe and often face martyrdom under the Antichrist. Eschatology (the doctrine of last things) is a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree without compromising the gospel. Apocalyptic texts such as Daniel, Matthew 24, and Revelation use symbolic imagery that has been interpreted in different ways throughout church history, while all orthodox views confess Christ’s personal, bodily return to judge the living and the dead.

Another historic Christian reading (amillennial or historic premillennial) sees no sharp separation between the church and a later group of tribulation saints. In this view the “great tribulation” describes either the entire age of the church’s suffering between Christ’s first and second coming or a climactic intensification that the church itself endures. All who trust in Christ are therefore saints who come through tribulation, cleansed by His blood (John 16:33; Revelation 7:14). There is one people of God, not two.

These differences do not affect the essentials: Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died as a penal substitution for sinners, rose bodily, and will return. Regardless of the precise timeline, Scripture calls every believer to persevere by grace. A helpful next step is to read Revelation 7 slowly in its larger context, then talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about how the passage encourages endurance today.

question: Who are the Black Hebrews / Black Israelites?
answer:
The Black Hebrews or Black Israelites (often called Hebrew Israelites) are a loosely related set of African American religious movements, mostly arising in the United States from the late 1800s onward, that claim people of African descent, especially African Americans, are the true ethnic descendants of the ancient Israelites of the Bible.

These groups are not one church or denomination. Some live quietly and emphasize Old Testament practices such as Sabbath-keeping and dietary laws. Others, especially certain street-preaching sects, teach that African Americans (and sometimes Latinos and Native Americans) are the lost tribes of Israel, that modern Jews are impostors, and that salvation or covenant blessing belongs to their ethnic group. A few of the more extreme voices have mixed this with racial hostility. Mainstream Judaism does not recognize them as Jewish, and their teachings usually stand apart from historic Christian orthodoxy.

Scripture presents the Israelites as a real people descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, through whom God brought the Messiah, Jesus Christ, who was born a Jew of the line of David (Matthew 1:1-17; Romans 9:4-5). The Bible never makes skin color the basis of covenant identity, nor does it restrict the Gospel to one ethnicity. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Christ died as a substitutionary atonement for sinners and rose bodily, so that whoever believes in Him, Jew or Gentile, is justified by grace through faith alone, not by ancestry or law-keeping (Romans 3:21-26; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8-9). In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Galatians 3:28). The church is now the people of God drawn from every nation (Matthew 28:19; Revelation 7:9-10). Ethnic pride, even when it arises from real historical pain, cannot replace this Gospel.

If this movement has shaped your view of God, identity, or Scripture, the next step is to read the New Testament itself, beginning with Romans and Galatians, and to talk with a pastor in a local church that holds to the historic Christian faith. True belonging is found in Christ, not in a racial reconstruction of Israel.

question: What does the Bible say about church-hopping?
answer:
The Bible does not use the term "church-hopping," but it calls believers to devoted, ongoing life in a local church rather than a pattern of continually moving from one congregation to another. Hebrews 10:24-25 says, "And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching."

Scripture presents the church as Christ's body, in which every believer is a member who belongs and contributes rather than remaining an independent consumer. 1 Corinthians 12:27 states, "Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it." Ephesians 4:16 adds that "the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part." Frequent hopping often prevents the very things God designed the local church to give: mutual encouragement, the use of spiritual gifts, and real accountability under shepherds who know you. Hebrews 13:17 instructs, "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who must give an account."

The earliest believers modeled this devoted belonging. Acts 2:42 records, "They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer." Valid reasons exist to leave a church (false teaching, relocation, or a congregation that no longer preaches the gospel), yet a restless habit of moving to avoid difficulty, preference, or accountability sits at odds with this New Testament pattern.

If this describes your situation, a wise next step is to pray for wisdom, then speak with the elders of a gospel-preaching church about membership and a concrete way you can serve. Plant yourself there, receive the Word, and let others know you, trusting that Christ uses imperfect local churches to grow His people.

question: Dance in worship - what does the Bible say?
answer:
The Bible records dancing as a joyful, bodily expression of praise after God's deliverance, as when Miriam and the women danced with tambourines after the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 15:20) and when David leaped and whirled before the Lord as the ark was brought to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:14-16). The Psalms likewise call God's people to praise His name with dancing (Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4). The New Testament, however, never mentions dance among the gathered church's practices, which center on the apostles' teaching, prayer, the Lord's Supper, fellowship, and singing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (Acts 2:42; Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16).

Dance in corporate worship is a tertiary matter of worship style, not an essential of the faith. Faithful Christians may disagree here because the New Testament gives less explicit instruction on physical expressions in the assembly than the Old Testament festival examples, and because churches differ on how much continuity to draw between Israel's celebrations and New Covenant gathered worship.

Some Christians, looking to the Psalms and David's example, view dance as a fitting, even wholehearted, form of doxology when it is decent, God-focused, and culturally appropriate, seeing the body as part of offering ourselves as living sacrifices.

Others, applying the regulative principle of worship, conclude that the church should use only those elements God has appointed in the New Testament for the assembly, so that dance, while perhaps a personal or cultural expression of joy, is not an element of Lord's Day worship, in order to keep the focus on the preached Word and to do all things decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

In matters of Christian liberty outside clear command or prohibition we are not to judge one another's consciences (Romans 14:3-5), yet corporate worship must still edify the whole body. Whatever practice a church adopts, the heart of worship remains spirit and truth (John 4:24), not the form itself.

A wise next step is to read 2 Samuel 6 and Psalm 150 in their contexts this week, then talk humbly with your church's elders about how your congregation can honor God together without distraction or division.

question: What is secular humanism?
answer:
Secular humanism is a non-theistic worldview that treats human reason, science, and experience as the highest authorities for knowledge, ethics, and meaning, typically without God, Scripture, or the supernatural.

It commonly affirms that people create their own values, that the universe is explained by natural processes, and that religion is unnecessary or even an obstacle to human progress. Documents such as the Humanist Manifestos have expressed this outlook, presenting humanity itself as the source of dignity and moral direction.

Scripture gives a different account. God has made Himself known through creation, yet people suppress that truth and exchange the glory of the Creator for created things, including the elevation of human autonomy itself (Romans 1:18–25). Humans do possess real dignity because they are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), yet that dignity is not self-generated. It is received from the holy, sovereign God who also justly judges sin.

Secular humanism often appeals because it promises compassion, science, and freedom from religious conflict. Those desires are understandable, yet they cannot finally ground objective morality or answer death and guilt. The Bible locates true human worth and hope in Christ, who is truly God and truly man, who died and rose bodily, and who alone reconciles sinners to God by grace through faith.

If you are weighing this worldview, read Romans 1–3 slowly and ask the Lord to show you whether human reason is a sufficient foundation, or whether we need the God who made us. A wise next step is to discuss these questions with a mature believer in a local church that holds the Scriptures as God’s inerrant Word.

question: Does the Bible predict the destruction of Damascus?
answer:
Yes, the Bible contains several oracles of judgment that predict the destruction of Damascus.

Isaiah 17:1 states, "This is an oracle concerning Damascus: “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.”" Parallel words of coming fire and ruin appear in Jeremiah 49:23-27 and Amos 1:3-5. These were spoken in the eighth and seventh centuries BC, when Damascus (capital of Aram) stood as an enemy of Israel and Judah. The Hebrew term often translated "oracle" is massa, a burdensome message of divine judgment that also appears in other oracles against the nations, underscoring the Lord's rule over every kingdom.

Faithful Christians differ on the timing of fulfillment, a tertiary matter of eschatological interpretation on which believers may disagree without compromising the essentials of the faith (Romans 14). One historic view holds that the words were fulfilled when Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III captured Damascus in 732 BC, ending Aram as a kingdom even though the city was later rebuilt. Another view, noting that Damascus remains one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, sees a still-future, more complete destruction.

In either reading, the passages display God's justice and sovereignty over the nations. They ultimately point us to the personal, bodily return of Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead. As you study these texts, read Isaiah 17 in its full literary context (including the linked judgment on northern Israel) and pray that the Lord would give you a deeper trust in His unchanging Word rather than in any earthly city or power.

question: What does it mean to watch and pray?
answer:
To watch and pray means to remain spiritually awake and on guard against temptation, while depending on God through continual prayer. Jesus gave this command in Gethsemane: "Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (Matthew 26:41).

In the original Greek, "watch" (gregoreo) means to stay awake like a night sentry, alert rather than drowsy or careless. Scripture joins this vigilance with prayer because our flesh is weak, the devil prowls, and Christ will return at an unexpected hour (1 Peter 5:8; Mark 13:33; Colossians 4:2). Watching without prayer becomes self-reliance; prayer without watching becomes unfocused. Together they belong to progressive sanctification: we rest in Christ's finished work while the Spirit uses these means of grace to keep us from falling.

A simple next step is to spend ten quiet minutes each evening this week praying through Psalm 139:23-24, asking the Lord to search your heart and then naming any temptation He brings to mind so you can watch against it.

question: How is eternity in Hell a fair punishment for sin?
answer:
This question weighs heavily on many hearts, because eternity in hell can seem far out of proportion to a finite lifetime of sin. You may wonder how finite acts could ever warrant infinite punishment, or how a God of love could allow anyone to suffer forever.

The Bible teaches that the seriousness of sin is measured not mainly by how long the act lasted, but by the infinite holiness and worth of the God against whom it is committed. Every sin is ultimately against Him: “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight” (Psalm 51:4). Because God is infinitely majestic, rebellion against Him is infinitely serious. Hell is not an arbitrary overreaction; it is the just expression of His unchanging holiness and justice. Scripture speaks of “eternal punishment” in the same breath as “eternal life” (Matthew 25:46), of “eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord” (2 Thessalonians 1:9), and of the second death in the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14-15). The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and that death is everlasting because the offense is against an everlasting God.

God is perfectly just; He never punishes more than is deserved. At the same time He is patient, “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). He has given every person the witness of creation and conscience (Romans 1:18-20; Romans 2:14-15). Heaven is never owed; it is sheer mercy. Hell is what justice requires when that mercy is finally refused.

That is why the cross is necessary. Only the infinite Son of God, truly God and truly man, could bear an infinite debt. Jesus lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary atonement in our place, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Ask God in prayer to give you a clearer sight of His holiness (perhaps by reading Isaiah 6 or Romans 3), and talk with a pastor in a Bible-believing church about these things. What part of this question is most on your mind right now?

question: How is Satan god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4)?
answer:
Satan is called the god of this age in 2 Corinthians 4:4 because he exercises a real yet limited and temporary influence as the ruler of the present fallen world system, blinding the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. This does not mean Satan is a true deity, an equal rival to the living God, or the rightful owner of creation. He is a created, fallen angel who gained sway through humanity’s sin and now operates as a usurper and deceiver within this present evil age.

Scripture consistently describes him in these terms without granting him independent sovereignty. Jesus called him the ruler of this world who stands already judged (John 12:31; John 16:11). Paul identifies him as the prince of the power of the air, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2). John writes that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19), and Paul speaks of this present evil age from which Christ delivers us (Galatians 1:4). The title therefore highlights the spiritual conflict of this age: the world as a system in rebellion against God, under Satan’s blinding influence, yet still fully subject to the Father’s sovereign rule. God remains holy, supreme, and in control; Satan can act only within the bounds God permits, as the book of Job makes plain.

This truth presses us toward both humility and hope. The gospel itself is the God-ordained means by which the Holy Spirit opens blinded eyes, and Christ’s death, burial, and bodily resurrection have already disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15). One practical step is to pray specifically for those around you who do not yet see Christ’s glory, asking the Lord to remove the veil while you speak the truth in love and refuse to conform to the world’s values (Romans 12:2).

question: Is faith intellectual assent?
answer:
No, saving faith is not merely intellectual assent to facts about God or the gospel. Biblical faith includes knowing the truth, agreeing that it is true, and personally trusting in Jesus Christ, receiving and resting on Him alone for justification (being declared righteous before God) and eternal life.

James 2:19 makes the distinction plain: “You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.” Demons possess accurate knowledge and even assent, yet they remain unsaved because they do not trust or submit to Christ. The New Testament repeatedly calls people to believe in Christ, not merely that certain statements about Him are true (John 1:12; John 3:16; Romans 10:9-10). This personal reliance, often called trust, is essential; without it, agreement with Christian teaching remains empty.

Such faith is itself a gift of God, produced by the Holy Spirit through the Word, so that we cast ourselves upon Christ rather than our own understanding or effort (Ephesians 2:8-9). If your faith has been only mental agreement so far, a concrete next step is to read John 3 slowly, asking God to grant you a heart that actually rests on His Son, and then speak with a pastor in a local church that preaches the gospel clearly.

question: What does it mean to be saved by grace?
answer:
To be saved by grace means that God freely gives undeserving sinners forgiveness, new life, and eternal standing with Him as a gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ rather than earned by our works, goodness, or religious effort. This is justification by grace alone: God declares the ungodly righteous solely because of what Christ has done, not because of anything we contribute.

All of us have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), and a holy God justly opposes sin. Yet in love He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, He lived a perfect life in our place, died on the cross as our substitute in penal substitutionary atonement, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is now exalted as Lord. Salvation is therefore “by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). Grace is God’s unmerited favor; faith is simply trusting Christ alone.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If you already belong to Him, rest in His finished work instead of striving to earn what He has already given, and keep growing in sanctification through the Word, prayer, and a faithful local church. Open Ephesians 2 today and thank God for this gift, then talk with a pastor or mature believer about how this grace is shaping your life.

question: What is the kalam cosmological argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The kalam cosmological argument is a philosophical argument for God's existence that reasons from the fact that the universe began to exist to the conclusion that it must have a transcendent cause. In its basic form it runs: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause.

That cause, the argument continues, must be spaceless, timeless, immaterial, enormously powerful, and personal (able to choose to create), which matches the God revealed in Scripture as the eternal, uncaused Creator. Genesis 1:1 declares, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." Hebrews 11:3 adds, "By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible."

This line of reasoning does not replace the Bible; it simply shows that reason and the observable beginning of the cosmos point in the same direction as the opening words of Scripture. The God who caused all things is the same God who later took on flesh in Jesus Christ, lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, and rose bodily from the dead. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

question: Why is the virgin birth so important?
answer:
The virgin birth is so important because it is the historical means of the Incarnation, by which the eternal Son of God took on a true human nature in the womb of the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, remaining fully God and becoming fully man in one person without original sin.

This event fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah 7:14 and is recorded as fact in Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:26-38, where Mary conceives as a virgin and the child is called Immanuel, God with us. The result is the hypostatic union: two natures, divine and human, united in Jesus Christ from conception onward. Because He had no earthly father, Jesus did not inherit Adam’s guilt, remaining the sinless last Adam who could represent us and offer Himself as the perfect substitute.

All people have sinned and stand separated from the holy God, unable to save themselves. Jesus, born of the virgin, lived a sinless life, died on the cross in our place, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing justification by grace through faith in Him alone.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, died, and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A helpful next step is to read Luke 1:26-38 slowly this week, asking God to deepen your wonder at this truth, and then talk it over with a mature believer in your local church. How does the virgin birth shape the way you worship and trust Jesus as both God and man?

question: How can I overcome disappointment with life?
answer:
Disappointment with life is a heavy burden, and that sense of let-down can leave even ordinary days feeling empty. Jesus acknowledged this reality plainly: in this world you will have tribulation, but take heart, He has overcome the world (John 16:33).

We face disappointment because we live in a fallen creation that groans under the effects of sin (Romans 8:22). God is holy and just, so the consequences of the fall are real. Yet He is also gracious and faithful. For those who belong to Christ, He works all things together for good, conforming us to the image of His Son through progressive sanctification even in painful seasons (Romans 8:28-29). Our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed (Romans 8:18). Jesus, truly God and truly man, experienced sorrow Himself and can sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). Because He died, was buried, and rose bodily, we have a living hope, and He will return to renew all things, wiping away every tear (1 Peter 1:3; Revelation 21:4).

When disappointment rises, pour out your heart to God as the psalmists did (Psalm 62:8). This week, read Romans 8 slowly, a few verses each day, asking the Lord to settle your heart in His sovereignty. Reach out to a pastor or mature believer in your local church, share what you are carrying, and ask them to pray with you. In your own prayers, tell God specifically what has disappointed you, ask Him for His perspective and strength, and thank Him for the hope secured by Christ’s resurrection.

question: What is the Gemara?
answer:
The Gemara is the body of rabbinic analysis, debate, and commentary on the Mishnah. Together they form the Talmud, the central compilation of Rabbinic Judaism.

The Mishnah, redacted around 200 AD, records the Oral Law in Hebrew. The Gemara, written mostly in Aramaic, was developed in the academies of the Land of Israel and Babylon over the following centuries. It discusses Jewish law (halakha), stories, ethics, and theology (aggadah). There are two versions: the Jerusalem Talmud (completed around the 4th century) and the more extensive Babylonian Talmud (completed around the 5th–6th century), which became the more widely studied text.

As Christians we hold the Bible alone, the Old and New Testaments, as the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, our ultimate authority for faith and practice. Jesus Christ is the Messiah who fulfilled the Law and the Prophets.

question: How can I stop being a people-pleaser?
answer:
People-pleasing is a heavy burden because it ties your peace to the shifting opinions of others rather than to the unchanging love of God.

Scripture names this clearly: The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high (Proverbs 29:25). The apostle Paul asked, Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10).

At its root, this habit is often an idolatry of human approval, looking to people for the justification and security that God freely gives those who trust in Jesus Christ. Because of Christ's penal substitutionary atonement, believers are already fully accepted by the Father, not because they performed well for others. Progressive sanctification then becomes the Spirit's work of replacing the fear of man with a holy fear of God.

Jesus Himself did not live to please the crowds. He lived to please His Father, even when it cost Him everything. A concrete way to begin is this: the next time you feel pressure to say yes just to avoid disappointing someone, pause and ask whether the choice serves Christ or merely keeps human peace.

One next step you can take today is to write down Galatians 1:10 and pray through it each morning this week, asking God to make you more concerned with being His servant than with winning people's praise. Share this desire with a mature believer in your local church who can pray with you and help you practice godly boundaries. He who began a good work in you will continue to perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1:6).

question: What is the golden chain of salvation?
answer:
The golden chain of salvation is the unbreakable sequence of God’s saving acts in Romans 8:29–30, linking His eternal purpose to the believer’s certain glorification: those He foreknew He also predestined, called, justified, and glorified.

Paul writes this immediately after assuring believers that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose (Romans 8:28). In the original setting, he was strengthening Roman Christians who faced suffering and weakness, showing that their hope rests not in changing circumstances but in God’s completed work from eternity to eternity. “For those God foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. And those He predestined He also called; those He called He also justified; those He justified He also glorified” (Romans 8:29–30).

Each link is God’s action, spoken in the past tense because the outcome is as certain as His character. Foreknowledge here is not mere advance information but God’s personal, electing love for His people. Predestination is His determination that they will be made like Christ. Calling is the Spirit’s effectual work that brings a person to faith through the gospel. Justification is God’s legal declaration that the sinner is righteous through faith in Christ’s penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection. Glorification is the final transformation of body and soul, already as good as done because God finishes what He starts.

This chain is often called the ordo salutis (the order of salvation). It undergirds the perseverance of the saints: everyone truly called and justified will be glorified, kept by God’s power rather than their own grip. If you are in Christ, this means your salvation does not hang on the strength of your faith today but on the God who called you. Read Romans 8 slowly this week, and thank God specifically for each link of the chain as you pray.

question: Should Mark 16:9-20 be in the Bible?
answer:
The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is absent from the earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts, including Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, which conclude the Gospel at Mark 16:8 with the women fleeing the empty tomb in fear. Later copies include these verses, and some early Christian writers such as Irenaeus knew a form of them, yet the abrupt ending at verse 8 fits Mark’s style and the manuscript evidence points to a later addition, most likely in the second century, to supply a smoother conclusion.

This is a non-essential question of textual transmission on which faithful Christians may disagree. It does not touch the inerrancy of the original autographs or any core doctrine of the faith. One historic view, reflected in most modern translations, treats Mark 16:9-20 as non-original and therefore prints it in brackets or with a footnote so readers know it was not part of Mark’s Gospel as first written. Another historic view, held by those who follow the traditional received text, includes the verses as Scripture because they appear in the great majority of later manuscripts and have been read in the churches for centuries.

No unique essential teaching hangs on this passage. The risen Christ’s appearances, His commission to preach the Gospel, and the call to baptize are clearly given in Matthew 28:18-20, Luke 24:46-49, and 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Even if one reads the longer ending, the signs listed in Mark 16:17-18 describe what God did through the apostles to confirm the message (Hebrews 2:3-4) rather than a standing command for every believer to handle serpents or drink poison. Jesus Himself refused to put the Lord to the test (Matthew 4:7).

You can trust that God has preserved His Word. Read Mark 16 in a study Bible that notes the evidence, compare it with the other Gospel endings, and talk with the elders of your local church if the footnotes trouble you. Ask the Lord for wisdom as you handle Scripture, knowing that the Holy Spirit uses the Word He inspired to make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15-17).

question: What is the difference between a sect and a cult?
answer:
A sect is typically a subgroup that has separated from a larger religious body over secondary matters while still affirming the same core truths, whereas a cult (in Christian usage) is a group that claims to be Christian yet denies essential doctrines of the faith, often adding extra-biblical authority or exercising high control over members.

The New Testament uses the Greek word hairesis (translated “sect”) for factions such as the Pharisees or even for the early church as outsiders saw it (Acts 24:5; Acts 24:14). Scripture also warns that false teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies that deny the Master who bought them (2 Peter 2:1). Historic Christianity therefore tests every group by whether it holds the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 1:3), including the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ (the hypostatic union), His penal substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection, and justification by grace alone through faith alone.

When you encounter a group, compare its teaching directly with Scripture rather than with personalities or experiences, and seek counsel from a local church that clearly preaches that Gospel.

question: Is "name it claim it" teaching biblical?
answer:
No, “name it and claim it” teaching is not biblical. Also known as Word of Faith or the prosperity gospel, it treats faith as a force you can speak in order to obligate God to give health, wealth, or success, as if your words create reality.

Scripture presents faith as humble trust in God’s character and promises, not a power we wield independently. Hebrews 11:1 describes faith as the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. We are to pray according to God’s will, not our own decrees: “If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). James 4:15 tells us to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39).

God is sovereign, and He often uses suffering to sanctify His people rather than removing every hardship. Paul pleaded for his thorn in the flesh to be taken away, yet the Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus told His disciples they would have tribulation in this world (John 16:33) and called them to take up their cross (Luke 9:23). The apostles suffered, the early church suffered, and Job’s story shows that even a blameless man can lose everything without it being a failure of faith.

The true Gospel is Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection to reconcile sinners to a holy God, not a guarantee of earthly abundance. God does provide for His people’s needs (Matthew 6:33; Philippians 4:19), and godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6). Paul warns against those who imagine that godliness is a means of financial gain (1 Timothy 6:5). Treating God like a vending machine can crush people when trials come, as if their suffering proves they lacked faith. That is neither the character of God nor the pattern of Scripture.

If this teaching has left you disappointed or confused, bring your actual needs to the Lord in honest prayer that includes “Your will be done,” and talk with a pastor in a local church that preaches the whole counsel of God. A simple next step is to read 2 Corinthians this week, noticing how Paul boasts in weakness rather than claiming it away.

question: What does the Bible say about cryonics or cryogenics?
answer:
The Bible does not mention cryonics or cryogenics, since these are modern technologies. Scripture does teach that it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Death entered through sin and remains the last enemy (Romans 5:12; 1 Corinthians 15:26). At death the body returns to dust while the spirit returns to God (Genesis 3:19; Ecclesiastes 12:7). For those in Christ, to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8).

The Christian hope is not human preservation of this present body, but the bodily resurrection God will accomplish when Christ returns. Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies” (John 11:25). The perishable body will be raised imperishable, and this mortal body will put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:42-44; 1 Corinthians 15:53). Only God possesses immortality in Himself (1 Timothy 6:16), and He grants eternal life as a gift through His Son.

Placing hope in cryonics therefore looks away from the appointed reality of death and from the resurrection that belongs to God alone. A wise next step is to read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly and talk with a pastor in a local church about any fear of death, so that hope rests in Christ’s victory rather than in unproven technology.

question: How can I obtain favor from the Lord (Proverbs 8:35)?
answer:
You obtain favor from the Lord by finding Wisdom, just as Proverbs 8:35 says: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD." In Proverbs, Wisdom is personified as calling out so that people may listen, live, and receive God's blessing rather than ruin. The New Testament identifies this Wisdom with Jesus Christ Himself, "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), in whom "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).

Because God is holy, we cannot earn His favor by our own efforts. All have sinned and fall short of His glory, and our sin separates us from Him (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as our substitute under God's just wrath against sin (penal substitution), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. God now grants His favor, life, and justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 5:1). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

If you already belong to Christ, keep seeking this Wisdom by fearing the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), and by receiving the Word, prayer, and fellowship as means of grace. Ask God directly for wisdom, for He "gives generously to all without finding fault" (James 1:5). A simple next step is to read Proverbs 8 slowly this week, then open the Gospel of John and ask the Lord to show you Christ as your Wisdom, while speaking with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about walking this out together. What has drawn you to this verse today?

question: Why is solo Christo important?
answer:
Solo Christo (Christ alone) is important because Jesus Christ is the only Savior and the one Mediator who can bring sinners to God. No other person, work, or path can reconcile us to a holy God.

Jesus Himself said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). The apostles preached the same exclusive claim: “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Paul adds, “For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

This is essential to the Gospel. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, leaving us unable to save ourselves (Romans 3:23). Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not, died on the cross in penal substitution as the atoning sacrifice for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation comes by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). His finished work is both necessary and completely sufficient.

Without solo Christo the Gospel is lost, because people would look to their own efforts, other mediators, or other religions. That would deny both the uniqueness of Christ’s person and the completeness of His atoning death and resurrection. For the believer this truth brings rest: you do not add your performance, feelings, or anyone else to Jesus. You simply receive Him.

Read John 14 and Hebrews 7–10 this week, noting how Christ alone fulfills and ends the need for any other priest or sacrifice. Then talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about how this shapes your daily trust. Pray directly to God, thanking Him for giving His Son as the only way and asking the Spirit to help you rest in Christ’s finished work rather than your own.

If you have not yet done so, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. What has been drawing your attention to this truth lately?

question: Does Genesis chapter 1 literally mean 24 hour days?
answer:
The question of whether the days in Genesis 1 are ordinary 24-hour periods is a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians who affirm the inerrancy of Scripture may disagree. It does not define the faith, because the Hebrew word yom can refer to a solar day or a longer period, and interpreters who all treat Genesis as historical revelation differ on how the literary features of the chapter function.
