One view, common among many believers, is that the six days are consecutive 24-hour days. This reading notes the repeated “evening and there was morning” formula, the sequential numbering of the days, and the later Sabbath command that patterns human rest after God’s work: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, but He rested on the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11; see also Genesis 1:5).

Another historic view held by many Christians is that the days serve as a literary framework or represent longer ages. This approach emphasizes God’s orderly, sovereign work rather than a strict chronological sequence of solar days, observing that light appears before the sun (Genesis 1:3-5, Genesis 1:14-19) and that Genesis 2:4 uses “day” for the entire creation period: “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made them.”

In such non-essential questions, Scripture calls us to charity and liberty rather than division: “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). All who trust the Bible can agree that God created everything by His word, that it was very good, and that He alone is worthy of worship.

Read Genesis 1–2 slowly in its own context, perhaps alongside a trusted pastor or mature believer in your local church, and ask the Lord for wisdom as you seek to honor Him as Creator.

question: What is the power of the Holy Spirit?
answer:
The power of the Holy Spirit is the personal, almighty working of God Himself, by which He creates, convicts, regenerates, sanctifies, and empowers His people to live holy lives and bear witness to Christ.

The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force or energy, but the third Person of the Trinity, fully God, co-equal and co-eternal with the Father and the Son. His power is the same divine power that hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), overshadowed Mary in the virgin conception of Jesus (Luke 1:35), and raised Christ from the dead (Romans 8:11). Jesus promised His disciples, “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). That same power now indwells every true believer (1 Corinthians 6:19), producing the fruit of Christlike character (Galatians 5:22–23) and enabling us to put sin to death (Romans 8:13).

This is the work of regeneration and progressive sanctification: the Spirit gives new life to those who were dead in sin (Titus 3:5; Ephesians 2:4–5) and then continually transforms us into the image of Christ, not by our own might but by His presence (Zechariah 4:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Practically, this means we do not rely on self-effort or willpower alone; we depend on Him through prayer, the Word, and the fellowship of the church, asking to be filled so that we may obey and speak for Jesus in ordinary daily life (Ephesians 5:18).

question: How is the word to be read and heard, that it may become effectual to salvation?
answer:
The Word of God is to be read and heard with diligence, preparation, and prayer, received with faith and love, laid up in the heart, and practiced in life, so that it may become effectual to salvation.

The Holy Scriptures are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15). All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and we need a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. The Holy Spirit uses the Word as the ordinary means of grace to convict of sin, reveal Christ, and grant saving faith. As you read and hear, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

Attend to the Word diligently, as the Bereans received the message with eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day (Acts 17:11). Prepare your heart by putting away sin and approaching with humility: “Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls” (James 1:21). Pray for illumination, as in Psalm 119:18: “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law.” Receive it with faith and love, not as the word of men but as the true word of God that is at work in those who believe (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Hide it in your heart (Psalm 119:11) and be doers of the word, not hearers only (James 1:22).

A practical next step is to set a regular time to read Scripture, beginning with prayer for a humble and obedient heart, then looking for how the passage points to Christ and calls you to trust and obey Him today. Gather with a local church to hear the Word preached faithfully. Pray to God yourself, asking Him to make His Word living and active in you by His Spirit. How has the Lord been using His Word in your life recently?

question: What is millennialism?
answer:
Millennialism refers to Christian interpretations of the thousand-year reign of Christ described in Revelation 20:1–6.

This belongs to eschatology and is a tertiary (non-essential) doctrine on which faithful Christians may disagree, because Revelation employs the symbolic, apocalyptic language common in Second Temple Jewish writings, and Scripture does not define every detail of the last days with the same explicitness as the gospel itself.

The three main historic views are premillennialism (Christ returns before a future earthly millennial kingdom), postmillennialism (the gospel gradually produces a golden age of Christian influence, after which Christ returns), and amillennialism (the thousand years symbolizes Christ’s present spiritual reign through the church until He returns). In such disputable matters Christians have liberty and should not quarrel over them (Romans 14:1–5).

What remains certain is that Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead and to renew all things (Acts 1:11; 2 Timothy 4:1; Revelation 21:1–5). A helpful next step is to read Revelation 19–21 in context, focusing on Christ’s victory rather than timelines, and to discuss it charitably with mature believers in your local church.

question: What does the Bible say about war?
answer:
The Bible presents war as a sorrowful reality in a fallen world, sometimes used by God as an instrument of His judgment, while calling believers to pursue peace and recognizing that governing authorities are given the sword to restrain evil.

In the Old Testament the Lord is described as a warrior. Exodus 15:3 The LORD is a warrior; the LORD is His name. He commanded Israel to wage specific wars of judgment against nations whose wickedness had reached its full measure, not because of Israel’s righteousness but because of the inhabitants’ sin. Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4-5. Scripture also declares that God hates the lover of violence. Psalm 11:5 The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked; His soul hates the lover of violence. There is a time for war and a time for peace. Ecclesiastes 3:8

In the New Testament Jesus blesses those who make peace. Matthew 5:9 Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. He taught His disciples not to resist evil with personal retaliation. Matthew 5:39 But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also. He also made clear that allegiance to Him would bring division rather than immediate peace on earth. Matthew 10:34 Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. At the same time, the apostle Paul teaches that God has established civil authorities as His servants who do not bear the sword in vain but serve as agents of wrath against wrongdoers. Romans 13:4 For he is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. He is God’s servant, an agent of wrath to bring punishment on the wrongdoer.

Believers are to live at peace with everyone insofar as it depends on them. Romans 12:18 If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone. The prophets promise a future day when the Messiah will end war among the nations. Isaiah 2:4 He will judge between the nations and will settle disputes for many peoples. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not take up sword against nation, nor will they train for war anymore.

Christians have historically held different views on whether and when believers may participate in war. Some conclude from Jesus’ words on non-resistance that Christians must be pacifists and refuse all military involvement. Others, looking to the God-ordained role of the magistrate in Romans 13 and examples of just defense, believe war can be a regrettable but necessary act of justice when conducted by legitimate authority, for a just cause, as a last resort, and with right intention and limited means.

Whatever view one holds, the consistent call of Scripture is to be peacemakers in daily life, to pray for those in authority, and to long for the return of the Prince of Peace. A helpful next step is to read Matthew 5:38-48 and Romans 12:9-13:7 together, asking God for wisdom, and to talk with a pastor or mature Christian in your church about how these truths apply in our day.

question: Are there errors in the Qur'an (Koran)?
answer:
Yes, from the historic Christian faith the Qur'an contains errors, because it contradicts the Bible (the inspired, inerrant Word of God) on the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.

Muslims commonly hold that the Qur'an is perfectly preserved and that earlier Scriptures were corrupted. Christians believe God has kept His Word intact, as the New Testament writings already circulated in the first century, centuries before Muhammad, and Jesus promised Scripture would not pass away (Matthew 5:18; Matthew 24:35).

The Bible teaches that Jesus is truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union), that He died by crucifixion as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Qur'an denies the crucifixion itself (Qur'an 4:157) and presents Jesus only as a prophet, not as God. These cannot both be true. The Qur'an also calls Mary the sister of Aaron (Qur'an 19:28), a historical mismatch of more than a thousand years with the biblical timeline, and it portrays Christians as taking Mary as a deity alongside Jesus (Qur'an 5:116), which does not match the Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

These differences are not minor. If Jesus did not die and rise, there is no forgiveness of sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). All people have sinned and stand separated from a holy God (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus lived the perfect life we could not, died in our place, and rose again. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 14:6).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If you are weighing these claims, read the Gospel of John and ask God to show you who Jesus is. What questions do you have about what the Bible says concerning Christ?

question: What is the spiritual significance to a déjà vu experience?
answer:
Déjà vu, that sudden sense of having already lived the present moment, is not given any particular spiritual meaning in Scripture, which never mentions the experience.

Interpreting everyday inner phenomena like this is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may disagree, because the Bible is silent on it and leaves room for different emphases on natural processes versus God’s ordinary providence. Many Christians therefore treat déjà vu as a common feature of the brain God created, a brief mismatch in how memory and perception work, carrying no special message. Others may loosely see it as a faint reminder that God already knows every moment of our lives.

I would not treat déjà vu as a mystical sign, a fragment of a past life, or a new revelation, because Scripture is sufficient for all we need to know God and live faithfully (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The idea of reincarnation or soul-memory from previous existences contradicts the Bible’s teaching that each person is appointed to die once and then face judgment (Hebrews 9:27). In Christian liberty (Romans 14) we can hold interpretations of such feelings loosely, without making them a test of faith.

When the sensation next comes, let it simply prompt you to live this present moment before the God who already knows it. Read Psalm 139 slowly and thank Him that He is present with you now, whether the moment feels familiar or entirely new. If the experience unsettles you, speak with a mature believer in your local church.

question: What are the four beasts in Daniel chapter 7?
answer:
The four beasts in Daniel chapter 7 represent four kings who will arise from the earth, according to the angelic interpretation given to Daniel (Daniel 7:17). They appear as a lion with eagle’s wings, a bear raised up on one side with three ribs in its mouth, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a uniquely dreadful beast with iron teeth, ten horns, and a boastful little horn that arises among them (Daniel 7:4–8).

This night vision came to Daniel during the Babylonian exile, using the image of chaotic seas and monstrous creatures (familiar in the ancient Near East for depicting threatening powers) to show that every earthly empire remains under God’s control. The scene then turns from the beasts to the Ancient of Days seated in judgment and one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive everlasting dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will never pass away (Daniel 7:9–14). That “son of man” is the Messiah, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, whose kingdom the saints of the Most High will possess forever (Daniel 7:18; Daniel 7:27).

Throughout church history many Christians have identified the four beasts with the successive empires of Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome (paralleling the statue in Daniel 2). Others have seen the fourth beast as pointing more fully to a still-future end-times power. These details of fulfillment belong to eschatology, a tertiary matter where faithful believers may differ without compromising the essentials of the faith. What remains clear and unifying is the sovereignty of God over the rise and fall of nations and the certainty of Christ’s return and final judgment.

When political powers seem overwhelming, this chapter calls us to live as citizens of the coming kingdom rather than placing ultimate hope in any earthly government. Read Daniel 7 slowly this week, asking the Lord to deepen your trust that He alone sits on the throne.

question: What did Paul mean when he said, “I die daily” in 1 Corinthians 15:31?
answer:
When Paul said “I die daily” in 1 Corinthians 15:31, he meant that he constantly faced real, physical danger of death through persecution and hardship in his apostolic ministry. In the immediate context he asks why he and others would endanger themselves every hour if the dead are not raised, then adds that he faces death every day as surely as he boasts about the Corinthians in Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:30-32).

This is not first of all a statement about dying to sin in daily sanctification (though Paul teaches that elsewhere). It is part of his defense of the bodily resurrection: if Christ has not been raised and the dead will not rise, then such daily risk is pointless, and one might as well live only for present pleasure. The language echoes the Old Testament pattern of the righteous facing death all day long for God’s sake (Psalm 44:22, which Paul also quotes in Romans 8:36) and matches his own record of imprisonments, beatings, and near-death experiences (2 Corinthians 11:23-28).

The resurrection of Christ, therefore, is not an optional extra but the foundation that makes Christian suffering meaningful. Because Jesus died, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, those united to Him can face loss, opposition, or even death without despair. When hardship comes because of your faith, remember that your labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Open 1 Corinthians 15 and read the whole chapter slowly, asking God to let the hope of the resurrection steady you in whatever you are facing today.

question: What does the Bible say about motivation?
answer:
The Bible teaches that God cares about the heart behind our actions, calling believers to be motivated by love for Him, gratitude for the Gospel, and a desire to glorify Him rather than by selfish ambition or human approval. Proverbs 16:2 says, "All a man’s ways are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the motives." Jesus warned against doing righteous acts merely to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1), while Paul wrote that "Christ’s love compels us" (2 Corinthians 5:14) and that we should "do it all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). Colossians 3:23-24 adds, "Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, as for the Lord and not for men, because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving." Philippians 2:3 further cautions, "Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in humility consider others more important than yourselves."

This flows from the Gospel itself: we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, not by our works, so our service becomes a grateful response rather than an attempt to earn standing with God. In progressive sanctification the Holy Spirit renews our desires so that we increasingly live for God's glory instead of our own.

A practical next step is to pray through Psalm 139:23-24 today, asking the Lord to search your current motives, then bring what He shows you to a trusted believer in your local church for encouragement and accountability.

question: What does it mean to put off the old man (Ephesians 4:22)?
answer:
Putting off the old man (also called the old self) in Ephesians 4:22 means laying aside the former sinful identity and lifestyle you had before Christ, a nature that is being corrupted by its deceitful desires. Paul uses the picture of taking off filthy clothes because you have already been taught the truth that is in Jesus.

This command sits in the larger call of Ephesians 4:17-24, where Paul contrasts the futile, darkened walk of the Gentiles with the new life of those who have learned Christ. The old man is the person we were in Adam, dead in trespasses and enslaved to sin (Ephesians 2:1-3). In union with Christ the old self has already been crucified (Romans 6:6; Colossians 3:9), yet remaining patterns of that nature must still be put off as part of progressive sanctification. The Holy Spirit renews the mind so that we put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness (Ephesians 4:23-24).

A concrete way this works is seen in the verses that follow: put off falsehood and speak truth, put off unrestrained anger and give no foothold to the devil, put off stealing and instead work in order to give (Ephesians 4:25-28). The same Spirit who regenerated you now enables you to mortify specific sins and walk in the corresponding graces.

This week, read Ephesians 4:17-32 slowly and ask the Lord to show you one lingering pattern of the old self. Confess it, then take one practical step of putting on the new self (for example, replacing a harsh word with an encouraging one) and share that step with a mature believer in your local church for prayer and accountability.

question: What is a freethinker?
answer:
A freethinker is a person who forms conclusions about God, morality, and reality through independent reason and evidence rather than submitting to religious authority, tradition, or revealed Scripture.

The label grew common in the Enlightenment among those who treated church teaching as an obstacle to be set aside. Christians are called to love God with the mind (Matthew 22:37) and to test all things (1 Thessalonians 5:21), yet Scripture also teaches that sin darkens human thinking (the noetic effects of sin). Therefore we do not lean on our own understanding but trust the Lord (Proverbs 3:5-6). Jesus Christ is the truth who actually sets people free (John 8:32; John 14:6). If you are weighing these ideas, read the Gospel of John and ask God to show you whether Christ’s claims match reality.

question: What is an overseer in the church?
answer:
An overseer in the church is a qualified man who holds the office of elder, called to teach sound doctrine, govern the congregation, and shepherd the people of God.

Some historic Christian traditions, especially Anglican, Roman Catholic, and Orthodox churches, understand the overseer (bishop) as a distinct higher office of apostolic succession that oversees multiple congregations in order to guard unity and orthodoxy.

I believe Scripture treats overseer, elder, and pastor as the same local-church office, because Paul tells Titus to appoint elders and then immediately gives the qualifications for an overseer (Titus 1:5-7), and because the elders of Ephesus are the very men the Holy Spirit has made overseers to shepherd the church (Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:1-2). This reading supports a plurality of elders in each congregation rather than a regional bishopric.

The Greek term episkopos simply means one who watches over or superintends, and the New Testament applies it to men who must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a lover of money, and proven managers of their own households (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:6-9). They are to serve willingly as examples, not as lords (1 Peter 5:2-3), because they will give an account for the souls entrusted to them (Hebrews 13:17).

Pray regularly for the overseers in your own church, and if you are a man sensing a possible call to this work, begin by measuring your life against these qualifications and seeking the counsel of your present elders.

question: Someone gave me a prophetic word/prophesied over me. What is the interpretation?
answer:
It can feel significant and even weighty when someone claims to speak a word from God over your life. Without the exact words that were spoken, I cannot interpret that particular message for you.

The Bible requires us to test every such claim rather than receive it uncritically. 1 John 4:1 Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21 Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good.

Faithful Christians differ on whether the New Testament gift of prophecy continues today. Continuationists argue that gifts like prophecy remain for the church's edification until Christ returns, drawing from 1 Corinthians 14, while insisting any word must be tested and never treated as equal to Scripture.

I hold the cessationist view as one historic Christian position: the revelatory gifts, including prophecy that functions as new divine revelation, ceased with the apostles and the closing of the New Testament canon. Scripture is now complete and sufficient. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work. Hebrews 1:1-2 On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.

Any word spoken over you must be judged solely by the Bible. If it contradicts Scripture, reject it. If it agrees with Scripture, the truth is already given there, which is more sure than any personal impression. 2 Peter 1:19 And we have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. You will do well to pay attention to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Do not let an extra-biblical word govern your identity, decisions, or future. Rest in Christ's finished work and the sufficiency of God's written Word.

Share the exact words with a trusted pastor or elder in your local church and ask them to help you compare it carefully with Scripture. In the meantime, read the Gospels daily so that you know Christ Himself more clearly than any claimed word about you.

Would you be willing to share the specific words that were spoken so we can weigh them together against the Bible?

question: What is/isn’t a Christian married couple allowed to do, sexually?
answer:
Sexual intimacy is a good gift God designed for marriage, to be enjoyed exclusively between one husband and one wife as part of their one-flesh union. Genesis 2:24 says, "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh." The marriage bed is to be kept pure and undefiled (Hebrews 13:4), meaning it belongs only to the couple and is not to be shared with anyone else, even in thought or through images.

Scripture does not give a detailed catalog of every permitted or forbidden act. It gives clear principles instead. Spouses are to give themselves to one another in love and not deprive each other except by mutual agreement for a time of prayer (1 Corinthians 7:3-5). Husbands are to love their wives sacrificially, as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25), and both are to treat one another with honor rather than selfish demand. Passages such as Proverbs 5:18-19 and the Song of Solomon celebrate joyful, exclusive delight in one's spouse. Everything is to be done to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

What is not allowed is anything that breaks that exclusivity or holiness: adultery, pornography (which involves lusting after others, contrary to Matthew 5:28), coercion, abuse, or treating your spouse as an object rather than a person made in God's image. Sexual activity that introduces a third party, even digitally, defiles the marriage bed.

Within those bounds, Christian couples have liberty to enjoy one another, guided by mutual consent, love, and a desire not to cause the other to stumble. Faithful believers may hold different convictions about particular practices; this is an area of Christian liberty where each should be fully convinced in their own mind and act in love (Romans 14). If a practice feels degrading, unloving, or contrary to holiness for either spouse, it should be set aside.

Talk openly and prayerfully with your spouse about desires, fears, and boundaries, putting the other's good first. Read 1 Corinthians 7 and Ephesians 5 together this week and ask the Lord to help you serve one another more faithfully in this gift He has given. If you need further wisdom, speak with a pastor in your local church.

question: Why is God going to give us a white stone with a new name (Revelation 2:17)?
answer:
Jesus promises in Revelation 2:17 to give the overcomer a white stone with a new name written on it, known only to the one who receives it. This is a personal pledge of victory, acceptance, and intimate belonging to God for those who remain faithful.

The text itself does not define the white stone, so this is a non-essential matter of interpretation where faithful Christians may differ, depending on first-century customs and related biblical themes.

One common understanding notes that white stones (or pebbles) served in the ancient world as a sign of acquittal in court, in contrast to a black stone for condemnation, or as a token of admission to a banquet. In this view God declares the believer justified and welcomes him to the heavenly feast, together with the hidden manna mentioned in the same verse.

Another understanding focuses on the new name as God conferring a transformed identity, just as He renamed Abram in Genesis 17:5 and Jacob in Genesis 32:28 to mark covenant relationship and purpose. The secrecy of the name underscores a unique, personal knowledge of God that cannot be shared or stolen, a theme also seen in Isaiah 62:2 and Revelation 3:12.

These pictures together assure believers that those who overcome by faith, as 1 John 5:4 describes, will receive honor, purity, and a new identity fully realized in Christ’s presence. This fulfills the new creation already begun in the believer, as 2 Corinthians 5:17 teaches. The church in Pergamum needed exactly this encouragement while under pressure to compromise.

The promise is real and calls us to find our worth in the name God writes rather than in earthly labels or approval. A helpful next step is to read the seven letters in Revelation 2 and 3, noting each promise to the overcomer, and then discuss with a mature believer in your church how these truths strengthen daily faithfulness.

question: What is the meaning of the strange fire in Leviticus 10:1?
answer:
The strange fire in Leviticus 10:1 is unauthorized fire that Nadab and Abihu offered before the Lord, fire He had not commanded them to bring. In Hebrew the phrase is *esh zarah*, meaning alien, foreign, or illegitimate fire, most likely incense burned with coals taken from some source other than the altar God had just consecrated.

Immediately after the Lord sent fire to consume the burnt offering and display His glory (Leviticus 9:24), Aaron’s newly ordained sons took their own censers, added incense, and approached God on terms He had never prescribed. Fire then came out from the presence of the Lord and consumed them (Leviticus 10:2). Moses explained the event with the Lord’s own words: “I will show My holiness to those who come near Me, and I will be glorified before all the people” (Leviticus 10:3). The subsequent command that priests must not drink wine when they enter the tent of meeting (Leviticus 10:9) suggests they may also have been impaired, unable to distinguish holy from common.

This real historical judgment underscores that God is holy and may be approached only as He has revealed, never by human invention. In the new covenant we draw near through Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, whose once-for-all sacrifice and resurrection open the way that no unauthorized offering ever could.

A practical next step is to read Leviticus 8–10 slowly this week, asking the Lord to give you a holy fear of His presence and a clearer love for the way He has provided in Christ. Speak with a pastor or mature believer in your church about how your gathered worship and daily life can more carefully honor what God has actually commanded rather than what we find convenient.

question: Is it possible to sell your soul to the devil?
answer:
No, it is not possible to sell your soul to the devil as a transaction or contract. Every soul belongs to God, who created it. Ezekiel 18:4 says, "Behold, every soul belongs to Me; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is Mine. The soul who sins is the one who will die."

Satan is a real but limited created being, a liar and accuser who seeks to devour, not a co-equal power who can buy what God owns (John 8:44; 1 Peter 5:8). The idea of a Faustian bargain belongs to folklore and literature, not to Scripture. People can reject God, live in rebellion, and come under the evil one's influence as slaves to sin, yet that never transfers ownership of the soul away from the Lord's sovereignty (Ephesians 2:1-2). Jesus Himself asked, "What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?" (Matthew 16:26). The soul is not a commodity we can barter.

Involvement with the occult, witchcraft, or any attempt to traffic with darkness is real sin that Scripture forbids and that opens a person to deception and oppression (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). It does not, however, place anyone beyond the reach of Christ's redeeming work. All of us have sinned and stand in need of a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. God delivers those who trust Him from the domain of darkness and transfers them into the kingdom of His Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins (Colossians 1:13-14). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

If this question comes from fear, curiosity about forbidden things, or a sense that you have already given yourself over to darkness, speak with a pastor in a local church that holds to the Bible, and begin reading the Gospel of John to see who Jesus is and what He has done. What prompted you to ask this?

question: What does the Bible say about obedience?
answer:
The Bible presents obedience as the fitting response of love and faith toward God, never as a way to earn salvation. God called Abraham to walk before Him and be blameless (Genesis 17:1), and He later told Israel that to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22). Jesus taught, “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15), and Paul spoke of “the obedience of faith” that the gospel produces (Romans 1:5).

This obedience belongs to sanctification, the Spirit’s work of conforming believers to Christ after they have already been justified by grace through faith alone. Christ Himself learned obedience through suffering and became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him (Hebrews 5:8-9; Philippians 2:8). Believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). When human commands conflict with God’s, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

A concrete next step is to read John 14–15 this week, note one command of Jesus, and ask the Lord in prayer to help you put it into practice in a specific relationship or responsibility today.

question: What does it mean that God is our refuge and strength and an ever-present help in trouble (Psalm 46:1)?
answer:
Psalm 46:1 means that the Lord Himself is a secure fortress for His people, the source of their power, and immediately available to aid them in every crisis. The psalm uses the language of a stronghold that cannot be stormed, strength that does not fail, and help that is already at hand rather than delayed or distant.

This opening line belongs to a song of confident trust in the midst of upheaval. The verses that follow picture the earth giving way, mountains falling into the sea, and nations raging, yet the people of God will not fear because “the LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (Psalm 46:7; Psalm 46:11). “Refuge” (a hiding place or fortress) and “strength” together show that God both shields His people and enables them to stand. “Ever-present help” stresses His nearness: He is not a far-off deity but the living God who is found when His people cry out. The same truth appears throughout Scripture: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe” (Proverbs 18:10); “God is our refuge and strength” is echoed in the New Testament when believers say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid” (Hebrews 13:6).

Theologically this verse displays God’s covenant faithfulness and His immanence (He is truly with His people). He does not change, so His help is not seasonal. For those who belong to Christ, this promise is even more personal: Jesus is Immanuel, God with us, who faced the greatest trouble at the cross so that sinners might have a sure refuge from sin, death, and judgment.

When trouble comes, the first movement is not to self-reliance or panic but to the God who is already there. Read Psalm 46 slowly today, name the specific distress you face, and ask the Lord to be your refuge and strength in it. Then share that need with a mature believer in your local church so you do not walk through it alone.

question: Should a Christian woman wear a bikini?
answer:
This is a tertiary matter of applying biblical principles of modesty rather than a specific command that lists garments, so faithful Christians may disagree without it defining orthodoxy. Scripture requires women who profess godliness to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, emphasizing inner character over outward display (1 Timothy 2:9-10; 1 Peter 3:3-4).

Some Christians conclude a bikini is inconsistent with this because it exposes the body in ways that can provoke lust in others and does not reflect the covering God provided after the fall, preferring more covering swimwear as an expression of holiness and love that avoids causing a brother to stumble (Matthew 5:28; Romans 14:13; 1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Other Christians view it as permissible in a swimming context, arguing that all functional swimwear is somewhat revealing by necessity, that modesty is chiefly a matter of the heart's intent rather than a rigid style, and that we must not judge one another in disputable matters of conscience (Romans 14:1-5; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

I would encourage greater caution, choosing covering that honors the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit and considers others, as one faithful way of pursuing holiness without treating a particular swimsuit as the test of genuine faith. Pray directly to the Lord about your motives and the effect on others, read 1 Timothy 2 and 1 Peter 3 this week, and seek counsel from a mature Christian woman in your local church (Titus 2:3-5).

question: Is Christian rap music appropriate?
answer:
The appropriateness of Christian rap music is a tertiary matter of worship style and Christian liberty, where faithful Christians may disagree without compromising the Gospel, because Scripture does not prescribe specific musical genres. It instead calls us to fill our hearts and gatherings with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs that teach the Word of Christ and give thanks to God (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16).

Some Christians, often those who emphasize cultural separation or a more traditional approach to gathered worship, view rap as unfitting because of its origins in hip-hop culture frequently marked by pride, aggression, and worldly themes. They argue we should not be conformed to the patterns of this world and should prefer music that keeps the focus on orderly, God-centered praise (Romans 12:2; 1 Corinthians 14:40).

Others treat musical style as a matter of Christian liberty (adiaphora), seeing rap as a culturally adaptable form that can proclaim Christ to particular audiences, much as the church has used various song forms across history, so long as the lyrics are theologically sound, Christ-exalting, and edifying rather than self-promoting.

Whatever the style, the decisive questions are the content and the fruit: does a given song align with Philippians 4:8 (what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable), and does it help you and others glorify God rather than the world (1 Corinthians 10:31)? Some tracks labeled “Christian rap” fail this test through unbiblical attitudes or language, while others can be used profitably in personal listening. Corporate worship involves additional considerations of unity, order, and the weaker brother (Romans 14:1-6; Romans 14:13).

A wise next step is to examine specific lyrics against Scripture with a mature believer or your church’s elders, then pray for discernment about what you personally consume and how it shapes your heart.

question: What is a "dark night of the soul"?
answer:
The "dark night of the soul" is a phrase from the 16th-century Spanish Carmelite mystic St. John of the Cross, describing a season of deep spiritual dryness, inner turmoil, and a felt sense that God has withdrawn, which he understood as God's purifying work to detach the soul from lesser things and draw it nearer to Himself.

The term itself does not appear in Scripture, yet the Bible honestly records similar experiences of lament and trial. The psalmist cries, "How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1), and Jesus Himself, in His real human suffering on the cross, quoted Psalm 22:1: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). God uses such seasons in progressive sanctification, producing endurance and proven character (James 1:2-4; Romans 5:3-5; Hebrews 12:5-11).

In the Catholic mystical tradition this is often treated as a distinct stage on the way to contemplative union with God. Many Protestants, especially in the Reformed stream, see these times as God's fatherly discipline or testing that drives believers back to the ordinary means of grace (the Word, prayer, and the gathered church) rather than as a required mystical itinerary. Faithful Christians may describe these trials in different ways, since Scripture does not mandate one technical map of interior stages, and we have liberty in non-essentials (Romans 14).

From a Reformed Baptist perspective this is one way God keeps His people through perseverance of the saints: even when we do not feel His presence, He does not abandon those who are truly in Christ (John 10:28-29; Philippians 1:6). If you are in a similar season, a concrete next step is to pray through a lament psalm such as Psalm 13 or Psalm 88 while staying connected to a local church that preaches the Bible.

question: What does the Bible say about self-defense?
answer:
The Bible teaches that human life is sacred because every person is made in the image of God, so murder is forbidden, yet Scripture distinguishes murder from other uses of force, including the protection of life (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 9:6; Exodus 20:13).

Old Testament law illustrates this distinction. Exodus 22:2-3 states, “If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him. But if this happens after sunrise, there is bloodguilt for him.” Lethal force in defending a household against a nighttime intruder, when the threat could not be clearly assessed, did not bring guilt.

Jesus told His disciples, “But now, whoever has a money bag should take it, and likewise a traveling bag. And whoever does not have a sword should sell his cloak and buy one” (Luke 22:36). Many have seen this as practical provision for a dangerous journey. At the same time, Jesus taught, “But I tell you not to resist an evil person. If someone slaps you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). In that setting a slap on the right cheek was typically an insult, not a lethal attack. He also rebuked Peter’s use of the sword in Gethsemane: “Put your sword back in its place. For all who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). Paul likewise writes, “Do not repay anyone evil for evil. \ldots Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:17, 19), while also affirming that the civil authority “does not bear the sword in vain” as God’s servant to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:4).

Faithful Christians have understood these texts in different ways. Some, especially in historic Anabaptist and peace-church traditions, conclude that Jesus’ call to love enemies and refuse retaliation means His followers should not use force even in self-defense. Others, reading the same passages alongside the whole counsel of Scripture, including the duty to protect the vulnerable and the distinction between personal vengeance and just restraint of evil, believe defending oneself, one’s family, or the innocent from unjust aggression is permitted and can even be an expression of love for neighbor.

This is not a core doctrine that defines Christian identity. Sincere believers may differ here, and we are called to charity and liberty in such matters (Romans 14:1-6, 19). In every case the heart of Scripture is the same: we do not take personal revenge, we value life as God’s image, and we trust the Lord as our refuge while seeking wisdom to act justly and peaceably.

question: What was the significance of Jesus being dead for three days?
answer:
Jesus remaining in the grave for three days before rising bodily on the third day fulfills Scripture and His own words, proving He truly died and that God raised Him as Lord and Savior.

Jesus Himself identified this as the sign of Jonah: "For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). He repeatedly told His disciples that He must suffer, be killed, and be raised on the third day (Matthew 16:21). Paul presents this as the core of the Gospel itself: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

The three days confirm that Jesus was genuinely dead, not merely unconscious or appearing to die, so His resurrection is a real triumph over death rather than a recovery. It also follows God's pattern of deliverance, as Hosea 6:2 says, "After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence." This bodily resurrection on the third day declares Jesus to be the Son of God with power (Romans 1:4), shows that His penal substitutionary death fully satisfied God's justice against sin, and is the ground of our justification (Romans 4:25).

Because He was dead and now lives, those who belong to Him have a living hope that death is not the end. All of us have sinned and stand under God's just judgment. Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died in our place, was buried, and rose on the third day. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

Read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly this week and talk with a pastor or mature believer about what the resurrection means for your own life. What does this truth stir in you as you consider it?

question: Is the idea of chi compatible with the Christian faith?
answer:
The traditional idea of chi (an impersonal vital energy or life force flowing through meridians, the body, and the cosmos) is not compatible with the Christian faith. Scripture presents God as the personal, triune Creator who alone gives breath and life, not an impersonal force that people balance or manipulate. Genesis 2:7 records that the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being. Colossians 1:17 and Hebrews 1:3 teach that Christ holds all things together by His power. Life is a personal gift from God, not an independent energy we channel.

Chi arises from Taoist and Chinese philosophical traditions that treat the universe through impersonal dualities such as yin and yang. That worldview clashes with the Bible’s revelation of one holy, sovereign God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is a divine Person who convicts, regenerates, and indwells believers (John 16:8; Titus 3:5; 1 Corinthians 6:19), not a force to be directed. Equating the Spirit with chi, or treating chi as a parallel reality, mixes truth with empty philosophy and human tradition, which Colossians 2:8 warns against.

Physical movements sometimes associated with chi (certain exercises or breathing techniques) can be used as ordinary activity if the accompanying spiritual claims are rejected. The metaphysical idea itself, however, and any practice that seeks to open, balance, or invoke that energy, pulls a person away from exclusive trust in Christ. Believers are called to worship God alone and to test every teaching by Scripture (Exodus 20:3; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1).

If this question arises from interest in martial arts, traditional medicine, or similar practices, bring it to your local church elders for counsel, and ask the Lord for wisdom as you read His Word. He is the true source of life and peace.

question: What is the peace that passes all understanding?
answer:
The peace that passes all understanding is the peace of God, which, according to Philippians 4:7, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. This is not a calm that comes from easy circumstances or human reasoning. It is a supernatural gift of God that transcends our ability to explain or produce it.

Paul writes this from prison, urging believers: “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God” (Philippians 4:6). The result is this guarding peace. It rests on the prior reality of peace with God. “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Through Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection, sinners are reconciled to a holy God. That objective peace with God then becomes the source of the experiential peace of God that steadies the heart.

This peace is also listed among the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). It does not mean life will be free of trouble. It means God Himself keeps watch over the inner life of those who belong to Christ, even when anxiety presses in.

When worry rises, take the next step Paul gives: bring the specific request to God in prayer, with thanksgiving for who He is and what He has already done in Christ. His peace, not your understanding, is what He promises to set as a guard.

question: Is an eclipse a sign of the end times?
answer:
A typical solar or lunar eclipse is a regular part of the order God established in creation, not in itself proof that the end times have arrived. Genesis 1:14 tells us the lights in the sky serve as signs to mark seasons, days, and years; eclipses have occurred throughout history without bringing the final Day of the Lord.

Scripture does use striking cosmic language for that Day. Joel 2:31 says, “The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD.” Jesus speaks of the sun darkened and the moon not giving its light after the tribulation (Matthew 24:29), and Revelation 6:12 describes the sun becoming black and the moon like blood. These passages belong to eschatology, a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may differ without compromising the core hope that Jesus will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead.

One view, often among those who read prophecy more literally and futuristically, treats these descriptions as events we might actually observe, sometimes linking notable eclipses or “blood moons” to approaching fulfillment. Another historic view sees the language as apocalyptic imagery drawn from Old Testament oracles of judgment (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10, 31). It portrays the shaking of the present order when Christ appears, rather than ordinary, predictable eclipses that have come and gone for centuries.

Jesus Himself cautions against alarm and date-setting: “You will hear of wars and rumors of wars, but see to it that you are not alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come” (Matthew 24:6). “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36). The signs He mentions serve to keep us watchful, not to let us calculate the calendar.

The sure hope is Christ’s finished work: He died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily, and He will return. Live ready by trusting Him, walking in holiness by the Spirit, and gathering with a local church. If an eclipse has stirred questions, read Matthew 24–25 and 1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11, then pray through those chapters, asking the Lord for peace in His timing rather than in the skies.

question: Who are the multitude of all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues in Revelation 7:9?
answer:
The multitude in Revelation 7:9 is the innumerable company of the redeemed, people from every nation, tribe, people, and language who have been saved by the blood of Jesus Christ and now stand in victory before the throne and the Lamb.

John sees them immediately after the vision of 144,000 sealed from the tribes of Israel (Revelation 7:1–8). An elder later identifies them as those who “have come out of the great tribulation” and “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). They cry out, “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7:10). This is a picture of the church triumphant, the elect gathered from all peoples, clothed in the righteousness of Christ.

Faithful Christians differ on the precise relationship between this multitude and the 144,000, because Revelation uses highly symbolic, apocalyptic language whose details are not spelled out with the same clarity as core gospel truths. One historic view (common among amillennial interpreters) sees the 144,000 as a symbolic picture of the complete people of God (the true Israel, Jew and Gentile together) and the great multitude as the same saints viewed from the vantage point of heavenly glory. Another common view (especially among premillennial interpreters) treats the 144,000 as a literal Jewish remnant sealed during a future tribulation and the multitude as a distinct group of Gentiles (and perhaps others) who come to faith in that same period.

Both readings agree that these are justified sinners whose robes have been made white only by Christ’s atoning blood, not by their own works. The vision fulfills God’s ancient promise that all families of the earth would be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3) and shows the Lamb’s success in purchasing people “from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Heaven will not be a homogeneous gathering; it will be a vast, multi-ethnic assembly united in worship of the one Savior.

This should move us to pray for the gospel to reach remaining unreached peoples and to cherish the diversity of Christ’s body already present in our local churches, knowing we will one day stand together before the throne.

question: What is the counsel of the ungodly, and how do we not walk in it (Psalm 1:1)?
answer:
The counsel of the ungodly (called the wicked in the Berean Standard Bible) in Psalm 1:1 is the advice, plans, values, and whole way of thinking that come from people who live as though God is irrelevant or nonexistent. We refuse to walk in it by declining to let that thinking set our direction, and instead delighting in the law of the Lord and meditating on it day and night.

Psalm 1:1 says, "Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of mockers." The verse traces a downward slide: first taking their advice as a guide for life (walking), then joining their path (standing), then settling into their company of those who scoff at God (sitting). The alternative appears immediately in Psalm 1:2: "But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night." This is the beginning of wisdom, for "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding" (Proverbs 9:10).

This contrast is not mere self-help. It is the path of sanctification, being set apart from the world's patterns so that our minds are renewed rather than squeezed into its mold (Romans 12:2). The blessed person is like a tree planted by streams of water, fruitful and stable, while the wicked are like chaff the wind drives away (Psalm 1:3-4). In practice, this means testing every source of counsel (friends, media, culture, even our own feelings) against Scripture, especially on identity, morality, money, relationships, and purpose. When a decision arises, ask whether the advice aligns with God's Word rather than whether it feels popular or comfortable.

This week, take one piece of counsel you are currently considering, read it beside Psalm 1 and Proverbs 3:5-6, and pray directly to God, asking Him to make His Word your delight and to give you a discerning heart. Share what you find with a mature believer in your local church so you do not walk this path alone.

question: Does heaven exist?
answer:
Yes, heaven exists. The Bible presents heaven as a real place, the dwelling of the living God and the home He prepares for those who belong to Christ.

You may wonder whether this is only a comforting idea, since it cannot be measured in a lab, or whether different religions simply invent their own afterlives. Christians believe the risen Jesus Himself spoke of heaven as certain fact, not metaphor. He said, “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in Me. In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with Me that you also may be where I am” (John 14:1–3). His bodily resurrection on the third day is the public confirmation that His words about the unseen world are true.

God is holy, and every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory, so we cannot enter His presence by our own goodness (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose again, conquering death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life with Him. What thoughts or questions does this raise for you?

question: Does the Bible teach geocentrism?
answer:
No, the Bible does not teach geocentrism as a scientific model of the universe. It speaks in ordinary observational language from an earthly viewpoint (the sun “rises” and “sets,” the earth is “established”), just as we still do today without intending a cosmological claim.

This is a non-essential matter of interpretation where faithful Christians may differ, because Scripture’s purpose is to reveal God, creation, sin, and salvation rather than to supply a technical astronomy textbook, and the relevant verses are often poetic or phenomenological rather than scientific propositions (Romans 14:1-5).

Some Christians have historically read verses such as Psalm 93:1 (“The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved”) or Joshua 10:12-13 as implying a stationary earth at the center. Others, including most who hold a high view of Scripture’s inerrancy, understand the same language as describing appearances and God’s sovereign control, not a physical model; Job 26:7 even speaks of God hanging the earth “upon nothing.”

The Bible’s clear teaching is that the triune God created the heavens and the earth, rules them, and made this world the stage of His redemptive work in Christ. Hold that firmly, read the cosmological language according to its genre and intent, and leave room for Christian liberty on the scientific details.

question: Why did Jesus say, “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13)?
answer:
Jesus said this to show that He came for those who know they need mercy, not for those who think they are already righteous on their own. In Matthew 9:9-13, after Jesus called the tax collector Matthew and sat at table with many sinners, the Pharisees objected. Jesus answered that the well have no need of a physician, but the sick do, and He quoted Hosea 6:6: God desires mercy, not sacrifice.

The “righteous” in view are the self-righteous, those who trust their own law-keeping and see no need to repent. The sinners are those who admit their guilt. Scripture is plain that “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10) and “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Jesus therefore came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10), calling every person to repentance, a turning from sin toward God.

This is the Gospel itself. God is holy. Our sin separates us from Him. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not live, died on the cross as our substitute in penal substitutionary atonement, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He now calls sinners to Himself. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Read Matthew 9:9-13 slowly this week and ask the Lord to show you any place you are still relying on your own goodness rather than coming to Him as a needy sinner. How does His call to repentance meet you today?

question: What is God?
answer:
God is the one true and living God, eternally existing as three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) who are co-equal and co-eternal, the self-existent Creator of heaven and earth. He is infinite, holy, sovereign, unchanging, all-knowing, all-powerful, just, gracious, and loving.

Scripture opens by declaring that God created all things (Genesis 1:1). He is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), yet He has revealed Himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Son is fully God who became flesh (John 1:1; John 1:14), and the Holy Spirit is God (Acts 5:3-4). This biblical teaching is summarized in the doctrine of the Trinity: one God in three persons, not three gods and not one person wearing three masks.

God’s character is holy (Isaiah 6:3), immutable (Malachi 3:6), and both merciful and just (Exodus 34:6-7). His wrath against sin is real (Romans 1:18), yet He is patient and abounding in steadfast love.

We know this God most clearly in Jesus Christ, who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15) and who said that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9). Because of our sin we stand separated from this holy God, but Christ lived a perfect life, died as a substitutionary atonement on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day so that sinners might be justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A good next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking God to show you who He is through His Word, and to talk with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about what you find.

What part of who God is would you like to explore further?

question: How does the preservation of the Qur’an compare to the preservation of the Bible?
answer:
The Bible has been preserved through an unusually large, early, and publicly examined manuscript tradition that allows the original wording to be recovered with very high , while the Qur’an was gathered after Muhammad’s death from oral recitation and scattered writings, then officially standardized by caliphal order with other copies destroyed.

God promised that His Word would endure. “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus said, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away” (Matthew 24:35). The historical record matches that promise. The Old Testament text is confirmed by the Dead Sea Scrolls (dating from the second century BC onward), which align closely with the later Masoretic tradition. The New Testament is supported by more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts (some fragments from the early second century), plus thousands of early translations and extensive quotations by church fathers. Variants exist, as they do in every ancient text copied by hand, yet the overwhelming majority are minor (spelling, word order, synonyms). No core doctrine of the Christian faith (the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, or justification by grace through faith) is altered by them. Textual criticism, practiced openly for centuries, reconstructs the original autographs with a degree of unmatched by most other ancient literature. Christians therefore hold that Scripture is inspired, inerrant in the original writings, and faithfully preserved so that the Gospel remains clear.

The Qur’an’s history is different. Islamic sources record that Muhammad received recitations over about 23 years and that they were written on various materials and memorized. After his death in 632, many reciters died in battle, prompting the first caliph, Abu Bakr, to have Zayd ibn Thabit compile a collection. Around 650, Caliph Uthman commissioned an official version in the Quraysh dialect, sent copies to major cities, and ordered the burning of other written materials to end disputes over recitations. Companion codices (such as those associated with Ibn Masud and Ubayy ibn Ka’b) are reported in hadith literature to have differed in content, order, or inclusion of certain passages. Early manuscripts, including the Sana’a palimpsest, contain readings that diverge from the later standard text. Today the Qur’an exists in several canonical qira’at (authorized readings, commonly seven or ten), which differ in wording, grammar, and occasionally meaning; the Hafs transmission is now dominant, but it is not the only one. Reports also exist of verses once recited (for example, a stoning verse) that were not retained in the final compilation.

The popular contrast that “the Qur’an is perfectly unchanged while the Bible is corrupted” therefore oversimplifies both histories. The Bible’s transmission was decentralized and abundantly documented, with variants catalogued rather than suppressed; the Qur’an’s involved a later, centralized recension that eliminated competing written versions. Both texts have been copied by human hands, yet the volume, earliness, and transparency of biblical evidence give strong warrant for trusting that we possess the message God intended. That message centers on Christ’s incarnation, sinless life, substitutionary death, burial, and bodily resurrection, by which sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him.

If you are weighing these claims, a concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John (or Mark) in a reliable translation alongside a basic introduction to New Testament manuscripts, then compare that evidence with the hadith accounts of the Qur’an’s compilation. Pray that the Lord would give you clarity as you examine the texts themselves.

question: What is the meaning of Azazel / the scapegoat?
answer:
Azazel is the Hebrew name for the live goat (often called the scapegoat) in the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16. After lots were cast, one goat was sacrificed to the LORD while the high priest laid both hands on the second goat, confessed Israel’s sins over it, and sent it into the wilderness, never to return (Leviticus 16:8–10, 21–22).

The word ʿăzāzēl most naturally means “the goat of departure” (from ʿēz, goat, and ʾāzal, to go away) or names the remote, barren region itself. Either way, the ceremony vividly pictured expiation: God removing guilt so that it would not remain among His people.

This old-covenant shadow finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. He is both the slain offering whose blood propitiates God’s wrath and the sin-bearer who carries our iniquities away by penal substitutionary atonement (Isaiah 53:6; 1 Peter 2:24; Hebrews 9:26–28; Hebrews 13:11–13). Because He has done this, “as far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

Some extra-biblical Jewish writings (such as 1 Enoch) later identified Azazel as a demonic figure, and a minority of interpreters therefore see the goat as banishing sin into the realm of evil. The biblical text itself, however, presents the entire rite as taking place before the LORD, not as an offering to any rival power.

If you belong to Christ, you may rest in the finished work of the true Scapegoat: your sins have been carried away, and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Read Leviticus 16 slowly this week, then Hebrews 9–10, and thank God specifically that Jesus has taken your guilt far from you.

question: Who are sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2)?
answer:
The sons of disobedience in Ephesians 2:2 are those whose lives are marked by persistent rebellion against God, walking according to the ways of this world, the influence of Satan (the ruler of the power of the air), and their own sinful desires. Paul uses this phrase for the unregenerate, the natural condition of every person apart from Christ, as he immediately adds that “all of us also lived among them at one time” and “we were by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:1–3).

This Semitic idiom (“sons of”) describes people characterized by unbelief and disobedience rather than a special subclass of sinners. In the flow of Ephesians, Paul is reminding Gentile believers of their former spiritual death so that God’s mercy in making them alive with Christ would shine all the brighter (Ephesians 2:4–5). The same language appears in Colossians 3:6, where God’s wrath comes upon the sons of disobedience because of the sins they practice.

This reality is what Scripture calls our condition under original sin and total inability: we cannot please God or come to Him by our own power. Yet the same chapter announces the Gospel: God, rich in mercy, made us alive together with Christ even when we were dead in trespasses; it is by grace we have been saved through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:4–9). Christ died as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death.

If this still describes you, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. Believers, remember you were once in that company so that gratitude, humility, and eagerness to walk in the good works God prepared for you (Ephesians 2:10) become your daily response. What has Ephesians 2 shown you about your own need for Christ or His grace toward you?

question: What does the Bible say about pettiness?
answer:
The Bible does not use the word pettiness, but it repeatedly condemns a small-minded, easily offended spirit that keeps score of minor wrongs, stirs up strife over trivial matters, and withholds the generous grace God has shown us.

Love “is not easily angered” and “keeps no record of wrongs” (1 Corinthians 13:5). Wisdom considers it a glory “to overlook an offense” (Proverbs 19:11). Jesus taught His disciples to forgive not seven times but seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21-22), and He rebuked religious leaders for straining out a gnat while swallowing a camel, exposing their petty focus on minor rules while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23-24). Paul urged believers to put away bitterness, rage, slander, and malice, and instead “be kind and compassionate to one another, forgiving each other, just as in Christ God forgave you” (Ephesians 4:31-32). We are to “bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against one another. Forgive as the Lord forgave you” (Colossians 3:13). Above all, “love covers over a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

This large-hearted forbearance is part of our sanctification. The Holy Spirit produces patience, kindness, and self-control rather than the works of the flesh such as discord, envy, and fits of anger (Galatians 5:19-23). Pettiness often reveals a heart still defending its own honor instead of resting in Christ’s finished work. Because Jesus died as our substitute and rose again, we no longer need to magnify every slight.

When a small irritation or old grievance tempts you to brood or snap, pause and remember how freely God has forgiven you in Christ, then choose to overlook it. This week, read 1 Corinthians 13 slowly each morning and ask the Lord to show you one relationship where you can cover a small offense rather than keep a record of it. Talk with Him about it in prayer, and if a particular conflict keeps circling the same small issues, seek counsel from a mature believer in your local church.

question: What is the “great and dreadful day of the Lord” (Malachi 4:5)?
answer:
The “great and dreadful day of the Lord” (Malachi 4:5) is the coming day of the Lord’s judgment, when He will consume the arrogant like stubble in a furnace yet bring healing to those who fear His name (Malachi 4:1-2). Malachi closes the Old Testament with the promise that Elijah will appear first, turning hearts of fathers and children so the land is not struck with a curse (Malachi 4:5-6). The prophets often used “day of the Lord” language for God’s decisive intervention of wrath against sin and salvation for His remnant (Joel 2:31; Zephaniah 1:14).

Jesus identified John the Baptist as coming in the spirit and power of Elijah to prepare the way (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14). At the same time, He indicated that Elijah’s restoring work still has a future aspect (Matthew 17:11).

Questions about the exact timing belong to eschatology, a tertiary doctrine on which faithful Christians may disagree without breaking fellowship, because Scripture is clearer on the certainty of Christ’s return than on every prophetic detail. One major view understands the great and dreadful day as fulfilled primarily in Christ’s first coming, with John’s ministry as the promised Elijah. Another major view sees it pointing chiefly to Christ’s second coming and the final judgment. Christians hold these interpretations in liberty (Romans 14:5), united in the core truth that Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead.

The abiding call is to fear the Lord now, turn from sin, and be ready, just as Elijah was sent to turn hearts.

question: What does the Bible say about self-righteousness?
answer:
The Bible teaches that self-righteousness is sinful pride that trusts in one's own moral performance or superiority rather than in God's grace, and it keeps people from true repentance and faith.

Jesus told a parable specifically to those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and looked down on others, in Luke 18:9-14. The Pharisee boasted of his own goodness while the tax collector simply pleaded, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner," and Jesus said the humble man went home justified rather than the self-righteous one. Isaiah 64:6 declares that all our righteous acts are like filthy rags. Romans 10:3 explains that those who seek to establish their own righteousness have not submitted to God's righteousness.

This stands at the heart of justification by faith alone. No one is made right with God by personal works or comparison with others. There is no one righteous, not even one, in Romans 3:10, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God in Romans 3:23. The only righteousness that God accepts is the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith, as Paul longed to have in Philippians 3:9, not a righteousness of his own from the law.

Self-righteousness often shows itself in feeling we have earned God's favor or in looking down on those we consider worse sinners. The Gospel offers the opposite: Jesus lived a perfect life, died as our substitute on the cross to pay for sin, and rose bodily from the dead. Turn from relying on your own goodness and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

If you see this tendency in your own heart, read Luke 18:9-14 slowly this week and ask God in prayer to reveal any self-reliance, then talk it over with a pastor or mature believer in a local church.

question: What is the meaning and purpose of saying grace before a meal?
answer:
Saying grace before a meal is a prayer of thanksgiving to God for the food He has provided, acknowledging Him as the source of every good gift. Its purpose is to express gratitude, remember our daily dependence on His providence, and do even ordinary things like eating to His glory.

Jesus Himself modeled this practice, looking to heaven and giving thanks before breaking bread to feed the crowds (Matthew 14:19) and again at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26–27). Paul teaches that every creation of God is good and is to be received with thanksgiving, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). Scripture also commands, “So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). In the Old Testament, God’s people were instructed, after eating and being satisfied, to bless the LORD for His provision (Deuteronomy 8:10). This simple act of thanksgiving therefore turns a meal into a moment of worship, reminding us that we live by God’s common grace and not by our own strength.

You might begin this week by pausing before one meal each day to thank God specifically for the food, those who prepared it, and the strength it gives to serve Him. Pray in your own words, perhaps using Psalm 145:15–16 as a guide: “The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season. You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing.” If you have a family, this can also become a brief, regular way to teach gratitude together.

question: What does the Bible say about fun and entertainment?
answer:
The Bible presents joy, rest, and celebration as good gifts from God to be received with thanksgiving, while calling believers to pursue leisure in ways that honor Christ rather than feed sin or worldliness. God Himself instituted rest and commanded His people to rejoice, yet He never treats entertainment as an end in itself or as something exempt from His lordship.

The Sabbath was given as a day of rest and delight in the Lord (Exodus 20:8-11; Isaiah 58:13-14). Israel’s feasts included eating, drinking, and rejoicing before God (Deuteronomy 16:14-15). Jesus attended a wedding feast and provided wine, sharing in ordinary human gladness (John 2:1-11). Ecclesiastes 3:4 speaks of “a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance.” God “richly provides us with all things to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). These passages show that laughter, play, music, and recreation are not inherently unspiritual.

At the same time, Scripture warns against the love of the world and its passing pleasures (1 John 2:15-17). “Everything is permissible for me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is permissible for me, but I will not be mastered by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Believers are to dwell on whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable (Philippians 4:8). Whatever we do, in word or deed, is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God (Colossians 3:17). Drunkenness, sexual immorality, greed, and foolish talk are named as sins to put away, not as entertainment options (Ephesians 5:3-18).

Specific choices about movies, sports, games, or other pastimes often fall under Christian liberty, where Scripture does not give a detailed list and faithful Christians may differ according to conscience and circumstance (Romans 14:5-6; Romans 14:13-23). Some believers emphasize greater caution, avoiding much of contemporary culture so as not to be conformed to it or to stumble others. Others exercise wider freedom, engaging culture while filtering it through holiness and love. Neither view is required of every Christian as a test of faithfulness; both must submit to the same standard of glorifying God and pursuing sanctification (1 Corinthians 10:31).
