A practical next step is to review one current form of entertainment this week by asking whether it draws your affections toward Christ or dulls them, then talk it over with a mature believer in your local church. Ask the Lord for wisdom in these matters (James 1:5) and thank Him for every good gift while keeping your heart free from being mastered by any of them.

question: Does Romans 2:7 teach works salvation?
answer:
No, Romans 2:7 does not teach works salvation. Paul states God's impartial principle of judgment: "To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life" (Romans 2:7), echoing that God "will repay each one according to his deeds" (Romans 2:6).

In the argument of Romans, this standard of judgment according to works exposes that no one actually meets it. Paul soon declares, "There is no one who does good, not even one" (Romans 3:12), "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23), and "no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law" (Romans 3:20). Justification (God's declaration that a sinner is righteous) is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, whose penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection provide the righteousness we lack (Romans 3:21-26; Romans 4:5; Romans 5:1). The perseverance in doing good in Romans 2:7 describes the fruit of those already justified by faith, not the meritorious cause of eternal life. God creates believers in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:8-10), and He keeps them so they will not finally fall away.

If this verse has raised questions about whether your own deeds could ever be enough, look away from yourself to Jesus Christ, who perfectly obeyed and died in the place of sinners. Read Romans 3:21-26 slowly this week and ask God to settle your heart on Christ's finished work rather than your own perseverance.

question: Why do Christians believe in proselytization?
answer:
Christians share the Gospel (evangelism) because Jesus commanded His followers to make disciples of all nations and because they are convinced that He alone saves people from sin and eternal separation from God. In Matthew 28:18-20 Jesus said, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Romans 10:14 adds the practical reason: people cannot believe in the One of whom they have not heard.

Some see this as arrogant, intolerant, or a leftover of cultural imperialism, assuming every religion is equally valid or that faith should stay private. Christians understand why that feels true in a pluralistic world, yet they hold that if Jesus truly rose from the dead, His claim in John 14:6 stands: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." Withholding that news would be unloving, not humble. They are called to do it with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), never by force or contempt.

The Bible teaches that God is holy and just, every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory (Romans 3:23), and the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin and death. Justification comes by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works. Out of love for God and neighbor, Christians therefore speak of this hope so others may repent and live.

If you have not trusted Him, turn from sin and put your faith in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What has shaped your view of Christians sharing their faith?

question: What does Exodus 23:2 teach us about not following the crowd?
answer:
Exodus 23:2 teaches that God’s people must not follow the crowd into doing evil, and must not twist justice simply because many people demand it. The verse says, “You shall not follow a crowd in doing evil. Nor shall you testify in a dispute so as to pervert justice by siding with a crowd.”

This command sits in the covenant laws given after the Ten Commandments, where the Lord requires impartial justice that reflects His own holy and just character. Truth and righteousness are never decided by majority vote or social pressure. The fear of man is a snare, but the one who trusts in the Lord is kept safe (Proverbs 29:25).

The same principle runs through the rest of Scripture. The broad road that many travel leads to destruction, while the way of life is narrow (Matthew 7:13-14). Believers are therefore called not to be conformed to this world, but to be transformed by the renewing of the mind so they can discern God’s good and perfect will (Romans 12:2). This is part of sanctification: being set apart to walk in holiness even when it is costly or lonely.

When friends, coworkers, or the wider culture press you to compromise because “everyone else is doing it,” this verse calls you to refuse. Ask the Lord for courage to stand on His Word rather than on popular opinion, and talk with a mature believer in your local church about one specific area where you feel that pressure.

question: What is Tisha B'Av?
answer:
Tisha B'Av, meaning “the ninth of Av,” is a major Jewish fast day of mourning that commemorates the destruction of Solomon’s Temple in 586 BC and the Second Temple in AD 70, along with later national tragedies.

Scripture records the burning of the First Temple as God’s judgment on covenant unfaithfulness in 2 Kings 25:8-9 and Jeremiah 52:12-13. Jesus Christ Himself prophesied the Second Temple’s destruction, saying that not one stone would be left upon another (Matthew 24:1-2; Mark 13:1-2), a word fulfilled in AD 70.

These events display God’s holiness and justice against sin, yet they also point to Christ as the true Temple whose body was destroyed and raised on the third day (John 2:19-21).

question: Should Christians care about physical appearance?
answer:
Yes, Christians should care about physical appearance as faithful stewards of the bodies God has given, yet without vanity, comparison, or treating looks as the measure of worth.

Our bodies belong to the Lord. 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 says, “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.” Reasonable care for health, hygiene, rest, and modest, fitting dress is part of presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1) and of not hindering our witness. Physical training even has some value (1 Timothy 4:8).

At the same time, Scripture will not let appearance become an idol or the source of identity. The LORD told Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him. The LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). 1 Peter 3:3-4 teaches, “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight.” Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but the one who fears the LORD is to be praised (Proverbs 31:30). Godliness holds promise for this life and the next in a way that physical appearance never can.

How much time or money is spent on appearance, beyond the clear calls to modesty and stewardship, is often a matter of Christian liberty and wisdom (Romans 14). The danger on one side is neglect that dishonors the body as God’s gift; the danger on the other is the world’s obsession with image, which feeds pride, anxiety, and judging others by what they wear (James 2:1-4). Our worth is already settled in Christ: we are fearfully and wonderfully made (Psalm 139:14) and, if we are in Him, a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

A practical next step is to bring this before the Lord in prayer. Ask Him to search your motives when you look in the mirror or choose clothes: does this honor Him and serve others, or feed self-focus? Thank Him specifically for your body as His temple, then give more time to the inner life through Scripture than to outward appearance. If this area has become a source of struggle, speak with a mature believer in your local church who can walk with you in the gospel.

question: What is the gospel of inclusion?
answer:
The phrase "gospel of inclusion" does not appear in Scripture. It is a modern term some teachers and churches use for a message that God accepts all people into salvation or the church without the call to repent of sin or to trust in Jesus Christ alone.

That message is not the Gospel of the Bible. It stands outside orthodox Christianity when it denies the necessity of personal faith, the reality of God's judgment, or the exclusive claims of Christ.

Scripture teaches that God is holy and that all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). In love He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Jesus lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By grace alone through faith alone in Him, sinners are justified and given new life. This good news is offered to people from every nation and background: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). Yet Jesus is the only way: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6); "Salvation exists in no one else" (Acts 4:12). God now commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What have you heard about this idea, and which Scriptures would you like to look at together?

question: What did Paul mean by the “Holy Scriptures” in 2 Timothy 3:15?
answer:
Paul meant the Old Testament Scriptures by the “Holy Scriptures” in 2 Timothy 3:15. These were the sacred Hebrew writings Timothy had known from childhood, the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings given by God to Israel.

The Greek phrase hiera grammata (“sacred writings”) was a common Second Temple Jewish way to name those books. Timothy received them through his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois (2 Timothy 1:5), long before most New Testament books were written. Paul says those same Scriptures “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15), because they testify about the Messiah who would come. Jesus Himself taught that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44; John 5:39).

This shows the unity and authority of God’s Word: the Old Testament is not a separate or lesser revelation but the Spirit-inspired foundation that finds its fulfillment in Christ’s incarnation, atoning death, and bodily resurrection. All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable (2 Timothy 3:16), so the whole Bible, Old and New Testaments together, trains us in the faith once for all delivered to the saints.

A simple next step is to read a portion of the Old Testament this week (perhaps Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22) while asking how it points to Jesus, then talk it over with a mature believer in your local church.

question: Is the priesthood of all believers biblical?
answer:
Yes, the priesthood of all believers is biblical. Scripture presents every Christian as part of a royal priesthood with direct access to God through Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, rather than through a separate class of human mediators.

God first called Israel a kingdom of priests in Exodus 19:6. The New Testament applies this to the church: 1 Peter 2:5 describes believers as a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ, and 1 Peter 2:9 calls us a royal priesthood. Revelation 1:6 and Revelation 5:10 likewise say Christ has made us a kingdom and priests to God. Because Jesus is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5) and our sympathetic High Priest who has opened the way (Hebrews 4:14-16; Hebrews 10:19-22), we may now approach the throne of grace with confidence. His once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:12) fulfills and ends the old Levitical priesthood.

Some historic Christians, particularly in Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions, hold that while all the baptized share a common priesthood, Christ also instituted a distinct ministerial priesthood through apostolic succession to offer the Eucharist as a sacrifice and administer the sacraments. As a Reformed Baptist I affirm the priesthood of all believers as the New Testament pattern: every Christian now functions as a priest by offering the spiritual sacrifices of praise, prayer, intercession, and a life of service (Hebrews 13:15; Romans 12:1), while pastors and elders serve the church by teaching and shepherding, not by mediating access to God.

This truth means you can pray, confess, and worship God directly today. Read 1 Peter 2 this week and ask the Lord to show you one concrete way to live as a priest in your family, work, or church, whether by interceding for someone or speaking of Christ’s virtues.

question: Why is there a curse associated with hanging on a tree?
answer:
The curse associated with hanging on a tree comes from Deuteronomy 21:22-23, where God commanded Israel that a person put to death for a capital crime and then hung on a tree is under God’s curse. The body was not to remain overnight, so that the land would not be defiled, because the hanging itself publicly marked the offender as under divine judgment.

This law displayed the holiness of God and the real weight of sin. Execution already declared the person guilty, and hanging the body added shame as a visible warning that such a one stood accursed before the Lord.

The New Testament shows this reaching its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. Galatians 3:13 states, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.’” Though sinless, He was crucified on a wooden cross (called a tree, using language that matches the Hebrew word for tree or wood in Deuteronomy). In this way He took the curse the law pronounces on sinners. This is penal substitutionary atonement: the righteous One bore the curse in the place of the unrighteous so that those who trust Him are redeemed and receive the blessing of justification by faith, not by works of the law (Galatians 3:10-14). 1 Peter 2:24 adds, “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.”

When the law’s demands or your own guilt feel heavy, look to Christ who hung on the tree for you. He has already borne the curse. Read Deuteronomy 21:22-23 and Galatians 3:10-14 together, and thank God directly in prayer for how Christ became a curse so that you might be blessed in Him.

question: How can we learn to trust God like the prophet Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:17-19)?
answer:
We learn to trust God like Habakkuk by fixing our joy on the Lord Himself as our salvation and strength, rather than on circumstances that can fail us completely.

Habakkuk began by wrestling with God's justice as Judah faced coming judgment, yet after recalling the Lord's mighty acts of old he declared, "Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will be joyful in the God of my salvation. GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights" (Habakkuk 3:17-19). This is living by faith, as the prophet had already heard: "the righteous will live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). God's sovereignty remains good and just even when He allows or brings loss; our trust rests in His character, not in the fruit of the field.

For us that same God of salvation is known most clearly in Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, whose substitutionary death on the cross and bodily resurrection secure hope that no drought or empty stall can take away. We grow in this trust through the ordinary means of grace: reading Scripture that displays His past faithfulness (from the Exodus Habakkuk remembered to the empty tomb), praying honestly as Habakkuk did, and walking with the local church. When your own "fig tree" fails, you can still say "yet I will rejoice," because joy is rooted in the unchanging Lord, not in changing gifts. This is part of progressive sanctification, as the Spirit uses trials to deepen our rest in grace rather than in ourselves.

This week read the whole book of Habakkuk slowly. Then take one present lack or fear, pray Habakkuk 3:17-19 over it, and thank God specifically for Christ as your salvation. Share what you are learning with a pastor or mature believer in your church so you do not walk this path alone.

question: Why are we supposed to give thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18)?
answer:
We give thanks in everything because this is God’s will for us in Christ Jesus, a grateful response to His sovereign goodness that shapes our whole life of faith. 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says, “Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.” This command sits with the call to rejoice always and pray continually (1 Thessalonians 5:16-17), showing that thanksgiving is not an extra religious habit but part of living as those already reconciled to God.

God remains holy, faithful, and good even when circumstances are painful. He works all things together for the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28), and every good gift comes from Him (James 1:17). Thanksgiving in hardship is therefore not pretending evil is pleasant. It is trust in divine providence: the same God who sent His Son to die and rise for us will not waste what He allows. Gratitude also flows from justification by faith. Because we have peace with God through Christ, we can rest in His purposes instead of growing bitter. Ingratitude, by contrast, is a mark of hearts that refuse to honor Him (Romans 1:21).

This practice is part of our sanctification. It trains us to see Christ’s lordship in ordinary and difficult days alike, producing endurance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3-5). When anxiety rises, thanksgiving with prayer becomes the path to the peace of God that guards our hearts (Philippians 4:6-7).

A concrete way to begin is this: when a disappointment or trial meets you this week, pause and thank God specifically for His unchanging presence and for one way He may be using it to draw you nearer to Himself. As a next step, read 1 Thessalonians 5:16-24 each day for a week, note one circumstance you face, and write a brief reason to thank God in it. Share that with a mature believer in your local church so you do not walk it alone. In your own prayers, ask the Lord to help you remember His benefits and to see His hand even in what you would not have chosen, using Psalm 103:1-5 as a guide.

question: Why did Jesus refer to the temple as “my Father’s house” (John 2:16)?
answer:
Jesus referred to the temple as “My Father’s house” because He is the unique, eternal Son of God who shares the Father’s nature and therefore holds rightful authority over the place where God chose to dwell among His people. This was a public claim of divine sonship, not a general religious phrase, and it immediately set Jesus apart from every prophet, priest, or teacher who had gone before Him.

In the Old Testament the temple is repeatedly called the house of the LORD, the sacred site of God’s presence and the center of Israel’s worship (1 Kings 8:10–13). Jesus takes that language and makes it intensely personal: it is *His* Father’s house. The same conviction appears even in His childhood, when He told Mary and Joseph, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49). By driving out the merchants and money changers who had turned the court of the Gentiles into a marketplace, Jesus acted with the zeal that belongs to the Son, fulfilling the Scripture, “Zeal for Your house will consume Me” (Psalm 69:9; John 2:17).

This declaration of unique sonship is a core affirmation of the deity of Christ and of the Trinity: the Father and the Son are distinct persons, yet one God. The religious authorities later understood the implication and sought to kill Him for “making Himself equal with God” (John 5:18). At the same time Jesus pointed beyond the stone building to Himself as the true temple, saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (John 2:19), speaking of His body that would be crucified and bodily raised.

The same truth still calls us to worship the Father through the Son with undivided hearts, treating the gathering of God’s people as holy rather than as a platform for profit or self-interest.

question: What does the Bible say about child abuse?
answer:
The Bible condemns child abuse as a grievous sin. Children are a heritage from the Lord and bear the image of God, so physical, sexual, emotional, or neglectful harm against them is an assault on their Creator and a violation of His holy law (Psalm 127:3; Genesis 1:27).

Jesus gave one of Scripture’s most severe warnings about harming the vulnerable: “But if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18:6). God is a Father to the fatherless and commands His people to defend the weak (Psalm 68:5; Psalm 82:3).

Parents receive a direct charge: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Biblical discipline is patient, purposeful training in righteousness, never rage, cruelty, or injury. Abuse is not discipline; it is sin that God will judge. Sexual abuse falls under the Bible’s clear prohibitions against sexual immorality and exploiting others (Leviticus 18; 1 Corinthians 6:18). Neglect of a child’s needs contradicts the command to provide for one’s household (1 Timothy 5:8).

God’s wrath against such evil is real, yet the Gospel holds out mercy. Christ, who is truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Even the darkest sins can be forgiven for those who repent and trust in Him alone.

If you have suffered abuse, the Lord is near to the brokenhearted and sees every injustice (Psalm 34:18). If you have committed it, turn from it at once, confess it, and submit to both God’s forgiveness and the just consequences of civil authority, which God has appointed to punish evildoers (Romans 13:4). In either case, speak with a pastor in a local church that takes child protection seriously, and if abuse is occurring, report it to the proper authorities immediately.

A practical next step is to pray through Psalm 10, asking God for justice, protection for the vulnerable, and wisdom to act righteously in your own family and church.

question: What is Christianophobia?
answer:
Christianophobia is hostility, prejudice, or discrimination directed against Christians or the Christian faith because of that faith. It can appear as mockery, social exclusion, legal pressure against biblical convictions, or outright violence, depending on the setting.

The Bible treats such opposition as a normal part of following Jesus rather than a surprise. Jesus told His disciples, “If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (John 15:18). Paul likewise wrote, “Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (2 Timothy 3:12). This hostility often arises because the gospel confronts human pride and sin; the cross itself is an offense (Galatians 5:11).

Not every disagreement with Christian teaching is Christianophobia. Honest critique and even sharp debate can be legitimate. The term points instead to prejudice that refuses to treat Christians fairly or that seeks to silence or punish them for holding to Scripture. Believers are called to respond with love for enemies, prayer, and steadfastness rather than bitterness (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:14). If you are facing this kind of pressure, stay planted in a local church that holds to the Word, and keep bringing the matter to God in prayer, asking Him for wisdom and a gentle, truthful witness.

question: How can I know that my future sins are forgiven?
answer:
You can know that your future sins are forgiven because Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice fully paid the penalty for every sin of those who trust Him, and justification is God’s complete, irreversible declaration that you stand righteous in Christ.

Hebrews 10:14 tells us, “For by a single offering He has made perfect forever those who are being sanctified.” At the cross Jesus accomplished penal substitution: He bore the wrath our sins deserved, and God imputes Christ’s perfect righteousness to everyone who believes. That standing before God is not piecemeal or probationary. Romans 8:1 therefore says, “Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” Colossians 2:13-14 adds that He has “forgiven us all our trespasses, having canceled the record of debt that stood against us.” All of them, not merely the ones already committed.

Some Christians, reading 1 John 1:9, fear that each new sin remains unforgiven until it is specifically named, as if justification were repeated or incomplete. That verse, however, is written to people already walking in the light. It concerns the restoration of family fellowship with the Father when we sin, not a fresh judicial pardon. Our Advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, already lives to intercede for us (1 John 2:1-2). The distinction matters: justification settles our legal status once; sanctification is the lifelong work of the Spirit making us actually holy. We still confess, hate, and turn from sin because we are children who love our Father, not because we are still trying to earn or keep His verdict.

This assurance never licenses carelessness (Romans 6:1-2). Those whom God justifies He also sanctifies; the same grace that covers future sins also produces repentance and growth. If you have truly trusted the Jesus who died, was buried, and rose on the third day, you are kept by God’s power and will not finally fall away (John 10:28-29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). Look away from your performance and to the finished work of Christ.

If you have never yet turned from sin and trusted Jesus Christ alone, do so now: we have all sinned and deserve judgment, yet He lived the life we could not live, died the death we deserved, and rose again so that whoever believes in Him has eternal life, not by works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to read Romans 8 slowly this week, asking the Lord to settle your heart in His promises, and then talk with a pastor or mature believer in your local church about the specific fears this question raises. What particular worry about future failure has been heaviest on you?

question: Book of Malachi - Bible Survey
answer:
The Book of Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament and the twelfth of the Minor Prophets, a four-chapter prophetic message delivered to post-exilic Judah around 430 BC. God speaks through the prophet Malachi (whose name means “My Messenger”) to a community that had rebuilt the temple yet grown spiritually indifferent under Persian rule.

After the ministries of Haggai and Zechariah, the people questioned God’s love, offered blemished sacrifices (Malachi 1:8), broke marriage covenants through divorce and intermarriage (Malachi 2:11; Malachi 2:14–16), and withheld tithes (Malachi 3:8–10). The book employs a covenant-lawsuit style of statement, objection, and reply, beginning with God’s electing love for Jacob over Esau (Malachi 1:2–3).

Its main movements confront priestly dishonor (Malachi 1:6–2:9), call the people to covenant faithfulness (Malachi 2:10–16), announce a purifying Messenger and the Day of the Lord (Malachi 2:17–3:5), urge a return in giving (Malachi 3:6–12), and distinguish the remnant who fear the Lord (Malachi 3:13–4:6). God declares His own immutability: “I the LORD do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

These oracles find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The messenger who prepares the way (Malachi 3:1) is John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2; Luke 7:27), and the Lord who comes suddenly to His temple is Christ Himself. The promised Elijah (Malachi 4:5–6) likewise points to John’s ministry (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14). Thus Malachi closes the Old Testament with a summons to repentance and a forward look to the Gospel, after which four centuries of silence preceded the incarnation.

When worship grows routine or giving reluctant, Malachi still calls God’s people to honor Him with undivided hearts, knowing He keeps a book of remembrance for those who fear His name (Malachi 3:16) and that the sun of righteousness has already risen with healing in Jesus (Malachi 4:2). Read the four chapters this week, noting each question the people ask and God’s reply, then bring those same areas of life before the Lord in prayer.

question: What are phylacteries?
answer:
Phylacteries (also called tefillin) are small leather boxes containing parchment with Torah verses, traditionally worn by Jewish men on the forehead and left arm during weekday morning prayers as a literal sign of devotion to God's Word.

This custom grew from commands such as Deuteronomy 6:8: "Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads." Similar language appears in Exodus 13:9, Exodus 13:16, and Deuteronomy 11:18. In the Second Temple period these boxes became a visible mark of piety among some Jews.

Jesus rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for enlarging their phylacteries to be noticed by others rather than walking in humble obedience (Matthew 23:5). The danger He named was hypocrisy: using religious symbols to display righteousness while the heart remained far from God.

Scripture calls believers to hide God's Word in the heart rather than merely on the body (Psalm 119:11). Let that Word shape your thoughts and actions today, and if you have not yet trusted Christ, turn from sin and rest in His finished work on the cross and His bodily resurrection for forgiveness and new life.

question: Who are true worshipers (John 4:23)?
answer:
True worshipers are those who worship the Father in spirit and in truth, the very people the Father Himself is seeking (John 4:23). Jesus spoke these words to a Samaritan woman who assumed worship depended on the right mountain (Gerizim versus Jerusalem). He answered that the hour had already arrived in Him, so location and ethnic ritual no longer define acceptable worship.

Because God is Spirit, worship must correspond to His nature: it arises from the inner person, is enabled by the Holy Spirit, and is offered according to the truth God has revealed, supremely in Jesus Christ who is the Truth (John 4:24; John 14:6). This is possible only for those who have been born again; unregenerate hearts cannot produce the worship God seeks (John 3:5-8). The apostle Paul later describes the same reality: “we who serve God by His Spirit, who boast in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3).

A practical next step is to open John 4, read the whole conversation slowly, and ask the Lord to show you whether your own worship (in gathered church, private prayer, or daily obedience) is flowing from a sincere, Scripture-shaped heart rather than mere habit.

question: Book of Obadiah - Bible Survey
answer:
The Book of Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, a single chapter of 21 verses. It is a prophetic oracle announcing the LORD’s judgment on Edom for arrogant violence against Judah, together with a promise of deliverance for God’s people and the coming of His kingdom (Obadiah 1:1; Obadiah 1:21).

Obadiah (“servant of the LORD”) is otherwise unknown in Scripture. The prophecy most likely comes from the years after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edomites (descendants of Esau) stood aloof, looted, and even handed over Judah’s fugitives. Some date it earlier, to the ninth century BC, but the language of calamity against “your brother Jacob” fits the later disaster especially well.

Edom occupied the rugged highlands of Seir south of the Dead Sea, trusting in its rock fortresses, trade wealth, and reputation for wisdom. The long hostility between Esau’s line and Jacob’s line (Numbers 20:14-21) boiled over into open betrayal. God therefore declares that Edom’s pride has deceived it (Obadiah 1:3). Its allies will fail, its wise men will be destroyed, and it will be cut off forever because of the violence done to its brother (Obadiah 1:8-10). The nations that joined in the plunder will drink the same cup of wrath on the Day of the LORD (Obadiah 1:15-16). Yet on Mount Zion there will be deliverance and holiness; the house of Jacob will possess its inheritance, including Edom itself, and “the kingdom will belong to the LORD” (Obadiah 1:17, Obadiah 1:21).

The book therefore displays God’s sovereign justice over every nation, His hatred of pride, and His covenant faithfulness to Israel. The “Day of the LORD” here is both near historical judgment and a pointer to the final day when Christ will rule. Edom’s later history (absorption by the Nabateans, the Idumean line of Herod) only confirms that the word spoken through Obadiah did not fail.

Pride still deceives hearts that feel secure in their own strength or position. When fellow believers suffer, we are not to stand at a distance or gloat. Read the whole of Obadiah in one sitting this week, then ask the Lord to show you any hidden arrogance or lack of brotherly compassion, and to fix your hope on the kingdom that already belongs to Him.

question: What does it mean to gain the whole world but lose your soul?
answer:
Jesus taught that to gain the whole world but lose your soul is to obtain every earthly treasure, success, and pleasure while forfeiting eternal life with God, an exchange that profits nothing.

He asked, “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matthew 16:26; see also Mark 8:36; Luke 9:25). These words come right after His call to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him (Matthew 16:24–25). In that setting, “the whole world” meant all that people chase instead of Christ: wealth, status, comfort, and self-rule. Your soul is the real you, created for God and destined to stand before Him forever. To lose it is to face His just judgment for sin, eternal separation from the God who made you.

Because we have all sinned, we stand in that danger (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). God is holy, and His wrath against sin is real. Yet He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who lived a perfect life, died on the cross as our substitute under the penalty we deserved (penal substitutionary atonement), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Justification comes by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by any worldly achievement.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. A next step is to read Matthew 16:13–28 slowly this week and pray that God would show you where you may be seeking the world instead of His kingdom (Matthew 6:33). If this question is weighing on you, share it with a pastor or mature believer in a local church. What has been stirring this in your own life?

question: Why did God send the flood when He knew sin would continue after the flood?
answer:
God sent the flood as a just judgment on the overflowing wickedness of Noah’s generation, while mercifully preserving a remnant so that His redemptive plan could continue, even though He knew the human heart would remain sinful afterward.

The LORD saw that “the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5). Violence and corruption filled the earth, and God, who is holy and just, determined to bring judgment (Genesis 6:11–13). Yet Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8), and through him God preserved the human race and the promised line that would lead to Christ.

After the flood God Himself declared that “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). The flood judged that particular generation; it was never meant to remove original sin or perfect humanity. God knew this because He knows the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:9–10). When Scripture says the LORD “regretted that He had made man” (Genesis 6:6), it expresses His holy grief over sin in language we can grasp. It does not mean He was surprised or that His unchanging nature shifted (Malachi 3:6; Numbers 23:19).

The flood therefore accomplished exactly what God intended: it displayed His justice against sin, His patience (He waited 120 years, Genesis 6:3), and His mercy in saving eight people. It also stands as a real historical warning of the greater judgment still to come and as a picture of salvation. Peter writes that God “did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, with seven others, when He brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:5), and he links that event to the coming judgment by fire (2 Peter 3:6–7). In the same way, “a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water. And this water symbolizes baptism that now saves you also… through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:20–21).

The persistence of sin after the flood shows that external judgment alone cannot change the heart. Only Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who lived a sinless life, died as a substitutionary sacrifice, was buried, and rose bodily, can deal with the root of sin. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone.

If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted Christ, repent and believe in Jesus who died and rose for you, that you may be saved from the coming judgment and receive new life. I encourage you to read Genesis 6–9 this week, asking the Lord to show you both His holiness and His grace, and to talk it over with a mature believer in your local church. What part of this most stirs questions or comfort for you?

question: Should a church tithe 10% of the offerings it receives?
answer:
The New Testament does not require a local church to tithe 10 percent of the offerings it receives. Church decisions about a set giving percentage belong among non-essential matters of stewardship and Christian liberty, where faithful congregations may differ because Scripture supplies principles of generous, cheerful giving rather than a fixed congregational tenth under the New Covenant.

Some churches apply the Old Testament tithe as a starting point of firstfruits, directing 10 percent toward missions or other gospel work in order to model obedience and keep resources moving outward. Other churches follow the New Testament pattern in which congregations gave according to ability and present need, as when the disciples decided to send relief “as each one was able” (Acts 11:29) and the Macedonian churches gave “even beyond their ability” (2 Corinthians 8:3), without a mandated percentage.

Romans 14:5 reminds us that in such disputable practices each should be fully convinced in his own mind and walk in faith toward the Lord without judging one another. Consistent with covenant theology that recognizes both continuity and the distinctiveness of the new covenant in Christ, I see the tithe as belonging to the Mosaic administration rather than as a binding law for churches today; every congregation remains free, and is called, to give generously and even sacrificially as an act of worship. Elders should lead in prayerful, transparent budgeting that supports pastors, cares for needy saints, and advances the gospel, reflecting that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If this question is before your church, a wise next step is for the elders to study 2 Corinthians 8:1–15 and 2 Corinthians 9:6–15 together, pray for wisdom, and then guide the body in a budget that honors Christ with the resources He has entrusted.

question: Easter Bible reading plan
answer:
A simple Easter Bible reading plan can guide you through the Gospel accounts of Jesus Christ’s final week in Jerusalem, His atoning death, and His bodily resurrection, all presented in Scripture as real historical events.

Whether or not a church follows a special calendar for these days is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty where faithful believers may differ (Romans 14:5-6). Some find an annual focus helpful for meditation, while others treat every Lord’s Day as the weekly celebration of the resurrection. Either way, these texts remain essential.

Palm Sunday: Matthew 21:1-11; Psalm 118:19-29. Jesus enters as the promised King.

Monday: Matthew 21:12-17. He cleanses the temple, showing His zeal for true worship.

Tuesday: Matthew 26:1-16. The plot against Him forms even as He is anointed for burial.

Wednesday: John 13:1-17. Jesus washes the disciples’ feet, displaying humble love on the night of betrayal.

Thursday: Matthew 26:17-30; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. The Last Supper institutes the Lord’s Supper as a proclamation of His death.

Good Friday: Matthew 27:27-56; Isaiah 53:3-12; Psalm 22:1-18. Christ is crucified, bearing sin in penal substitutionary atonement.

Saturday: Matthew 27:57-66; Psalm 16:7-11. He lies in the tomb, yet the Father will not abandon Him to decay.

Easter Sunday: Matthew 28:1-10; John 20:1-18; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, 12-20. The tomb is empty. Jesus is risen bodily, the firstfruits of those who sleep.

These readings display the heart of the Gospel: the Son of God, truly God and truly man, died in our place and rose again, securing justification by grace alone through faith alone (Romans 4:25). His resurrection confirms both His deity and the believer’s future hope.

Set aside 15-20 minutes each day to read the passage slowly. Note one truth about Christ’s work, thank the Father for it in your own words, and share that insight with a family member or fellow church member. Gather with a local congregation this Lord’s Day to hear the Word and remember the risen Christ together.

question: What is ignosticism? What is an ignostic?
answer:
Ignosticism is the view that questions about God's existence are meaningless until a coherent, agreed-upon definition of "God" is given, because the word is often used in vague, contradictory, or empty ways. An ignostic is a person who holds this position and therefore refuses to take a side in the usual theist-versus-atheist debate until that definition is supplied.

The Bible does not treat "God" as an undefined placeholder. It presents Him as the living, personal, holy Creator who has made Himself known through creation and, above all, through His spoken Word and the incarnation of His Son. God is incomprehensible in His infinite essence, yet truly knowable because He has chosen to reveal Himself (Romans 1:19–20; Hebrews 1:1–2). Jesus Christ is the climactic self-disclosure of God: "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). The attributes Scripture assigns to Him (holy, just, merciful, faithful, sovereign) are not optional add-ons; they are the content of that revelation.

If the many competing uses of the word "God" have left the term feeling empty to you, that experience is understandable. The Christian claim is not that every religious sentence about "God" is equally clear, but that the God who actually exists has spoken with sufficient clarity in Scripture and in Christ. A next step worth taking is simply to read the Gospel of John and ask whether the person it describes matches the undefined "God" of ignosticism or the living God who has made Himself known.

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath?
answer:
Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath means that He, as the divine Son of Man, holds complete authority over the Sabbath, the day He established at creation as a gift of rest and worship, and that the Sabbath finds its true purpose and fulfillment in Him.

In the Gospels, the Pharisees accused Jesus’ disciples of breaking the Sabbath by plucking heads of grain to eat. Jesus answered that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28; Matthew 12:8; Luke 6:5). In first-century Judaism, groups such as the Pharisees had layered many extra traditions onto the Sabbath command, turning a blessing into a burden. Jesus rejected that legalism, pointing back to David eating the consecrated bread and to the priests who worked in the temple on the Sabbath, then claiming an authority greater than the temple itself.

This claim reveals the deity of Christ. Only God is Lord of the Sabbath He created when He rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11). As the eternal Word through whom all things were made, Jesus has every right to interpret, fulfill, and rule over it (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The Sabbath pointed to rest from labor and delight in God; Jesus is that rest. He invites the weary, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God because the one who finished His work now sits at the Father’s right hand (Hebrews 4:9-10).

When busyness or extra rules leave you exhausted, remember that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath. Come to Him rather than striving in your own strength. Read Mark 2:23-28 slowly this week and ask the Lord to help you rest in His finished work and His present lordship over every day.

question: What does it mean that Jesus Christ conquered death?
answer:
Jesus Christ conquered death through His bodily resurrection from the grave on the third day after the crucifixion, breaking the power of sin and death so that all who trust in Him share in His victory and will rise to eternal life.

Death entered the world through human sin (Romans 5:12), and the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died as our substitutionary sacrifice, was buried, and rose again in the body, just as the apostles preached (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). His resurrection is the firstfruits, the guarantee that those united to Him by faith will also be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20-22). He now holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18) and has destroyed the devil’s power over death so that His people need no longer live as slaves to the fear of dying (Hebrews 2:14-15). For the believer, death is a defeated enemy; to be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord, and at Christ’s return we will receive glorified bodies (2 Corinthians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17).

This truth means you can face your own mortality with hope rather than terror. A simple next step is to read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly this week, asking God to let the reality of the empty tomb steady your heart and shape how you live today.

If you have not yet trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. What part of His victory over death most encourages or challenges you right now?

question: What are the books of the Bible? What does it mean that the Bible is composed of different books?
answer:
The Bible consists of 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament.

The Old Testament books are Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

The New Testament books are Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude, and Revelation.

That the Bible is composed of different books means it is a library of distinct writings by about 40 human authors across roughly 1,500 years, using varied genres such as law, history, poetry, prophecy, gospel, and epistle, yet forming one unified Word because God is the ultimate Author. Hebrews 1:1-2 teaches that God spoke in many portions and in many ways through the prophets, and now has spoken by His Son. All Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), the product of divine inspiration in which the Holy Spirit carried the writers along so that their words are exactly God’s intended revelation (2 Peter 1:21). This collection, called the canon of Scripture, presents one coherent story of creation, fall, redemption, and restoration in Christ. A concrete next step is to begin reading a single book such as the Gospel of John, noticing how it fulfills the promises of the earlier books and calling you to trust the Savior they all proclaim.

question: What is the creation mandate / cultural mandate?
answer:
The creation mandate, also known as the cultural mandate, is God’s command in Genesis 1:28 that humanity, created in His image, is to be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion over every living creature.

This calling, given before the Fall, establishes people as God’s vice-regents and stewards (imago Dei) who cultivate the world, raise families, and develop culture to His glory. Unlike surrounding ancient Near Eastern stories that treated humans as slaves of the gods, Scripture presents mankind as royal representatives entrusted with the earth. Genesis 1:27-28 records, “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. God blessed them and said to them, ‘Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that crawls upon the earth.’” Genesis 2:15 adds that the Lord God placed the man in the garden “to work it and watch over it.”

The Fall brought toil and frustration to this work (Genesis 3:17-19), yet the mandate itself remains. In Christ, who is the true image of God and now holds all authority, believers can engage every sphere of life (home, vocation, arts, science, and just neighbor-love) as an act of worship rather than mere secular activity. Practically, you can live this out this week by treating your ordinary responsibilities as opportunities to bring order and blessing in Jesus’ name, doing them “as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

question: What does it mean that friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4)?
answer:
Friendship with the world means choosing loyalty to the fallen world's rebellious values, desires, and approval rather than exclusive devotion to God, which places a person in hostility toward Him as spiritual unfaithfulness.

James 4:4 says, "You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God." James uses the language of adultery because God relates to His people as a husband to a bride, so dividing our affection with the world is covenant-breaking unfaithfulness, just as the prophets described Israel's idolatry. The "world" here is not God's good creation or the people He loves (John 3:16), but the organized system of human life in rebellion against Him, marked by the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:15-17). You cannot serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). This is why such friendship is enmity: God is holy and jealous for His people's whole heart, and the world stands opposed to His will.

This warning comes in a passage addressing quarreling, coveting, and praying with selfish motives among believers, showing that worldliness often hides in ordinary ambitions and compromises rather than obvious rebellion. It calls us to progressive sanctification, being set apart from the world's pattern by the renewing of our minds (Romans 12:2). A concrete next step is to read James 4 slowly this week, asking God to show any place where you have made peace with sin, pride, or cultural pressure in order to fit in, then draw near to Him in repentance, knowing He gives more grace to the humble (James 4:6-8). Pray directly about this, seeking also the counsel of mature believers in your local church.

question: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?
answer:
God hardened Pharaoh’s heart to display His power, gain glory over Pharaoh and Egypt, and make His name known in all the earth as He delivered Israel, according to the purpose He Himself declared.

Exodus 9:16 records God’s word to Pharaoh: “But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” God announced this beforehand (Exodus 4:21; Exodus 7:3) so that the plagues would fully reveal His supremacy over Egypt’s gods and its king, who claimed divine status himself. Exodus 14:4 adds that God would harden Pharaoh so that He would “gain glory for Myself through Pharaoh and all his army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.”

Pharaoh was no innocent victim. He was already a proud oppressor who refused God’s command, and he repeatedly hardened his own heart as well (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 8:32; Exodus 9:34). God’s action was judicial hardening: a righteous confirmation of a wicked man in the rebellion he already loved. The New Testament cites this same event to show that God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills (Romans 9:17–18). Divine sovereignty and human responsibility stand together here without contradiction.

This should humble us before God’s majesty. He is not thwarted by human defiance; He uses even the hardest opposition to magnify His glory in both judgment and salvation. A wise next step is to read Exodus 7–14 slowly, noticing both God’s initiative and Pharaoh’s willing stubbornness, then turn to Hebrews 3:7–15 and ask the Lord to keep your own heart soft to His Word today rather than resistant. If this account raises questions about God’s justice, speak with a pastor or mature believer in your local church and pray through these passages yourself, asking God for a clearer sight of His holiness.

question: How should we treat our enemies according to Proverbs 25:21–22?
answer:
Proverbs 25:21–22 teaches that if your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for in so doing you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you. This is a call to practical kindness instead of revenge, meeting real needs even toward those who oppose us.

The apostle Paul quotes these verses in Romans 12:20, placing them in the larger command not to repay anyone evil for evil but to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Jesus likewise commands, “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), reflecting the Father who “causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good” (Matthew 5:45). Such enemy-love is part of our sanctification as we are conformed to Christ, who died for us while we were still His enemies (Romans 5:8; Romans 5:10).

A concrete next step is to name one person who has wronged you, pray for their good today, and look for one simple way to meet a need they have this week, leaving justice and results in the Lord’s hands.

question: What does the Bible say about indecision / being indecisive?
answer:
The Bible warns against indecision as double-mindedness that produces instability and divided loyalty, calling God's people instead to wholehearted faith and obedience.

James 1:6-8 says the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind, and "He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways." Writing to believers under pressure, James ties this wavering to a lack of trusting faith when we ask God for wisdom.

Elijah confronted Israel's divided hearts in 1 Kings 18:21: "How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him; but if Baal is God, follow him." Jesus likewise taught that split allegiance is impossible in Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money." Revelation 3:15-16 rebukes lukewarmness that is neither hot nor cold.

Scripture therefore calls us to trust the Lord with all our heart rather than lean on our own understanding, for He makes the paths of those who acknowledge Him straight (Proverbs 3:5-6). When you face a decision, ask God for wisdom without doubting (James 1:5-6), search the Scriptures, seek counsel from mature believers in your local church, and then take the next faithful step rather than remaining paralyzed.

question: What does it mean that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4)?
answer:
In Revelation 21:4, God wiping away every tear means that in the new heaven and new earth He will personally and completely remove every sorrow from His people, so that death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone forever because the former things have passed away.

This is the tender, fatherly consolation of God Himself dwelling with His redeemed, not a vague hope but the sure reality of the new creation after the final judgment. The verse echoes Isaiah 25:8, where God promises to swallow up death forever and wipe tears from all faces, showing that the curse of Genesis 3 will be fully reversed. Revelation 21:3-4 places this in the context of God making His dwelling with humanity, and Revelation 7:17 already previews the same comfort for those who come out of the great tribulation.

This describes the glorification of the saints, the final stage of salvation in which justification by faith and progressive sanctification reach their completion: no remaining sin, no remaining effects of the Fall, only unbroken fellowship with the Triune God. Faithful Christians may differ on the sequence of events leading to this (some expecting a millennial reign of Christ on earth first, others seeing the new creation arrive directly at His return), yet they share this hope of God’s personal comfort in eternity, a matter of Christian liberty that need not divide us.

When present grief feels overwhelming, this promise invites you to bring those tears to the Lord now in prayer, asking Him to use Revelation 21:4 to steady your heart until the day He wipes them away for good.

question: What is the meaning of “there but for the grace of God go I”?
answer:
The saying “there but for the grace of God go I” means that, apart from God’s undeserved favor, I could just as easily be in the same painful, sinful, or ruined condition as the person I am observing. It is a confession of humility, not superiority: any safety, restraint from worse sin, or difference in circumstance comes from God, not from our own wisdom or strength.

It is commonly linked to the English Reformer John Bradford (who was later martyred), who is said to have spoken similar words when he saw prisoners being led to execution. The thought itself is thoroughly biblical. Scripture teaches that all people are sinners who fall short of God’s glory (Romans 3:23), that we have nothing we did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7), and that we are what we are only by the grace of God (1 Corinthians 15:10). Left to ourselves we would remain dead in trespasses; God made us alive by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:1–9).

This should kill self-righteousness. When you see someone trapped in addiction, poverty, crime, or public failure, the right response is not “I would never,” but a quiet recognition of common grace (God’s restraining kindness even to those who do not yet know Him) and saving grace (His particular mercy to those He has brought to Christ). Galatians 6:1 calls those who are spiritual to restore the fallen gently while watching themselves, lest they also be tempted.

A simple next step is this: the next time you notice someone whose life looks wrecked, thank God specifically for His grace in your own story, then pray for that person by name if you can, asking the Lord to show them the same mercy that has kept you.

question: How can we walk in God’s ways (Psalm 128:1)?
answer:
We walk in God’s ways by fearing the Lord with reverent awe and ordering our daily lives according to His Word, as Psalm 128:1 teaches. This is not self-powered effort but the fruit of justification by faith in Christ, as the Holy Spirit works progressive sanctification in us through the means of grace.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), a humble, trusting reverence that leads to glad obedience rather than mere rule-keeping. Jesus said, “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15). We learn His ways in Scripture, which is a lamp to our feet (Psalm 119:105), and we walk them by the Spirit so that we do not gratify the flesh (Galatians 5:16). Christ already walked this path perfectly for us; now He lives in those who trust Him (Galatians 2:20), producing the fruit of love, joy, and self-control.

A concrete next step is to pray Psalm 25:4 directly to God today, asking Him to show you His ways, then read one chapter of the Gospels and put one of Jesus’ commands into practice this week in a specific relationship at home or work. Share that step with a mature believer in your local church for encouragement and accountability.

question: What does the Bible say about the ice age?
answer:
The Bible does not mention an ice age by that name, as the term comes from modern geology rather than Scripture. It does teach that God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1), sent a worldwide flood in the days of Noah (Genesis 7:17-24), established the ongoing cycle of seasons after the flood (Genesis 8:22), and rules over ice, snow, frost, and the weather (Job 38:29-30; Psalm 147:16-18).

How an ice age might relate to biblical history is a tertiary matter, a non-essential on which faithful Christians may disagree. The Bible gives no explicit description or timeline of such an event, so differences arise from interpretive emphasis on Genesis and how one relates Scripture to the geological record.

One view, common among those who hold a recent six-day creation, is that a single ice age followed the Flood as a result of volcanic activity, warmer oceans, and climatic disruption after the waters receded. Another view, held by Christians who see the creation days as longer periods or who accept an older earth, is that ice ages occurred over extended timescales as part of God’s work in the world He made, without being tightly tied to the Flood in the same way.

In both cases we affirm the authority of Scripture, the historicity of creation and the Flood, and God’s sovereignty over all of nature. These details need not divide us; Romans 14:1-5 calls us to accept one another in disputable matters while holding fast to the essentials. As you think through this, read Genesis 1-11 slowly, asking the Lord to show you His power in making and judging the world, and His faithfulness in preserving it.

question: What is the significance of the city of Nineveh in the Bible?
answer:
Nineveh was the capital of the ancient Assyrian Empire, a vast and powerful city on the Tigris River whose biblical significance centers on God’s mercy toward repentant sinners and His just judgment against persistent wickedness. It first appears in Genesis 10:11 as a city associated with Nimrod, then becomes the focus of Jonah’s reluctant mission and Nahum’s later oracle of destruction.

In Jonah, God sends the prophet to this “great city” because its evil had come up before Him (Jonah 1:2; Jonah 3:3). After Jonah’s preaching, the people of Nineveh, from the king downward, believed God, fasted, put on sackcloth, and turned from their violence; God then relented from the disaster He had threatened (Jonah 3:5–10). This event displays the Lord’s compassion even toward a brutal pagan nation that had oppressed Israel, revealing Him as gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in love (Jonah 4:2). The Assyrians were notorious in the ancient Near East for military cruelty and mass deportations, including the fall of the northern kingdom in 722 BC, which makes their repentance all the more striking as an act of God’s sovereign mercy.

Later, Nahum prophesied Nineveh’s complete overthrow because the city had returned to bloodshed, idolatry, and oppression (Nahum 1:1; Nahum 3:1–7). That word was fulfilled in 612 BC when Babylonians and Medes razed the city, confirming that divine patience has limits and that God rules over the rise and fall of empires.

Jesus Himself treated Nineveh as a lasting witness: the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn an unbelieving generation, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, yet one greater than Jonah is here (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). The city’s story therefore underscores repentance as the proper response to God’s warning, His concern for the nations, and the certainty that He will both forgive the humble and judge the unrepentant.

A simple next step is to read the short book of Jonah this week, noticing both Jonah’s resistance and God’s heart for people far from Him, then ask the Lord to give you that same compassion toward those you find hardest to love.

question: What is Epicureanism? What did Epicurus teach?
answer:
Epicureanism is the philosophical system begun by the Greek thinker Epicurus, who lived from 341 to 270 BC, and it teaches that the greatest good is a calm life of modest pleasure free from pain and anxiety. Epicurus taught that the world is made of atoms moving in empty space, that gods exist but take no interest in human lives, that the soul perishes at death so there is nothing to fear afterward, and that wisdom consists in simple diet, loyal friendship, and avoiding unnecessary desires and public strife.

When the apostle Paul preached in Athens, some Epicurean philosophers argued with him, as Acts 17:18 records, because they found the news of Jesus and the resurrection strange. The Bible teaches instead that the one true God rules all things by His providence (Psalm 103:19), that after death comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27), and that Christ’s bodily resurrection is the firstfruits of those who belong to Him (1 Corinthians 15:20). Christians therefore need not live only for present comfort; we can rest in the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

question: Book of Philippians - Bible Survey
answer:
The Book of Philippians is the Apostle Paul’s letter to the church in Philippi, written from Roman imprisonment around AD 61–62 to thank them for their gift and to call them to joy, unity, and humility in Christ.

Paul founded this first European congregation during his second missionary journey after the Macedonian vision, as recorded in Acts 16:9–40. Philippi was a proud Roman colony that prized earthly citizenship, a reality Paul turns to gospel use when he writes that “our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).

Joy in the Lord runs through the whole letter even while Paul sits in chains. He thanks God for their “partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (Philippians 1:5) and testifies that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel. In Philippians 1 he declares that “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Chapter 2 urges the church toward one mind by pointing to the incarnation: Christ, existing in the form of God, emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on a cross, after which God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:5–11). This is the humiliation and exaltation of the incarnate Son, the pattern for every believer. Chapter 3 warns against confidence in the flesh; Paul counts his impressive Jewish credentials as loss “that I may gain Christ and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:8–9). Justification is by grace through faith alone. He then presses on toward the goal of the upward call. Chapter 4 addresses a personal rift, commands “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4), promises the peace of God that guards hearts and minds, and models contentment in every circumstance through Christ who strengthens him (Philippians 4:11–13).

The letter therefore holds together the deity and true humanity of Christ, justification by faith, and the believer’s progressive sanctification as we “work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Read the entire letter in one sitting this week, marking every mention of joy or rejoice. Then pray that the Holy Spirit would form that same glad dependence on Christ in you and in your local church.

question: In what ways was Moses like Jesus?
answer:
Moses was like Jesus as a type of the Messiah, serving as prophet, mediator, and deliverer in ways that pointed forward to Christ’s greater work.

God promised through Moses, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Peter applied this promise directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22).

Both were preserved as infants from a ruler’s decree of death (Exodus 2:1-10; Matthew 2:13-16). Moses led Israel out of slavery in Egypt through signs and wonders (Exodus 7:1-5), just as Jesus delivers His people from slavery to sin (John 8:34-36; Colossians 1:13-14). Moses mediated the old covenant (Exodus 24:8; Galatians 3:19), while Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant in His blood (Hebrews 9:15; Luke 22:20). Moses interceded for Israel after their sin, even offering himself (Exodus 32:32), pointing to Jesus who always lives to intercede as our great High Priest (Hebrews 7:25).

Both were initially rejected by those they came to save (Acts 7:35; John 1:11). Yet Jesus is far greater: Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over it (Hebrews 3:5-6). At the transfiguration Moses appeared with Jesus, and the Father declared, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” (Matthew 17:5).

These typological connections show that the Scriptures testify about Jesus (Luke 24:27). Read Hebrews 3 this week and pray that the Holy Spirit would help you see Christ throughout the Old Testament.

question: What is Socinianism?
answer:
Socinianism is a 16th- and 17th-century anti-Trinitarian heresy named after Faustus Socinus that denies the Trinity, the eternal deity of Jesus Christ, original sin, and penal substitutionary atonement. It treats Jesus as a uniquely inspired man, miraculously born of the Virgin Mary, who lived in perfect obedience, died as a moral example, and was later exalted by God, rather than as the eternal Son who is truly God and truly man.

This movement arose in Reformation-era Italy and Poland (especially among the Polish Brethren) and was summarized in the Racovian Catechism of 1605. It later fed into Unitarianism. Socinians subordinated Scripture to human reason, rejected mysteries such as the Trinity, and recast the cross as an example of love or obedience rather than a propitiatory sacrifice that satisfies God’s justice.

These claims stand outside orthodox Christianity because they deny core doctrines. Scripture presents one God eternally existing in three persons and Jesus Christ as the eternal Word who became flesh (John 1:1; John 1:14). In Him the fullness of Deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9), He claimed the divine name (John 8:58), and Thomas confessed Him as “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). God presented Christ as a propitiation through faith in His blood (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2), so that the One who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). The hypostatic union (two natures in one person) and penal substitution are not later inventions; they summarize what the apostles taught.

A denial of Christ’s deity and atoning work cannot save. Read the Gospel of John, noting every claim about who Jesus is, and talk these truths over with a pastor or mature believer in a local church that confesses the biblical Christ.

question: Can an unmarried man be a deacon or elder?
answer:
Yes, an unmarried man can serve as a deacon or elder if he meets the other qualifications of godly character and gifting in Scripture.

Some faithful Christians argue that a man must be married (often with well-ordered, believing children) because an overseer or deacon is called “the husband of one wife” and must manage his household well as the proving ground for leading God’s church.

I hold that an unmarried man may serve in these offices, because the phrase describes a “one-woman man” of sexual faithfulness and purity rather than a requirement to be married, the household instructions apply to those who have families, and the New Testament honors the gift of singleness for undivided devotion to the Lord. The Greek expression behind “husband of one wife” in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 highlights moral integrity in relationships, not current marital status. An overseer must be “above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2), qualities a single man can display through a life of self-control. Deacons likewise must be “the husband of but one wife and must manage his children and his own household well” (1 Timothy 3:12), yet this does not exclude those without a wife or children. Paul, who remained unmarried, wrote that “the unmarried man is concerned about the affairs of the Lord, how he can please the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:32). A local church, under its elders, should therefore examine a candidate’s overall blamelessness and service according to 1 Timothy 3:1-13 and Titus 1:5-9, whether married or single.

If you are considering this yourself, open these passages with the elders of your church and seek their counsel together with the congregation’s prayerful recognition of God’s gifting.

question: Is it better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich?
answer:
It is not inherently better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich. Our standing with God rests on faith in Christ and a heart of contentment, not on how much or how little we possess.

This is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians have differed, often because of different emphases in Scripture and church history. Some have viewed voluntary poverty as spiritually advantageous, seeing it as a way to loosen earthly attachments and depend more fully on God, as in Jesus’ word to the rich young ruler (Matthew 19:21). Others have seen wealth as a providence from God that can serve His kingdom when handled with humility and generosity, as with Abraham (Genesis 13:2) and the charge given to the rich (1 Timothy 6:17-19). In such matters of application, Romans 14:5 calls each believer to be fully convinced before the Lord without judging another.

Scripture itself treats neither poverty nor riches as the spiritually superior state. Jesus blessed the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3), those who know their need of God, not merely those who lack money. He also warned that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom because wealth easily becomes an idol (Matthew 19:23-24), yet He immediately added that with God all things are possible (Matthew 19:26). Poverty can tempt toward envy, anxiety, or even theft, which is why Agur prayed, “Give me neither poverty nor riches” lest he deny the Lord in plenty or profane His name in want (Proverbs 30:8-9). Riches can tempt toward pride and self-reliance, for “those who want to be rich fall into temptation” and “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:9-10).

The better path in every circumstance is godliness with contentment (1 Timothy 6:6-8). Paul learned to be content whether in plenty or in need through Christ who strengthened him (Philippians 4:11-13). God has often chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith (James 2:5), yet He has also used the wealthy who feared Him. The real issue is the heart: whether we are storing up treasure on earth or being rich toward God (Luke 12:15; Luke 12:21).

If you have little, thank God for daily provision and resist coveting. If you have much, thank God and look for ways to be generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:18). A simple next step is to read 1 Timothy 6 this week, pray to the Lord for a content and generous heart in whatever He has given you, and talk it over with a mature believer in your local church.

question: Will the sun really be turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:31)?
answer:
Yes, the Bible prophesies that the sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD (Joel 2:31). Peter quotes this very promise in Acts 2:20, Jesus describes corresponding signs in Matthew 24:29, and John records them in the vision of Revelation 6:12.

These words belong to biblical teaching on the last things. The exact manner in which the signs will appear is a tertiary matter of eschatology, where faithful Christians may differ in charity because prophetic and apocalyptic texts often combine straightforward declaration with vivid imagery drawn from earlier judgments, and the details are not given with the same clarity as the Gospel itself.

One historic Christian reading takes the language in its more straightforward sense as pointing to actual, observable darkening of the sun and a blood-red moon as supernatural portents of Christ’s personal, bodily return and the final judgment. Another equally orthodox reading understands the same language as traditional prophetic symbolism for the overthrow of earthly powers and the unveiling of God’s rule, just as similar cosmic descriptions in Isaiah 13:10 pictured the fall of Babylon.

In either case the prophecy is certain because God has spoken it, and the Creator who made the sun and moon (Genesis 1:16) will fulfill His Word in His time. The practical call is watchfulness: read 2 Peter 3:8-13, which sets the Day of the Lord before us, and pray that the Lord would keep you faithful in His Word, prayer, and the fellowship of a local church until He comes.

question: How can I overcome spiritual apathy?
answer:
Spiritual apathy can leave your heart feeling cold and unmoved toward God, even when you still long to love Him.

You are not alone in this. The psalmist cried out, “My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?” (Psalm 42:2).
