Seasons of dryness are a real part of the Christian life as the Holy Spirit continues His work of progressive sanctification, patiently conforming us to Christ and exposing how much we need Him.

God is gracious and does not despise a broken and contrite heart (Psalm 51:17). He has given ordinary means of grace to revive us.

Return to His Word even when it feels dry. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). The Scriptures are living, and the Spirit uses them to stir what has grown dull.

Pray honestly. Tell the Father about the apathy itself. He already knows, and He invites you to draw near with confidence (Hebrews 4:16).

Stay connected to Christ’s people. Isolation feeds coldness. “Let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds, not neglecting to meet together, as some have made a habit, but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:24-25).

Remember the Gospel that first captured you. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died in your place, rose bodily from the grave, and now lives to intercede for you. His love is what rekindles ours (2 Corinthians 5:14-15).

A concrete next step: tomorrow morning, read John 15:1-11 slowly and ask the Lord to help you abide in Him as the true Vine. Then speak with a mature believer or your pastor about this struggle and ask them to pray with you.

Use Scripture in your own prayer, such as “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit” (Psalm 51:12). Talk to God directly about this.

What has this apathy looked like in your daily walk with the Lord lately?

question: How can I experience healing and recovery after an abortion?
answer:
The grief, regret, and sense of inner brokenness after an abortion are real and heavy, and the Lord sees that pain. God formed every life in the womb, knitting each person together with purpose (Psalm 139:13-16; Jeremiah 1:5). Abortion takes an innocent human life and is therefore sin, a violation of God’s command, “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). He is holy and just, and our sin separates us from Him.

Yet the same God is merciful and gracious. All have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). God shows His love in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). The eternal Son of God took on true humanity through the virgin birth, lived a sinless life, and offered Himself as a penal substitutionary atonement, dying in our place on the cross. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead. He is now exalted as Lord. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our efforts to make up for the past.

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). True healing and recovery rest in that finished work of justification, then grow through progressive sanctification as the Holy Spirit applies the Word, prayer, and the fellowship of the church.

This week, contact the pastor of a local church that holds Scripture as the final authority, share your burden with a mature believer there, and begin reading the Gospel of John to meet Jesus’ compassion for the broken. Pray directly to God, confessing this sin and all others, thanking Him for the blood of Christ that cleanses, and asking Him to restore your soul. If the weight remains overwhelming, seek a certified biblical counselor through your church or an ACBC-trained counselor who can walk with you in the Gospel.

What would taking that first step toward a church family look like for you right now?

question: What does God mean when He says, “Seek me and live” (Amos 5:4)?
answer:
In Amos 5:4, God means that His people must turn from empty religion, idolatry, and injustice to pursue Him in genuine repentance and covenant loyalty, because He alone is the giver of life and the only refuge from coming judgment.

Amos spoke this word to the northern kingdom of Israel in a season of outward prosperity yet deep spiritual decay. The LORD says, “Seek Me and live! Do not seek Bethel, do not go to Gilgal, do not journey to Beersheba. For Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing” (Amos 5:4-5). The Hebrew word for “seek” (darash) carries the sense of diligent inquiry and devoted turning, not casual interest. Israel had mixed true worship of Yahweh with calf idols and Canaanite practices at those very shrines, while oppressing the poor. God therefore contrasts seeking Him with seeking those places, and He repeats the warning: “Seek the LORD and live, or He will sweep through the house of Joseph like a fire” (Amos 5:6). Later He adds, “Seek good, not evil, so that you may live. Then the LORD God of Hosts will be with you, as you have claimed. Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate” (Amos 5:14-15). Life here is both deliverance from exile and death and the fullness of walking with the holy, just, and merciful God who had bound Himself to them by covenant.

This call reveals God’s character: His wrath against sin is real, yet He patiently invites sinners to Himself rather than immediately consuming them. The same invitation echoes through Scripture, and it finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who is “the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). In Him was life (John 1:4), and He died and rose so that all who repent and trust in Him receive that life as a gift of grace, not as a wage of works.

A simple next step is to read Amos 5 slowly this week, asking the Lord to show you any rival “shrines” (idols of security, success, or self-righteousness) that keep you from seeking Him first. Then pray directly to Him, using the psalms of repentance such as Psalm 51, that He would give you a heart that hates evil, loves good, and clings to Christ.

question: If aborted babies go to heaven, why is abortion wrong?
answer:
Abortion is wrong because it is the unjust killing of an innocent human being made in the image of God. God forbids murder, and the unborn child is already a living person, not potential life or disposable tissue. The eternal destiny of that child, even if we hope they are received into heaven by God's mercy, does not make the act of killing them righteous or permissible.

Scripture treats the child in the womb as a real person whom God Himself forms and knows. "For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psalm 139:13-14). God told Jeremiah, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you" (Jeremiah 1:5). John the Baptist leaped in Elizabeth’s womb at the presence of the unborn Christ (Luke 1:41-44). The sixth commandment remains: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13). God hates "hands that shed innocent blood" (Proverbs 6:16-17).

Some Christians hope, on the basis of God’s character and passages such as 2 Samuel 12:23, that infants who die are covered by Christ’s mercy rather than condemned for Adam’s sin in the same way as those who personally reject Him. That hope, however, is not a license to kill. Morality is not determined by the victim’s destination. If it were, murdering a believer would be an act of kindness because they go to heaven. We are not God. He alone numbers our days (Psalm 139:16; Job 14:5). Taking innocent life into our own hands is rebellion against His sovereignty and a denial of the worth He has already given that child.

The act also wounds the mother, the family, and a culture that begins to treat the weak as expendable. None of that is undone by the child’s possible salvation.

If this question comes from personal involvement or deep regret, there is real forgiveness. Christ’s death on the cross was sufficient for this sin too; He rose bodily, and all who repent and trust in Him alone are justified by grace through faith, not by works. Turn from this sin and from every other, and trust Jesus Christ who died and rose for you. Speak with a faithful pastor in a local church who can walk with you in Scripture, prayer, and the ordinary means of grace.

question: Should communion be open or closed?
answer:
The Lord's Supper should be closed rather than open, reserved for those who have been baptized as believers upon profession of faith and who are walking in good standing with a gospel church.

Those who practice open communion argue charitably that the table belongs to the Lord Himself, so every true believer should be welcomed as a visible sign that there is one body and one loaf (1 Corinthians 10:17).

I hold to close communion as one faithful historic option within orthodox Christianity because baptism is the New Testament initiatory ordinance that publicly identifies a person with Christ and His people, after which they share the ongoing church meal, following the pattern of those who received the word, were baptized, and then devoted themselves to the breaking of bread (Acts 2:41-42); the gathered church also has a real responsibility to fence the table so that participants examine themselves and unrepentant sin does not profane the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). This treats both ordinances as churchly acts rather than purely private ones, while still allowing visiting baptized believers from like-minded churches to participate. If this question is live in your congregation, study these passages together with your elders and seek unity in how the table is overseen.

question: What is the Remnant Fellowship?
answer:
Remnant Fellowship is a church founded in 1999 by Gwen Shamblin Lara in Brentwood, Tennessee, which grew out of her Weigh Down Workshop, a program that treated overeating as spiritual idolatry rather than a mere diet issue. The group presents itself as a faithful remnant restoring true, obedient Christianity amid widespread apostasy, with heavy emphasis on thinness, self-control, hierarchical submission, and separation from other churches.

Its founder publicly rejected the Trinity as a later, unbiblical invention rather than the teaching of Scripture. Historic Christianity holds the Trinity as a non-negotiable core doctrine: one God eternally existing as three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Scripture presents Jesus as truly God and truly man (John 1:1; John 1:14; Colossians 2:9), and the Holy Spirit as God (Acts 5:3-4). Denial of this places the group's teaching outside orthodox Christianity.

The Bible calls believers to test every teaching against Scripture rather than follow a leader's claims of exclusive remnant status (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1). After Shamblin Lara's death in a 2021 plane crash, the organization has continued under remaining leadership, but the same doctrinal problem remains.

If you are encountering their materials or know someone involved, compare their statements on God, Christ, and the gospel directly with the whole of Scripture, and talk with a pastor in a local church that confesses the historic faith.

question: Who wrote the book of 2 John? Who was the author of 2 John?
answer:
The Apostle John wrote the book of 2 John. He identifies himself as “the elder” in 2 John 1:1, the same apostle who wrote the Gospel of John, 1 John, 3 John, and Revelation.

Early church testimony (including Irenaeus, who learned from Polycarp, a disciple of John) consistently ascribes these letters to John the son of Zebedee, the beloved disciple. Because the letter is apostolic Scripture, it carries the full authority of God’s inspired and inerrant Word, calling the church to walk in truth and love while rejecting anyone who denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (2 John 7–11). That warning protects the core confession of Christ’s true deity and true humanity. As you read 2 John, hold fast to that same truth and test every teaching by it.

question: What is false guilt, and how can I avoid it?
answer:
False guilt is a sense of condemnation or shame that does not come from actually breaking God’s commands as given in Scripture. It typically arises from extra-biblical rules, other people’s expectations, perfectionism, or the accusations of the enemy rather than from the Holy Spirit.

True guilt is different and is real: every person has sinned against our holy God and needs a Savior (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross in our place, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by our works. If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, repent and believe in Him today for forgiveness and new life.

For those who belong to Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The Spirit convicts of genuine sin so that we confess and are cleansed (John 16:8; 1 John 1:9), producing godly sorrow that leads to repentance rather than despair (2 Corinthians 7:10). When our hearts still condemn us after we have confessed, God is greater than our hearts (1 John 3:20). Justification by faith means Christ’s righteousness is counted as ours, so we rest in His finished work rather than in our performance.

To avoid false guilt, test every inner accusation against the actual words of Scripture. If it does not match a clear command you have broken, or if you have already confessed that sin, refuse it as not from the Lord and return your thoughts to the gospel. Fill your mind daily with passages that declare your standing in Christ.

A concrete next step is to write down one recurring feeling of guilt this week, compare it directly with Scripture, then speak with a pastor or mature believer in your local church for perspective, while praying that God would align your conscience with His Word rather than with fear or human standards. What particular situations most often stir these feelings for you?

question: Are baptism and communion means of grace?
answer:
Yes, baptism and communion (the Lord's Supper) are means of grace.
Some memorialist Christians argue charitably that these ordinances are simply vivid pictures and acts of obedience that commemorate Christ's work, with grace coming only through the Word and Spirit rather than through the signs themselves.
This Reformed view is one faithful option within historic Christianity: they are Christ's appointed ordinances that the Holy Spirit uses to increase and strengthen the faith of believers who receive them by faith, confirming our union with Him rather than working automatically or meriting justification (which is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone).
Paul describes the cup as a participation in the blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16), and baptism visibly portrays our burial and resurrection with Him so that we walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4).
Prepare your heart with self-examination and faith before the next Lord's Supper in a gospel-preaching church, looking to Christ Himself rather than the elements.

question: What is the spirit of the law?
answer:
The spirit of the law is the inner purpose, intent, and heart-attitude God requires in His commandments (love for Him and neighbor), rather than mere external, checklist obedience to the written code.

Paul explains that God “has made us competent as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). The written code exposes sin and condemns, but cannot give the power to obey; the Holy Spirit writes God’s law on the heart in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10) so that believers fulfill its righteous requirement by walking according to the Spirit (Romans 8:4). Jesus demonstrated this by pressing the law to the heart in the Sermon on the Mount: anger is murder, lust is adultery, and the Sabbath exists for human good, not human bondage (Matthew 5:21-28; Mark 2:27). Love is the fulfillment of the law (Romans 13:8-10).

This does not mean the moral law is discarded. Those justified by grace through faith in Christ’s atoning death and resurrection now obey from a new heart as a rule of life, not as a way to earn standing with God. A concrete next step is to take one command you are currently facing, ask what love for God and others it is meant to produce, and pray through that passage asking the Spirit to change your motives rather than merely your behavior.

question: Should pastors be paid a salary?
answer:
Yes, churches should pay pastors a salary (or equivalent support) so those who labor in preaching and teaching can live from the gospel.

Some historic Christians, especially in certain free-church or house-church settings, have held that elders should remain unpaid and bi-vocational to avoid a professional clergy class and to keep every member equally engaged in ministry, pointing to times when Paul supported himself by tentmaking.

I believe the ordinary biblical pattern is for the church to provide comfortable support so pastors are not entangled in secular work. The Lord commanded that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14). Elders who lead well, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching, are worthy of double honor, for the worker is worthy of his wages (1 Timothy 5:17-18). Those who receive instruction in the word must share all good things with their instructor (Galatians 6:6). This frees pastors to devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the Word (Acts 6:4) while still requiring them not to be greedy for money (1 Timothy 3:3). Bi-vocational service remains a faithful option when a church cannot yet afford full support, yet the church’s duty is still to give according to its ability.

If you belong to a local church, one concrete next step is to review your own giving and ask how the congregation can honor its pastor with generous, regular support rather than leaving him anxious about provision.

question: What does it mean that man shall not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3)?
answer:
Deuteronomy 8:3 means that human life cannot be sustained by physical food alone. We live by every word that comes from the mouth of God, depending on His revelation, commands, and faithful provision rather than on material things.

God allowed Israel to hunger in the wilderness and then supplied manna, a food neither they nor their fathers had known, in order to humble them and teach this lesson of trust (Deuteronomy 8:3). Physical bread meets a real bodily need, yet it is not enough for true life. The people of God flourish only as they receive and obey what He has spoken.

Jesus quoted this same verse when Satan tempted Him to turn stones into bread after forty days of fasting. He refused to meet His hunger apart from the Father’s will, showing that even legitimate physical needs must bow to the Word of God (Matthew 4:4). The episode underscores the sufficiency of Scripture: God’s spoken Word gives life, directs our steps, and proves more reliable than our circumstances.

A concrete next step is to treat daily Scripture reading as essential nourishment, not an optional extra. Open the Bible each morning as you would sit down to a meal, asking the Lord to feed your soul with His truth so that you walk in dependence on Him rather than on what you can see or provide for yourself.

question: What does the Bible say about parenting?
answer:
The Bible presents parenting as a sacred stewardship from God, in which mothers and fathers train their children in His ways through daily instruction, godly example, and loving discipline, treating them as a heritage rather than possessions. Psalm 127:3 declares that children are a heritage from the LORD and the fruit of the womb a reward.

Parents are commanded to keep God's words on their own hearts and teach them diligently to their children in ordinary life, speaking of them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and in the morning (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Ephesians 6:4 specifically charges fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. The Greek terms paideia (training or formative discipline) and nouthesia (admonition or warning) describe a whole-life shaping that points children to Christ rather than mere rule-keeping.

Scripture balances this with a warning against harshness that embitters a child (Colossians 3:21) while still commending wise, diligent correction as an act of love (Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 22:15). Mothers share fully in this work, as seen when Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice passed genuine faith to him through the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 2 Timothy 3:14-15). Children, in turn, are called to honor their father and mother (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:1-3).

This calling is gospel-centered: parents themselves are sinners who need the same Savior, and they are to teach their children of human sin, Christ's sacrificial death on the cross, His burial, and His bodily resurrection, so that the young may trust Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

A practical next step is to read Deuteronomy 6:4-9 aloud with your family this week and choose one simple, daily moment (a meal, a walk, or bedtime) to speak of God's Word together. Ask the Lord directly for wisdom in this work (James 1:5), and talk with a mature believer or your church's elders for encouragement and accountability.

question: Who was Jeremiah in the Bible?
answer:
Jeremiah was a major prophet of the Old Testament who served in Judah from the thirteenth year of King Josiah until after Jerusalem fell to Babylon. God called him as a young man from a priestly family in Anathoth to proclaim both coming judgment and future hope.

His ministry spanned roughly forty years under Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. He confronted Judah’s idolatry and unfaithfulness, urged genuine repentance, and announced the seventy-year exile, all while facing rejection, imprisonment, and deep personal grief. Scripture records his oracles in the Book of Jeremiah and his lament over the ruined city in Lamentations. God had set him apart from the womb: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart; I appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5).

Jeremiah also announced the new covenant, in which the Lord would write His law on His people’s hearts and remember their sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). That promise finds its fulfillment in Christ’s atoning work. His life therefore displays both God’s holy justice against sin and His faithful mercy toward those who turn to Him.

Jeremiah’s steadfastness amid opposition invites us to speak God’s truth with compassion even when it is costly, remaining rooted in the local church and the Scriptures.

question: Why did Jesus allow the demons to enter the herd of pigs?
answer:
Jesus permitted the demons to enter the herd of pigs because they begged Him not to send them into the Abyss before the appointed time of their judgment, and He granted their request, thereby displaying His complete authority over every spiritual power.

In Matthew 8:29 the demons cried out, “What do You want with us, Son of God? Have You come here to torment us before the appointed time?” Luke 8:31 records that they pleaded with Him not to order them into the Abyss. When they saw the large herd of pigs, they asked to enter them instead (Matthew 8:31; Mark 5:12; Luke 8:32). Jesus gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out of the man, entered the pigs, and drove the whole herd down the steep bank into the sea, where they drowned (Mark 5:13).

This was never a negotiation between equals. A legion of demons could not even enter animals without Jesus’ word. By allowing it, He made the man’s deliverance publicly visible and revealed the true nature of the demonic: they destroy whatever they inhabit. At the same time, Jesus showed that one human soul, created in the image of God, is of far greater worth than two thousand pigs. The people of that Gentile region in the Decapolis, however, were more distressed by their lost livelihood than by the miracle, and they asked Jesus to leave (Mark 5:17). He did not force Himself on them, yet He left the restored man as a living witness to proclaim throughout the region what God had done for him (Mark 5:19-20).

The account underscores the lordship of Christ over the unseen realm. His first coming was to seek and save the lost, not yet to execute final judgment on the demons; that day still lies ahead. We can therefore rest in the truth that no darkness operates beyond the limits He sets, and that He still delights to set captives free.

Read the full narrative in Mark 5 and ask the Lord to impress His authority on your own heart, then talk with a pastor in a local church that faithfully preaches this same Jesus.

question: What are the Analects of Confucius?
answer:
The Analects of Confucius (also called the Lunyu) is a collection of sayings, conversations, and teachings attributed to the Chinese philosopher Confucius (Kong Fuzi, 551–479 BC) and his disciples. Compiled by later followers rather than written by Confucius himself, it became the foundational text of Confucianism, emphasizing moral self-cultivation, social harmony, filial piety, ritual propriety, and virtuous government.

These writings reflect humanity’s search for wisdom and order, which Christians understand as part of God’s general revelation through conscience and the created world (Romans 2:14–15). They do not, however, reveal the holiness of the triune God, the reality of sin, or the necessity of Christ’s atoning death and bodily resurrection for salvation. True and saving wisdom is found in Scripture alone.

question: Can faith change God's plan?
answer:
Faith cannot change God’s eternal plan, because God is sovereign and unchanging. His purposes stand forever, and He works all things according to the counsel of His will.

The Bible is clear that God declares the end from the beginning. Isaiah 46:10 records His words: “I declare the end from the beginning, and from ancient times what is still to come. I say, ‘My purpose will stand, and I will do all that I please.’” Proverbs 19:21 adds, “Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.” God is immutable. Malachi 3:6 says, “Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed.” James 1:17 describes Him as the Father of lights “with whom there is no variation or shifting shadow.”

God has nevertheless ordained faith and prayer as the very means He uses to accomplish what He has already decreed. Faith is not a force that bends God’s will or surprises Him with new information. It is a gift that aligns us with His will. 1 John 5:14 says, “This is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.” When Scripture describes God “relenting” after intercession (as with Moses or Hezekiah), it shows Him relating to us in time and using our prayers as part of His unchanging decree. Those prayers were never outside His plan.

This reflects God’s immutability and His sovereign decree, which includes secondary causes such as the faith of His people. We do not manipulate God. We come to Him as children, trusting that He delights to work through the prayers He Himself stirs up.

Pray with both boldness and submission, as Jesus did in Gethsemane: “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). Bring a specific concern to the Lord today, thanking Him that His plan is wise and good, and ask Him to increase your trust in His timing.

question: What is Pneumatology?
answer:
Pneumatology is the theological study of the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity. It examines His full deity, His personal nature, and His work in creation, Scripture, salvation, and the daily life of the church.

The term comes from the Greek pneuma (spirit, breath, or wind) and logos (word or study). Scripture presents the Holy Spirit as fully God, not an impersonal force. He can be lied to (Acts 5:3-4), grieved (Ephesians 4:30), and resisted (Acts 7:51). He was active at creation, hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2). He inspired the writing of Scripture (2 Peter 1:21) and now applies Christ’s finished work to God’s people.

Jesus called Him the Helper who would come after His ascension, teaching, reminding, convicting of sin, and glorifying Christ (John 14:26; John 16:7-14). The Spirit regenerates sinners, giving new birth (John 3:5-8; Titus 3:5), and He produces progressive sanctification, bearing fruit such as love, joy, and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23). He also seals believers as a guarantee of their inheritance until the day of redemption (Ephesians 1:13-14).

This doctrine matters because no one comes to Christ or grows in holiness apart from the Spirit’s power. Believers therefore depend on Him rather than their own strength, walking by the Spirit so they do not gratify the flesh (Galatians 5:16). As you read Scripture, ask the Holy Spirit to illuminate the text and to give you both the will and the power to obey it.

question: What does the Bible say about children's church?
answer:
The Bible does not mention children's church or any age-separated program during the gathered worship of the church. Scripture instead consistently includes children in the assemblies of God's people and places the primary duty of discipleship on parents.

This is a tertiary matter of church practice. Faithful Christians may disagree because the Bible gives clear principles for worship, the preaching of the Word, and family instruction, yet it does not prescribe a detailed Sunday schedule or age grouping.

One common approach is family-integrated worship, in which children remain with their parents throughout the service. This follows the pattern of Israel assembling men, women, children, and foreigners so they could hear and learn to fear the Lord (Deuteronomy 31:12; Joshua 8:35). New Testament letters written to churches also address children directly, assuming they are present to hear (Ephesians 6:1; Colossians 3:20). Jesus Himself welcomed little children rather than sending them away (Mark 10:14).

Another common approach is children's church or Sunday school, offering age-suited teaching so young ones can grasp the gospel more readily while adults hear undistracted preaching. This is viewed as a wise use of Christian liberty in the circumstances of how a church organizes its teaching (Romans 14:5).

Both approaches can serve Christ if they support rather than replace parental responsibility. The preaching of the Word is a means of grace for the whole church, and fathers are commanded to bring their children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4; Deuteronomy 6:6-7). The church comes alongside families; it does not take their place.

A practical next step is to talk with your children after the service about what they heard concerning Jesus, then begin or strengthen a simple daily time of Scripture reading and prayer at home. Speak with your church's elders about their philosophy of involving children, and ask the Lord for wisdom and patience to disciple the children in your care.

question: Why is the humanity of Jesus important?
answer:
The humanity of Jesus is essential because only a true man could represent us before God, obey the law we have broken, die as our substitute, and rise again as the guarantee of our own resurrection. In the incarnation the eternal Son of God took on a complete human nature, remaining one person with two natures (the hypostatic union), fully God and fully man.

Scripture is clear that He had to share our flesh and blood: “Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. ... For this reason He had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 2:14–17). Born of a woman and born under the law, He redeemed those under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). As the last Adam His perfect obedience and penal substitutionary death reverse the condemnation that entered through the first Adam (Romans 5:18–19; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22). There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

Because He is fully human He is also a sympathetic High Priest who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, so we may approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). He knows hunger, weariness, sorrow, and rejection from the inside.

We have all sinned and fall short of God’s glory, yet Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived the life we should have lived, died the death we deserved on the cross, and rose bodily on the third day. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

When you next feel weak or tempted, pause and remember that Jesus faced real human trials, then ask Him for the help He promises. You might also read Hebrews 2:10–18 slowly and thank God in your own words that His Son became flesh for you. What aspect of Jesus’ humanity most encourages you right now?

question: What is the new birth?
answer:
The new birth (also called regeneration) is the Holy Spirit’s sovereign work of imparting spiritual life to a person who is dead in sin, so that they become a child of God and a new creation able to see and enter the kingdom of God.

Jesus taught this plainly to Nicodemus: “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3). Nicodemus thought of ordinary physical birth, yet Jesus spoke of a birth “from above,” born of the Spirit rather than the flesh (John 3:5-8). We need this because we are spiritually dead and cannot come to God by our own will or effort (Ephesians 2:1; John 1:13). God, according to His mercy, gives this new life through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5), ordinarily using the living Word of God (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). The Old Testament already promised it: God would give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

This regeneration is not produced by human decision, ritual, or moral improvement. It is God’s gracious act that enables a sinner to repent and believe in Jesus Christ, who died as a substitutionary atonement for our sins and rose bodily on the third day. Those born of God receive a new nature that loves God, hates sin, and perseveres in faith, showing itself in a changed life (1 John 3:9; 1 John 5:1; 2 Corinthians 5:17).

If you have never been born again, turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Read John 3:1-21 slowly this week and ask God to make this truth real in your own heart. What has prompted you to ask about the new birth?

question: What does the Bible say about education?
answer:
The Bible presents education as beginning with the fear of the Lord and as the diligent, daily instruction of God's Word, especially from parents to children. True knowledge is never merely academic; it is meant to form the heart in wisdom, righteousness, and love for God.

In the covenant setting of Israel, God commanded, "These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts. And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). This home-centered discipleship is echoed in the call to "Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it" (Proverbs 22:6) and in the New Testament charge, "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Scripture itself is the essential curriculum: "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Proverbs 1:7 adds that "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline."

The Bible therefore values learning, as seen in Jesus Himself growing in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and in believers being urged to let the word of Christ dwell richly among them (Colossians 3:16). At the same time it warns against empty philosophy that sets itself against Christ (Colossians 2:8). Education in Scripture is ultimately a means of discipleship, aiming at sanctification rather than mere information.

How families apply these principles in formal schooling (home, Christian school, or public) is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty on which faithful believers may differ, because Scripture gives the priority of biblical instruction without prescribing a modern educational system (Romans 14:1-12). Some emphasize homeschooling to keep Deuteronomy 6 at the center of every subject; others see broader schooling as an opportunity to be salt and light while parents and the church supply the primary spiritual training. Neither approach is required of all Christians. Whatever setting you choose, keep God's Word first.

A concrete next step is to read a short passage of Proverbs or a Gospel with your children (or those you teach) each day and simply ask how it applies to their studies, friendships, and choices, then pray together for wisdom.

question: What is the Edenic covenant?
answer:
The Edenic covenant is the pre-Fall arrangement God made with Adam in the Garden of Eden, requiring perfect obedience for life and threatening death for disobedience, as recorded in Genesis 2:16-17.

Some Christians, especially those outside Reformed covenant theology, do not regard Genesis 2 as a formal covenant at all, treating it simply as a divine command or test given to the first man without covenantal structure.

From a Reformed Baptist understanding, it is the Covenant of Works, in which Adam served as the federal head of the entire human race so that his obedience or failure would represent all who descend from him. This reading best accounts for the blessings and curses attached to the command, Adam’s representative role, and later Scripture that treats his transgression as a covenant-breaking act (Hosea 6:7; Romans 5:12-19; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22).

Adam’s failure in that covenant brought sin, death, and condemnation upon all humanity, which is why God in mercy established the Covenant of Grace, fulfilled by Jesus Christ, the last Adam, whose perfect obedience and substitutionary death secure justification for all who trust in Him. This truth means we cannot recover ourselves by our own works; we must rest in Christ’s finished righteousness rather than our own.

question: What is Wahhabism? What is Wahhabi Islam?
answer:
Wahhabism is a revivalist movement within Sunni Islam that began in the 18th century in the Najd region of Arabia under Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792). He taught a return to what he saw as the original practices of the Quran and the earliest Muslims, stressing strict monotheism (tawhid) and rejecting later customs he regarded as innovations, such as veneration of saints, visits to tombs, and many Sufi practices.

Wahhabi Islam is simply the name given to that same interpretation and way of life. Its adherents often prefer the label Salafi, meaning they seek to follow the salaf (the first generations of Muslims). Through an alliance with the Al Saud family it became the dominant religious teaching of Saudi Arabia and has shaped many mosques, schools, and publications funded from there.

The movement is known for its emphasis on the oneness of God, opposition to anything it views as associating partners with God, and a call to purify worship according to its reading of the earliest sources. Like other Islamic traditions, it denies the Trinity, the deity of Christ, and His death and resurrection as the Bible records them.

If you would like to compare this with what the Bible teaches about God, Christ, or salvation, I am glad to walk through those passages with you.

question: What is the Watchtower Bible and Tract Society?
answer:
The Watchtower Bible and Tract Society is the main legal corporation and publishing organization of Jehovah's Witnesses. Incorporated in Pennsylvania in 1884 under Charles Taze Russell, it produces their magazines (such as The Watchtower), books, and the New World Translation, while directing their worldwide preaching work and property.

Jehovah's Witnesses present themselves as Bible-based Christians, yet their official teachings deny several core doctrines of historic Christianity. They reject the Trinity (one God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) and the full deity of Jesus Christ, teaching instead that He is a created being (Michael the archangel). They also deny His bodily resurrection, claiming He was raised as a spirit.

Scripture teaches otherwise. Jesus is truly God: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Thomas confessed to the risen Christ, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). The risen Jesus Himself said, "Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have" (Luke 24:39). Baptism is commanded "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), showing the three persons of the one God.

These differences are not minor. They place Watchtower teaching outside orthodox Christianity. The Bible calls us to test every teaching against Scripture itself (Acts 17:11). If you have encountered their literature or representatives, read the Gospel of John in a standard translation and see who Jesus claimed to be.

question: What sort of interfaith ministries are appropriate?
answer:
Faithful Christians may disagree on which interfaith ministries are appropriate, because Scripture commands both love for our neighbor and remaining distinct from false worship, yet it does not spell out every modern partnership. Some Christians, emphasizing common grace, believe it is fitting to work alongside people of other religions in practical mercy such as feeding the hungry, medical clinics, or disaster relief, doing good to everyone as we have opportunity (Galatians 6:10) while remaining ready to give a defense for the hope we have (1 Peter 3:15). Others, taking the call not to be unequally yoked more strictly, prefer that churches carry out such ministries independently so the witness stays unmistakably Christian and avoids any appearance of syncretism (2 Corinthians 6:14-18).

What is never appropriate is joint worship, shared prayers that treat other gods as equal, or any implication that other religions save, because there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). A wise next step is to bring any specific opportunity to your church’s elders for counsel, and in your own prayers ask God for wisdom to love well without compromising the exclusivity of Christ (James 1:5).

question: What is presuppositional apologetics?
answer:
Presuppositional apologetics is a method of defending the Christian faith that begins with the truth of Scripture as the ultimate authority and treats the triune God as the necessary precondition for knowledge, logic, science, and morality. It argues that every person already operates with presuppositions, that the unbeliever cannot consistently account for reality without borrowing from the Christian worldview, and that the Christian therefore should not grant autonomous human reason as a neutral starting point.

This approach, developed most fully by Cornelius Van Til in the twentieth century and later by Greg Bahnsen, employs a transcendental argument: it shows that the alternative to biblical theism collapses into inconsistency or absurdity. It takes seriously the noetic effects of sin, the way the fall darkens the mind so that people suppress what they already know of God. Proverbs 1:7 teaches that “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline.” Romans 1:18-21 explains that God’s wrath is revealed against those who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, even though what may be known about God is plain to them. Colossians 2:8 warns against being taken captive by philosophy according to human tradition rather than according to Christ. In practice, a believer using this method might gently ask an atheist how the laws of logic or moral obligation can exist in a purely material universe, then invite the person to consider that only the God of Scripture makes such things intelligible.

Other historic Christian approaches exist. Classical apologetics typically first offers philosophical proofs for God’s existence and then historical evidences for Christianity. Evidential apologetics focuses more directly on historical and scientific data, such as the resurrection. These methods differ in starting point, yet all seek to obey the command of 1 Peter 3:15 to be prepared to give a defense for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and respect. Faithful Christians may employ different methods without compromising the gospel itself. The authority of Scripture and the lordship of Christ remain the non-negotiable center, whatever tools we use to commend Him. If you are considering how to grow in this area, begin by reading 1 Peter 3:15 and Romans 1 slowly, then discuss with a mature believer in your local church how these truths shape conversations about the faith.

question: What does the Bible say about chanting? Should a Christian chant?
answer:
The Bible does not use the word "chanting," but it commands believers to sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, making melody in their hearts to the Lord, and to let the word of Christ dwell richly among them (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). Jesus also warns against empty, repetitive prayer like the pagans, who think they will be heard for their many words (Matthew 6:7).

Chanting Scripture or biblical songs with understanding can be a fitting way to hide God's Word in the heart and offer praise, as the Psalms themselves were meant to be sung and recited (Psalm 47:6-7; Psalm 119:11). Historic Christian practice has included psalm chanting for this reason. However, Christians must not join in mantras, trance-inducing repetitions, or chants from other religions or occult sources. Those practices often empty the mind, treat words as magic, or invoke other spirits, which Scripture forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; 1 John 4:1). Biblical meditation fills the mind with God's truth rather than emptying it.

Worship style is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may differ, since Scripture gives less detail on musical form than on content, heart, and intelligibility. Some traditions use slow liturgical chant to savor the words of Scripture in worship. Others prefer varied hymns and congregational songs that invite fuller participation. Romans 14:5-6 calls us to liberty and charity in such things, provided worship remains biblical, understandable, and offered to God in spirit and truth (John 4:24; 1 Corinthians 14:15-19).

The key is not the style but whether Christ is honored and the mind is engaged with His Word. Recite or sing a psalm slowly this week (Psalm 23 or Psalm 103), asking the Lord to help you grasp and live it. Talk with your pastor about how your church approaches Scripture in worship.

question: Who is Jesus — Day 4 — Jesus the Prophet
answer:
Jesus is the Prophet promised by God, the One we must listen to because He perfectly reveals the Father and speaks with the full authority of God Himself.

Moses announced this coming Prophet: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). In Jesus’ day many Jews were waiting for that figure, and after the feeding of the five thousand some declared, “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6:14). Peter later applied Moses’ words directly to Jesus (Acts 3:22). God had spoken in many times and in many ways through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). Jesus is not merely another messenger; He is the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). At the transfiguration the Father’s voice confirmed the same call Moses had given: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” (Matthew 17:5).

Unlike earlier prophets who said “Thus says the Lord,” Jesus spoke as God incarnate. He taught with unique authority, called sinners to repentance, and accurately foretold His own death, burial, and bodily resurrection on the third day. Those events happened exactly as He said, confirming that His prophetic word is true. This is the prophetic office of Christ as our Mediator: He is the final and sufficient revelation of God. We therefore listen to Him in the Scriptures He inspired, not looking for new prophets to add to that Word.

Because Jesus is this Prophet, He not only announced salvation but accomplished it. All of us have sinned and stand separated from the holy God; Jesus lived the perfect life we could not live, died on the cross as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily, conquering sin and death. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A simple next step is to open one of the Gospels today (John 1 or Matthew 5–7 are good places) and read as one who is listening to the Prophet Himself, asking the Holy Spirit to help you hear and obey. What word of Jesus has recently confronted or comforted you?

question: Will there be a second chance for salvation after death?
answer:
No, the Bible does not teach a second chance for salvation after death. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that to face judgment (Hebrews 9:27).

This present life is the season God has given us to hear the Gospel, repent, and believe. Jesus described a great chasm fixed after death so that none can cross from torment to comfort (Luke 16:26). Now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

All have sinned and stand under God’s just wrath, yet Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died in our place as our substitute (penal substitutionary atonement), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works or later opportunity.

If you have not yet trusted Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. Seek the Lord while He may be found (Isaiah 55:6), and talk with a pastor in a local church that faithfully preaches this Gospel. What has prompted this question for you?

question: What is biblical homemaking?
answer:
Biblical homemaking is the God-given stewardship of the household as a place of order, provision, hospitality, instruction, and worship that honors Christ and serves the family.

Scripture presents the home as a creation ordinance, not a cultural invention. God formed the family before the fall, giving the man and woman complementary callings so that the household would flourish under His design (Genesis 2:18; Genesis 2:24). The virtuous woman of Proverbs 31 watches over the affairs of her household with industry, wisdom, and the fear of the Lord, providing for her family and extending generosity beyond her doors (Proverbs 31:10-31). Likewise, Paul instructs older women to train younger women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled and pure, and to be managers of their households so that the word of God will not be discredited (Titus 2:3-5; 1 Timothy 5:14). Husbands are called to sacrificial headship that images Christ's love for the church, providing, protecting, and washing the family with the Word (Ephesians 5:25-33).

Faithful Christians have differed on the precise outworking of these texts in modern life. Some emphasize the wife's primary vocation in the home as a high and honorable calling that frees her to nurture children and cultivate hospitality. Others stress shared responsibility in which both spouses labor together, adapting to seasons of work, health, or necessity while still honoring biblical order and priorities. These differences often arise from interpretive emphasis and cultural setting rather than from denial of Scripture's authority, so they belong in the realm of Christian liberty where we must not bind one another's consciences (Romans 14:1-6). What remains non-negotiable is that the home itself is to be a center of discipleship, not merely a lodging place.

A concrete next step is to open Proverbs 31 or Titus 2 with your family this week, ask the Lord to show you one ordinary task (a meal, a chore, or evening prayer) that can become an act of worship and instruction, and then talk with a mature believer in your local church about how to grow in this stewardship together.

question: How should Christians view statues of Jesus?
answer:
Christians should view statues of Jesus as unauthorized and unwise, since Scripture forbids making images of God and gives no warrant for depicting the incarnate Christ this way.

The main opposing view, held by many Catholics, Orthodox, and some Protestants, is that because Jesus became truly man His physical form may be represented in art to instruct the faithful and honor the incarnation, provided the image itself receives no worship.

I hold that we should not use statues of Jesus. The second commandment still applies to the triune God, we possess no authentic likeness of our Lord, Christ appointed the preaching of the Word and the Lord's Supper as the ways we are to remember Him, and a statue inevitably portrays only His humanity rather than the fullness of the hypostatic union.

God said, "You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the waters below. You shall not bow down to them or worship them" (Exodus 20:4-5). Deuteronomy 4:15-16 reminds Israel they saw no form when the Lord spoke, so they must not make a carved image. Although Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), that image is Christ Himself, not a figure we fashion. "Therefore, being God’s offspring, we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination" (Acts 17:29). "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5:21).

Christ gave us His Word and the Lord's Supper to remember Him (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24-25). If a statue is in your home or church, a wise next step is to read John 4:19-24 and ask God for wisdom to worship Him in spirit and truth, then talk with your pastor or elders about whether it helps or hinders true devotion to the living Christ.

question: I am in the process of getting a divorce. Can I start dating, or do I have to wait until the divorce is final?
answer:
I am sorry you are walking through the painful process of a divorce. That season often brings grief, loneliness, and uncertainty.

You should not begin dating while the divorce is still in process. You remain married until it is legally finalized, and Scripture treats that remaining covenant as binding. Jesus said, “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6). Paul likewise instructed that if a spouse separates, “she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:11). Pursuing a romantic relationship now would be unfaithful to the marriage God still recognizes and would risk the sin of adultery, even in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28; Exodus 20:14).

The reasons for the divorce matter in God’s sight. Scripture permits it only in limited cases such as sexual immorality or abandonment by an unbelieving spouse, and even then the call is toward faithfulness rather than rushing into a new relationship. God hates divorce (Malachi 2:16), yet He is gracious to those who repent and seek to honor Him.

I know this time can feel isolating. As a next step, speak with your pastor or church elders this week, laying out the details of your situation so they can give wise, biblical counsel. In your own prayers, ask the Lord for wisdom (James 1:5) and for the strength to remain faithful where you are right now, perhaps meditating on 1 Corinthians 7.

question: What is the importance of the empty tomb?
answer:
The empty tomb of Jesus Christ is of first importance because it is the historical evidence of His bodily resurrection, proving that He is the Son of God and that His death fully atoned for sin.

The four Gospels record that Jesus was crucified, buried in a real tomb, and that on the third day the tomb was found empty. The angel announced, “He is not here; He has risen, just as He said. Come, see the place where He lay” (Matthew 28:6). This is attested across Matthew 28:1-10; Mark 16:1-8; Luke 24:1-12; John 20:1-18. The apostle Paul places the burial and resurrection at the heart of the Gospel itself: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and we remain in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17).

The empty tomb therefore confirms Jesus’ identity, demonstrates His victory over death, and shows that God accepted His penal substitutionary sacrifice. Because He lives, those who belong to Him will also be raised.

All people have sinned and stand in need of a Savior. Jesus, truly God and truly man, died in our place, was buried, and rose again, as the empty tomb declares. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

How does the empty tomb shape your hope today?

question: What is traducianism?
answer:
Traducianism is the view that a child’s soul is generated and transmitted from the parents through ordinary procreation, together with the body, rather than being created immediately by God for each person.

This is a tertiary matter on which faithful Christians may disagree without compromising the essentials of the faith, because Scripture clearly teaches that every person is a body-soul unity created in God’s image, fallen in Adam, and in need of new birth, yet it does not give a detailed, explicit account of the precise origin of each individual soul.

Traducianism has been held by some early writers such as Tertullian and by various later Protestants. Its advocates often argue that it best explains how original sin is conveyed to all of Adam’s descendants by ordinary generation, as in Romans 5:12 (“Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned”) and Psalm 51:5 (“Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me”). Some also point to passages such as Hebrews 7:9-10, where Levi is described as already in the loins of Abraham.

The main historic alternative is creationism of souls (God immediately creates a new soul for each person). This view has been held by many Reformed theologians, Augustine, and much of the broader church. Its advocates typically emphasize that God alone forms the spirit of man, as in Zechariah 12:1 (“The LORD, who stretches out the heavens, who lays the foundation of the earth, and who forms the spirit of man within him”) and Ecclesiastes 12:7 (the spirit returns to God who gave it). They also note that the soul is a simple, spiritual substance not generated in the same way as the body.

Both views confess the same core truths: God is the Creator of every human being, the whole person (body and soul) is affected by original sin through Adam’s federal headship, and salvation comes only through Christ’s penal substitutionary atonement received by grace alone through faith alone. The practical difference is small. Children are not born morally neutral; they need the gospel, baptism upon profession of faith, and patient discipleship in the local church. Hold whatever conclusion you reach with charity, study the relevant passages in their context, and discuss the question with your pastors rather than treating it as a test of orthodoxy. Romans 14 reminds us that in non-essentials each should be fully convinced in his own mind while pursuing peace.

question: I am a Buddhist, why should I consider becoming a Christian?
answer:
As a Buddhist, you may find real wisdom in the recognition of suffering, the call to compassion, and the disciplined pursuit of insight and ethical living. You might also wonder whether Christianity is simply one more path among many, or why it would claim that Jesus is uniquely necessary rather than another teacher pointing toward enlightenment.

The Bible teaches that there is one personal, holy God who made us for relationship with Himself. All of us have sinned and fallen short of His glory, so we stand separated from Him and under just judgment (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Our own efforts, however sincere, cannot remove that guilt or restore us to God.

In love, God the Father sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. He lived a sinless life, then died on the cross as our substitute, bearing the penalty we deserved (this is called penal substitutionary atonement). He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, proving His victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He now reigns as Lord.

Salvation is a gift of grace received through faith in Christ alone, not by works or accumulated merit (Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus said, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6). There is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

Turn from relying on your own path and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life with God.

A simple next step is to read the Gospel of John, perhaps a chapter at a time, and ask God to show you whether these things are true. What questions does this raise for you about Jesus or about the Christian claim?

question: How should a Christian view the intellect?
answer:
Christians should view the intellect as a good gift from God, given so that we may know Him, understand His world, and love Him with our whole being, yet a gift that must be humbled and renewed because of sin.

God created humanity in His image with the capacity to reason, learn, and discern (Genesis 1:26-27). Jesus Himself commands us to love the Lord our God with all our mind (Matthew 22:37). The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7). At the same time, the Fall produced the noetic effects of sin, darkening our understanding so that we do not naturally think God's thoughts after Him (Ephesians 4:17-18). Therefore the Christian mind is not autonomous. It must be transformed by the renewing work of the Holy Spirit as we submit to Scripture (Romans 12:2). We take every thought captive to make it obedient to Christ rather than letting human philosophy or empty speculation take us captive (2 Corinthians 10:5; Colossians 2:8).

This means we refuse both anti-intellectualism (as if faith required us to stop thinking) and rationalism (as if unaided reason were the final court of appeal). Careful thinking, study, and even debate are acts of stewardship when they serve the knowledge of God.

When you encounter an idea at work, in a book, or in conversation, pause and ask whether it accords with what God has revealed. A concrete next step is to pray each morning for wisdom, using James 1:5 as your guide, then read a portion of Scripture slowly and ask the Lord to shape your thinking that day. Seek out mature believers in your local church who can help you grow in this, for iron sharpens iron.

question: What does the Bible say about being zealous / having zeal?
answer:
The Bible commends zeal as fervent, wholehearted devotion to God and His purposes when it is according to knowledge, while warning that zeal without truth can become misguided and even destructive.

God Himself is zealous. Isaiah 9:7 declares, “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” Jesus displayed this same burning intensity when He cleansed the temple; His disciples remembered that it is written, “Zeal for Your house will consume Me” (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9). The Hebrew word qinah and the Greek word zelos both speak of a holy heat or jealousy that Scripture applies first to God’s own character and then to the corresponding passion He produces in His people.

Believers are therefore called to the same fervor: “Do not let your zeal subside; keep your spiritual fervor, serving the Lord” (Romans 12:11). Christ “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people who are His own, zealous for good deeds” (Titus 2:14). It is always good to be zealous provided the purpose is good (Galatians 4:18). This godly zeal is not self-generated effort but a fruit of the Holy Spirit in progressive sanctification, flowing from the Gospel rather than earning it.

At the same time, Scripture is clear that zeal can go wrong. Paul testified of Israel that “they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge” (Romans 10:2), and he himself once had zeal that persecuted the church (Philippians 3:6). True zeal is therefore tested by whether it submits to the Word of God.

A concrete next step is to read Romans 12:11 and Titus 2:14 slowly this week, then ask the Lord in your own words to rekindle genuine fervor for serving Him and His people, perhaps by taking one specific act of service in your local church. Pray directly to God about any area where your passion has grown cold, and consider sharing that prayer with a mature believer who can walk with you.

question: What is the grace of God?
answer:
The grace of God is His free, unmerited favor and kindness toward people who deserve only judgment, given most fully in the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.

Scripture presents this grace as a gift, not a wage: "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). It appeared in history when "the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone" (Titus 2:11), and it is seen in Christ's own self-giving: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). Mercy withholds the punishment we deserve; grace goes further and gives us the blessing we could never earn.

This grace is the foundation of justification, in which God declares sinners righteous solely through faith in Christ's finished work, not our performance. Christians also recognize common grace (God's general kindness in creation and providence to all people, such as rain and sunshine in Matthew 5:45), yet saving grace is particular, applied by the Holy Spirit so that we are born again, forgiven, and kept.

A concrete way this applies is that when you fail or feel unworthy, you do not have to hide or try harder to earn God's smile. You can confess your sin, rest in what Christ has already done, and keep walking with Him in thankful obedience, because His grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9).

question: How young can you be to ask Jesus to be your Savior? Can a 3 or 4 year old truly believe?
answer:
A child of any age can come to Jesus in saving faith, because the Bible never sets a minimum age and because faith itself is a gift of God rather than a product of mature reasoning. Yes, a 3 or 4 year old can truly believe.

Jesus welcomed little children and declared that the kingdom of God belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14; Matthew 19:14). He did not treat their coming as pretend or incomplete. Saving faith involves knowledge of the Gospel, assent that it is true, and personal trust in Christ. A young child can possess these at a simple level: they can know they have sinned, that Jesus is God’s Son who died on the cross for sinners and rose again, and they can rest in Him. The Holy Spirit is able to grant regeneration even to the youngest heart (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 3:8). Timothy knew the sacred writings from childhood, which were able to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15).

A child’s faith will look childlike. It may be expressed in simple words and will grow in understanding over time. We do not look for adult vocabulary or exhaustive theology, but for a genuine turning to Jesus. True faith, once given, is kept by God’s power and will not finally fall away.

If you are a parent or caregiver, keep sharing the Gospel plainly and often. Read the accounts of Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection together from a children’s Bible, pray with your child about their need for a Savior, and involve them in the life of a local church where they can hear the Word. Speak with your pastors or elders so they can help you discern and nurture what God may be doing. Rejoice if your child expresses trust in Christ, then continue patiently teaching, correcting, and pointing them to Jesus as they grow.

question: Is it wrong for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches?
answer:
It is not inherently sinful for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches, because Scripture never issues a direct command that spouses must belong to the same local congregation. This is a tertiary matter of wisdom and Christian liberty rather than an essential of the faith. Faithful believers may differ here because the Bible gives less explicit detail on the practical outworking of church attendance within marriage than it does on the gospel itself.

One historic Christian view is that a husband and wife should worship together as a family. This honors their one-flesh union, allows the husband to exercise spiritual headship in leading his household, and provides a consistent example for children in discipleship. Another view holds that attending different gospel-preaching churches can be acceptable when there are sincere differences of conscience on secondary matters (such as baptism or church practice), provided both congregations are orthodox, the couple remains united in Christ, and they continue to encourage one another.

I believe it is generally wiser for a husband and wife to attend the same church whenever possible. The marriage covenant calls them to walk together, and the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church (Ephesians 5:23). Separate attendance can make shared prayer, family teaching, and mutual edification more difficult, even if it is not a sin. Christian liberty still applies, however, especially when both churches faithfully preach Christ crucified and risen (Romans 14:5; Romans 14:19). Each should be fully convinced in his own mind and pursue what leads to peace.

If this describes your situation, talk openly with your spouse about the reasons, pray together for unity and wisdom, and consider seeking counsel from the elders of both churches. You might also visit one another’s congregations so you can better understand and support each other’s walk with the Lord. Hebrews 10:24-25 still calls every believer not to neglect meeting together, and Ephesians 5:31 reminds us that the two have become one flesh. Let that union shape how you decide.

question: What is the Druze religion?
answer:
The Druze religion is a monotheistic, ethnoreligious faith that arose in 11th-century Egypt from Ismaili Shia Islam and is now practiced by a closed community mainly in Lebanon, Syria, Israel, and Jordan. Its followers, who call themselves Muwahhidun (Unitarians), emphasize the absolute oneness of God (tawhid), the reincarnation of souls until they reach purity, and the idea that God has manifested in human form, especially in the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah. Conversion is not permitted; one must be born Druze. Inner teachings, drawn from the Epistles of Wisdom, are esoteric and reserved for initiated members (uqqal), while the faith honors a range of figures including biblical prophets, Jesus, Muhammad, and certain Greek philosophers.

The Bible presents a different revelation of God and of how people are reconciled to Him. God is one in essence yet eternally three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus Christ is the unique, once-for-all incarnation of the eternal Son, truly God and truly man in the hypostatic union, born of the Virgin Mary. He did not appear as one manifestation among others. His sacrificial death on the cross was a penal substitutionary atonement sufficient to pay for sin, and His bodily resurrection on the third day demonstrated His victory over death. Scripture teaches that people die once and then face judgment, not repeated rebirths: “Just as man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by cycles of reincarnation or secret knowledge. Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

Druze people, like all people, are made in God’s image and deserve respect. The historic Christian claim is that the Father has spoken fully and finally in His Son. If you would like to look at what Scripture says about knowing God, I am glad to walk through it with you.

question: What is an invocation prayer?
answer:
An invocation prayer is a prayer that calls upon God to be present, to bless those gathered, and to grant His help by the Holy Spirit, most often offered at the opening of a worship service, meeting, or other Christian gathering.

Scripture regularly shows God's people calling upon His name in this way, as when the psalmist prays, "May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us" (Psalm 67:1). We come to the Father through the Son, asking in Jesus' name so that the Father may be glorified (John 14:13-14). Such a prayer acknowledges our dependence on God rather than ourselves and seeks His glory in whatever follows.

If you are leading a gathering, you can keep it simple and specific: ask the Father to draw near, to open His Word, and to make hearts attentive by His Spirit for Jesus' sake.

question: What is the spiritual gift of prophecy?
answer:
The spiritual gift of prophecy is a Holy Spirit-given ability to receive and speak a message from God that strengthens, encourages, and comforts His people (1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 Corinthians 14:3). In the New Testament this gift functioned alongside the apostles as God laid the foundation of the church and completed the canon of Scripture (Ephesians 2:20; 1 Corinthians 14:29–32).

Cessationists hold that such revelatory gifts belonged to that foundational period and ceased once the apostles died and Scripture was complete, because the church now possesses the sufficient, finished Word of God. Continuationists argue that 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 locates the end of prophecy at Christ’s return rather than the close of the canon, so a lesser, fallible form of prophecy may still edify the church today provided it is tested by Scripture.

As a Reformed Baptist I hold the cessationist view as one faithful option within historic Christianity, because the foundation of the apostles and prophets has already been laid and because 2 Timothy 3:16–17 teaches that the completed Scriptures thoroughly equip us for every good work; no further binding revelation is needed or given. In practice this means we weigh every claimed prophetic word against the Bible, reject anything that contradicts or adds to it, and devote ourselves to knowing and proclaiming the already-revealed Word, which is the prophetic word made more sure (2 Peter 1:19).

question: What does the Bible say about purification?
answer:
The Bible teaches purification as God's provision to make His people clean and holy, first through ceremonial washings and sacrifices in the Old Testament that illustrated sin's defilement, and ultimately through the blood of Jesus Christ who truly purifies the heart and conscience. These Old Testament rituals, given in Israel's covenant context to set them apart as holy to the LORD who dwelt among them, could cleanse only outwardly and pointed forward to a greater atonement.

On the Day of Atonement, God declared, "because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, that you may be clean from all your sins before the LORD" (Leviticus 16:30). David, after his own sin, prayed, "Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow" (Psalm 51:7). Yet these shadows could not remove guilt from the conscience.

The New Testament reveals the fulfillment in Christ's penal substitutionary atonement. Hebrews 9:13-14 explains, "For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean sanctify them so that they are outwardly clean, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!" This purification is received by faith and continues in our sanctification as we walk with Him. "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

Practically, this calls us to turn from known sin each day, not by our own efforts but by trusting Christ's finished work, perhaps by reading Psalm 51 and 1 John 1 this week while asking God to search and cleanse your heart through His Word.

question: Does the Bible say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times?
answer:
The Bible does not say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times. The passage most often connected to this idea is Daniel 12:4: "But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will roam to and fro, and knowledge will increase."

One interpretation, common among Christians who read prophecy in a strongly futurist way, takes "roam to and fro" as worldwide travel and "knowledge will increase" as the modern explosion of science and technology, treating both as markers that the last days have arrived. Another interpretation, held by many other believers, sees the increase in knowledge as a growing understanding of the very prophecies Daniel was told to seal, or as people searching the Scriptures more widely, rather than as a prediction of technological progress itself.
