Some Christians in the Arminian tradition argue that salvation remains conditional on continued faith and obedience in every age, so that even Old Testament believers could forfeit it through persistent unbelief.

I hold the Reformed Baptist view as one faithful option within historic Christianity that they did have it, for the perseverance of the saints rests on God's eternal election and the covenant of grace that spans both testaments rather than on the believer's era or strength. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3), and those saints died in faith without yet receiving the promises, yet God prepared a city for them (Hebrews 11:13-16). The Lord loves justice and will not forsake His saints; they are preserved forever (Psalm 37:28). This same preserving grace that kept David after his sins and Abraham through his failings keeps God's people today, so rest in Christ's finished work and continue looking to Him in the ordinary means of grace.

question: What does it mean that the church is the bride of Christ?
answer:
The church is the bride of Christ, a biblical picture of the exclusive covenant union between Jesus and His redeemed people, in which He loves the church as a husband loves his wife, having given Himself for her to make her holy.

This language appears most clearly in Ephesians 5:25-27, where Paul writes that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to Himself as a radiant church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless. The same imagery is used in 2 Corinthians 11:2, where the church is described as betrothed to Christ as a pure virgin, and it reaches its climax in Revelation 19:7-9 and Revelation 21:2,9, where the marriage of the Lamb arrives and the New Jerusalem comes down as a bride adorned for her husband. The Old Testament already prepared this picture by calling the Lord the husband of His people (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19-20), so the New Testament presents Christ as the true Bridegroom who fulfills that covenant faithfulness.

Theologically, this is the church’s union with Christ. He is the Head who laid down His life in penal substitutionary atonement; the church is His body and bride, already joined to Him by faith yet still awaiting the full consummation when He returns. Because of that union, believers are called to live in exclusive devotion and growing holiness, not as those who belong to themselves but as those purchased and set apart for Him.

A concrete next step is to read Ephesians 5:22-33 slowly this week, asking God to shape your love for Christ and your local church after the pattern of His own sacrificial love. Pray directly to Him for the church’s purity and unity, and talk with a mature believer or your pastors about how this identity should mark your daily faithfulness.

question: How can I believe in the goodness of God when there is so much evil in the world?
answer:
The evil and suffering in the world can make God's goodness feel distant or even questionable, and your honest struggle with that is understandable. Many have asked how a good God could allow such pain, or whether the scale of injustice means He is not truly good or not truly in control.

The Bible teaches that God is perfectly good, holy, and just. Psalm 34:8; Psalm 100:5; Psalm 145:9. Evil did not originate with Him. It entered through humanity's rebellion against God, bringing death, brokenness, and the groaning we still see. Genesis 3; Romans 5:12. God is not the author of sin, yet He remains sovereign over all things, and His wrath against evil is real because He is holy.

God's goodness is most clearly displayed at the cross. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, entered our suffering world, lived without sin, and died as a substitute, bearing the penalty our sins deserved (penal substitutionary atonement). He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin, death, and evil. Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4. The worst act of evil in history, the crucifixion of the innocent Son of God, became the means of the greatest good: the salvation of sinners. God does not stand aloof from our pain; He has entered it and overcome it.

Even now He works all things together for the good of those who love Him, and one day Christ will return to judge evil finally and make all things new, wiping away every tear. Romans 8:28; Revelation 21:4-5. Until then, we live in a fallen world, yet we can trust His character because He has revealed it in Scripture and in Christ.

A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John, watching how Jesus meets suffering with both compassion and authority, and to pray honestly to God, telling Him your doubts and asking Him to help you see His goodness (you might use Psalm 13 as a guide for lament). Seek a faithful local church where the Word is preached and you can walk with other believers who have faced the same questions.

If this wrestling has left you unsure of your standing with God, salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. What part of the evil you see weighs on you most right now?

question: What does "communion of the saints" mean in the ancient creeds?
answer:
The phrase "communion of the saints" in the Apostles' Creed means the spiritual fellowship and unity of all true believers in Christ, the holy people of God joined as one body both on earth and in heaven. The Nicene Creed expresses the same reality when it confesses "one holy catholic and apostolic Church."

In Scripture every Christian is a saint (hagioi, those set apart by God), not a special class of heroes. Paul greets ordinary believers this way in 1 Corinthians 1:2 and Philippians 1:1. This communion (koinonia) is our shared participation in Christ and in one another through the Holy Spirit, as "we were all baptized by one Spirit into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13). The first church lived it when they "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer" (Acts 2:42). Hebrews 12:22-23 includes the saints already with the Lord, so the church on earth and the church in glory form one communion under Christ their Head.

This is the church as the mystical body of Christ. Practically, it means you are not meant to walk the Christian life alone; commit yourself to a local congregation where you share worship, the Lord's Supper, prayer, and mutual care.

Some later traditions have added the practice of asking departed saints to intercede, yet the creeds themselves, read with Scripture, point us to Christ as the one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). The historic Protestant understanding, which I hold, sees this communion as the fellowship of all who are truly united to Jesus, expressed most clearly in the life of the local church.

question: How can I gain a passion for winning souls?
answer:
A genuine passion for winning souls is not something we generate by guilt or technique. It grows as we behold the heart of Christ and ask the Holy Spirit to share His compassion with us.

Jesus was moved with compassion when He saw the crowds, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He then told His disciples that the harvest is plentiful but the workers are few, and He commanded them to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers (Matthew 9:36-38). The Apostle Paul felt great sorrow for those still outside of Christ and described the love of Christ as the thing that controls us, so that we now serve as ambassadors through whom God makes His appeal (Romans 10:1; 2 Corinthians 5:14; 2 Corinthians 5:20). This is the same Lord who sends us in the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19-20).

That passion rests on three biblical realities. First, God is holy and His wrath against sin is real; apart from Christ, people remain under judgment (John 3:36). Second, the Gospel itself is glorious: the eternal Son took on human nature, lived a perfect life, died as our penal substitute, was buried, and rose bodily. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Him. When that news grips us again, silence becomes impossible. Third, every person bears the imago Dei and is therefore of infinite worth, yet desperately needs the Savior (Genesis 1:27; Romans 3:23).

Pray specifically for this burden. Ask the Father each day to give you His heart for the lost, to open doors, and to fill you with the Spirit’s love (Romans 5:5). Abide in Christ; apart from Him we can do nothing (John 15:5). Meditate on Luke 15, where Jesus seeks the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. Then take one concrete step this week: write down the names of two or three people you know who do not yet know Christ. Pray for their salvation by name every day, and watch for a natural opportunity to speak of how Jesus has forgiven you. Share this desire with a mature believer in your local church so you can be encouraged and held accountable.

The Lord delights to answer such prayers. He who began a good work in you will carry it on, and He can kindle in you the same love that sent His Son into the world.

question: What is reprobation? What does it mean to be reprobate?
answer:
Reprobation is God's eternal, sovereign decree to pass over some fallen sinners, withholding the electing grace given to others and justly ordaining them to condemnation for their own sin, to the praise of His glorious justice. To be reprobate, in this theological sense, means to be among those not chosen in Christ, left in spiritual death and unbelief, and therefore facing God's righteous wrath.

Scripture teaches this alongside election. God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills (Romans 9:18). He endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of His glory on vessels of mercy prepared beforehand (Romans 9:22-23). Certain ungodly people were designated long ago for condemnation (Jude 4), and some stumble at the word because they were appointed to that end (1 Peter 2:8). This is not God authoring sin; people remain fully responsible for their rebellion, and reprobation displays His justice just as election displays His grace.

The New Testament also uses a related term (often rendered "reprobate" or "depraved") for those who fail the test of genuine faith or are given over to a rejected mind (Romans 1:28; 2 Timothy 3:8; 2 Corinthians 13:5). Theologically, that describes those under the decree of reprobation.

Faithful Christians differ here. Many (including Arminian and Wesleyan believers) hold that God elects on the basis of foreseen faith and reprobates on the basis of foreseen unbelief, emphasizing texts such as 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9 to preserve God's desire that all be saved and the reality of human response. The Reformed Baptist view I hold is that both election and reprobation rest in God's independent will, not in anything foreseen in us, because "it does not, therefore, depend on human desire or effort, but on God’s mercy" (Romans 9:16) and His purpose of election stands before anyone has done good or evil (Romans 9:11). This upholds salvation by grace alone.

This truth should produce humility, not speculation about others, and it never excuses neglecting the gospel. We do not know who is elect or reprobate in this life, so we proclaim Christ to all without distinction and call every person to repent and believe. If the doctrine troubles you, read Romans 9–11 slowly while asking God to show you both His mercy and His justice, then discuss it with a pastor in a local church that loves Scripture.

question: What does the Bible say about how to get baptized / how to baptize?
answer:
The Bible teaches that baptism is to be given by immersing in water those who have already repented and believed in Jesus Christ, done in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, as a public sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection.

Faithful Christians who baptize infants, especially in Presbyterian and Reformed churches, argue that baptism replaced circumcision as the covenant sign and should therefore be given to the children of believers, often by sprinkling or pouring, pointing to household baptisms such as the Philippian jailer’s in Acts 16:33 and God’s pattern of including families in His covenants.

I hold that the New Testament calls for believer’s baptism by immersion because every baptism follows a personal profession of faith, the word used means to dip or immerse, and the ordinance pictures being buried with Christ and raised to new life. After Philip preached Jesus, the Ethiopian eunuch believed and then asked, “Look, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?” before they both went down into the water (Acts 8:36–38). Those who received Peter’s word were told, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ,” and about three thousand were baptized that day (Acts 2:38; Acts 2:41). Jesus commanded His disciples to make disciples of all nations, “baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Paul explains that we were “buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4; see also Colossians 2:12).

Baptism does not save anyone; it is an act of obedience that follows salvation by grace through faith in Christ’s death and resurrection alone (Ephesians 2:8–9). To be baptized, first trust in Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior, then ask the pastors or elders of a local church that practices believer’s baptism to administer it as a public testimony. The one who baptizes (ordinarily a pastor or elder) immerses the believer fully in water and raises him or her up while speaking the triune name, usually in the gathered church.

If you have believed, speak with a pastor this week, share how Christ has saved you, and request baptism as your next step of discipleship.

question: What is prevenient grace?
answer:
Prevenient grace is the teaching, especially in Arminian and Wesleyan theology, that God gives a universal, preceding grace to every person that restores enough freedom for them to accept or reject the gospel.

Those who hold this view argue that it honors both God’s necessary initiative (no one comes unless drawn) and the many biblical calls that treat people as genuinely able to repent, so that the difference between belief and unbelief finally rests in the human will.

Reformed Baptist theology understands preceding grace differently. Because Scripture describes us as dead in trespasses and sins and unable of ourselves to receive spiritual things, God must first regenerate the heart, so that faith itself is the fruit of His effectual, particular work rather than a response made possible by merely enabling grace given equally to all (Ephesians 2:1; 1 Corinthians 2:14; John 6:44; John 6:65; Ezekiel 36:26-27). This is why we pray and preach expecting God to open hearts as He opened Lydia’s, knowing the new birth is His sovereign gift (Acts 16:14).

question: What does it mean that Jesus died for our sins?
answer:
Jesus dying for our sins means that He, the sinless Son of God, bore the penalty our rebellion deserved as our substitute, so that sinners who trust in Him are forgiven, justified, and reconciled to God.

God is holy, just, and good. His wrath against sin is real because sin is lawlessness that separates us from Him (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). We cannot earn our way back by works. In love the Father sent the Son, who is truly God and truly man. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, Jesus lived a perfect life and then offered Himself on the cross. This is penal substitutionary atonement: He took our punishment in our place. Scripture says, “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, proving His victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is now the exalted Lord.

Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our efforts. Those who repent and believe are declared righteous because His finished work is counted as theirs.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life with God.

Because this is true, you do not have to carry guilt as if the debt were still unpaid. Confess sin, rest in His righteousness, and live in grateful obedience. This week, read Isaiah 53 slowly and ask the Lord to impress on you both the weight of sin and the depth of His love.

What part of this truth feels most needed or most confusing for you right now?

question: What is Calvinism, and is it biblical?
answer:
Calvinism is the historic Reformed teaching on salvation that emphasizes God's sovereign grace in choosing, redeeming, and keeping sinners, commonly summarized in the five points of TULIP.

Arminian Christians teach that God elects based on His foreknowledge of who will freely believe, that Jesus died for all humanity equally, and that people can resist or fall from grace, seeing this as faithful to God's universal love and human accountability in passages like John 3:16 and 1 Timothy 2:4.

I believe Calvinism is biblical because it best explains the Bible's emphasis on God's free and particular grace, such as His choosing us before the world began according to His purpose in Ephesians 1:4-5 and His drawing of people so that they come in John 6:44.

Total depravity means that because of the fall, humans are spiritually dead and unable to choose God without His prior work (Ephesians 2:1; Romans 8:7-8). Unconditional election means God chooses specific people for salvation not because of anything in them but solely from His mercy (Romans 9:15-16). Limited atonement, or particular redemption, means Christ's death on the cross actually secured the salvation of the elect rather than merely making it possible (John 10:14-15; Matthew 1:21). Irresistible grace, or effectual calling, means the Holy Spirit effectively regenerates the elect, overcoming their resistance so they come willingly to faith (John 6:37; Ezekiel 36:26-27). Perseverance of the saints means God preserves those He has saved so they continue in faith to the end (John 10:28; 1 Peter 1:5).

These doctrines produce humility, since we contribute nothing to our justification, and they fuel evangelism, because God uses the preaching of the Gospel as the means to call His people (Romans 10:14-17). A good next step is to read Romans 8-9 and Ephesians 1 slowly, asking God for understanding, and to talk through the passages with a pastor or mature believer in a local church that submits to Scripture.

question: Who was Ishtar, and is there any connection between Ishtar and Easter?
answer:
Ishtar was an ancient Mesopotamian goddess of love, fertility, and war (earlier called Inanna by the Sumerians). There is no historical, linguistic, or religious connection between Ishtar and Easter.

A common claim online is that Easter came from Ishtar because the English names sound alike and both get linked to spring fertility symbols such as eggs. That claim does not hold up. The English word Easter most likely comes from Old English Ēostre (possibly a dawn or spring figure noted by the 8th-century writer Bede, or simply the east and the season). The Christian feast itself is far older than that English name and has a completely different origin. It commemorates Jesus Christ’s bodily resurrection, which took place at the time of the Jewish Passover, as the Gospels record as a real historical event (Matthew 28:1-10; Mark 16:1-8; Luke 24:1-12; John 20:1-18). The New Testament presents this as the fulfillment of Scripture, and the early church called the observance Pascha (from the Hebrew Pesach, Passover). Most languages still use a form of that name.

Ishtar’s own symbols were typically the eight-pointed star, lions, and a descent-to-the-underworld myth; they do not match later European folk customs of eggs and rabbits, which grew up independently in Christianized cultures. Those customs are not the origin or the meaning of the day.

Faithful Christians may differ on the English name “Easter” or on extra-biblical spring customs; that belongs to Christian liberty in non-essentials (Romans 14:5). What remains essential is the event itself: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). When the season comes, let the empty tomb and the risen Lord be the center rather than later trappings.

question: Who are the Alawites, and what do they believe?
answer:
The Alawites (also called Alawis or historically Nusayris) are an ethnoreligious minority concentrated mainly along the Syrian coast, with smaller communities in Lebanon and Turkey. They emerged in the 9th–10th century as a secretive offshoot of Twelver Shia Islam, associated with Muhammad ibn Nusayr, and today make up roughly a tenth of Syria’s population.

Their theology is esoteric, initiatory, and not fully disclosed to outsiders. It centers on the deification of Ali ibn Abi Talib (Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law) as a divine manifestation, together with a triad of Ali (the Meaning), Muhammad (the Name), and Salman al-Farisi (the Gate). Alawites hold to reincarnation (the transmigration of souls according to one’s deeds) and practice a syncretic faith that mixes Shia elements with Gnostic, Neoplatonic, and some Christian or older Near Eastern motifs; certain festivals overlap with Christmas or Epiphany. They regard themselves as Muslims, though many Sunni and Shia authorities have historically viewed them as outside orthodox Islam.

Scripture teaches that there is one God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). Jesus Christ is the unique, eternal Son who became truly man in the incarnation, died as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, and rose bodily (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by secret knowledge or cycles of rebirth (Ephesians 2:8–9; Hebrews 9:27). Alawite teaching therefore stands outside the biblical Gospel.

Every Alawite, like every other person, is made in God’s image and needs the same Savior. Christians can love their Alawite neighbors by praying that they would hear of Christ’s death and resurrection and by sharing that hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

question: Why is sola fide important?
answer:
Sola fide is important because it is the biblical truth that God justifies sinners by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from any meritorious works of their own. Justification is God’s legal declaration that a guilty person is righteous in His sight, and Scripture presents faith as the sole instrument by which we receive the perfect righteousness of Jesus, not as something we contribute or complete.

The Bible is clear: “For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). “A man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16). God is holy and just, and His wrath against sin is real. Every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory, so no amount of law-keeping, religious effort, or moral improvement can make us right with Him. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived the perfect life we could not live, died as our substitute under the penalty of our sin (penal substitution), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. By faith alone His righteousness is imputed to the believer, and our sin is counted to Him.

This doctrine matters because it protects the sufficiency of Christ’s atonement and the glory of God in salvation. If justification depended even partly on our works, we would either boast in ourselves or live in despair, never knowing whether we had done enough. Sola fide gives true assurance, because it rests on Christ’s finished work rather than our fluctuating performance. True saving faith is never idle; it produces good works as its fruit and evidence (James 2:17), yet those works are the result of justification, never its basis.

When guilt, striving, or self-reliance rises in your heart, look away from yourself to Christ crucified and risen, and rest in His merit. If you have been relying on your own efforts rather than on Jesus, turn from sin and self-trust and place your faith in Him alone who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Talk with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about this, and ask God to give you a clearer grasp of justification as you read Romans 3–5 this week. What part of this truth is most on your mind right now?

question: Does the Bible say anything about clairvoyance?
answer:
The Bible does not use the modern term clairvoyance, yet it clearly forbids the related practices of seeking hidden knowledge, distant events, or the future through occult means such as divination, soothsaying, omens, or consulting mediums. These are presented as detestable to God because they bypass His appointed ways of revealing truth and often involve demonic influence rather than His Spirit.

Deuteronomy 18:10-12 states, "Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, who practices divination or interprets omens, who engages in witchcraft, or casts spells, or who is a medium or spiritist or who consults the dead. Anyone who does these things is detestable to the LORD, and because of these detestable practices the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you." Leviticus 19:31 adds, "You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God." Isaiah 8:19 asks, "When they say to you, 'Consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter,' should not a people consult their God? Should they consult the dead on behalf of the living?"

In the New Testament a slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination earned money by fortune-telling until Paul commanded the spirit to leave her in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 16:16-18). Scripture consistently contrasts such practices with true revelation that comes from God alone, whether through His prophets in the Old Testament or through the completed Word and the Holy Spirit today. Human attempts to gain extrasensory knowledge independently of Him are treated as rebellion, not a spiritual gift.

God is sovereign over all hidden things and the future; He invites His people to seek wisdom from Him rather than occult sources (James 1:5). If this topic has arisen because of curiosity, a personal experience, or someone offering such services, the next step is to bring it to the Lord in prayer, asking Him for discernment, and to discuss it with a pastor or mature believer in your local church who can help you stay rooted in Scripture.

question: What is the Shahada in Islam?
answer:
The Shahada is Islam’s central declaration of faith and the first of its Five Pillars. It is the testimony, “I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” In Islamic teaching, sincere recitation of this creed is what makes a person a Muslim.

Christians also confess that there is one true God, yet the Bible reveals Him as the Trinity, one God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, and He alone is the way to the Father (John 14:6).

question: What is the dispensation of Grace?
answer:
The dispensation of Grace, in dispensational theology, is the present church age from the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost until the rapture, characterized by salvation through faith in Christ apart from the Law of Moses.

Covenant theologians argue that Scripture reveals one covenant of grace throughout redemptive history, fulfilled in the new covenant, so that the stewardship of God’s grace in Ephesians 3:2 refers to Paul’s ministry of the previously hidden mystery of Gentile inclusion in Christ rather than a new and separate era.

I hold to covenant theology because the apostles present the church as the continuation of God’s people, with believing Gentiles now fellow heirs of the promise (Ephesians 3:6; Galatians 3:29), and justification always by faith as it was for Abraham (Romans 4:1-5). This perspective helps us read the Old Testament as Christian Scripture that points to Jesus and to live in the liberty of the gospel, depending on Christ’s finished work for our standing before God.

question: What does the Bible say about repentance? What does it mean to repent?
answer:
The Bible teaches that to repent is to turn from sin toward God with a changed mind and heart, and this turning is commanded of all people. Jesus said, “Repent and believe in the gospel!” (Mark 1:15), and God “now commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

The New Testament word often translated “repent” is metanoia, a change of mind that produces a change of direction in life, not mere regret or emotion. In the Old Testament the prophets used shuv, calling people to return to the Lord from idolatry and rebellion (Isaiah 55:7; Ezekiel 18:30–32). John the Baptist and Jesus both demanded fruit in keeping with repentance (Matthew 3:8; Luke 3:8). Godly sorrow produces this repentance that leads to salvation, unlike worldly grief that produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Scripture also shows that God Himself grants repentance as a gift (Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25).

This matters because God is holy and we are not. Every person has sinned and is separated from Him, facing His just wrath. In love the eternal Son took on human nature through the virgin birth, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as our substitute in penal substitution, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and is now exalted as Lord. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works. True faith always includes this Spirit-given repentance, through which sinners are justified and begin the lifelong work of sanctification.

If the Spirit is convicting you of a particular sin, name it to God, turn from it, and rest in Christ’s finished work rather than your own resolve. A concrete next step is to read Psalm 51 slowly this week and then speak with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about walking in that new direction.

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. What about this call to turn toward God feels most pressing or unclear to you right now?

question: Is there an argument for the existence of God?
answer:
Yes, there are several strong arguments for the existence of God, drawn from reason, the created world, moral experience, and especially the historical person of Jesus Christ.

Some people object that science has made a Creator unnecessary, that suffering and evil make a good God unlikely, or that we cannot prove anything beyond the material world. Those concerns are understandable, yet they do not erase the evidence God has given.

Scripture itself treats God’s existence as clearly displayed in creation. “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1). “For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (Romans 1:20). This is what Christians call general revelation: God has not left Himself without witness in the world He made.

The cosmological argument notes that everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe had a beginning, so it requires a cause that itself did not begin, an eternal, uncaused Creator. The teleological (design) argument observes the astonishing fine-tuning of the universe’s physical constants and the specified complexity of living things, pointing to an intelligent Designer rather than unguided chance. The moral argument observes that we all recognize objective right and wrong (it is really wrong to torture the innocent for pleasure). Such moral obligation is best explained by a transcendent Moral Lawgiver.

The most decisive evidence is historical: Jesus of Nazareth claimed to be God, was crucified, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day. The empty tomb, the appearances to many witnesses, and the sudden transformation of fearful disciples into bold proclaimers are well-attested facts that confirm both God’s existence and His action in history (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

The Bible opens with the straightforward declaration, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). “And without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him” (Hebrews 11:6).

Knowing that God exists is not yet knowing Him personally. All of us have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A simple next step is to read the Gospel of John this week, asking God to show you who Jesus is. Seek out a local church that preaches the Bible, and talk with a pastor or mature believer. You can also pray directly to God, asking Him to make Himself known to you as you seek Him.

What particular argument or objection is most on your mind?

question: Is Christmas a pagan holiday?
answer:
No, Christmas is not a pagan holiday. Christians who observe it do so to remember the real, historical incarnation of Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God who took on human nature and was born of the Virgin Mary.

The Bible never assigns a date to Jesus’ birth, and the earliest Christians did not keep December 25. By the fourth century the church in Rome had begun marking that day, possibly because of an older calculation that placed the Annunciation on March 25, or possibly to offer a Christian alternative to existing winter festivals. Historians still debate the exact reasons. Some later customs (evergreen decorations, for example) have mixed cultural roots, yet the heart of the observance, when it is Christian, is the gospel event recorded in Scripture: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The angel’s announcement remains the same: “Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:11).

Whether a believer sets aside December 25 for this remembrance is a tertiary matter of Christian liberty, not an essential of the faith. Scripture neither commands nor forbids a special day for Christ’s birth, and the New Testament treats the observance of days as something each person should be fully convinced about in his own mind (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17). Faithful Christians have therefore reached different conclusions.

One historic view is that the season can be a fitting time to proclaim the incarnation, gather for worship, and give thanks that God sent His Son. Another historic view, held by many Puritans and some later Baptists, is that we should not treat the day as a holy day because it is not commanded in Scripture and because of concerns about syncretism or worldly excess.

I believe Christians are free in Christ to remember His birth on that day or on any other, provided the focus remains on the true God and His gospel rather than on empty tradition or commercial frenzy. The incarnation itself is not optional; it is a core truth. The Son of God became truly man so that He could live a perfect life, die as a substitute for sinners, and rise bodily for our justification.

Whatever you decide, keep Christ central. Read the nativity accounts in Luke 2 and Matthew 1–2, and let the wonder of God with us shape your worship all year. If you are unsure, talk it through with the elders of a local church that holds the Scriptures as its final authority.

question: What is a Calvinist?
answer: A Calvinist is a Christian who holds that God sovereignly and unconditionally elects, calls, and preserves sinners for salvation by His grace alone, as taught in the Reformed tradition stemming from John Calvin. Arminian Christians, by contrast, maintain that God elects those He foresees will believe, that Christ atoned for all humanity, and that people can freely accept or reject His grace, thereby upholding the universal offer of the gospel and genuine human choice. I hold to Calvinism as one faithful historic Christian option because the Bible teaches that faith is granted by God (Philippians 1:29) and that the Father draws His people to the Son (John 6:44), a monergistic work that exalts God's glory in our salvation and gives unshakable hope. These truths are often summarized as total depravity, unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, and perseverance of the saints. Practically, this leads a believer to share the good news widely, trusting God to save, and to find comfort that nothing can separate us from His love (Romans 8:38-39).

question: What is Reformed epistemology apologetics?
answer:
Reformed epistemology is an approach to Christian apologetics, associated especially with Alvin Plantinga and Nicholas Wolterstorff, that holds belief in God can be rational and warranted as a properly basic belief, without first needing arguments or evidence to justify it.

This view draws from Reformed theology’s teaching that God has given all people an innate awareness of Himself (what Calvin called the *sensus divinitatis*). Scripture presents this as real knowledge, not mere inference: “For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse” (Romans 1:19–20; see also Psalm 19:1). The noetic effects of sin suppress this knowledge, yet the Holy Spirit’s internal testimony can restore and confirm it in the believer (Romans 8:16).

Unlike classical evidentialism, which treats arguments for God’s existence as necessary for rational faith, Reformed epistemology treats such arguments as optional rather than required. It also differs from some forms of presuppositional apologetics by focusing on the conditions of warrant (what makes a belief knowledge) rather than primarily on transcendental or worldview-level confrontation. The practical fruit is that a Christian’s trust in God need not wait on answering every skeptical objection; faith can rest on God’s self-revelation while still engaging objections as they arise.

If you are wrestling with whether your own faith is “rational enough,” a helpful next step is to read slowly through Romans 1 and Psalm 19, asking God to make His self-disclosure in creation and Scripture freshly clear to you, and to talk it through with a mature believer in your local church.

question: Can a person be saved through general revelation?
answer:
No, a person cannot be saved through general revelation. Creation and conscience display God’s eternal power, divine nature, and moral law, yet they do not reveal Jesus Christ or the way of justification by grace through faith in Him.

Psalm 19:1–4 and Romans 1:19–20 show that what may be known about God is plain in the things He has made, so that people are without excuse. Yet because of sin they suppress the truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18), become futile in their thinking, and do not seek God (Romans 3:10–12). General revelation therefore leaves every person under just condemnation; it cannot produce saving faith.

Salvation comes only through special revelation of the Gospel: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ (Romans 10:17). There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12), and Jesus Himself said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

You may wonder about those who never hear the name of Jesus. Scripture does not teach that a sincere response to nature or conscience can save them. God remains perfectly just (Romans 2:5–11), all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23), and He has appointed the preaching of the Gospel as the ordinary means by which He calls His people. That is why the church must go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19–20).

If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted in the crucified and risen Christ, do so today. He alone is the Savior who reconciles sinners to God. What has raised this question for you?

question: What is Christianization?
answer:
Christianization is the process by which individuals and societies are converted to the Christian faith through the Gospel, so that people come to trust in Jesus Christ and their lives and communities are reshaped according to Scripture.

Jesus commanded this work in the Great Commission: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19-20). The New Testament shows it beginning at Pentecost as the apostles preached repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Christ, and the Lord added to the church those who were being saved (Acts 2:38; Acts 2:41; Acts 2:47). True Christianization is not merely a change of customs or political alignment. It requires the Holy Spirit’s work of regeneration, in which a sinner is born again, justified by grace through faith alone, and then grows in sanctification (John 3:3-8; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9).

Historically the term also describes large-scale movements such as the conversion of the Roman world after the apostles, or later missionary advances among the nations. Scripture itself distinguishes genuine conversion from mere outward conformity: Christ’s kingdom is not advanced by the sword (John 18:36). Forced or purely cultural change cannot produce living faith.

A concrete next step for a believer is to join a faithful local church in praying for and supporting Gospel work among the unreached, while personally sharing the good news of Christ’s death and resurrection with those God places nearby.

question: What are the satanic verses?
answer:
The Satanic Verses primarily refer to an alleged incident in some early Islamic historical sources in which Muhammad temporarily recited verses that acknowledged three pagan Meccan goddesses before later claiming Satan had inspired those words. The term is also the title of Salman Rushdie’s 1988 novel that drew on related themes and provoked widespread controversy.

According to accounts preserved by historians such as al-Tabari, while reciting what became Surah 53, Muhammad added lines praising Allat, al-Uzza, and Manat as “high-flying cranes” whose intercession could be hoped for. The polytheists of Mecca were said to rejoice, and some even joined the Muslims in prostration. Muhammad later recanted the lines, attributing them to Satan’s interference, after which they were removed. Most Muslims today reject the story as inauthentic, holding that the Quran was perfectly protected from such error.

Christians believe God’s true revelation is never mixed with Satan’s deception. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). Jesus taught that Satan is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). The apostle Paul warned that even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse (Galatians 1:8). Deuteronomy 13:1-3 further cautions that if a prophet arises and a sign comes to pass, yet he says, “Let us follow other gods” and worship them, you must not listen, for the Lord your God is testing you.

This contrast underscores the Bible’s claim of inerrancy: the living God does not accommodate idolatry or require later corrections from the adversary. The Scriptures consistently call people from false gods to the one true God who has spoken finally in His Son.

question: Is the "Way of the Master" evangelism method biblical?
answer:
The Way of the Master method is biblical in its core pattern of using God's moral law to expose sin, then pointing sinners to Jesus Christ as the only Savior.

It rests on the law-gospel distinction Scripture itself employs. Romans 3:20 says that through the law we become conscious of our sin. Galatians 3:24 describes the law as our guardian until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith. Jesus used the commandments with the rich young ruler in Mark 10:17-22 to reveal the man's self-righteousness and need. The method then presents Christ's penal substitutionary death, burial, and bodily resurrection, calling people to repent and trust Him alone, which matches the apostolic Gospel.

Evangelism technique itself is a tertiary matter. Faithful Christians may disagree on starting points without compromising the faith, because Scripture gives the message we must preach but does not prescribe one conversation formula for every hearer (Romans 14). Some begin with the law as Way of the Master does. Others start with God's love (John 3:16) or with the Creator and general revelation, as Paul did in Athens (Acts 17:22-31). Both can be used when they still declare human sin, Christ's cross and resurrection, and the call to faith.

I appreciate this method because it takes God's holiness and our guilt seriously rather than assuming people already feel their need. Use it, or any other biblical approach, with the gentleness 1 Peter 3:15 requires. A wise next step is to read the evangelistic sermons in Acts, noting how the apostles kept the same Gospel while adapting the doorway, then share that Gospel with someone this week.

question: Is there a God?
answer:
Yes, there is a God. The Bible opens with the clear declaration that God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1).

You may wonder how a loving God could allow so much suffering, or whether the universe can be explained by natural processes alone without a Creator. Those are honest questions many people carry.

The Bible teaches that God has made His existence evident in creation itself. His eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen from His workmanship, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20). God is not an impersonal force but the one true God, eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He is holy, just, and His wrath against sin is real, yet He is also gracious, merciful, and loving.

We were made to know Him, but all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), leaving us separated from Him and unable to save ourselves. In love, God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, He lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a penal substitution for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He now reigns as Lord. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

Talk to God directly in prayer, asking Him to open your eyes to the truth of His Word. A concrete next step is to begin reading the Gospel of John. If you have a local church, speak with a pastor there as well.

What has led you to ask this question?

question: Does God exist?
answer:
Yes, God exists. The Bible opens by declaring that in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1), and it states that anyone who would come to Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him (Hebrews 11:6).

You may wonder how anyone can know an unseen God, or why a good God would allow so much pain and evil in the world. Those are honest questions many people raise.

The Bible teaches that God’s eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen in what He has made, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20). He has also spoken through Scripture and, most clearly, through His Son.

God is holy, yet every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory, earning death as the wage of sin (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). In love He sent Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Jesus lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a penal substitution for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is now exalted as Lord. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

What has prompted you to ask this question? Open a Bible to the Gospel of John and read it, asking God to make Himself known as you do.

question: Is there any conclusive proof of God?
answer:
The Bible teaches that God has made His existence known through the created world and through Jesus Christ, though He does not provide the kind of coercive laboratory proof that would remove all need for faith. Many people look for repeatable scientific evidence that would leave no room for doubt, and others see suffering and evil in the world as a reason to question a good God.

Christians believe God has given general revelation in nature, so that His eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20). The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands (Psalm 19:1). Special revelation comes through Scripture and, above all, in the incarnation of the Son of God. Because of sin, people suppress this truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18). All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and we stand in need of a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, demonstrating His victory over sin and death. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John, a chapter at a time, and talk to God directly, asking Him to open your eyes to who Jesus is.

What has led you to ask this question?

question: How is belief in God any different from belief in a Flying Spaghetti Monster?
answer:
The Flying Spaghetti Monster is often raised to argue that God is just as unfalsifiable, unevidenced, and arbitrarily invented as a pasta creature, especially if one insists on laboratory-style proof before believing anything. You may also feel that every religion simply picks its own deity the way someone might invent a monster, so none of them deserve more weight than a joke.

Christians believe the comparison does not hold. The God of Scripture is not a contingent physical being inside the universe (the way a spaghetti monster would be). He is the eternal, self-existent Creator who made all things and needs no cause Himself (Genesis 1:1; Psalm 90:2). A Flying Spaghetti Monster, even if it existed, would still require an origin and explanation; the God of the Bible is presented as the necessary ground of existence, not one more object within it.

The Bible also teaches that this God has not left Himself without witness. His eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in the created order, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). He has written a moral law on human hearts (Romans 2:14-15). Most decisively, He has entered history in the person of Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union). Jesus lived a perfect life, died as a penal substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, appearing to many eyewitnesses (John 1:1; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Those are public, historical claims that can be examined, unlike a 2005 parody with no ancient sources, no fulfilled prophecy, and no empty tomb.

This is why belief in the God of the Bible is not interchangeable with belief in a Flying Spaghetti Monster. One is a recent satirical invention. The other is the holy, personal God who made us, whom we have all sinned against, and who has acted in space and time to save. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or by inventing a nicer deity.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What about the Flying Spaghetti Monster comparison feels most convincing to you right now?

question: Was Yahweh originally a Edomite or Canaanite god?
answer:
No. The Bible presents Yahweh as the one true, eternal, and self-existent God who created all things and called Abraham, not as a deity that originated among the Edomites or Canaanites.

Some scholars, drawing on Egyptian inscriptions that mention Yhw among Shasu nomads linked to Edom or Seir, and on poetic texts that speak of the LORD coming from Seir or Edom, have proposed that Yahweh worship began as a southern or Midianite/Kenite cult later adopted by Israel, or that it developed out of Canaanite worship of El and Baal.

Scripture, however, identifies Yahweh as the God of the patriarchs from the outset. When He revealed His name to Moses, He said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6; Exodus 3:15). The language of God marching from Seir, Sinai, or Teman (Judges 5:4; Deuteronomy 33:2; Habakkuk 3:3) recounts His historical theophany and deliverance of Israel from Egypt in the southern wilderness, not the origin of a local tribal god. Canaanite practices, including the worship of Baal and Asherah, are repeatedly forbidden as abominations that Israel must reject (Exodus 20:3; Deuteronomy 12:29-31). Yahweh alone is God; the gods of the nations are idols, and there is no other besides Him (Psalm 96:5; Deuteronomy 4:35; Isaiah 45:5-6).

This uniqueness means the God of Scripture is not a product of cultural evolution or syncretism, but the living Creator who has spoken and who remains the same. Reading Exodus 3 and Deuteronomy 4–6 in context helps us see how He presents Himself.

question: Is God dead?
answer:
No, God is not dead. The Bible reveals Him as the living God, eternal, sovereign, and unchanging.

You may be thinking of Friedrich Nietzsche’s claim that “God is dead,” reflecting a culture that has dismissed Him as irrelevant, or you may be wrestling with whether God is real or present amid suffering and doubt.

The Bible teaches that the LORD is the living God. Jeremiah 10:10 states, “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and everlasting King. At His wrath the earth quakes, and the nations cannot endure His indignation.” Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man, died in His humanity through the hypostatic union, yet He rose bodily from the dead. He declares in Revelation 1:18, “I am the Living One. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.” God’s divine nature is immortal and immutable, as He says in Malachi 3:6, “For I, the LORD, do not change.”

All people have sinned and stand separated from this holy God. In love, God the Son took on human nature, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a substitutionary atonement for sinners, was buried, and rose on the third day, conquering sin and death.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

A good next step is to read the Gospel of John, seeing Jesus as the living Word, and to talk directly to God about your questions, for He hears. What has been on your mind as you asked this?

question: Why does God allow evil?
answer:
The question of why God allows evil often rises from real pain, injustice, or the sense that a good and powerful God should stop it all. A common objection is that an all-loving, all-powerful God would never permit such suffering, especially of the innocent. Another is that the sheer scale of evil seems to count against His existence or His care.

The Bible teaches that God is holy, good, sovereign, and just, and that His wrath against sin is real. He created the world very good (Genesis 1:31). Evil did not originate in God. It entered through the rebellion of Satan and then of humanity in the garden, bringing sin, death, and the groaning of creation (Genesis 3:1–19; Romans 5:12; Romans 8:20–22). God is not the author of evil: “When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’ For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (James 1:13). In His sovereignty He permits what He hates in order to accomplish purposes that display His justice, His patience, and His redeeming love, even while the “secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29).

The clearest window into this is the cross. The murder of the sinless Son of God was the greatest evil ever committed, yet God ordained it for the greatest good: “This Man was handed over to you by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, with the help of wicked men, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross. But God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 2:23–24). In the incarnation Jesus, truly God and truly man, entered our suffering. His death was a penal substitutionary atonement, bearing the penalty of sin in the place of sinners, and His bodily resurrection demonstrated victory over sin, evil, and death.

God will not allow evil forever. Christ will return to judge the living and the dead and to make all things new, where “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). Until then, for those who love Him, “God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28).

Evil in the world also exposes the evil in us: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Jesus lived a perfect life, died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

If this question is personal for you right now, bring your grief and your questions directly to God, using the honest language of the Psalms as a guide, and talk with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk with you. How has this question been weighing on you?

question: Why does God allow the innocent to suffer?
answer:
This question cuts deeply, especially when we see children or others who seem to have done nothing to deserve such pain. You may wonder how a loving God could allow it, or whether His power is somehow limited in the face of such injustice.

The Bible teaches that God is both infinitely good and fully sovereign. He made the world very good, yet through Adam’s rebellion sin, death, and the curse entered, so that the whole creation now groans (Genesis 3:17-19; Romans 5:12; Romans 8:22). No one is ultimately innocent before a holy God, for all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Original sin means even the youngest inherit a fallen nature. God is never the author of evil, yet He permits it and remains in complete control, weaving it into purposes we cannot fully see this side of eternity (Deuteronomy 29:29; Isaiah 55:8-9).

Scripture refuses to treat such suffering as trivial. Job was a blameless man who suffered not because of his own particular sins, yet God was never absent. Jesus Himself, the only truly innocent One, entered our pain and bore the penalty of our sin in His body on the cross. His sacrificial death and bodily resurrection on the third day display both God’s justice against sin and His mercy toward sinners (1 Peter 2:24; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That is penal substitution: the righteous suffering in the place of the guilty so that we might be justified by grace through faith in Him alone.

In this fallen world God uses even unjust suffering to produce endurance, to expose our need for a Savior, and to work all things together for the good of those who love Him (Romans 5:3-5; Romans 8:28). One day He will wipe away every tear and make all things new (Revelation 21:4). Until then we weep with those who weep and point them to the cross, where God Himself did not remain distant from suffering.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life. If this question has arisen from a particular grief you are carrying, bring it honestly to God in prayer (perhaps beginning with Psalm 13 or Psalm 22) and share it with a pastor or mature believer in a local church. What has stirred this question in your own heart?

question: Why won't God heal amputees?
answer:
God is fully able to heal amputees. He created every limb, and Jesus restored a withered hand, made the lame walk, gave sight to the blind, and even raised the dead (Mark 3:5; Matthew 11:4-5; John 11:43-44). The reason we do not see missing limbs regularly restored is not that God lacks power, but that He has not willed it as the ordinary pattern of this present age.

This question is often raised as a challenge: if prayer and miracles were real, an amputee’s limb would grow back in a way no one could deny. Some conclude from this that God is either unable, uncaring, or imaginary. Christians believe the opposite. God is both all-powerful and perfectly good, yet He has subjected the present creation to frustration because of human sin (Romans 8:20-22; Genesis 3:17-19; Romans 5:12). Bodies break, limbs are lost, and death comes to everyone. Jesus’ miracles were signs that authenticated Him as Messiah and previewed the coming Kingdom; they were not a promise that every physical defect would be reversed on demand in this life. Even Jesus refused to perform signs merely to satisfy skeptics (Matthew 12:38-39).

God sometimes withholds the healing we want. The apostle Paul, who saw many healed, was not delivered from his own affliction; the Lord told him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). We are to pray, yet always as Jesus did: “Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). Physical restoration in this life is a mercy when it comes, not a right. The far greater work is already done: Christ lived without sin, died as a substitute bearing the penalty our sin deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That resurrection guarantees that everyone who trusts Him will receive a glorified body free from every defect when He returns (1 Corinthians 15:42-44; Revelation 21:4).

Until that day, God is present with those who suffer. If this question comes from your own pain or from watching someone you love live with amputation, He sees it. The real separation that needs healing is our sin against a holy God. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and the sure hope of complete restoration.

Read the Gospel of John this week, asking God to show you who Jesus is. If you are able, speak with a pastor in a Bible-believing church about how Scripture speaks to suffering. What has made this question pressing for you?

question: Is Jesus real?
answer:
Yes, Jesus is real. The Bible presents Him as a historical person who was born, lived, taught, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and rose from the dead in first-century Judea.

You may have heard claims that Jesus is only a myth, or that the Gospel accounts are later legends with no real historical basis.

The Bible teaches that Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God who entered history in the incarnation, remaining fully God while taking on full humanity as truly God and truly man (John 1:14). God is holy, and every person has sinned and fallen short of His glory, leaving us separated from Him and in need of a Savior (Romans 3:23). Jesus lived a sinless life, died on the cross as our substitute under the penalty of sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He is now exalted as Lord, and we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone who died and rose for you for forgiveness and new life.

What has led you to ask this, and what questions do you have about Him?

question: Did Jesus really exist? Is there any historical evidence of Jesus Christ?
answer:
Yes, Jesus of Nazareth really existed as a historical person in first-century Judea under Roman rule. Multiple independent sources, both Christian and non-Christian, confirm this within decades of his life.

You may wonder whether Jesus is only a legend, since no Roman government records from his exact lifetime survive, the Gospels were written by his followers, or some compare him to pagan dying-and-rising gods. Those questions are understandable in an ancient setting with limited documentation, yet they do not erase the evidence we do have.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing around 93 AD, mentions Jesus as a teacher crucified under Pontius Pilate and refers to James as “the brother of Jesus who was called Christ.” The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116 AD, records that Christus was executed by Pontius Pilate during Tiberius’s reign and that this movement spread from Judea to Rome. Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor around 112 AD, describes Christians gathering to worship Christ as a god. These are hostile or neutral sources, not Christian propaganda.

Even earlier, the apostle Paul’s letters (written in the 50s AD, about twenty years after the crucifixion) treat Jesus as a real man born of a woman, descended from David, crucified, buried, and raised, and they name his brother James (Galatians 4:4; Galatians 1:19; 1 Corinthians 15:3-8). The Gospels present themselves as orderly historical accounts drawn from eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1-4). The vast majority of historians, including many who are not Christians, accept that Jesus existed; the idea that he never lived at all is a fringe view.

This historical Jesus is the One the Bible presents as truly God and truly man, the eternal Son who took on human nature in the incarnation, lived without sin, and gave himself as a substitutionary atonement. All people have sinned and fall short of God’s holiness (Romans 3:23). Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What stands out to you in these sources, and how does it shape what you think about who Jesus is?

question: What is the Skeptics' Annotated Bible?
answer:
The Skeptics' Annotated Bible is a website and printed book by Steve Wells that prints the King James Version of the Bible with notes from an atheistic, skeptical viewpoint, listing what the author regards as contradictions, scientific or historical errors, cruelty, absurdities, and other problems. It treats Scripture as a merely human text to be critiqued rather than received as God's Word, and it applies a similar method to the Quran and the Book of Mormon.

Christians do not accept that approach. The Bible is the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, our final authority for faith and practice. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). No prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Jesus Himself treated the Scriptures as true and unbreakable (John 10:35; Matthew 5:18).

Many of the annotations take verses out of their literary context, ignore genre (history, poetry, parable, apocalypse), or assume that a difficulty equals an error. Historic Christianity has long confessed the inerrancy of the original manuscripts and the reliability of the text we have. If particular notes from this resource have raised questions for you, take them to a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk through the passages with you in the whole counsel of God. Read the Bible itself prayerfully, asking the Lord to open His Word to you.

question: Is the Bible a fairy tale?
answer:
No, the Bible is not a fairy tale. It is the inspired, inerrant Word of God, recording real historical events and God's own revelation rather than invented folklore.

You may see it as a fairy tale because its miracles (creation, the flood, or Jesus rising from the dead) seem impossible by ordinary experience, or because other ancient cultures also told legendary stories. The Bible, however, presents itself as truth, not myth. It is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), and its writers explicitly deny inventing clever stories: they reported what they witnessed (2 Peter 1:16). Jesus treated the Old Testament as historically accurate, speaking of Abraham, Moses, Jonah, and others as real people who lived. The Gospels are written as careful historical accounts; Luke investigated everything from the beginning so that readers would know the certainty of these things (Luke 1:1–4).

Because Scripture is true, it shows us a holy God, our sin that separates us from Him, and Jesus Christ who died as a substitute for sinners and rose bodily on the third day. If you are weighing these claims, read the Gospel of John for yourself and ask God to open your eyes to its truth. What in particular makes the Bible seem like a fairy tale to you?

question: Is the Bible mind control?
answer:
No, the Bible is not mind control. It is the inspired and inerrant Word of God that reveals truth and invites a willing response of faith, producing freedom rather than coercion.

Some people associate religious texts with psychological manipulation after encountering cults or groups that isolate members, punish questions, and demand unquestioning loyalty. Others, from a secular viewpoint, treat any book that claims to change a person’s life as a form of indoctrination.

The Bible itself, however, repeatedly calls for examination and reason rather than blind submission. Jesus said, “If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31-32). The Bereans were commended because they “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). God even invites, “Come now, let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18). Scripture also commands, “test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

Mind control typically depends on deception, isolation, and the suppression of critical thought. The Bible is publicly available, historically anchored in real events (including Christ’s death, burial, and bodily resurrection), and it encourages open community rather than secrecy. The change it produces is not robotic obedience but the Holy Spirit’s illumination and the renewing of the mind, so that a person can freely know and love God (Romans 12:2).

If this question arises from distrust or past hurt, read the Gospel of John for yourself and ask God to show you whether it is true. Speak with a mature believer in a local church who will welcome your questions rather than shut them down.

question: Does the Bible contain errors, contradictions, or discrepancies?
answer:
The Bible does not contain errors, contradictions, or discrepancies. It is the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, completely true in all that it affirms.

Many people raise objections about apparent discrepancies, such as variations in the four Gospel accounts of the same events or numerical differences in Old Testament records. These are not actual contradictions. The Gospel writers, carried along by the Holy Spirit, gave complementary eyewitness testimony shaped by their distinct purposes and audiences, not identical transcripts. Apparent numerical issues often arise from different methods of counting, rounding, or later copyist notes, while the original writings remain without fault. Apparent tensions with modern science or history likewise dissolve when the text is read in its own historical, literary, and theological context rather than forced into later categories.

Scripture itself claims this reliability. 2 Timothy 3:16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness. 2 Peter 1:21 For no prophecy was ever brought about through human initiative, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. John 17:17 Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth.

This inerrancy means God, who cannot lie, has given us a Word we can fully trust as our final authority for knowing Him, for salvation in Christ, and for faithful living. If a particular passage still puzzles you, read it in its full context with a reliable study Bible and talk it over with a pastor or mature believer in a local church. Pray directly to God, asking Him to open your eyes to the wonders of His law as you read (Psalm 119:18).

question: What is Christian apologetics?
answer:
Christian apologetics is the reasoned defense and explanation of the Christian faith, giving a clear account of why the Gospel is true and answering honest questions or objections about God, Scripture, Christ, and salvation.

The New Testament uses the Greek word apologia for this kind of defense. Peter writes, “But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But respond with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). In the Greco-Roman world this term described a formal courtroom defense; Peter applies it to every believer’s everyday witness, especially under pressure.

Apologetics therefore belongs to ordinary Christian discipleship. It is not mere debate. It aims to remove stumbling blocks so that people can hear the good news of Christ’s incarnation, His penal substitutionary death on the cross, His burial, and His bodily resurrection. Paul modeled this when he reasoned from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 17:2-3) and took every thought captive to obey Him (2 Corinthians 10:5).

A concrete next step is to prepare a brief, gracious answer to one common question you actually hear (for example, “How can you trust an ancient book?” or “Why does God allow suffering?”). Ground it in Scripture, keep Christ at the center, and speak with the gentleness Peter requires. Seek out a mature believer or your local church to practice together.

question: Does the Bible call Christians to defend the faith / argue for the faith?
answer:
Yes, the Bible calls Christians to defend the faith by always being prepared to give a reasoned answer for the hope they have in Christ, and to contend for the truth of the gospel.

In 1 Peter 3:15 the apostle Peter writes that believers are to honor Christ as Lord in their hearts and always be ready to give a defense to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope within them, doing so with gentleness and respect. The word translated “defense” is the Greek apologia, a term drawn from the legal and public settings of the Greco-Roman world, meaning a clear, reasoned explanation rather than an angry quarrel. This is the biblical root of what later came to be called Christian apologetics. Jude 1:3 likewise urges believers to contend earnestly for the faith once for all delivered to the saints. At the same time Scripture forbids quarrelsome arguing: 2 Timothy 2:24-25 teaches that the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring, and correcting opponents with gentleness.

This calling flows from the authority of Scripture and the uniqueness of Christ’s saving work. Christians do not invent the faith; they bear witness to the historical death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus and the justification that comes by grace through faith in Him alone. The defense is therefore an act of love, both for the truth of God and for the neighbor who needs to hear it.

A practical next step is to read 1 Peter 3 in its full context, then begin a simple habit of studying one gospel account alongside a clear summary of the gospel so you can explain the hope of Christ with both clarity and kindness whenever the Lord opens a door.

question: What are the cosmological arguments for the existence of God?
answer:
Cosmological arguments for the existence of God begin with the reality of the universe itself and conclude that it requires a First Cause, Unmoved Mover, or Necessary Being outside of space and time, whom Christians know as the God revealed in Scripture.

The Kalam cosmological argument reasons that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, and therefore the universe has a cause. That cause must be eternal, spaceless, immaterial, immensely powerful, and personal. Thomas Aquinas developed related arguments from motion (everything moved is moved by another, so there must be an Unmoved Mover) and from efficient causation (there cannot be an infinite regress of causes, so there must be a First Cause). A further form, often associated with Leibniz, appeals to contingency: everything we observe depends on something else for its existence, so there must be a necessary being who exists of Himself and explains why there is something rather than nothing.

These philosophical lines of thought align with the Bible’s plain teaching that God created all things from nothing.
